note: Records removed in the October 2026 audit because they did not show an outside party getting its people, money or control inside a government, international body or company. Each carries the reason.

cases.n: Ergenekon verdict — ex-army chief Basbug sentenced to life
cases.rank: former Chief of the General Staff
cases.d: On 5 August 2013 Istanbul's 13th High Criminal Court ruled on 275 defendants accused of belonging to an 'Ergenekon' network plotting to overthrow the government. Former Chief of General Staff Ilker Basbug was sentenced to life. Retired general Veli Kucuk received a double aggravated life sentence plus 99 years, and Workers' Party leader Dogu Perincek aggravated life plus 30 years. These convictions were overturned in 2016 (see separate record).
cases.cite: Istanbul 13th High Criminal Court, verdict 5 August 2013
cases.drop_reason: A trial of an alleged plot network that the appeals court later found never existed; no proven outside party got inside an institution.

cases.n: Ergenekon verdict — sitting CHP MPs jailed
cases.d: Three opposition CHP MPs were among those convicted in the 5 August 2013 Ergenekon verdict: Mustafa Balbay (34 years 8 months), Mehmet Haberal (12 years 6 months) and Sinan Aygun (13 years 6 months). The appeals court overturned the Ergenekon convictions in April 2016, finding no evidence that the organisation existed.
cases.cite: Istanbul 13th High Criminal Court, 5 August 2013; Court of Cassation, 21 April 2016
cases.drop_reason: Convictions of opposition MPs in a case later overturned for lack of evidence that the network existed; no proven infiltration.

cases.n: Sledgehammer (Balyoz) — 300 officers convicted of coup plot
cases.d: On 21 September 2012 an Istanbul Heavy Penal Court sentenced about 300 of 365 military defendants for an alleged 2003 coup plan called Sledgehammer. Retired generals Cetin Dogan, Ibrahim Firtina and Ozden Ornek were given aggravated life, reduced to 20 years; 78 others got 18 years and 214 got 16 years. The convictions were later quashed (see separate record).
cases.cite: Istanbul Heavy Penal Court, verdict 21 September 2012
cases.org_note: grouped with the Ergenekon-era 'deep state' trials.
cases.drop_reason: A coup-plot trial based on evidence later found forged; the record names no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Sledgehammer retrial — all 236 acquitted, evidence found forged
cases.d: On 19 June 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled the defendants' rights had been violated and they were released. On 31 March 2015 an Istanbul court acquitted all 236 remaining defendants after the prosecutor said the digital evidence was faked. Experts found documents dated 2003 that used later fonts and named a navy ship, TCG Alanya, that did not exist until 2005.
cases.cite: Constitutional Court of Turkey, 19 June 2014; Istanbul court acquittal, 31 March 2015
cases.drop_reason: Acquittal over forged evidence; the record does not say who forged it or show any outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Egypt designates Muslim Brotherhood a terrorist organisation
cases.d: On 25 December 2013 Deputy Prime Minister Hossam Eissa announced that the interim cabinet had declared the Muslim Brotherhood a terrorist organisation, two days after a car bomb at the Mansoura police headquarters killed 14 people. Ansar Bait al-Maqdis claimed the bombing. Membership became punishable by up to five years in prison; a court had already banned the group and seized its assets in September 2013.
cases.cite: Egyptian cabinet decision, 25 December 2013
cases.drop_reason: A government designating a group as terrorist is not infiltration.

cases.n: Morsi Qatar case — ex-president's life term upheld
cases.d: Morsi and others were accused of passing state secrets to Qatar while he was president. On 16 September 2017 Egypt's Court of Cassation upheld his life sentence (handed down in June 2016) for leading an illegal group, but threw out a 15-year term for stealing secret documents. Three co-defendants' death sentences were upheld. Qatar denied the accusations.
cases.cite: Egyptian Court of Cassation, 16 September 2017
cases.drop_reason: The record shows a conviction for leading an illegal group; the secrets-to-Qatar charge was thrown out, so any infiltration angle would be invented.

cases.n: Safari Club — Egypt's intelligence chief Kamal Hassan Ali
cases.d: General Kamal Hassan Ali, head of Egypt's Mukhabarat, was one of five intelligence chiefs who signed the Safari Club charter dated 1 September 1976, with France, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran. In 1977 France flew Egyptian and Moroccan troops into Zaire's Shaba province to back Mobutu. Saudi Arabia paid Egypt $75 million for old Soviet weapons sent to Somalia's Siad Barre. Mohamed Heikal documented the club from the Shah's seized archives (Iran: The Untold Story, 1982).
cases.cite: Mohamed Hassanein Heikal, Iran: The Untold Story (1982); Prince Turki al-Faisal, Georgetown University speech, 2002
cases.drop_reason: The Safari Club was a declared alliance among five governments' intelligence services, not an outside party getting inside one.

cases.n: Safari Club — Saudi intelligence chief Kamal Adham
cases.d: Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence from 1965 until his dismissal on 19 January 1979, signed the 1976 Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Egypt, Morocco and Iran. In a 2002 speech at Georgetown University, his successor-but-one Prince Turki al-Faisal publicly confirmed the club and said it 'included France, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Morocco, and Iran.'
cases.cite: Prince Turki al-Faisal, former Saudi intelligence chief, Georgetown University speech, 2002
cases.drop_reason: The Safari Club was a declared alliance among five governments' intelligence services, not an outside party getting inside one.

cases.n: Saudi Arabia lists Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist
cases.rank: designation by the government (no officials named)
cases.d: On 7 March 2014 the Saudi Press Agency published a list of terrorist organisations including the Muslim Brotherhood, Jabhat al-Nusra, ISIS and the Houthis. It came a day after Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Bahrain withdrew their ambassadors from Qatar. The designation did not name any Saudi officials.
cases.cite: Saudi government designation published by the Saudi Press Agency, 7 March 2014
cases.drop_reason: A government designating a group as terrorist is not infiltration.

cases.n: UAE cabinet lists Muslim Brotherhood and Islah as terrorist
cases.d: On 16 November 2014 the UAE cabinet approved a list of about 80 terrorist organisations, released through the WAM news agency. It included the Muslim Brotherhood and its local affiliates, and the Emirati group al-Islah.
cases.cite: UAE cabinet terrorist list, 16 November 2014
cases.drop_reason: A government designating groups as terrorist is not infiltration.

cases.n: Ennahda-led government in Tunisia
cases.d: After winning the October 2011 Constituent Assembly election, Ennahda led Tunisia's government: Hamadi Jebali was prime minister from December 2011 to March 2013, and Ali Laarayedh from March 2013 to January 2014. Rafik Abdessalem, son-in-law of party leader Rached Ghannouchi, was foreign minister 2011-2013. Ennahda grew out of the Brotherhood tradition but says it has no organisational link to the Egyptian Brotherhood.
cases.cite: Tunisian government records; academic and press histories of Ennahda
cases.drop_reason: Ennahda formed a government after winning an open election; nothing hidden or undeclared.

cases.n: Ghannouchi, ex-speaker, given 22 more years ('Instalingo' case)
cases.rank: former speaker of parliament; former foreign minister
cases.d: On 5 February 2025 a Tunisian court sentenced Ennahda leader Rached Ghannouchi, speaker of parliament from 2019 to 2021, to a further 22 years for 'plotting against state security' in the Instalingo case. Ex-foreign minister Rafik Abdessalem got 34 years and ex-prime minister Hichem Mechichi 35 years in absentia. Ghannouchi has been jailed since April 2023; Ennahda calls the case political. In July 2025 he received another 14-year sentence.
cases.cite: Tunisian criminal court, Instalingo case verdict, 5 February 2025
cases.drop_reason: A prosecution of an opposition leader on state-security charges; the record shows no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Safari Club — SAVAK chief Nematollah Nassiri
cases.d: General Nematollah Nassiri, head of the Shah's SAVAK, signed the 1976 Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco. The club's documents were found in the Shah's archives after the 1979 revolution, where journalist Mohamed Heikal read them for his 1982 book Iran: The Untold Story.
cases.cite: Mohamed Hassanein Heikal, Iran: The Untold Story (1982); Prince Turki al-Faisal, Georgetown speech, 2002
cases.drop_reason: The Safari Club was a declared alliance among five governments' intelligence services, not an outside party getting inside one.

cases.n: Safari Club — Moroccan intelligence chief Ahmed Dlimi
cases.d: General Ahmed Dlimi, head of Morocco's DGED, signed the 1976 Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Iran. In 1977 France airlifted Moroccan troops into Zaire's Shaba province to defend Mobutu, the club's first major operation.
cases.cite: Mohamed Hassanein Heikal, Iran: The Untold Story (1982); Prince Turki al-Faisal, Georgetown speech, 2002
cases.drop_reason: The Safari Club was a declared alliance among five governments' intelligence services, not an outside party getting inside one.

cases.n: Senegal closes Gulen schools, hands them to Turkey's Maarif
cases.d: In 2017 Senegal's government closed more than a dozen schools linked to the Gulen movement, attended by about 3,000 children, after Turkish requests. President Erdogan said they were transferred to Turkey's state-backed Maarif Foundation, which opened three schools in Senegal in November 2017.
cases.cite: Senegalese government closure, 2017, reported by AFP/IOL, 18 March 2018
cases.drop_reason: Turkey openly asked Senegal to close schools, and Senegal's government did so; an open request between governments, not infiltration.

cases.n: Chad's president orders Gulen schools handed to Maarif
cases.d: In November 2017 a statement on the Chadian presidency's website said President Idriss Deby had agreed to hand schools run by the Gulen movement to Turkey's Maarif Foundation by 18 December 2017 and to expel people linked to the movement.
cases.cite: Statement of the Presidency of Chad, November 2017
cases.drop_reason: Chad's president openly agreed to Turkey's request to hand over schools; an open agreement between governments, not infiltration.

cases.n: Niger hands Gulen schools to Turkey's Maarif Foundation
cases.d: By June 2017 Gulen-linked schools in Niger had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry, as also happened in Guinea, Sudan and Somalia.
cases.cite: Turkish government and Maarif Foundation statements, June 2017
cases.drop_reason: Schools were handed to Turkey's foundation after open talks between governments; not infiltration.

cases.d: By June 2017 Gulen-linked schools in Guinea had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry.

cases.d: By June 2017 Gulen-linked schools in Sudan had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry.

cases.n: Morocco shuts Gulen-linked schools
cases.d: Morocco's government ordered Gulen-linked schools in the country shut down, one of several African states (with Tunisia and Sierra Leone) reported in June 2017 to have closed them.
cases.cite: Turkish government statements reported June 2017
cases.drop_reason: A government closing schools is not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Shinzo Abe assassination — Yamagami life sentence
cases.d: Former prime minister Shinzo Abe was shot dead in Nara on 8 July 2022 by Tetsuya Yamagami. Yamagami said he acted after seeing a video message Abe sent to a group affiliated with the Unification Church, which he blamed for his family's ruin, and that he wanted to expose the church's ties to Abe. He said he first planned to target the church's leader but switched to Abe. On 21 January 2026 the Nara District Court sentenced him to life in prison after he pleaded guilty to murder.
cases.cite: Nara District Court verdict, 21 January 2026 (AP report)
cases.drop_reason: A murder trial; the killer's motive concerned the church, but the record shows no one placed or paid inside an institution.

cases.n: Unification Church dissolution order — Tokyo courts
cases.rank: ruling party (context of the government case)
cases.d: After the 2022 revelations about church ties to LDP lawmakers, the culture ministry asked the courts to dissolve the church. In March 2025 the Tokyo District Court issued the first dissolution order based on a group's illegal acts under the Civil Code, finding roughly 40 years of damage: 1,559 victims of unlawful donation solicitation and about 20.4 billion yen taken. On 4 March 2026 the Tokyo High Court upheld the order, stripping the church of religious-corporation status and starting liquidation. The 'inquiry' status here marks a court finding against the organization, not a criminal conviction of any official.
cases.cite: Tokyo District Court dissolution order, March 2025; Tokyo High Court ruling, 4 March 2026 (Adnkronos/Jiji)
cases.drop_reason: A court dissolving the church over harm to its own followers is not infiltration of an institution.

cases.n: Operation Condor trial — 15 convicted incl. ex-dictator Bignone
cases.rank: former de facto president; army officers
cases.d: On 27 May 2016 an Argentine federal court convicted 15 former military officers in the first verdict focused on Operation Condor itself. Former de facto president Reynaldo Bignone received 20 years. The court found that state terror in Argentina was a criminal conspiracy coordinated with other regional dictatorships, covering the disappearance of 105 people.
cases.cite: Argentine Federal Oral Court, Operation Condor trial verdict, 27 May 2016

arch.t: Operation Condor — CIA-Coordinated Assassination Network Across Seven South American Countries

cases.drop_reason: A trial over coordinated state terror between dictatorships; governments cooperating is not an outside party getting inside one.

cases.n: TFP Argentina — Buenos Aires police inquiry into military training
cases.d: The Argentine branch of Tradition, Family, Property was founded in 1967 and gained the apparent support of the military government in the late 1960s after calling for a purge of progressive clergy. In 1973 the Buenos Aires Provincial Police investigated military-style training activities run by the group.
cases.cite: Buenos Aires Provincial Police investigation, 1973 (as reported in histories of TFP)
cases.drop_reason: A police inquiry into a religious group's military-style training is not anyone getting inside a government body.

cases.n: Licio Gelli's Montevideo archive seized by Uruguayan police
cases.d: After an Italian arrest warrant was issued on 22 May 1981, Gelli took refuge in Uruguay. Uruguayan police seized files at his Montevideo villa, reportedly on a CIA tip. Italian military intelligence (SISMI) sent a mission to recover them; it found only about 300 files left, the rest reportedly taken by the CIA, and recovered about 70 incomplete files, including ones on Francesco Cossiga.
cases.cite: Reporting in Domani on the SISMI recovery mission; P2 histories

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

cases.drop_reason: The record covers Uruguayan police seizing Gelli's files and their later recovery, not P2 or anyone getting inside an institution in Uruguay.

cases.d: Juan Carlos Blanco, Uruguay's former foreign minister, was one of 24 people given life sentences by a Rome appeals court in July 2019 in the Operation Condor case. The case covered the disappearance of 43 people, 23 of them Italian citizens. Most defendants were sentenced in absentia.

cases.d: Gregorio Álvarez, former army commander and Uruguay's last de facto president, was sentenced in October 2009 to 25 years for 37 homicides, including forced disappearances. Uruguay's Supreme Court upheld the sentence on 2 September 2011. Several victims were moved to Argentina in 1978 under the Condor plan.

cases.n: Archives of Terror found in Paraguayan police station
cases.d: On 22 December 1992 lawyer Martín Almada and judge José Agustín Fernández found the records of Stroessner's secret police in a police station in Lambaré, outside Asunción. The files proved Operation Condor existed; they include a letter from Chilean intelligence chief Manuel Contreras inviting Paraguayan officials to a secret meeting in Santiago on 25 November 1975. Paraguay's Truth and Justice Commission (from 2003) used them to document 9,923 people who suffered 14,338 violations.
cases.cite: Judicial seizure, Asunción, Dec 1992; Paraguayan Truth and Justice Commission final report

arch.t: Operation Condor — CIA-Coordinated Assassination Network Across Seven South American Countries

cases.drop_reason: Operation Condor was a pact among South American military governments to hunt their own opponents; the record covers state repression and later trials, not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: BCCI and Paraguay's central bank under Stroessner
cases.d: The US Senate BCCI report lists a $5,000,000 deposit by the Central Bank of Paraguay at BCCI dated 10 October 1989. It reports that BCCI's Paraguay ties were developed by Saudi businessman Ghaith Pharaon through his friendship with dictator Alfredo Stroessner.
cases.cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

cases.n: Letelier killing — DINA chief Contreras convicted
cases.d: Former Chilean foreign minister Orlando Letelier was killed by a car bomb in Washington DC in September 1976. On 30 May 1995 Chile's Supreme Court upheld the convictions of Manuel Contreras, retired general and head of the DINA intelligence agency, to seven years, and his deputy Brig. Gen. Pedro Espinoza, then still on active duty, to six years.

cases.n: Pinochet indicted for Operation Condor crimes
cases.d: On 13 December 2004 Chilean judge Juan Guzmán indicted former dictator Augusto Pinochet for nine kidnappings and one homicide linked to Operation Condor and ordered him under house arrest in Santiago. Pinochet died in 2006 without being convicted.
cases.cite: Indictment by Judge Juan Guzmán, Santiago Court of Appeals, 13 Dec 2004

cases.n: Colonia Dignidad — sect compound used by DINA for torture
cases.d: Chile's Rettig truth commission (1991) concluded that people seized by the DINA were held at Colonia Dignidad, a German sect compound near Parral, and that some residents helped torture them. In 2006 sect leader Paul Schäfer was sentenced to 20 years after a 2004 child-abuse conviction. In 2013 Chile's Supreme Court ruled to prosecute 16 Chilean and German members, and in March 2017 the German Bundestag acknowledged Germany's failures toward the colony.
cases.cite: National Commission for Truth and Reconciliation (Rettig Report), 1991; Chilean court rulings 2004–2013
cases.org_note: colonia_dignidad: closed German religious sect (Sociedad Benefactora y Educacional Dignidad) that collaborated with Pinochet's DINA; none of the listed keys fits
cases.drop_reason: The record shows Chile's own intelligence service using a sect compound for detention and torture, which is state repression with the sect's help, not an outside party getting inside the state.

cases.n: TFP banned by Frei's government in Chile
cases.d: A Chilean TFP chapter formed in 1967 from the group behind the magazine Fiducia. In the late 1960s the Christian Democratic government of Eduardo Frei Montalva confiscated a TFP book and banned the group (exact year not confirmed). The TFP welcomed the 1973 coup, and in March 1976 Chile's bishops said its members had 'placed themselves outside the Catholic Church'.
cases.cite: Frei government ban, late 1960s; Chilean Bishops' Conference statement, March 1976
cases.drop_reason: A government ban on a group is a designation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Banco Ambrosiano Andino — guarantee for Peru's Exocet purchase
cases.d: Banco Ambrosiano Andino in Lima was a subsidiary of Roberto Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano. During the 1982 Falklands war, British intelligence found that the guarantee for Exocet missiles bought by Peru, which France then blocked to stop their transfer to Argentina, was a $200 million deposit from Banco Ambrosiano Andino. Ambrosiano's Latin American banks had lent to Panamanian shell companies that the Vatican Bank's letters of patronage described as under its control.
cases.cite: Histories of the Banco Ambrosiano collapse; Time magazine, 1982

cases.d: Luis Arce Gómez was interior minister and chief of repression under Luis García Meza after the 17 July 1980 coup, which Argentina's junta backed. In July 2019 a Rome appeals court gave him a life sentence in the Operation Condor case, one of 24 such sentences.

cases.n: Brazil — prosecutors cite Malhães files as proof of Condor role
cases.d: On 24 November 2014 Brazil's federal prosecutors in Rio de Janeiro released documents found at the home of retired colonel Paulo Malhães. They describe 'Operation Gringo', run by the Rio de Janeiro Army Intelligence Center to track foreign nationals, which Attorney-General Rodrigo Janot called the strongest evidence that Operation Condor existed. Brazil's armed forces and foreign ministry deny the collaboration.
cases.cite: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office, Rio de Janeiro (MPF/RJ), 24 Nov 2014

cases.n: TFP Brazil and the 1964 military coup
cases.d: Brazil's Tradition, Family, Property campaign against President João Goulart's land reform is described by historians as helping set the stage for the 1964 military coup. The TFP later urged the military government to arrest Archbishop Hélder Câmara.
cases.cite: Academic histories of TFP
cases.drop_reason: Open public campaigning against land reform before a coup is not getting inside a government body.

cases.n: BCCI — Noriega's account in the name of Panama's Defense Forces
cases.d: General Manuel Noriega opened a BCCI account in early 1982 in the name of the Panamanian Defense Forces. The US Senate report found he held about $25 million in it at its height, mostly cash deposits, with one deposit of about $4 million. BCCI also lent to Noriega associates Enrique Pretelt and César Rodríguez and absorbed about $10 million in losses.
cases.cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

cases.drop_reason: Noriega holding an account and borrowing from BCCI is a client using a bank, with no hidden placement or payment inside an institution in the record.

cases.n: BCCI handled Jamaica's state foreign-currency accounts under Seaga
cases.d: Under Prime Minister Edward Seaga, BCCI handled Jamaica's US commodity financing and most government foreign-currency accounts. A BCCI officer told the Senate: 'we handled every penny that came into or out of Jamaica in terms of foreign currency.' The report lists loans of $33.9 million to the Bank of Jamaica and $45.4 million to state oil firm Petrojam.
cases.cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

arch.t: Bank of Credit and Commerce International — Abedi and Iqbal: BCCI Was the Largest Bank Fraud in History; CIA Used It for Covert Operations; 62 Countries Affected

cases.drop_reason: BCCI handling Jamaica's foreign-currency accounts and lending to state bodies was an open banking relationship; the record shows no bribes or hidden control.

cases.n: Ambrosiano's Managua bank — licence cancelled by presidential decree
cases.d: Ambrosiano Group Banco Comercial, a unit of Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano Holding of Luxembourg, was licensed in Nicaragua in 1977–78. Ambrosiano provided funds to both the Somoza government and the Sandinista opposition. Presidential Agreement No. 39, signed by Daniel Ortega on 2 August 1985, approved moving the bank's seat out of Nicaragua and cancelled its operating licence.
cases.cite: Acuerdo Presidencial No. 39, La Gaceta No. 157, 20 Aug 1985

cases.drop_reason: A bank operating in Nicaragua, lending to both sides and later losing its licence is open business and a regulatory decision, not infiltration.

cases.n: Ambrosiano Overseas, Nassau — Vatican Bank chief on board; suspended
cases.d: Banco Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau was a Calvi subsidiary; Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, president of the Vatican Bank (IOR), had been a director. After Ambrosiano's 1982 collapse, Bahamian banking authorities suspended its operations. The Nassau and Luxembourg units owed about half of the $1.2–1.4 billion lent to Panamanian shell companies.
cases.cite: Bahamian banking authorities' suspension, 1982; Time magazine, 9 Aug 1982

cases.drop_reason: The Vatican Bank president sat openly on the board of a Calvi subsidiary, which the regulator later suspended; this is a declared directorship and a bank collapse, not infiltration.

cases.n: Venezuela — government inquiry into TFP, 1984
cases.d: After parents complained that the group cut teenagers off from their families, a three-month investigation under President Jaime Lusinchi found Venezuela's TFP was operating outside the constitution, and the government was reported to plan a ban. In December 1984 Caracas police arrested a man carrying a TFP card over a possible plot against Pope John Paul II; TFP denied involvement. Whether a ban took effect is not confirmed.
cases.cite: Venezuelan government investigation, 1984 (as reported)
cases.drop_reason: A government inquiry into a religious group and a planned ban is designation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Scientology — 1993 IRS closing agreement and tax exemption
cases.rank: IRS Commissioner and Exempt Organizations division
cases.d: After decades of litigation (about 200 suits by the church and roughly 2,300 by individual Scientologists), the IRS granted the church religious tax exemption in October 1993. Negotiations began after David Miscavige walked into IRS headquarters and met Commissioner Fred Goldberg, likely in 1991. Under the secret closing agreement the church paid $12.5 million and dropped all its lawsuits against the IRS. The terms became public only when The Wall Street Journal published them on 30 December 1997.
cases.cite: IRS–Church of Scientology closing agreement, October 1993; terms published by The Wall Street Journal, 30 Dec 1997
cases.drop_reason: The 1993 IRS settlement came from open litigation and negotiation; secret terms do not show Scientology placed people or money inside the IRS.

cases.n: Fraser Report — Moon Organization worked with South Korean agencies
cases.rank: U.S. Congress (lobbying of members and offices)
cases.d: The House Subcommittee on International Organizations, chaired by Rep. Donald Fraser, found that Sun Myung Moon's organization had at times acted 'in cooperation with, or at the direction of, ROK agencies and officials'. It found the Moon group set up the Korean Culture and Freedom Foundation, presented as a nonprofit, and used it to advance its own interests and those of the South Korean government. The subcommittee also found the group had 'extensively used the names of Senators, Congressmen, U.S. Presidents' to raise money. It asked the Justice Department, SEC and IRS to form an interagency task force.
cases.cite: House Committee on International Relations, Subcommittee on International Organizations, 'Investigation of Korean-American Relations' (Fraser Report), 31 Oct 1978
cases.drop_reason: Lobbying Congress through a foundation acting for South Korea is outside influence; the record shows no one placed or paid inside Congress (Koreagate payments are covered by separate entries).

cases.n: Sun Myung Moon — federal tax conviction
cases.rank: Federal tax authorities (false returns filed with the IRS)
cases.d: A federal jury in New York convicted Moon in 1982 on three counts of filing false tax returns for 1973–75 and one count of conspiracy, which covered obstruction of justice and false statements to a grand jury. He was sentenced to 18 months and a $15,000 fine; aide Takeru Kamiyama was convicted of conspiracy, obstruction and perjury. The Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal in 1984, and Moon served 13 months at FCI Danbury.
cases.cite: United States v. Sun Myung Moon, S.D.N.Y. 1982; 718 F.2d 1210 (2d Cir. 1983); cert. denied, 466 U.S. 971 (1984)
cases.drop_reason: Moon's conviction for false tax returns is his own crime, not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Washington Times — Moon-founded paper read daily by Reagan
cases.rank: President of the United States (Ronald Reagan, as reader)
cases.d: Moon founded The Washington Times through his company News World Communications; its first edition appeared on 17 May 1982, with Bo Hi Pak as founding president. The paper ran at a heavy loss covered by Unification Church income from Japan; Moon had spent an estimated $900 million to $1 billion on it by 1991. Reagan read it every day of his presidency. The paper is still owned by an entity of the Unification movement.
cases.cite: Major-outlet and reference reporting on The Washington Times' ownership and funding
cases.drop_reason: Openly founding and owning a newspaper that a president reads is not infiltration.

cases.n: Bohemian Grove — Manhattan Project planning meeting, 1942
cases.rank: Wartime atomic bomb programme (S-1 Executive Committee, U.S. military)
cases.d: In September 1942 the Bohemian Club's Grove in Monte Rio, California, hosted a meeting on early Manhattan Project planning. Ernest Lawrence and J. Robert Oppenheimer hosted it in the Clubhouse; attendees included members of the S-1 Executive Committee and representatives of universities, industry and the military. The U.S. Department of Energy's Manhattan Project history carries a photo of the S-1 Committee at the Grove.
cases.cite: Gregg Herken, Brotherhood of the Bomb (2002), ch. 4; U.S. DOE/OSTI Manhattan Project history, S-1 Committee page

arch.t: Bohemian Grove — Elite Annual Occult Ritual; Nixon on White House Tapes

cases.drop_reason: Holding a wartime planning meeting at a private club's grounds is use of a venue, not the club getting inside government.

cases.n: BCCI — CIA kept using the bank after knowing it was criminal
cases.d: The Senate report found that by 1985 the CIA knew more about BCCI's U.S. goals than any other part of government, but shared it with Treasury and the OCC rather than the Fed or Justice Department. It found the CIA kept using BCCI and First American for its own operations after it knew BCCI was a criminal enterprise, and that its first information to Congress was untrue.
cases.cite: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, 'The BCCI Affair', December 1992

arch.t: Bank of Credit and Commerce International — Abedi and Iqbal: BCCI Was the Largest Bank Fraud in History; CIA Used It for Covert Operations; 62 Countries Affected

cases.drop_reason: The CIA using BCCI as a client and withholding information is a government agency's own conduct, not BCCI getting inside the CIA.

cases.n: John Singlaub — WACL chief used as cover for White House Contra aid
cases.rank: White House National Security Council operation (Contra supply)
cases.d: Retired Major General John Singlaub, removed from his Korea command by Carter in 1977, founded the U.S. Council for World Freedom in 1981 as the U.S. chapter of the World Anti-Communist League, and later chaired both. While Congress barred U.S. military aid to the Nicaraguan Contras, he raised private support for them and enlisted members of Congress. An Associated Press report found that 'Singlaub's private group became the public cover for the White House operation'.
cases.cite: Associated Press reporting during the Iran-Contra affair, 1986–87; CIA reading-room press clippings
cases.drop_reason: Here the White House used a private anti-communist group as cover for its own Contra operation, the reverse of an outside party getting inside government.

cases.n: Saskatchewan Klan — 1929 election that ousted the Liberals
cases.d: Klan leaders claimed about 40,000 members in over 100 Saskatchewan towns by 1928. In the 1929 election, Conservatives and Progressives campaigned on issues the Klan had stirred among Protestant voters and defeated Premier J. G. Gardiner's Liberals; Gardiner accused the Klan of being a Conservative tool, which the Klan and Conservative leader J. T. M. Anderson denied. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan states no proof of an alliance existed, but a 1930 Klan convention praised the Anderson government's school and immigration changes.
cases.cite: Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan (University of Regina), 'Ku Klux Klan'
cases.org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)
cases.drop_reason: The record says no proof of a Klan alliance with the Saskatchewan government exists; stirring voters' issues in an election is not getting inside government.

cases.n: UK masonic declaration rule for new judges, police, prosecutors
cases.rank: new judicial, police, CPS, probation and prison appointees
cases.d: After the 1997 Committee report, Home Secretary Jack Straw's government set a policy, stated to the Commons by minister Alun Michael on 6 May 1998, that all new appointees to the judiciary, the police, legally qualified Crown Prosecution Service staff and the probation and prison services must declare membership of the Freemasons. Serving office holders were only invited to declare on voluntary registers. In March 1999 Home Office minister Paul Boateng told Parliament that disclosure by existing police staff was 'entirely voluntary at present'.
cases.cite: Hansard, HC Deb 6 May 1998 vol 311 cc838–44 (adjournment debate, Freemasons); HC Deb 23 March 1999 written answer

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

cases.drop_reason: The record covers inquiries and disclosure rules about Freemasons in UK police and courts, not a case where a lodge got inside an institution and steered its decisions.

cases.n: Daniel Morgan Independent Panel — Freemasonry in the Met
cases.d: The Daniel Morgan Independent Panel reported in June 2021 on the 1987 axe murder of private investigator Daniel Morgan and the Metropolitan Police's handling of it. The Panel found no evidence that Masonic channels were used corruptly in the case. It nonetheless said membership was 'not conducive to a culture of integrity' and recommended that police officers and staff be required to disclose Freemason membership confidentially.
cases.cite: The Report of the Daniel Morgan Independent Panel, HC 11, June 2021

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

cases.drop_reason: The record covers inquiries and disclosure rules about Freemasons in UK police and courts, not a case where a lodge got inside an institution and steered its decisions.

cases.n: Service d'Action Civique — Gaullist militia dissolved after Auriol
cases.org_note: Service d'Action Civique (SAC): Gaullist security association created 1960, led in practice by Jacques Foccart; a parallel network that recruited police officers.
cases.d: The SAC was founded in January 1960 by Jacques Foccart, de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, and Pierre Debizet; its members included Charles Pasqua. On the night of 18 July 1981 police inspector Jacques Massié, the SAC's leader in Marseille, and his family were murdered at Auriol by an SAC commando. A National Assembly commission of inquiry reported in 1982, and the government dissolved the SAC by decree no. 82-670 of 3 August 1982 under the law on private militias. On 1 May 1985 five commando members were sentenced to terms from 15 years to life.
cases.cite: National Assembly commission of inquiry on the SAC, report 1982; Decree no. 82-670 of 3 August 1982; assize court verdict, 1 May 1985
cases.drop_reason: A party-linked militia whose own commando murdered its Marseille leader; the record shows no outside party getting inside a government body.

cases.n: OAS — secret army formed by French generals
cases.org_note: Organisation armée secrète: clandestine organisation formed in 1961 by French army officers to block Algerian independence.
cases.rank: army general, former commander-in-chief in Algeria
cases.d: Generals Raoul Salan, Maurice Challe, André Zeller and Edmond Jouhaud organised the failed Algiers putsch of April 1961, after which Salan became chief of the clandestine Organisation armée secrète. Salan was sentenced to death in absentia, arrested in April 1962, tried for treason and sentenced to life imprisonment. He was pardoned and released in June 1968 and later amnestied by Parliament and reinstated as a general in 1982.
cases.cite: French treason verdict against Salan, 1962; pardon June 1968
cases.drop_reason: An armed revolt by French generals and a clandestine army fighting the state, not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Dutch stay-behind (I&O) — Lubbers tells parliament, 1990
cases.rank: secret Intelligence (I) and Operations (O) units of the state
cases.d: In November 1990 Prime Minister Ruud Lubbers told parliament the Dutch stay-behind network was being given a new direction. In April 1992 Defence Minister Relus ter Beek wrote to members that it had become obsolete. It operated from 1945 to 1992 with several hundred recruited citizens and dozens of weapons caches; according to de Volkskrant, the government covered up the theft of some guns later used by members of Willem Holleeder's gang. In February 2021 Prime Minister Mark Rutte and Defence Minister Ank Bijleveld acknowledged the group in a letter to relatives, and in 2022 the government asked the Netherlands Institute for Military History to inventory its records.
cases.cite: Statement of Prime Minister Lubbers to the Tweede Kamer, November 1990; Rutte–Bijleveld letter, February 2021
cases.drop_reason: Describes a Dutch government-run secret network; the record names no outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Bommeleeër trial — gendarmerie officers accused of 18 bombings
cases.rank: officers of the Gendarmerie mobile brigade (BMG)
cases.d: In 2013 two former members of the Gendarmerie's mobile brigade (BMG), Jos Wilmes and Marc Scheer, went on trial for 18 bombings in Luxembourg between May 1984 and April 1986, targeting sites such as Cegedel power pylons. The defence argued the attacks were the work of NATO's Stay Behind network; a 2006 recording of Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, Justice Minister Luc Frieden and intelligence (SREL) chief Marco Mille speculating about Stay Behind involvement was played in court. Prosecutor Robert Biever said 88 of 125 pieces of evidence had disappeared. The trial was suspended in 2014; later, eight former gendarmerie and public-force officers were referred to trial for false testimony, but not for the bombings.
cases.cite: Luxembourg District Court, 9th criminal chamber, Bommeleeër trial (2013–14); Council Chamber referral order
cases.drop_reason: Gendarmes accused of bombings plus a speculative defence claim about Stay Behind; no outside party is shown inside an institution and no verdict was reached.

cases.n: Swiss parliament (PUK EMD) uncovers secret army P-26
cases.d: A parliamentary commission of inquiry into the Defence Department (PUK EMD), set up in March 1990 after the secret files scandal, reported in November 1990 that a secret cadre organisation, P-26, existed outside parliamentary and government control. It was led from October 1979 by Colonel Efrem Cattelan, organised in about 40 regions with up to about 1,000 members (about 300 had taken courses by 1990), and cost about 54.3 million francs of federal money from 1979 to 1990. P-26 was dissolved in November 1990.
cases.cite: Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the Federal Military Department (PUK EMD), report of 17 November 1990
cases.drop_reason: A domestic Swiss secret army under the Defence Department; the record names no outside party (the British link is in the Cornu report entry).

cases.n: German government confirms BND stay-behind, orders dissolution
cases.d: Answering a parliamentary question from Ingrid Köppe and the Bündnis 90/Die Grünen group, the federal government stated on 17 May 1991 that the dissolution of the stay-behind organisation had been ordered and that the BND, which ran it, would complete it before the end of 1991. The government said no staff of the organisation had been deployed in the former GDR and disputed the European Parliament's resolution of 22 November 1990 as resting on incorrect premises for Germany.
cases.cite: Deutscher Bundestag, Drucksache 12/560, 17 May 1991 (answer to Kleine Anfrage 12/393)
cases.drop_reason: The German government confirming dissolution of a network its own intelligence service ran; no outside party is shown.

cases.n: Austria's OeWSGV — Olah's secret army, later Interior Minister
cases.rank: Minister of the Interior; trade union federation (ÖGB) president
cases.d: In 1951 trade unionist Franz Olah raised a secret anti-communist paramilitary force under the cover name Österreichischer Wander-, Sport- und Geselligkeitsverein (OeWSGV), funded through the camouflage firms Atlanta and Omnia; it operated until 1964. Olah became ÖGB president in 1959 and Interior Minister in 1963, resigning in September 1964 over misuse of union funds. In his 1969 trial, which ended in a one-year sentence for fraud, he defended the OeWSGV as a patriotic measure. In 1991 the defence and interior ministers denied such an army had existed.
cases.cite: Vienna criminal court, Olah trial 1969; statements of Austrian defence and interior ministers, 1991
cases.drop_reason: A domestic secret paramilitary set up by a trade unionist who later became minister; the record names no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: US discloses 80+ hidden stay-behind arms caches in Austria
cases.d: In January 1996 reports revealed that more than 80 caches of US weapons, including machine guns, explosives, mortars and radio equipment, had been hidden in Austria in the early Cold War for a stay-behind network; Austrian officials said they had not been told. US Ambassador Swanee Hunt then made Cold War US intelligence documents public showing that the US created over one hundred secret weapons depots during its occupation. The Austrian government commissioned historian Oliver Rathkolb to seek further US documents; the CIA replied that none were available.
cases.cite: Boston Globe/Seattle Times, 21 January 1996; US Embassy Vienna document release, 1996
cases.drop_reason: US weapons caches hidden on Austrian soil; the record shows no one placed or paid inside an Austrian institution.

cases.n: Finland's Weapons Cache Case — officers hide arms after 1944
cases.org_note: Asekätkentä (Weapons Cache Case): secret network organised from Finnish Military Headquarters after the 1944 armistice to hide weapons for a guerrilla force.
cases.rank: officers of the operational department, Finnish Military Headquarters
cases.d: After the Moscow Armistice of 19 September 1944, Colonel Valo Nihtilä and Lieutenant Colonel Usko Haahti of the operational department of Finnish Military Headquarters began hiding weapons across the country, planned for 8,000 men but estimated to equip about 35,000. Between 5,000 and 10,000 people took part. The scheme was exposed in spring 1945 to the Allied Control Commission; the security police questioned more than 5,000 people and, under a retroactive law of January 1947, 1,488 people were convicted, most receiving 1–4 months in prison.
cases.cite: Finnish courts under the Act of January 1947; Valpo (State Police) investigation
cases.drop_reason: Finnish officers hiding their own army's weapons; no outside party got inside an institution.

cases.n: Serbian officers' May Coup kills King Alexander Obrenović
cases.org_note: The 1903 officer conspiracy led by Dragutin Dimitrijević (Apis) was the core from which the Black Hand (Unification or Death) was formed in 1911.
cases.d: On 11 June 1903 (29 May Old Style), Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis' and junior officers stormed the royal palace in Belgrade and killed King Alexander Obrenović, Queen Draga and others, bringing the Karađorđević dynasty to the throne. In 1911 Dimitrijević and fellow officers founded the secret society Unification or Death (Black Hand), which Britannica describes as dominating the army and pressuring the government through intimidation.
cases.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica; standard histories of Serbia
cases.drop_reason: A coup by Serbian officers against their own king before the Black Hand existed; no outside party is involved.

cases.n: Michele Sindona — banker convicted of Ambrosoli murder
cases.d: Sindona, a P2 member who advised the Vatican on its investments, had his Italian banks liquidated by lawyer Giorgio Ambrosoli, appointed by the Bank of Italy. Ambrosoli was shot dead in Milan on 11 July 1979. On 18 March 1986 a Milan court sentenced Sindona to life as the instigator. He drank cyanide-laced coffee in Voghera prison and died on 22 March 1986. He had already been convicted in New York in 1980 on 65 counts over the Franklin National Bank failure.
cases.cite: Milan Court of Assizes, 18 March 1986; US District Court SDNY, 1980

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

cases.drop_reason: Sindona's crimes concerned his own banks and the murder of their liquidator; the record shows no outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Silvio Berlusconi — P2 member, false testimony finding
cases.d: Berlusconi, then a television entrepreneur, was on the 1981 list; inquiry findings and his own earlier testimony showed membership from 1978. In a 1989 libel case in Verona he testified he had joined only briefly and paid no fee. In 1990 the Venice Court of Appeal found this was false testimony but could not sentence him because a 1989 amnesty had extinguished the offence.
cases.cite: Venice Court of Appeal, 1990 (offence extinguished by 1989 amnesty)

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

cases.drop_reason: Berlusconi was a private businessman when on the P2 list and the case concerns his false testimony, not P2 getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Bellini verdict — court calls Gelli 'conscious financier'
cases.d: Paolo Bellini, formerly of Avanguardia Nazionale, was sentenced to life in 2022 as a fifth perpetrator of the 1980 Bologna bombing; the appeal court upheld it and the Court of Cassation made it final in 2025. The appeal judges called P2 head Licio Gelli 'il consapevole finanziatore della strage' (the knowing financier of the massacre). Gelli died in 2015 and was never tried for it.
cases.cite: Bologna Court of Assizes 2022; Bologna Appeal Court of Assizes 2024; Court of Cassation 2025

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

cases.drop_reason: Concerns a bomber's conviction and terrorist financing; no one is shown inside an institution (the P2 state angle is in the 2020 Bologna and D'Amato entries).

cases.n: Peteano bombing — Casson uncovers Gladio
cases.d: On 31 May 1972 a car bomb at Peteano killed three Carabinieri. Venice magistrate Felice Casson reopened the case and identified neo-fascist Vincenzo Vinciguerra, who confessed and is serving life. In 1984 Vinciguerra described a 'secret force parallel to the armed forces' helped by the secret services; Casson's inquiry led to Gladio's exposure.
cases.cite: Venice judiciary (Judge Felice Casson); Vinciguerra life sentence

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

cases.drop_reason: A neo-fascist's car bombing and confession; the record names no outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: President Cossiga — Gladio role and impeachment motion
cases.d: After Andreotti's disclosure, President Francesco Cossiga acknowledged he had been involved in setting up Gladio (he became defence undersecretary in 1966). The Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) filed an impeachment motion; it was dismissed.
cases.cite: Parliamentary impeachment motion (PDS), 1991, dismissed

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

cases.drop_reason: The Italian president's own role in setting up a national network and a dismissed impeachment motion; no outside party is shown.

cases.n: Spain's stay-behind network — Serra inquiry
cases.d: After the Italian disclosure in 1990, Defence Minister Narcís Serra opened an inquiry into whether Spain had a Gladio network. Former prime minister Adolfo Suárez said he had never heard of it; former prime minister Leopoldo Calvo Sotelo said the Franco regime 'itself was Gladio'.
cases.cite: Spanish Ministry of Defence inquiry, 1990

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

cases.drop_reason: An inquiry into whether Spain had a Gladio network that found nothing; no one is shown inside an institution.

cases.n: Aginter Press — Lisbon 'news agency' training bombers
cases.d: Aginter Press was set up in Lisbon in September 1966 under Salazar's Estado Novo and run by former French officer and OAS member Yves Guérin-Sérac. It presented itself as a press agency but trained members in bombing and sabotage. Its documents were found at the end of 1974 after the Carnation Revolution, when Guérin-Sérac and associates left Portugal.
cases.cite: Academic history; documents recovered in Lisbon 1974
cases.drop_reason: A front 'news agency' that trained bombers under Salazar's regime; that is not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Aginter Press links to Italian bombings — Salvini testimony
cases.d: Italian magistrate Guido Salvini, investigating the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing, told the Italian parliamentary commission on terrorism in 1997 that his inquiries confirmed links between Aginter Press, Ordine Nuovo and Avanguardia Nazionale. He said Aginter instructors taught Avanguardia Nazionale members to use explosives in Rome in 1967–68.
cases.cite: Italian Parliamentary Commission on Terrorism, Salvini testimony 1997
cases.drop_reason: Testimony on training links between Aginter Press and Italian neo-fascist groups; no institution was infiltrated according to the record.

cases.n: Junta leaders convicted of high treason (1975)
cases.d: In the trial held at Korydallos Prison from 28 July to 23 August 1975, Georgios Papadopoulos, Stylianos Pattakos and Nikolaos Makarezos were sentenced to death for high treason and mutiny, commuted to life by the Karamanlis government. Dimitrios Ioannidis, former head of the military police, received life. In the separate Polytechnic trial (verdict 31 December 1975) Ioannidis received seven life terms.
cases.cite: Athens court, Trial of the Instigators and Polytechnic trial, 1975
cases.org_note: IDEA: secret society of Greek army officers
cases.drop_reason: A treason trial of coup leaders; the record names no outside party getting inside an institution (the IDEA angle is in its own entry).

cases.n: LOK stay-behind unit seized Defence Ministry in 1967
cases.d: The LOK special forces, integrated into the European stay-behind network after 1952, took over the Greek Defence Ministry during the 21 April 1967 coup under Brigadier General Kostas Aslanides, according to the historical record.
cases.cite: Academic history
cases.drop_reason: A Greek army unit took part in its own country's coup; the record shows no outside party steering it.

cases.n: Operation Sheepskin — Greek Gladio confirmed
cases.d: After Andreotti's 1990 disclosure in Italy, the Greek defence minister confirmed that a Greek stay-behind branch, Operation Sheepskin ('Red Sheepskin'), had operated until 1988. Former prime minister Andreas Papandreou said he learned of it in 1984 and ordered it dissolved.
cases.cite: Statement of the Greek Minister of Defence, 1990

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

cases.drop_reason: Confirms a Greek stay-behind branch existed and was dissolved; the record names no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Golden Dawn convicted as a criminal organisation
cases.d: Golden Dawn won 21 seats in May 2012, 18 in June 2012 and 17 in January 2015. On 7 October 2020 the Athens Court of Appeals found leader Nikolaos Michaloliakos and six other leading members and former MPs guilty of directing a criminal organisation 'dressed in the mantle of a political party', in a trial of 68 defendants that included the 2013 murder of rapper Pavlos Fyssas. On 4 March 2026 an appeal court upheld the convictions of 42 defendants.
cases.cite: Athens Court of Appeals, 7 October 2020; appeal ruling 4 March 2026
cases.org_note: Golden Dawn: neo-Nazi party ruled a criminal organisation
cases.drop_reason: Golden Dawn was openly elected to parliament and convicted as a criminal organisation, which is not infiltration (its police ties are a separate entry).

cases.n: Apollo Quiboloy — spiritual adviser to President Duterte
cases.d: Quiboloy, founder of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ church, was described by Rodrigo Duterte as his spiritual adviser and lent him his jet during the 2016 campaign. A US federal grand jury indicted him in 2021 on sex-trafficking and other counts; Philippine police arrested him in September 2024 after a two-week siege of his Davao compound on domestic child-abuse and trafficking charges.
cases.cite: US v. Quiboloy, C.D. Cal., indictment 2021; Philippine National Police arrest, September 2024
cases.drop_reason: Quiboloy was openly Duterte's spiritual adviser and his charges concern his own church, not getting inside government.

cases.n: Indonesia bans Hizb ut-Tahrir Indonesia
cases.rank: civil servants and members of the security forces
cases.d: The government revoked Hizb ut-Tahrir Indonesia's legal status in July 2017 under a new decree on mass organisations, citing its aim of replacing the state with a caliphate. Officials then warned that civil servants who were members would be dismissed; the ban was upheld by the courts in 2018.
cases.cite: Government Regulation in Lieu of Law (Perppu) 2/2017; Ministry of Law and Human Rights decision, 19 July 2017; Jakarta State Administrative Court, May 2018
cases.drop_reason: The banning of an organisation; the record shows no members steering decisions inside government.

cases.n: Iglesia ni Cristo endorses Marcos Jr., Duterte and 12 Senate bets
cases.d: On 3 May 2022 the Iglesia ni Cristo announced on its NET 25 channel that it backed Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for president, Sara Duterte for vice-president and 12 Senate candidates, including Jinggoy Estrada, Loren Legarda, Francis Escudero, Juan Miguel Zubiri, Joel Villanueva and Robin Padilla. The church calls its bloc voting the 'Unity Vote'; the 2015 census counted about 2.6 million members. It had backed Benigno Aquino III in 2010 and Rodrigo Duterte in 2016.
cases.cite: Manila Bulletin, 3 May 2022; Wikipedia 'Iglesia ni Cristo' (endorsement history)
cases.drop_reason: A church openly endorsing candidates is public campaigning, not infiltration.

cases.n: INC protest at the Justice Department and EDSA over De Lima probe
cases.d: From 27 to 31 August 2015 Iglesia ni Cristo members protested outside the Department of Justice and then occupied parts of EDSA after Justice Secretary Leila de Lima acted on an illegal-detention complaint by Isaias Samson Jr., a minister the church had expelled. Police put the crowd at about 15,400 at its peak. Vice-President Jejomar Binay backed the church's 'mass action'; the church ended the protest after talks with government officials, and the presidential palace said no deal had been struck.
cases.cite: Wikipedia '2015 Iglesia ni Cristo protests' (citing Inquirer, Philstar, Rappler)
cases.drop_reason: An open street protest against a government inquiry is public pressure, not getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Pakistan Supreme Court orders Gulen group banned, schools to Maarif
cases.d: A three-judge Supreme Court bench headed by Chief Justice Mian Saqib Nisar ordered the government on 28 December 2018 to ban the Gulen movement (FETO) and the Pak-Turk International Cag Education Foundation, which ran the Pak-Turk schools, and to hand its schools and other institutions to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation. The court said Pakistan was bound by an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation declaration naming the group.
cases.cite: Supreme Court of Pakistan, order of December 2018; Arab News Pakistan, 28 December 2018
cases.drop_reason: A court ordering a group banned and its schools handed over is a designation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Malaysia deports three Turks accused of Gulen links
cases.d: Malaysian police arrested Turgay Karaman and Ihsan Aslan, and two days later academic Ismet Ozcelik, in May 2017 under a security law allowing 28 days' detention without trial. They were deported to Turkey on the night of 11 May 2017; police chief Khalid Abu Bakar said Ankara had cancelled their travel documents, so they were treated as illegal immigrants. Turkey accused them of Gulen ('FETO') links; Human Rights Watch condemned the deportations.
cases.cite: Royal Malaysia Police statement, 11–12 May 2017; Al Jazeera, 12 May 2017
cases.drop_reason: Malaysia deporting Turks accused of Gülen links at Ankara's request; no one got inside an institution.

cases.n: Veysel Akcay — Mongolia grounds plane to stop removal to Turkey
cases.rank: Mongolian civil aviation and security authorities
cases.d: On 27 July 2018 Veysel Akcay, general manager of the Empathy Worldwide Educational Institution, which ran Turkish-Mongolian schools linked to the Gulen movement, was seized in Ulaanbaatar. Mongolian authorities temporarily grounded a plane at the airport and he was released the same day. Turkish Minute and the Stockholm Center for Freedom reported that Turkey's MIT intelligence service carried out the abduction; Mongolian authorities said they had no specific knowledge of an abduction and were investigating.
cases.cite: Euronews, 28 July 2018; Turkish Minute, 27 July 2018
cases.drop_reason: An abduction reportedly by Turkish intelligence; no one was placed inside a Mongolian institution.

cases.n: Orhan Inandi — Sapat schools head taken from Bishkek to Turkey
cases.rank: State Committee for National Security border service
cases.d: Orhan Inandi, president of the Sapat network of Turkish-founded schools in Kyrgyzstan and a Kyrgyz citizen, disappeared in Bishkek in mid-2021. On 5 July 2021 President Erdogan said on TRT Haber that Inandi, whom he called a FETO leader, had been 'captured and taken to Turkey'. In August 2021 Kyrgyzstan's Military Prosecutor's Office opened proceedings for negligence and breach of border-service rules against border officers of the State Committee for National Security who allowed him to be taken out of the country.
cases.cite: Kyrgyz Military Prosecutor's Office, pre-trial proceedings, August 2021 (24.kg, 17 August 2021); Erdogan on TRT Haber, 5 July 2021
cases.drop_reason: Turkish intelligence removed a man from Kyrgyzstan with border officers accused of negligence; no recruitment or payment of insiders is recorded.

cases.n: Azerbaijan state oil company takes over Gulen-linked schools
cases.d: On 18 June 2014 Gulen-linked educational facilities in Azerbaijan — 11 high schools, 13 university-entrance preparation centres and a private university — were taken over by the Azerbaijan International Education Company, in which the state oil company SOCAR holds shares. The company gave financial viability as the reason; the takeover followed requests from Turkish Prime Minister Erdogan for help against the Gulen movement.
cases.cite: Eurasianet, 19 June 2014
cases.drop_reason: A state-linked company taking over Gülen-linked schools at Turkey's request; no one got inside an institution.

cases.n: Tajikistan closes seven Gulen-linked schools by presidential decree
cases.d: In May 2015 President Emomali Rahmon issued a decree overruling a 1994 cabinet decision that had let the schools operate, closing seven Gulen-linked Turkish schools from September 2015. The schools were transferred to the state and rebranded as schools for gifted children; they had been under investigation since January 2015.
cases.cite: Presidential decree, May 2015; The Diplomat, August 2015
cases.drop_reason: A presidential decree closing Gülen-linked schools; a state action against a group, not infiltration.

cases.n: Turkmenistan closes Gulen schools and jails 18 men
cases.d: Turkmenistan closed or nationalised most of the Gulen-linked schools opened in the 1990s in 2011. After more than 100 people, most with some Gulen affiliation, were detained in late 2016, 18 men were convicted in closed trials and given 12 to 25 years for inciting hatred and involvement in a criminal organisation, according to a joint statement by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the Norwegian Helsinki Committee.
cases.cite: Joint statement of Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Norwegian Helsinki Committee, 2017, as reported by The Diplomat, June 2017
cases.drop_reason: Closure of Gülen-linked schools and jailing of 18 men; a state crackdown, not infiltration.

cases.n: Kazakhstan — 33 Turkish-Kazakh schools renamed after coup attempt
cases.d: After Turkey's July 2016 coup attempt Ankara asked Central Asian governments to close Gulen-linked schools; Kazakhstan declined to close them. On 18 October 2016 the sponsoring foundation KATEV announced that its 33 Turkish-Kazakh lyceums, co-founded by the Gulen movement, would be renamed 'Bilim' Innovative Lyceums. RFE/RL reported no Kazakh government order behind the renaming.
cases.cite: RFE/RL, 18 October 2016
cases.drop_reason: A Gülen-linked foundation renamed its own schools; no outside party got inside a government body, and the record says no government order was involved.

cases.n: Cardinal Becciu convicted over London property, then mistrial
cases.rank: Substitute for General Affairs, Secretariat of State; later prefect
cases.d: Cardinal Angelo Becciu, Substitute at the Secretariat of State from 2011 to 2018, was convicted of embezzlement by the Vatican tribunal on 16 December 2023 and sentenced to five and a half years, with eight other defendants also convicted. The case centred on the Secretariat of State's €350 million investment in a London building, where prosecutors said brokers and officials cost the Holy See tens of millions in fees and extorted €15 million to give up control. On 17 March 2026 the Vatican appeals tribunal nullified the indictment over unpublished papal decrees and undisclosed evidence and ordered a retrial from 22 June 2026.
cases.cite: Vatican City tribunal verdict 16 December 2023; Vatican appeals tribunal ruling 17 March 2026 (PBS NewsHour/AP); Wikipedia 'Giovanni Angelo Becciu'
cases.org_note: Holy See finance case filed under the ior key for the Vatican's financial institutions; the money came from the Secretariat of State, not the IOR.
cases.drop_reason: Embezzlement and losses by the Vatican's own officials and brokers over a property deal, with no outside party placed inside to steer the institution.

cases.n: Angelo Caloia — ex-IOR president convicted of embezzlement
cases.rank: president of the Institute for the Works of Religion (Vatican Bank)
cases.d: On 21 January 2021 the Vatican City tribunal convicted Angelo Caloia, former president of the IOR, and lawyer Gabriele Liuzzo of embezzlement from the IOR, aggravated embezzlement and self-laundering over IOR property sales between 2002 and 2007; each was sentenced to eight years and eleven months and fined €12,500. Liuzzo's son Lamberto received five years and two months for money laundering. The court ordered forfeiture of about €38 million.
cases.cite: Vatican City State tribunal, judgment of 21 January 2021 (Vatican News)

arch.t: Catholic Church Financial Fraud — Vatican Bank Scandal: IOR Documented Helping Italian Politicians Hide Money and Evade Taxes; Marcinkus Indicted; Never Extradited (PROVEN)

cases.drop_reason: Embezzlement by the Vatican Bank's own president and a lawyer; ordinary fraud by insiders with no outside party.

cases.n: Vatileaks 2 — finance commission secretary jailed for leaks
cases.rank: secretary of the Prefecture for the Economic Affairs of the Holy See
cases.d: Monsignor Lucio Vallejo Balda, a senior official in the Holy See's economic prefecture and member of the papal commission reviewing Vatican finances, was sentenced by the Vatican court in July 2016 to 18 months for leaking confidential documents used in books by Gianluigi Nuzzi and Emiliano Fittipaldi; he began serving in a Vatican cell on 22 August 2016 and was later granted clemency. The court acquitted the two journalists, saying it lacked jurisdiction. In the first 'Vatileaks' case, papal butler Paolo Gabriele was convicted of theft on 6 October 2012 and later pardoned.
cases.cite: Vatican City tribunal verdicts of 6 October 2012 and July 2016; Wikipedia 'Vatican leaks scandal'
cases.org_note: Filed under ior as a Holy See finance case.
cases.drop_reason: Leaks of documents by a Vatican official and a butler; insider wrongdoing with no outside party getting inside.

cases.n: Rome prosecutors seize €23m from IOR, investigate its president
cases.rank: president of the Vatican Bank (Ettore Gotti Tedeschi)
cases.d: In 2010 Italian magistrates in Rome seized €23 million held by the IOR at an Italian bank, saying anti-money-laundering laws had been broken, and placed IOR president Ettore Gotti Tedeschi and another IOR manager under investigation for money laundering. A Rome court later convicted former IOR officials Paolo Cipriani and Massimo Tulli over reporting omissions on three small transfers, acquitting them of money laundering.
cases.cite: Rome prosecutors' seizure order, 2010; Rome court verdict on Cipriani and Tulli; Wikipedia 'Vatican Bank'

arch.t: Catholic Church Financial Fraud — Vatican Bank Scandal: IOR Documented Helping Italian Politicians Hide Money and Evade Taxes; Marcinkus Indicted; Never Extradited (PROVEN)

cases.drop_reason: A seizure and reporting-omission case over weak anti-money-laundering controls at the Vatican Bank, with no crime group shown placing or paying staff inside it.

cases.n: Uniter — KSK soldier's network put under domestic intelligence watch
cases.rank: Special Forces Command (KSK) soldiers; police and reservists
cases.d: Uniter, an association founded by André Schmitt ('Hannibal'), a former soldier of the Bundeswehr's Special Forces Command (KSK), ran chat groups with soldiers and police that investigators found in 2017; Schmitt himself was an informant in mid-2017. In February 2020 the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution had classed Uniter internally as a review case; in early July 2020 it placed Uniter under surveillance. That same week Defence Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer disbanded a KSK company after a May raid on a sergeant major's property found PETN explosive, an AK-47 and thousands of rounds believed stolen from the army.
cases.cite: Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution classification 2020; German Defence Ministry, July 2020; Star Tribune (AP), 3 July 2020; t-online, 19 February 2020
cases.drop_reason: An association founded by a former special-forces soldier was put under surveillance, but the record does not show it steering decisions inside the KSK or the police, and the arms find was a separate case.

cases.n: Heinz Lembke — 33 arms caches on Lüneburg Heath
cases.d: In 1981 forester Heinz Lembke led investigators to 33 illegal arms dumps near Uelzen on the Lüneburg Heath holding automatic weapons, 13,520 rounds, 50 anti-tank weapons, 156 kg of explosives and 258 grenades. Members of the Deutsche Aktionsgruppe had said the day after the 26 September 1980 Oktoberfest bombing that Lembke offered them weapons. He was found hanged in his cell on 1 November 1981, the day before a hearing at which he had said he would name his backers; the inquiry into them was closed. The size and military grade of the caches led to suggestions of a link to NATO stay-behind stocks, which was never officially confirmed.
cases.cite: Federal prosecutor's investigation 1981; Wikipedia 'Heinz Lembke'
cases.drop_reason: An arms-cache case with no one shown inside an institution; the suggested NATO stay-behind link was never confirmed.

cases.n: Norway — Meyer arms cache and defence minister on stay-behind
cases.d: In 1978 Norwegian police found an arms cache and radio equipment at a mountain cabin and arrested businessman Hans Otto Meyer, who said Norwegian intelligence had supplied the weapons. Defence Minister Rolf Hansen then said the network 'was not in any way answerable to NATO and had no CIA connection'. Back in 1957 intelligence chief Vilhelm Evang had protested to NATO about stay-behind-related activity by officers at the Kolsås headquarters, settled in 1958 with assurances on how the networks would be run.
cases.cite: Statement of Defence Minister Rolf Hansen, 1978; Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio'
cases.drop_reason: Norway's own intelligence service ran the arms cache; the record shows no outside party inside Norwegian institutions, and the minister denied NATO or CIA control.

cases.n: Denmark — stay-behind 'Absalon' inside military intelligence
cases.d: Denmark's stay-behind network, code-named Absalon and led by E. J. Harder, was hidden inside the military intelligence service Forsvarets Efterretningstjeneste, according to historians cited by Wikipedia. Time reported in November 1990 that the Danish and Norwegian units were built 'with official cooperation'. The Guardian reported in January 1992 that after Italy's disclosure Denmark was among the countries that investigated and disbanded their national organisations.
cases.cite: Time, November 1990; The Guardian, 30 January 1992 (as quoted in the Mannheim Pro-Government Militias Database); Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio'
cases.drop_reason: Denmark's own stay-behind network built inside its intelligence service with official cooperation; no outside party is shown getting inside.

cases.n: Nigeria's constitution bars secret-society members from elected office
cases.rank: President, governors, National and State Assembly members; all public officers
cases.d: Sections 66(1)(g), 107(1)(g), 137(1)(h) and 182(1)(h) of Nigeria's 1999 Constitution disqualify members of secret societies from election to the National Assembly, State Houses of Assembly, the presidency and governorships, and Section 38(4) bars anyone from belonging to one; Section 318 defines the term. Paragraph 10 of the Code of Conduct for Public Officers (Fifth Schedule) says a public officer shall not belong to any society 'the membership of which is incompatible with the functions or dignity of his office'. Commentators name the Ogboni fraternities, Freemasons and AMORC among the societies at issue.
cases.cite: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, ss. 38(4), 66, 107, 137, 182, 318 and Fifth Schedule para. 10; ThisDay, 18 October 2022
cases.org_note: Covers Reformed Ogboni Fraternity, Aborigine Ogboni Fraternity and Masonic lodges together.
cases.drop_reason: A constitutional ban on secret-society members holding office is a law, not a case of anyone getting inside a government.

cases.n: Falae petition alleges president-elect Obasanjo is an Ogboni member
cases.d: After the February 1999 presidential election, runner-up Olu Falae's election petition alleged that Olusegun Obasanjo was an Ogboni member and therefore disqualified, since election rules barred secret-society members from running. The election tribunal dismissed the petition. The Reformed Ogboni Fraternity's general secretary said in March 1999 that it was non-political and not a secret society.
cases.cite: Falae election petition and tribunal ruling, 1999, as summarised by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (ecoi.net)
cases.org_note: Ogboni fraternity; filed under the generic freemasonry key.
cases.drop_reason: An election-petition allegation of secret-society membership that the tribunal dismissed; nothing in the record shows the society got inside government.

cases.n: Paraguayan Senate votes to expropriate Moon land at Puerto Casado
cases.d: Moon's representatives bought about 600,000 hectares in northern Paraguay, including the town of Puerto Casado, from the Argentine firm Carlos Casado in 2000 for US$22.5 million. In early August 2005 the Senate voted 24 to 14 to expropriate 52,000 hectares around the town for its roughly 6,000 residents; the bill then went to the lower house. President Nicanor Duarte's government sent troops to the area after a community radio station was attacked.
cases.cite: Paraguayan Senate vote, August 2005; MercoPress, 6 August 2005
cases.drop_reason: An open land purchase and a Senate vote to expropriate it; no one got inside a government body.

cases.n: AIFLD trainees and the 1964 coup against Goulart
cases.rank: President João Goulart (overthrown by the military, 1 April 1964)
cases.d: The American Institute for Free Labor Development was chartered in August 1962 by the AFL-CIO and contracted directly with USAID; it ran training institutes in Recife and São Paulo. Its director William Doherty Jr. later said the institute's Brazilian trainees were 'intimately involved' in the military and civilian conspiracy against President Goulart. Historian Cliff Welch writes that exactly what they did 'remains unclear' and their role was probably less central than Doherty claimed; after the coup, AIFLD graduates helped take over unions whose leftist leaders had been purged. This rests on Doherty's own statement and later historians, not on a court or inquiry finding.
cases.cite: Cliff Welch, 'Labor Internationalism: U.S. Involvement in Brazilian Unions, 1945-1965', Latin American Research Review; Philip Agee, Inside the Company (1974)
cases.drop_reason: AIFLD was openly chartered by the AFL-CIO and contracted with USAID; the coup role rests on its director's own claim, which historians doubt.

cases.n: NED founder: 'what we do today was done covertly by the CIA'
cases.rank: Overt successor to CIA political-action funding
cases.d: The National Endowment for Democracy was created by Congress in 1983 and is funded almost wholly by congressional appropriations. In a September 1991 Washington Post article by David Ignatius, NED founder Allen Weinstein said: 'A lot of what we do today was done covertly 25 years ago by the CIA.' In 1986 NED president Carl Gershman had said NED was set up because it would be 'terrible for democratic groups around the world to be seen as subsidized by the CIA'.
cases.cite: David Ignatius, 'Innocence Abroad: The New World of Spyless Coups', Washington Post, 22 Sept 1991
cases.drop_reason: NED is openly funded by Congress and its grants are public; a founder's quote about the CIA is not a case of anyone getting inside an institution.

cases.n: US-funded opposition before Nicaragua's 1990 election
cases.rank: Presidential election won by Violeta Chamorro (UNO), February 1990
cases.d: Historian William LeoGrande writes that NED's roughly $2 million in Nicaragua in 1984-88 was the main source of open aid to the civic opposition, about half of it to La Prensa, the paper run by Violeta Chamorro. In October 1989 the US House voted 263-156 for President Bush's plan to spend a further $9 million to boost the opposition before the 25 February 1990 election, which Chamorro's National Opposition Union won. Critics compared NED's Nicaraguan funding with earlier CIA operations in Chile; NED says its grants are public and nonpartisan.
cases.cite: William M. LeoGrande, Our Own Backyard (1998); Associated Press, 'Nicaragua aid passes House', 6 Oct 1989
cases.drop_reason: Open, congressionally voted US aid to Nicaragua's opposition; declared funding, not hidden placement inside a government body.

cases.n: Russia bans NED as 'undesirable'
cases.rank: Russian government designation (Prosecutor General / Justice Ministry list)
cases.d: In July 2015 Russia declared the National Endowment for Democracy an 'undesirable' organisation, the first group banned under the undesirable-organisations law signed two months earlier. Russian officials and state media blamed NED grants for, among other things, the 2014 Euromaidan protests in Ukraine. The designation is the Russian government's assertion; no court or independent body has found that NED worked inside Russian state institutions.
cases.cite: Russian Ministry of Justice list of undesirable organisations, July 2015; The Guardian, 28 July 2015
cases.drop_reason: A Russian government designation of NED as 'undesirable'; the record states no body found NED inside Russian state institutions.

cases.n: China sanctions NED over Hong Kong
cases.d: In December 2019 China sanctioned NED and other US groups after Congress passed the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act. In August 2019 its Foreign Ministry had circulated a report naming NED as a US intelligence front and listing 20 years of NED grants to political groups in Hong Kong. This is the Chinese government's assertion, not the finding of an independent forum.
cases.cite: Chinese Foreign Ministry statement, 2 Dec 2019; Washington Post, 2 Dec 2019
cases.drop_reason: Chinese government sanctions and assertions about NED; a designation, not a finding that anyone got inside an institution.

cases.n: John Perkins's 'economic hit man' account of Chas. T. Main
cases.rank: Economic forecasts used for foreign borrowing (Perkins's claim)
cases.d: John Perkins worked for the Boston engineering firm Chas. T. Main in the 1970s and became its chief economist. In Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004) he says his job was to inflate growth forecasts so that countries such as Indonesia, Ecuador, Panama and Saudi Arabia would take large loans for infrastructure, and that the National Security Agency screened him for the job. A 2006 New York Times check found 'the arc of Mr. Perkins's career seems to be described accurately' but found no evidence for his 'fancier claims', including the NSA link; Main's former vice president Einar Greve agreed the debt story was 'basically' true but denied the NSA link, and the US State Department called much of the book 'a total fabrication'. All of the hit-man claims are Perkins's own.
cases.cite: John Perkins, Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004); New York Times, 'Confessing to the Converted', 19 Feb 2006; Boston Magazine, May 2006; US State Department, Feb 2006
cases.drop_reason: Rests on John Perkins's own unverified claims about an openly contracted consulting firm; the NSA link was not supported.
