cases.n: US-Saudi Joint Commission (JECOR) run from the US Treasury
cases.rank: Saudi Ministry of Finance and National Economy (co-chaired with the US Treasury Secretary)
cases.d: The US-Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation was set up in 1974, after the Arab oil embargo, with the US Treasury Secretary and the Saudi Minister of Finance as co-chairs. A March 1979 Government Accounting Office report found that US technical assistance under it was 'funded almost entirely from the Saudi Arabian Trust Account in the U.S. Treasury', that it recycled petrodollars and steered US goods, services and technology to Saudi Arabia, and that it had 16 formal projects. John Perkins says Chas. T. Main worked on Saudi projects in this period; that is his claim, while the commission and its Treasury-held Saudi funding are documented by the GAO.
cases.cite: US General Accounting Office, 'The U.S.-Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation', ID-79-7, 22 March 1979
cases.drop_reason: An openly agreed US-Saudi commission co-chaired by both governments and funded by Saudi money; declared cooperation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Interpol refuses 773 Turkish Red Notice requests on Gülen suspects
cases.d: After the July 2016 coup attempt Turkey asked Interpol for Red Notices against people it accuses of links to the Gülen movement. In June 2021 Lütfi Çiçek, head of the Interpol department of Turkey's Interior Ministry, said Interpol had refused 773 such requests after finding them political, plus 240 more aimed at people linked to Kurdish and leftist groups. Interpol also refused a Turkish request concerning NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom.
cases.cite: Statement of Lütfi Çiçek, Turkish Interior Ministry, June 2021 (reported by Stockholm Center for Freedom)
cases.drop_reason: Turkey's Red Notice requests were refused by Interpol; misuse attempted from outside, with no one inside the organisation.

cases.n: Interpol deletes China's Red Notice for Uyghur leader Dolkun Isa
cases.rank: Chinese Ministry of Public Security request
cases.d: China had sought Dolkun Isa, a leader of the World Uyghur Congress living in Germany, through an Interpol Red Notice, calling him a terrorist; no Western country acted on it. In February 2018, while China's Meng Hongwei was Interpol president, Interpol removed the notice, and China protested. Rights groups say China has used Interpol channels against Uyghurs abroad and record 1,546 detentions or deportations of Uyghurs from 28 countries since 1997.
cases.cite: Reuters, 'China upset as Interpol removes wanted alert for exiled Uighur leader', 24 Feb 2018
cases.drop_reason: China's Red Notice request was removed by Interpol; no one is shown inside Interpol acting for China.

cases.n: Bahrain's Red Notice for refugee footballer Hakeem al-Araibi
cases.d: Bahrain obtained a Red Notice for Hakeem al-Araibi, a footballer and dissident who had fled Bahrain in 2014 and was a refugee in Australia. Thai police arrested him on arrival in Bangkok in November 2018. Interpol withdrew the notice days later because its 2015 policy bars notices sought by the country a refugee fled; Thailand still held extradition proceedings until prosecutors dropped the case on 11 February 2019.
cases.cite: Interpol refugee policy (2015); Thai Office of the Attorney General, 11 Feb 2019
cases.drop_reason: Bahrain's Red Notice request, withdrawn by Interpol; misuse attempted from outside, with no one inside the organisation.

cases.n: Russia's use of Interpol against critics; Prokopchuk candidacy
cases.rank: Russian Interior Ministry; Interpol vice-president Alexander Prokopchuk
cases.d: Interpol refused Russia's repeated requests for a Red Notice against financier Bill Browder as 'predominantly political'. In November 2018 four US senators said Interpol vice-president Alexander Prokopchuk, a Russian Interior Ministry general, had abused Red Notices, and he lost the presidency vote to Kim Jong Yang. In January 2026 the BBC reported leaked files showing Interpol received more complaints about Russia than any other country and that some extra checks added after 2022 were dropped in 2025.
cases.cite: BBC, 'Likely next Interpol chief Prokopchuk fox in the henhouse, US senators say', 20 Nov 2018; Council of Europe PACE and OSCE PA resolutions (2010-2017)
cases.drop_reason: Refused Red Notice requests and an openly contested Interpol election that Russia's candidate lost; no hidden placement is shown.

cases.n: Council of Europe Assembly criticises WHO H1N1 handling
cases.rank: WHO and European health ministries (pandemic vaccine decisions)
cases.d: On 24 June 2010 the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe voted 60-1 for a resolution, from a health committee report by Paul Flynn, saying the H1N1 response of WHO, EU agencies and national governments wasted large sums of public money. It found 'grave shortcomings' in the transparency of decision-making that 'generated concerns about the influence of the pharmaceutical industry', and noted that WHO withheld the names of its Emergency Committee members. The Assembly did not find proven industry control; WHO denied any improper influence but accepted it needed stronger transparency rules.
cases.cite: Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, Resolution 1749 (2010), 'Handling of the H1N1 pandemic: more transparency needed'
cases.drop_reason: The Council of Europe found transparency failings and concerns but no proven industry influence inside WHO.

cases.n: Quigley: CFR as the New York branch of the Round Table network
cases.rank: Council on Foreign Relations board (Morgan partners and associates)
cases.d: In Tragedy and Hope (1966) Carroll Quigley wrote that the Council on Foreign Relations 'was a front for J. P. Morgan and Company in association with the very small American Round Table Group', and that in 1928 its board included John W. Davis, Paul Cravath, Russell Leffingwell, Norman Davis and Allen Dulles. He says he studied the network for twenty years and examined 'its papers and secret records' for two years in the early 1960s. CFR's own centennial history records that Morgan partner Russell Leffingwell sat on its board. The 'front' description is Quigley's.
cases.cite: Quigley, Tragedy and Hope (Macmillan, 1966), pp. 950–952; G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021)

arch.t: Council on Foreign Relations — Submergence of US Sovereignty (Insider Testimony)

cases.drop_reason: Describes the make-up of the CFR's own board, a private body, not anyone getting inside a government body, international body or company.

cases.n: Pilgrims Society — US ambassadors admitted ex officio
cases.rank: US Ambassador to the Court of St James's; US Secretary of State
cases.d: The Pilgrims of Great Britain (London, 16 July 1902) and of the United States (New York, 13 January 1903) hold dinners to welcome each new US ambassador to Britain, and US secretaries of state and ambassadors in London are customarily admitted ex officio. Winston Churchill addressed the Society as Prime Minister on 18 March 1941. Members have included Henry Kissinger, George Shultz, Caspar Weinberger, Margaret Thatcher and Paul Volcker.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Pilgrims Society'
cases.drop_reason: A dining club that openly admits ambassadors ex officio; no hidden placement or steering of decisions is recorded.

cases.n: Wagner guards the CAR president and fights for the army
cases.rank: presidential close protection and army operations
cases.d: About 1,000 Wagner fighters have been in the Central African Republic since 2018, after a Russia–CAR military agreement in August 2018. Their tasks included close protection for President Touadéra and fighting rebels alongside the national army, for example at Boyali in January 2021. Reporting links the deployment to gold, diamond and timber concessions, including a Lobaye logging operation. Russia's defence ministry is moving these structures under its Africa Corps; the CAR remains its largest African deployment, estimated at 1,500–2,000.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Wagner Group activities in the Central African Republic', citing The Guardian (Feb 2023), Al Jazeera and ISPI
cases.drop_reason: Wagner fighters guarding the president and fighting rebels under an open Russia–CAR military agreement is mercenary contracting, not infiltration.

cases.n: Mali's defence minister sanctioned for bringing in Wagner
cases.rank: defence minister; air force chief and deputy chief
cases.d: On 24 July 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned Mali's defence minister, Colonel Sadio Camara, saying he planned and organised Wagner's deployment and made several trips to Russia in 2021 to finalise it. It also sanctioned air force chief of staff Colonel Alou Boi Diarra, who it said promoted Wagner inside the armed forces and worked with Wagner's Mali head Ivan Maslov, and deputy chief Lieutenant Colonel Adama Bagayoko. Mali's military government had asked UN peacekeepers to leave a month earlier.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release JY1645, 24 July 2023
cases.drop_reason: A government openly bringing in a mercenary force; the record does not show Wagner paying or controlling the ministers sanctioned.

cases.n: Mali — Wagner leaves, Russia's Africa Corps stays with the junta
cases.rank: armed forces partner of the military government
cases.d: Africa Corps is the Russian defence ministry's unit that took over most of Wagner's African operations after Prigozhin's death in 2023. On 6 June 2025 Wagner announced it was leaving Mali; Africa Corps, which had deployed about 1,000 troops in December 2024, became the only Russian force there, with about 2,000 Russian troops remaining. Several Wagner commanders moved across to it. Human Rights Watch and Le Monde have reported killings of civilians by Malian soldiers and Africa Corps members in 2025–26.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Africa Corps (Russia)', citing BBC News and Al Jazeera (June 2025)
cases.drop_reason: An open military deployment of Russian troops partnering a junta, not infiltration of an institution.

cases.n: Burkina Faso — Russia's Africa Corps base near the capital
cases.rank: military partner of the transitional government
cases.d: Burkina Faso's military government under Captain Ibrahim Traoré ordered French troops out in early 2023. Africa Corps personnel arrived on 24 January 2024, an initial 100 to be expanded to 300, and set up their first African base at Loumbila, north-east of Ouagadougou. Ghana's president had earlier alleged a mine was allotted to Wagner as payment, which Burkina's mines minister denied.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Africa Corps (Russia)' and 'Wagner Group activities in Mali'
cases.drop_reason: An open Russian military deployment and base agreed with Burkina Faso's government, not infiltration.

cases.n: Niger — Africa Corps moves into Niamey air base
cases.rank: military partner of the ruling junta
cases.d: After the July 2023 coup, Niger's junta ended military cooperation with the US and France. Dozens of Africa Corps troops arrived in Niamey in April 2024 and were stationed at Air Base 101 before US forces had left it. Estimates for 2025 put them at 200–300, mostly in intelligence, training and surveillance. Wikipedia's article says they took part in fighting during a January 2026 attack on Niamey airport.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Africa Corps (Russia)'
cases.drop_reason: An open Russian troop deployment at the junta's invitation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Equatorial Guinea — Russian troops protect President Obiang
cases.d: Teodoro Obiang has ruled Equatorial Guinea since 1979. In autumn 2024 Russia deployed up to 200 Africa Corps troops to protect his presidency and to train elite units in Malabo and Bata, according to the CTC Sentinel and other analyses. Obiang officially received the Africa Corps commander in Malabo in November 2025.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Africa Corps (Russia)', citing CTC Sentinel (Dec 2024)
cases.drop_reason: Russian troops openly deployed to protect a president are a security arrangement, not infiltration.

cases.n: Libya — UN monitors count up to 1,200 Wagner fighters with Haftar
cases.rank: fighting force for the Libyan National Army
cases.d: Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army controls eastern Libya. A May 2020 UN report counted 800–1,200 Wagner fighters supporting it, including sniper teams, and Syrians recruited by Wagner flown in on at least 33 flights. In July 2020 the US sanctioned Wagner people and firms over landmines planted around Tripoli. In December 2020 a Pentagon report said the UAE was the main funder of Wagner in Libya. Africa Corps began replacing Wagner there in spring 2024 and Russia uses eastern Libyan bases as logistics hubs.
cases.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya (2020), US Treasury (July 2020), US Defense Department Inspector General (Dec 2020), as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: Mercenary fighters supporting an armed faction and a sanctions case; no one placed inside an institution.

cases.n: Sudan — Prigozhin's gold firm sanctioned over plan to crush protests
cases.d: On 15 July 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned M Invest, a company linked to Yevgeny Prigozhin, and its Sudanese gold-mining subsidiary Meroe Gold. Treasury said the network had tried to help suppress the protesters who sought democratic reform in Sudan in 2018–19. Wagner personnel first arrived in Sudan in 2017 and numbered about 300 by 2022.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, 15 July 2020, reported by The Sentry
cases.drop_reason: Sanctions on a gold-mining firm over help suppressing protests; the record shows no one placed inside a Sudanese institution.

cases.n: Facebook removes Prigozhin networks run in eight African countries
cases.rank: election campaigns and political news in eight states
cases.d: On 30 October 2019 Facebook removed three networks of almost 200 fake and compromised accounts, with over a million followers, that it traced to entities tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin. They targeted Madagascar, the Central African Republic, Mozambique, DR Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Sudan and Libya, and meddled in the Mozambique and Madagascar elections. Stanford Internet Observatory found operators worked with local people and some accounts appeared linked to Wagner. Placed at Maputo because Mozambique's October 2019 election was a named target.
cases.cite: Facebook announcement, 30 Oct 2019; Stanford Internet Observatory; reported by Al Jazeera
cases.drop_reason: Fake social-media accounts removed by Facebook are a disinformation campaign, with no one inside a government body.

cases.n: AFRIC — Prigozhin-linked 'election observers' at Zimbabwe's 2018 vote
cases.d: AFRIC (Association for Free Research and International Cooperation) presented itself as an independent African research and election-monitoring body. It sent about 40 observers to Zimbabwe's 2018 general election. The European Platform for Democratic Elections reports that investigative journalists later found AFRIC was organised by people and structures linked to Yevgeny Prigozhin.
cases.cite: European Platform for Democratic Elections, 'Fake election observation as Russia's tool of election interference: the case of AFRIC' (2020)
cases.drop_reason: A front group posing as election observers; no one was placed inside a government, international body or company.

cases.n: Nyerere Leadership School — CCP trains six ruling parties' cadres
cases.d: The Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School in Kibaha, Tanzania, took its first class on 22 February 2022. It was built with a $40 million grant from the Chinese Communist Party's Central Party School, and CCP theoreticians teach there. It is a joint project of the CCP and six ruling parties: Tanzania's CCM, South Africa's ANC, Angola's MPLA, Mozambique's FRELIMO, Namibia's SWAPO and Zimbabwe's ZANU-PF.
cases.cite: Africa Center for Strategic Studies, 'China's first political school in Africa' (2022)
cases.drop_reason: An openly declared joint party school between the CCP and six ruling parties; nothing hidden is recorded.

cases.n: ANC leadership attends CCP-funded party school (2024)
cases.rank: ANC secretary-general and national executive members
cases.d: The ANC is South Africa's largest party and led every government from 1994 to 2024. From 23 to 25 January 2024 ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula led a five-person delegation, including NEC members David Makhura and Nobuhle Nkabane, to the annual meeting of the Nyerere Leadership School, which the ANC says the Communist Party of China supported at its 2022 launch. The ANC says the school has trained over 1,405 participants, including ANC members.
cases.cite: ANC statement, 23 January 2024
cases.drop_reason: A party delegation attending an openly co-funded training school is not infiltration.

cases.n: African Union HQ — China-built building sent data to Shanghai
cases.d: China built and paid for the African Union headquarters in Addis Ababa, opened in 2012. In January 2018 Le Monde, confirmed by the Financial Times, reported that the AU's IT staff found in 2017 that its computers had been sending data nightly to servers in Shanghai, and that microphones were found hidden in walls and furniture. The AU replaced the system. China's ambassador called the report 'ridiculous and preposterous'; Huawei also denied wrongdoing.
cases.cite: Le Monde, 26 January 2018 (Tilouine and Kadiri), as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: Data secretly sent from AU computers is espionage; nothing shows China steering African Union decisions through it.

cases.n: Uganda — Huawei technicians help police crack opposition phones
cases.d: Huawei is China's largest telecoms equipment maker. In August 2019 the Wall Street Journal reported that Huawei technicians working inside Uganda's police headquarters helped its cyber unit get into the encrypted messages of opposition MP Bobi Wine, and that Huawei staff also helped Zambia's government with domestic spying. The Journal found no evidence that Huawei executives in China or the Chinese state directed this. Huawei denied the report.
cases.cite: Wall Street Journal, 14 Aug 2019, as reported by CNBC
cases.drop_reason: Huawei staff helped the Ugandan government that hired them; no outside party steered the police for its own ends.

cases.n: Bell Pottinger expelled over campaign for Gupta firm
cases.rank: public-opinion campaign for the President's allies
cases.d: Bell Pottinger was a London public relations firm. From 2016 it was paid about £100,000 a month by the Gupta-owned Oakbay Investments and ran a campaign about 'white monopoly capital' using fake bloggers and Twitter accounts to defend the Guptas and President Zuma's circle. After a complaint from the Democratic Alliance, the industry body PRCA expelled it on 4 September 2017, and the firm went into administration on 12 September 2017.
cases.cite: Public Relations and Communications Association ruling, 4 Sept 2017; Herbert Smith Freehills review (2017)
cases.drop_reason: A paid PR and fake-account campaign for a client is propaganda, not anyone getting inside a government body.

cases.n: Lebanon's cabinet orders army plan to disarm Hezbollah
cases.rank: armed force outside the state's control
cases.d: On 7 August 2025 Lebanon's cabinet approved the aim that only the state hold weapons, and Hezbollah- and Amal-aligned ministers walked out. On 5 September 2025 army commander General Rodolphe Haykal presented the 'Homeland Shield' plan to disarm all militias, chiefly Hezbollah, which the cabinet welcomed without a timeline. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem rejected disarmament. In March 2026 Prime Minister Salam said Hezbollah's rocket and drone strikes were outside the state's authority.
cases.cite: Lebanese cabinet decisions of 7 Aug and 5 Sept 2025, reported by AP and Al Jazeera, as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: A cabinet decision to disarm a militia is not an outside party getting inside government.

cases.n: Kenya convicts two Iranians said to be Quds Force over explosives
cases.rank: operatives of Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force (as alleged)
cases.d: The Quds Force is the foreign operations branch of Iran's Revolutionary Guards. In May 2013 a Kenyan court convicted Iranian nationals Ahmad Abolfathi Mohammad and Sayed Mansour Mousavi of plotting attacks and sentenced them to life. Officials believed more than 100 kg of RDX explosive had been shipped into Kenya; about 15 kg was recovered. The men were alleged to be Quds Force members.
cases.cite: Kenyan court judgment, May 2013, as compiled by Iran Watch (Wisconsin Project)
cases.drop_reason: A bomb plot by foreign operatives with no one inside a Kenyan institution.

cases.n: US lists Lebanon's Brotherhood (al-Jamaa al-Islamiya) as terrorist
cases.d: The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 with branches across the region. On 13 January 2026 the US designated its Lebanese branch, which operates as the party al-Jamaa al-Islamiya ('The Islamic Group'), both a Foreign Terrorist Organization and a Specially Designated Global Terrorist, and Treasury named its secretary-general Muhammad Fawzi Taqqosh. These were the first US terrorist designations of any Brotherhood branch.
cases.cite: US State Department and Treasury designations, 13 Jan 2026, as reported by FDD
cases.drop_reason: A terrorist designation of a party; organisations being designated does not count.

cases.n: US lists Egyptian and Jordanian Brotherhood branches as terrorists
cases.rank: Brotherhood branches; linked party holds seats in parliament
cases.d: On 13 January 2026 the US Treasury designated the Egyptian and Jordanian branches of the Muslim Brotherhood as Specially Designated Global Terrorists. Egypt has banned the group since 2013, and Jordan banned all its activities in April 2025; Jordan's government spokesman said the group 'has been dissolved for years'. The Brotherhood-linked Islamic Action Front won 31 seats in Jordan's 2024 parliamentary election.
cases.cite: US Treasury designation, 13 Jan 2026, as reported by FDD
cases.drop_reason: A terrorist designation of banned or dissolved branches; designation does not count.

cases.n: UN monitors: 'credible' evidence UAE armed Sudan's RSF via Chad
cases.rank: Rapid Support Forces, paramilitary at war with the army
cases.d: The Rapid Support Forces grew out of Bashir-era militias and have fought Sudan's army since April 2023. A UN Panel of Experts report to the Security Council, leaked in January 2024, found 'credible' evidence that the UAE sent weapons to the RSF 'several times per week' through Amdjarass in northern Chad. The UAE denied it and said 122 flights carried aid. Sudan's genocide case against the UAE was dismissed by the International Court of Justice on 5 May 2025 for lack of jurisdiction, without ruling on the facts.
cases.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Sudan report (Jan 2024), reported by Al Jazeera; ICJ order, 5 May 2025
cases.drop_reason: Arms smuggling to a paramilitary force, with no one inside an institution.

cases.n: Saad Hariri announces resignation as Lebanese PM from Riyadh
cases.d: On 4 November 2017 Lebanon's prime minister Saad Hariri announced his resignation on television from Saudi Arabia, blaming Iran and Hezbollah. President Michel Aoun told ambassadors Hariri was being held by Saudi Arabia; The New Yorker cited a US official saying he was held for hours and slapped. Hariri returned, suspended the resignation on 21 November and withdrew it on 5 December 2017. Saudi Arabia denied holding him.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, '2017 Lebanon–Saudi Arabia dispute', citing Robert Fisk and The New Yorker
cases.drop_reason: Saudi Arabia allegedly pressed Lebanon's prime minister into resigning while he was on its soil; coercion of a visiting leader, not placing people, money or control inside Lebanon's government.

cases.n: Kenya hands four Gülen-linked refugees to Turkey
cases.d: Turkey lists the Gülen movement as a terrorist group, blames it for the 2016 coup attempt, and seeks its members abroad. On 18 October 2024 four Turkish nationals living in Kenya as refugees were returned to Turkey after seven people were abducted in Nairobi. Kenya's foreign affairs principal secretary Korir Sing'oei confirmed the repatriation was 'at the request of the government of Türkiye'. The UN said it was 'deeply concerned'.
cases.cite: Kenyan Foreign Affairs PS statement, 21 Oct 2024, reported by Stockholm Center for Freedom
cases.drop_reason: Kenya handed over refugees openly at Turkey's request; a rendition, not infiltration of an institution.

cases.n: Turkish intelligence brings Gülen's nephew back from Kenya
cases.d: In May 2021 Turkey's state news agency Anadolu reported that the intelligence agency MIT had seized Selahaddin Gülen, a nephew of Fethullah Gülen, in an overseas operation and brought him to Turkey for prosecution; he had been living in Kenya. A Turkish court later jailed him and the top court upheld the sentence.
cases.cite: Anadolu Agency report, 31 May 2021, as reported by VOA
cases.drop_reason: An abduction abroad by Turkish intelligence, not infiltration of an institution.

cases.n: NSO Group put on US blacklist over Pegasus sales to governments
cases.rank: spyware supplier to state intelligence and police services
cases.d: NSO Group is an Israeli company that sells Pegasus phone-hacking spyware only to governments, under Israeli defence ministry export licences. Investigations tied its use by state clients to surveillance of journalists and dissidents, including the circle of Jamal Khashoggi before Saudi agents killed him in 2018. In November 2021 the US Commerce Department added NSO to its Entity List for acting against US interests. A New York Times investigation found Pegasus sales coincided with some governments' warmer ties with Israel.
cases.cite: US Commerce Department Entity List addition, Nov 2021; Citizen Lab; New York Times, as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: Selling spyware to governments is an open sale, which the brief excludes.

cases.n: Morocco named as Pegasus client targeting 6,000 Algerian phones
cases.rank: Algerian politicians and senior military officers
cases.d: The 2021 Pegasus Project, a consortium of journalists working with Amnesty International, reported that Morocco had selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones, including politicians and senior military officers, as Pegasus targets; Le Monde also reported Morocco selected President Macron and 14 French ministers. Morocco denied using Pegasus. Algeria cut diplomatic relations with Morocco in August 2021, citing alleged Pegasus use among its reasons.
cases.cite: Pegasus Project (Forbidden Stories / Amnesty International), July 2021, as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: Hacking or targeting officials' phones is espionage, not placing people, money or control inside Algeria's government.

cases.n: Team Jorge — Israeli firm hacks Kenyan presidential aide's Telegram
cases.rank: digital strategist of the winning presidential campaign
cases.d: Team Jorge is an Israeli hacking and disinformation outfit led by ex-special forces operative Tal Hanan, exposed in February 2023 by a Forbidden Stories consortium after undercover reporters filmed him. Hanan claimed work on 33 presidential elections, many in Africa. In the meeting he showed access to the Telegram account of Dennis Itumbi, digital strategist for William Ruto in Kenya's 2022 election; Itumbi confirmed the account had been compromised.
cases.cite: Forbidden Stories 'Story Killers' investigation; The Guardian, 17 Feb 2023, as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: Hacking a campaign strategist's Telegram account is not getting inside a government body, international body or company.

cases.n: Cambridge Analytica and Team Jorge in Nigeria's 2015 election
cases.d: Cambridge Analytica was a British data firm, part of SCL Group. Emails leaked to The Guardian in 2023 showed it worked with Israel's Team Jorge in the 2015 Nigerian election on a campaign to re-elect President Goodluck Jonathan by discrediting Muhammadu Buhari, who won. Cambridge Analytica closed in 2018.
cases.cite: The Guardian, 16 and 18 Feb 2023, as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: A data firm hired for an election campaign is contracted campaign work, not infiltration of a government body.

cases.n: Cambridge Analytica ran Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns' data work
cases.d: Cambridge Analytica ran campaigns in secret in Kenya's 2013 and 2017 elections, both won by Uhuru Kenyatta, and said it surveyed 47,000 Kenyans in 2013. After staff boasted of their role on undercover footage in March 2018, the opposition called for an investigation; Kenyatta's Jubilee Party said it had hired the parent company for branding.
cases.cite: Channel 4 News undercover investigation (March 2018), as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: A data firm hired by a presidential campaign is contracted work, not infiltration.

cases.n: Archimedes Group banned by Facebook for African election meddling
cases.rank: election campaigns in several African states
cases.d: Archimedes Group was an Israeli political consulting firm. In May 2019 Facebook removed its networks for 'coordinated inauthentic behavior' aimed mainly at elections in sub-Saharan Africa, including Nigeria, as well as Latin America and Southeast Asia, and found it had spent about $1.1 million on ads. Placed at Abuja because Nigeria's February 2019 election was among those targeted.
cases.cite: Facebook takedown, 16 May 2019, reported by CNN; Atlantic Council DFRLab, as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: Fake-account campaigns removed by Facebook, with no one inside an institution.

cases.n: Senegal's new president makes early call on the Mouride khalife
cases.d: The Mourides are a Sufi brotherhood centred on the holy city of Touba with millions of followers; their leader, the Khalife général, has long been courted by Senegal's presidents, and Abdoulaye Wade went to Touba the day after his 2000 election. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, sworn in on 2 April 2024, visited Khalife Serigne Mountakha Mbacké on 15 April 2024, again in August 2024 and March 2025, and pledged state help with Touba's water and sanitation ahead of the Grand Magal pilgrimage.
cases.cite: Le Soleil (Senegal state daily), Aug 2025; Wikipedia, 'Mouride'
cases.drop_reason: A president openly visiting a religious leader is ordinary courtship, not infiltration.

cases.n: Manhattan 'secret Chinese police station' — two men convicted
cases.rank: overseas outpost of the Fuzhou Public Security Bureau (Chinese police)
cases.d: Safeguard Defenders, a human-rights group, reported in 2022 that Chinese local police ran 'service stations' abroad to pressure people to return to China. The FBI raided one on a floor of the American Changle Association office in Manhattan's Chinatown in October 2022, and it closed. In April 2023 Lu Jianwang and Chen Jinping, both US citizens, were charged with conspiring to act as unregistered agents of China and with deleting messages exchanged with a Ministry of Public Security official; the same day the Justice Department charged 34 Ministry officers. Chen pleaded guilty in December 2024 and a jury convicted Lu in May 2026.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice, Eastern District of New York charges (April 2023); Chen guilty plea December 2024; Lu jury verdict May 2026; Wikipedia 'Chinese police overseas service stations'
cases.drop_reason: A Chinese police outpost in a community association office pressured diaspora members; no government body, international body or company was infiltrated.

cases.n: Elliott Broidy — RNC finance official pleads guilty as foreign agent
cases.rank: deputy finance chair of the Republican National Committee
cases.d: Broidy was a deputy finance chair of the Republican National Committee, the party's national fundraising body, from April 2017 to April 2018. In October 2020 he pleaded guilty to acting as an unregistered foreign agent: he took money to press the Trump administration to drop the 1MDB investigation of Malaysian financier Jho Low and to have the Chinese dissident Guo Wengui sent back to China, and he forfeited more than $6 million. Trump pardoned him in January 2021, at the end of his first term. Rapper Pras Michel, who prosecutors said paid Broidy, was convicted on 10 counts in April 2023 and sentenced to 14 years in November 2025.
cases.cite: US v. Broidy, D.D.C., guilty plea October 2020; presidential pardon January 2021; US v. Michel, D.D.C., verdict 26 April 2023; Wikipedia 'Elliott Broidy', 'Pras Michel'
cases.org_note: Malaysian (Jho Low) and Chinese government interests
cases.drop_reason: Broidy lobbied the administration from outside as an unregistered agent; the record shows no official paid or placed inside government.

cases.n: David Rivera — ex-congressman convicted of secret Venezuela lobbying
cases.rank: former US representative (Florida) lobbying Congress and the White House
cases.d: PDV USA, the US arm of Venezuela's state oil company PDVSA, signed a three-month, $50 million consulting contract with former congressman David Rivera's one-man firm in 2017. Prosecutors said he worked to ease US sanctions on the Maduro government without registering as a foreign agent, enlisting Texas congressman Pete Sessions to broker meetings and deliver a letter from Maduro to Trump. A Miami federal jury convicted Rivera on all counts, including failing to register as a foreign agent and money-laundering conspiracy, on 1 May 2026; co-defendant Esther Nuhfer was tried with him.
cases.cite: US v. Rivera and Nuhfer, Southern District of Florida, jury verdict 1 May 2026 (AP via PBS NewsHour)
cases.org_note: Government of Venezuela via state oil company PDVSA
cases.drop_reason: Rivera lobbied from outside as an unregistered agent; the record shows no official paid or placed inside government.

cases.n: Michael McMahon — ex-NYPD sergeant convicted in China's 'Fox Hunt'
cases.rank: retired New York police sergeant working as a private investigator
cases.d: Operation Fox Hunt is the Chinese government's campaign to force people it accuses of crimes to return to China. A Brooklyn jury convicted McMahon in June 2023 of acting as an illegal agent of China, stalking and conspiracy: he tracked a former Chinese city official living in New Jersey and reported to a Chinese police officer and prosecutor, for more than $19,000. He was sentenced to 18 months on 16 April 2025; President Trump pardoned him on 7 November 2025.
cases.cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York, sentencing release 16 April 2025; pardon reported by AP, 7 November 2025
cases.drop_reason: A retired officer working as a private investigator stalked a target for China; no institution was infiltrated.

cases.n: Vikash Yadav — Indian intelligence officer charged in New York murder plot
cases.rank: Indian government intelligence officer (Research and Analysis Wing)
cases.d: US prosecutors unsealed an indictment in October 2024 charging Vikash Yadav, described as a senior field officer of India's foreign intelligence service (RAW) and former paramilitary officer, with directing a 2023 plan to kill Sikh separatist and US citizen Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York. The indictment says Yadav gave go-between Nikhil Gupta Pannun's address and routine and sent him video of Hardeep Singh Nijjar's body after Nijjar was killed in Canada. India said Yadav 'is no longer an employee of the Government of India'; he remains at large, while Gupta pleaded guilty in the US in early 2026.
cases.cite: US v. Yadav and Gupta, Southern District of New York, superseding indictment unsealed 17 October 2024 (Al Jazeera); Gupta guilty plea reported February 2026 (The Wire)
cases.org_note: Government of India — Research and Analysis Wing (RAW)
cases.drop_reason: An assassination plot by a foreign intelligence officer, not infiltration of an institution.

cases.n: Confucius Institutes named a foreign mission; most US branches closed
cases.rank: Chinese-government-funded language centres at US universities, incl. Pentagon-funded programmes
cases.d: Confucius Institutes are Chinese-language centres placed in foreign universities and funded through China's education ministry. On 13 August 2020 the State Department designated the Confucius Institute U.S. Center a 'foreign mission' of China, with Secretary Pompeo calling the network part of the Communist Party's influence and propaganda apparatus. Defense spending laws barred Pentagon language funds for campuses hosting an institute, and none of 13 universities that asked for waivers got one. The National Association of Scholars counted 104 of 118 US institutes closed by June 2022, while reporting that some reopened under new names.
cases.cite: US State Department foreign-mission designation, 13 August 2020 (RFA); National Association of Scholars count, June 2022 (The Diplomat, November 2023)
cases.drop_reason: Confucius Institutes sit in universities, not a government body, international body or company, and the record is about a designation.

cases.n: National Prayer Breakfast — Congress takes it from the Fellowship
cases.rank: members of Congress who host the annual breakfast attended by the President
cases.d: The Fellowship (also called the Family) is a private Christian network that organised the National Prayer Breakfast for Congress for decades through its Fellowship Foundation. After controversies over who was invited and how the event was paid for, and a boycott call signed by 30 groups, members of Congress moved the official event in 2023 to a new National Prayer Breakfast Foundation. Every president since Eisenhower has taken part; Trump spoke at the breakfast on 5 February 2026.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'National Prayer Breakfast'; Salon, 2 February 2023
cases.drop_reason: Records Congress moving the prayer breakfast away from the Fellowship; it shows no placement of people or control inside government.

cases.n: India — six diplomats expelled over Nijjar killing and threats
cases.rank: Indian High Commissioner and five other diplomats
cases.d: Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar, a Canadian citizen, was shot dead outside a gurdwara in Surrey, British Columbia, on 18 June 2023. Prime Minister Trudeau told Parliament on 18 September 2023 of 'credible allegations' linking agents of India's government to the killing, and the RCMP charged Indian nationals with murder in May 2024. In October 2024 Canada expelled High Commissioner Sanjay Kumar Verma and five other diplomats; officials said Indian diplomats had pushed Canadians to gather information for India's RAW intelligence agency and that targets were then attacked by the Lawrence Bishnoi gang. India denied it and expelled six Canadians; the two countries restored ties in 2025.
cases.cite: Government of Canada expulsions, October 2024; Trudeau statement to the House of Commons, 18 September 2023; Wikipedia 'Killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar'
cases.org_note: Government of India — High Commission and RAW
cases.drop_reason: Diplomatic expulsions over a killing and threats to Canadians; transnational repression, not placement inside a Canadian institution.

cases.n: Bishnoi gang listed as a terrorist entity by Canada
cases.rank: criminal group named by Canadian officials as used by Indian agents
cases.d: On 29 September 2025 Canada listed the Bishnoi Gang, which it describes as a transnational criminal organisation 'operating primarily out of India', as a terrorist entity under the Criminal Code, letting authorities freeze its property and bring terrorism charges. It became the 87th listed entity. In October 2024 Canadian officials had said Indian diplomats passed information on targets in Canada that the gang then attacked.
cases.cite: Public Safety Canada, news release, 29 September 2025
cases.drop_reason: A terrorist listing of a crime group; designation does not count.

cases.n: Hogue inquiry — China the 'most active' interferer, via the United Front
cases.d: The United Front Work Department is the Chinese Communist Party body that builds influence over overseas Chinese communities and foreign elites. Justice Hogue's final report of 28 January 2025 concluded that China is the 'most active perpetrator of state-based foreign interference' in Canada, working through proxies, diplomats and the United Front Work Department to 'control and influence' the diaspora. She found Canadian institutions had not been seriously affected and criticised the federal government's response as 'far from perfect'. China's embassy called the findings 'groundless accusations'.
cases.cite: Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference, Final Report, 28 January 2025 (Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, 30 January 2025)
cases.drop_reason: The finding concerns pressure on diaspora communities and says Canadian institutions were not seriously affected; no placement inside an institution is recorded.

cases.n: Zhao Wei — Chinese consular officer expelled over plan to target MP Chong
cases.rank: Member of Parliament Michael Chong and his relatives
cases.d: A top-secret CSIS assessment, reported in the press and confirmed in substance by Foreign Minister Mélanie Joly, said Zhao Wei, a diplomat at China's consulate in Toronto, was involved with Beijing's intelligence service in targeting Conservative MP Michael Chong and his relatives in Hong Kong. Canada declared Zhao persona non grata on 8 May 2023. China called the report baseless and expelled a Canadian diplomat in return.
cases.cite: Global Affairs Canada, persona non grata declaration, 8 May 2023 (Global News)
cases.drop_reason: Targeting an MP's relatives is intimidation, not placing people, money or control inside Parliament.

cases.n: Chinese 'police stations' in Toronto and Montreal — RCMP probe closed
cases.rank: overseas outposts attributed to Fuzhou city police
cases.d: Safeguard Defenders listed three outposts in Toronto run for the Fuzhou Public Security Bureau. Canada sent a cease-and-desist warning in 2022 and summoned China's ambassador, and in March 2023 the RCMP announced investigations into two alleged stations in the Montreal area. In July 2024 Canada said it had mapped the stations and would share the information with the G7. In September 2025 the RCMP closed its investigation without recommending charges; two Montreal community groups that denied the claims threatened to sue the RCMP.
cases.cite: RCMP statements, March 2023 and September 2025; Wikipedia 'Chinese police overseas service stations'
cases.drop_reason: Alleged police outposts pressuring diaspora members, with the probe closed without charges; no institution was infiltrated.

cases.n: William Majcher — ex-RCMP officer acquitted of helping China
cases.d: The RCMP arrested former officer William Majcher at Vancouver airport in 2023, alleging he used his police knowledge and contacts to get intelligence or services for China's government. At trial the case narrowed to one Security of Information Act count over a 2017 effort to pressure Vancouver resident Kevin Sun, whom China accused of fleeing with tens of millions of dollars, to return. On 13 May 2026 a B.C. judge acquitted him, calling the evidence 'entirely circumstantial'; federal prosecutors filed an appeal in June 2026.
cases.cite: R. v. Majcher, Supreme Court of British Columbia, acquittal 13 May 2026; Crown notice of appeal June 2026 (Global News)
cases.drop_reason: A retired officer acquitted over pressuring a resident to return to China; no institution was infiltrated.

cases.n: Cristina Fernández de Kirchner — ordered to trial over Iran pact
cases.d: In 1994 the AMIA Jewish centre in Buenos Aires was bombed, killing 85 people; Argentine courts charged Iranian officials. In 2013 President Fernández de Kirchner's government signed a memorandum with Iran on questioning the suspects, which prosecutor Alberto Nisman denounced as a cover-up before his death in 2015. A trial court dismissed the case, saying the pact was not a crime, but the Federal Court of Cassation ordered a trial, and on 5 December 2024 the Supreme Court upheld that order, so she must stand trial for aggravated cover-up.
cases.cite: Supreme Court of Argentina, ruling of 5 December 2024 (El Cronista)
cases.org_note: Government of Iran (AMIA bombing suspects)
cases.drop_reason: The Iran memorandum was an openly signed agreement and the case is a cover-up charge; the record shows no Iranian people or money inside Argentina's government.

cases.n: José Antonio Kast — Schoenstatt-raised President of Chile
cases.d: Schoenstatt is a Catholic lay movement founded in Germany in 1914 by priest Josef Kentenich and active in more than 100 countries, with nearly 80 of its shrines in Chile, Argentina and Brazil. BBC Mundo reported that Kast and several siblings were raised under Schoenstatt's guidelines; his brother Miguel Kast, Pinochet's planning minister and Central Bank president, was the only other member to hold high office in Chile. Kast won the 14 December 2025 runoff and took office on 11 March 2026.
cases.cite: BBC Mundo, 18 December 2025 (republished by Acento)
cases.drop_reason: A president's Catholic upbringing is not infiltration; no outside party is shown getting people, money or control inside government.

cases.n: Russian Interior Ministry training centre in Managua — US sanctions
cases.d: Russia's Interior Ministry opened a police training centre in the Las Colinas district of Managua in October 2017, attended by Russia's ambassador and Laureano Ortega Murillo, the president's son; it was set up as an affiliate of the Russian ministry, with courses for Nicaraguan police and later for Central American and Caribbean officers. On 15 May 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned the centre, saying it trains Ortega-Murillo government officials under the Russian government's 'playbook of oppression' and is a key actor in repressing civil society.
cases.cite: US Treasury sanctions, 15 May 2024 (La Prensa, Nicaragua); Confidencial, 25 October 2017
cases.org_note: Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs
cases.drop_reason: An openly agreed Russian police training centre in Nicaragua is declared state cooperation, not hidden infiltration.

cases.n: Chinese police 'service stations' listed in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Ecuador
cases.rank: overseas outposts attributed to Chinese county and city police bureaus
cases.d: Safeguard Defenders' 2022 reports listed Chinese police outposts in Rio de Janeiro (Qingtian County police) and São Paulo (Fuzhou city police), and also in Buenos Aires, Viña del Mar in Chile, and Guayaquil and Quito in Ecuador. The group said Chinese police recorded 230,000 fraud suspects 'persuaded to return' between April 2021 and July 2022. A Yale legal scholar found factual errors in the first report, which the group then revised. No Latin American government has announced findings on these sites.
cases.cite: Safeguard Defenders, '110 Overseas' (September 2022) and 'Patrol and Persuade' (December 2022); Wikipedia 'Chinese police overseas service stations'
cases.drop_reason: Undeclared Chinese police outposts pressured diaspora members but the record shows no one placed inside a Latin American government body.

cases.n: Chinese police inside Solomon Islands policing
cases.d: China sent its first police advisory team to the Solomon Islands in February 2022, after the November 2021 riots, and signed a security agreement in 2022 that lets Honiara ask for Chinese police and military personnel. In 2025 Chinese Ministry of Public Security police in the country began a local pilot of the 'Fengqiao' model of community surveillance policing; it was suspended after local objections. In May 2026 Matthew Wale, a critic of the China relationship, became prime minister and promised to review the security agreement.
cases.cite: East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024; Wikipedia: China–Solomon Islands relations
cases.drop_reason: Chinese police were sent under an openly signed security agreement; the record does not show work beyond what was agreed.

cases.n: Kiribati — Chinese uniformed police working with local force
cases.d: Kiribati switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019 and asked China for policing help in 2022. Kiribati's acting police commissioner Eeri Aritiera confirmed to Reuters in 2024 that up to a dozen uniformed Chinese police officers work alongside local police on six-month rotations, doing community policing, martial-arts training and IT support for a crime database.
cases.cite: Kiribati Police Service statement to Reuters (NBC News, 2024)
cases.drop_reason: Chinese police work with Kiribati's force at the government's open request; declared cooperation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Vanuatu — China's public security minister offers policing pact
cases.d: China has sent police advisers to Vanuatu since 2023. On 19 September 2025 Vanuatu's internal affairs minister Andrew Solomon Napuat met China's Minister of Public Security Wang Xiaohong in Beijing; China donated police equipment worth about NZ$720,000, including motorcycles and drones, and the two sides said they were discussing a wider policing partnership.
cases.cite: Pacific Media Network, 23 September 2025; East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024
cases.drop_reason: An openly announced equipment donation and policing talks between governments is not infiltration.

cases.n: Fiji — Chinese officers removed from police, 2011 pact kept
cases.d: Under a 2011 police cooperation agreement signed during military rule, China's Ministry of Public Security attached two officers at a time to the Fiji Police Force from 2013 and posted a police liaison officer to its embassy in 2021. In 2017 Chinese police working with local officials arrested 77 Chinese nationals in Fiji and flew them to China. In March 2024 Home Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua said Fiji had asked China to withdraw its embedded officers but would keep the agreement, reviewing it every six months, and Fijian officers continue to train in China.
cases.cite: Fiji Home Affairs Minister, ABC interview (BenarNews/RFA, 20 March 2024); East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024
cases.drop_reason: Chinese officers were attached to Fiji's police under an open 2011 agreement; declared cooperation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Philip Chan — Singapore's first 'politically significant person'
cases.d: Singapore's Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act of 2021 lets the Home Affairs Ministry designate people at risk of being used by foreign actors, who must then disclose donations and foreign links. On 26 February 2024 the ministry designated Hong Kong-born businessman Philip Chan Man Ping, the first person listed. He was president of the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce in Singapore and the Kowloon Club, a patron of two government-linked grassroots bodies, and had attended China's Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, a united front body, as an overseas delegate. The ministry said he had shown he was susceptible to being cultivated by foreign actors.
cases.cite: Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs designation, 26 February 2024
cases.drop_reason: A legal designation of a person at risk of being used by foreign actors is a designation, with no finding that he acted inside government for anyone.

cases.n: Harry Roque — ex-presidential spokesman charged over POGO hub
cases.d: Harry Roque was spokesman for President Rodrigo Duterte, under whom POGOs were legalised and expanded. In May 2025 the Angeles City Regional Trial Court, Branch 118, issued arrest warrants for Roque, businesswoman Cassandra Ong and 48 others on 11 counts of qualified human trafficking over Lucky South 99, a POGO hub in Porac, Pampanga, raided in June 2024. Prosecutors say Roque helped it seek a licence and was named as head of its legal department in a reapplication that the gaming regulator PAGCOR denied. Roque denies being its lawyer and has sought asylum in the Netherlands.
cases.cite: Angeles City RTC Branch 118 arrest warrants (GMA News, 15 May 2025)
cases.drop_reason: Roque is charged with human trafficking and with helping a gambling hub seek a licence after leaving office; no one is shown inside a government body for the hub.

cases.n: Philippines bans POGOs after Senate inquiry
cases.d: The state gaming regulator PAGCOR licensed offshore gaming operators from 2016, and President Duterte declined China's 2019 request to shut them. After 2024 Senate hearings led by Risa Hontiveros and Sherwin Gatchalian, President Marcos announced a total ban in July 2024 and signed Executive Order 74 in November 2024 requiring all operations to stop by 31 December 2024. Congress made the ban law in the Anti-POGO Act, signed in October 2025.
cases.cite: Philippine Senate hearings 2024; Executive Order No. 74 (2024); Anti-POGO Act (2025)
cases.drop_reason: A government banning an industry is a policy response, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: Huione — firm co-run by PM Hun Manet's cousin named a laundering hub
cases.rank: prime minister's cousin, director of Huione Pay
cases.d: Huione Group is a Phnom Penh financial conglomerate whose payment arm Huione Pay has Hun To, a cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet, as a major shareholder and director. In March 2025 the National Bank of Cambodia revoked Huione Pay's banking licence. In May 2025 the US Treasury's FinCEN found Huione Group to be a financial institution of primary money laundering concern, saying it laundered over US$4 billion in illicit funds between August 2021 and January 2025, including money from North Korean hackers and scam operations.
cases.cite: FinCEN finding, 1 May 2025; National Bank of Cambodia, March 2025
cases.drop_reason: A money-laundering finding against a financial firm; the record shows no outside party placed or paying anyone inside the government, only a relative of the prime minister owning shares.

cases.n: Canada expels six Indian diplomats over use of Bishnoi gang
cases.d: Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar was shot dead in Surrey, British Columbia on 18 June 2023. In October 2024 the RCMP said 'agents of the Government of India' had used criminal groups, including the gang of Lawrence Bishnoi, who is held in an Indian prison, to target pro-Khalistan Sikhs in Canada, and Canada expelled six Indian diplomats including High Commissioner Sanjay Kumar Verma. India denies involvement and expelled Canadian diplomats in return. Canada listed the Bishnoi gang as a terrorist entity in September 2025, and in July 2026 US prosecutors charged Bishnoi with directing Nijjar's killing; that indictment does not allege an Indian government role.
cases.cite: RCMP statement and Global Affairs Canada expulsions, October 2024; Canada terrorist-entity listing, September 2025
cases.drop_reason: Alleged use of a gang to attack Sikhs in Canada is a violent crime by a state, with no one placed inside a Canadian institution.

cases.n: Pannun plot — Nikhil Gupta pleads guilty; RAW officer charged
cases.d: US prosecutors charged that Vikash Yadav, an employee of India's Cabinet Secretariat, which houses the foreign intelligence agency RAW, directed a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen and lawyer for the pro-Khalistan group Sikhs for Justice, in New York in 2023. His go-between, Nikhil Gupta, agreed to pay $100,000 to a hitman who was really an undercover officer, with a $15,000 cash advance on 9 June 2023. Gupta was extradited from the Czech Republic in June 2024 and on 13 February 2026 pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court to murder-for-hire, conspiracy and money-laundering conspiracy. Yadav was charged in a superseding indictment unsealed in 2024 and has not been brought to the US.
cases.cite: US District Court, Southern District of New York: Gupta guilty plea, 13 February 2026
cases.org_note: The Indian state's intelligence service is the actor; the brief allows state cases where named in the task
cases.drop_reason: A murder-for-hire plot directed by an Indian official is not anyone getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Gnanasara — presidential pardon voided, BBS leader back in prison
cases.d: In 2018 the Court of Appeal jailed BBS leader Gnanasara for six years for contempt of court during the case over the disappearance of journalist Prageeth Eknaligoda; President Maithripala Sirisena pardoned him in May 2019. He was jailed again for four years in March 2024 over statements about Islam, and for nine months in January 2025 for inciting religious hatred. On 10 September 2026 the Supreme Court declared the 2019 pardon arbitrary and invalid, and on 5 October 2026 the Court of Appeal ordered him to serve the rest of the contempt sentence.
cases.cite: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, 10 September 2026; Court of Appeal order, 5 October 2026
cases.drop_reason: A court voiding a pardon is a legal outcome for one man, not infiltration.

cases.n: Gotabaya Rajapaksa — defence secretary opens BBS training centre
cases.d: On 9 March 2013 Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa, brother of President Mahinda Rajapaksa, opened Meth Sevana, the Bodu Bala Sena's cultural and training centre in Galle District, as chief guest. In January 2013 President Rajapaksa and ministers met BBS leaders at the official residence, Temple Trees. Gotabaya Rajapaksa later served as president from 2019 to 2022.
cases.cite: Colombo Telegraph, 14 March 2013; Wikipedia: Bodu Bala Sena
cases.drop_reason: A defence secretary opening a monks' group's centre is open state patronage, not the group getting inside government.

cases.n: Myanmar army spokesman donates to banned Ma Ba Tha successor
cases.d: Myanmar's state Buddhist clergy council ordered Ma Ba Tha disbanded in May 2017, and officials said its renamed successor was also outlawed. In June 2019, after members protested the civilian government's sedition case against the monk Wirathu, army spokesman Brigadier General Zaw Min Tun donated 30 million kyats to the successor group, the Buddha Dhamma Parahita Foundation. Zaw Min Tun is now the spokesman of the military government that took power in 2021.
cases.cite: Wikipedia: Ma Ba Tha (citing Myanmar press)
cases.drop_reason: An army spokesman donating to a banned group is money flowing out of the state, not an outside party getting inside it.

cases.n: Wirathu — junta drops sedition case and gives him top honour
cases.d: Wirathu is a monk of the 969 movement and a leading figure of Ma Ba Tha, known for anti-Muslim sermons. In September 2021, seven months after the coup, the military government dropped the sedition charges against him and released him. In November 2022 he was awarded the title Thiri Pyanchi, one of the country's highest honours.
cases.cite: Military government announcements, 2021–22; Wikipedia: Wirathu
cases.drop_reason: A junta dropping charges and awarding an honour is open favour, not infiltration.

cases.n: Vietnam designates exile party Viet Tan a terrorist group
cases.d: Viet Tan is a pro-democracy party founded by Vietnamese exiles in 1982 and based in the United States. On 4 October 2016 Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security designated it a terrorist organisation, saying it trained people to enter Vietnam and plotted sabotage. Human rights groups and foreign governments dispute the designation; the US government has said there is no evidence it is a terrorist group. Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of membership.
cases.cite: Vietnam Ministry of Public Security, 4 October 2016
cases.drop_reason: A government designating an exile party as terrorist is a designation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Front National — €9m loan from First Czech Russian Bank
cases.rank: national party leadership (Front National, now Rassemblement National)
cases.d: In November 2014 Marine Le Pen confirmed that her party had taken a €9 million loan from the First Czech Russian Bank in Moscow. Party officials told Mediapart it was the first part of a €40 million package, which Le Pen disputed. She said French banks had refused to lend and that the money came from a private bank, not the Russian state; the party is now the largest group in France's National Assembly.
cases.cite: Statement by Marine Le Pen, November 2014; Mediapart investigation
cases.drop_reason: A declared commercial loan from a bank to a party then outside government; the record does not show Russian state control or decisions made for it.

cases.n: Lega signs cooperation pact with Putin's United Russia
cases.rank: party leader Matteo Salvini (later deputy prime minister)
cases.d: United Russia is Vladimir Putin's ruling party. On 6 March 2017 Lega leader Matteo Salvini signed a ten-point cooperation agreement with it in Moscow, covering party delegations, links between Duma deputies and Italian legislators, and trade and investment. The pact runs for five years and renews unless one side gives notice; the Lega gave none, so Il Foglio reported it was tacitly renewed in March 2022 to run until 2027. Salvini is deputy prime minister in the current Italian government.
cases.cite: Text of the Lega–United Russia agreement, published by Il Foglio, 30 July 2022
cases.drop_reason: An openly signed party-to-party cooperation pact is declared, not hidden.

cases.n: FPÖ's five-year pact with United Russia (2016–2021)
cases.d: On 19 December 2016 the leadership of Austria's Freedom Party (FPÖ) signed an 'Agreement on Collaboration and Cooperation' with United Russia, covering delegation exchanges, legislative experience and economic ties. FPÖ ministers then sat in government from 2017 to 2019. The agreement expired at the end of 2021 when leader Herbert Kickl chose not to renew it, which United Russia's Andrey Klimov confirmed.
cases.cite: FPÖ and United Russia statements; Vindobona report on the expiry
cases.drop_reason: An openly signed party-to-party cooperation pact is declared, not hidden.

cases.n: Nikolay Malinov — Russophile leader cleared of spying for RISS
cases.rank: former member of parliament; leader of the Russophiles movement
cases.d: The Russian Institute for Strategic Studies (RISS) is a Russian state think tank. Bulgarian prosecutors charged Nikolay Malinov, a former MP and head of Bulgaria's largest pro-Russia NGO, in 2019 with collecting state secrets for RISS between 2013 and 2019. While on bail in 2019 he travelled to Moscow, where Vladimir Putin gave him the Order of Friendship. A Sofia court acquitted him of all charges in May 2026.
cases.cite: Bulgarian Specialised Prosecution Office indictment, 2019; Sofia court acquittal, May 2026
cases.drop_reason: The charge was collecting state secrets for a Russian think tank, not getting inside an institution, and the court acquitted him.

cases.n: Ireland orders China's Dublin 'police station' to close
cases.d: In September 2022 the human-rights group Safeguard Defenders reported that police bureaus in Chinese cities ran unofficial 'overseas service stations' abroad, used to pressure people wanted by China to return. One was listed on Capel Street, Dublin, run for the Fuzhou city police. In late October 2022 Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs ordered it to close.
cases.cite: Irish Department of Foreign Affairs order, October 2022; Safeguard Defenders report 'Patrol and Persuade', September 2022
cases.drop_reason: An undeclared Chinese police outpost aimed at the diaspora; no one placed inside an Irish government body.

cases.n: Netherlands orders two Chinese 'police stations' shut
cases.d: After the Safeguard Defenders report, the Dutch foreign ministry said two Chinese 'overseas service stations' in the Netherlands had been operating illegally because China never notified the Dutch government of them. Foreign minister Wopke Hoekstra ordered both closed and said the matter would be investigated further.
cases.cite: Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements, November 2022
cases.drop_reason: Undeclared Chinese police outposts aimed at the diaspora; no one placed inside a Dutch government body.

cases.n: Italy ends joint street patrols with Chinese police
cases.d: Under an agreement with China, Chinese police officers had joined Italian police on patrols in Italian cities with large Chinese communities. Safeguard Defenders listed four Chinese 'police stations' in Italy (Rome, Milan, Florence, Prato). In December 2022 Italy said the joint patrols would end; interior minister Matteo Piantedosi said they were unrelated to the stations. A 2023 ProPublica investigation found the leaders of the Fuzhou police station in Prato had ties to organised crime.
cases.cite: Italian Interior Ministry statement, December 2022; ProPublica investigation, 2023
cases.drop_reason: Joint patrols under an open bilateral agreement are declared cooperation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Hungary agrees joint patrols with Chinese police (2024)
cases.d: In mid-February 2024 Hungarian Interior Minister Sándor Pintér and China's Minister of Public Security reached a policing cooperation agreement that lets Chinese officers patrol alongside Hungarian police in tourist areas and at large events. The ministry denied that Chinese police stations exist in Hungary; Safeguard Defenders had listed two in Budapest, in the Józsefváros and Kőbánya districts.
cases.cite: Hungarian Interior Ministry statement, February–March 2024; Safeguard Defenders report, 2022
cases.drop_reason: Joint patrols under an openly announced agreement are declared cooperation, not infiltration.

cases.n: DITIB imams investigated for spying on Gülen followers
cases.rank: imams paid as Turkish civil servants; imams working in German prisons and schools
cases.d: DITIB runs about 900 mosques in Germany; its imams are trained in Ankara and paid as civil servants of Turkey's state religious authority, the Diyanet. In 2017 German federal prosecutors investigated DITIB imams suspected of passing information on Gülen supporters in Germany to Turkish authorities, and police searched imams' homes. Several imams left Germany, and in December 2017 prosecutors dropped the case for lack of evidence and because some suspects were out of reach. North Rhine-Westphalia introduced security checks for imams working in state prisons.
cases.cite: German Federal Prosecutor's Office investigation, 2017, closed December 2017
cases.drop_reason: Suspected spying on Gülen supporters in Germany targeted a community, not a German government body, and the case was dropped.

cases.n: France dissolves the Grey Wolves by cabinet decree
cases.d: The Grey Wolves (Ülkü Ocakları) are the youth movement of Turkey's Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), which governs Turkey in alliance with President Erdoğan. On 4 November 2020 the French Council of Ministers dissolved the movement in France, after an Armenian genocide memorial was defaced; Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin said it incited discrimination and hatred and took part in violent acts. The ban remains in force.
cases.cite: French Council of Ministers dissolution decree, 4 November 2020
cases.drop_reason: A government dissolving a movement is a ban, not infiltration.

cases.n: Austria bans the Grey Wolves salute and symbols
cases.d: From 1 March 2019 Austrian law banned the Grey Wolves hand salute and symbols, with fines of up to €4,000. Turkey's foreign ministry condemned the ban because the symbol belongs to the MHP, a legal party in Turkey's governing alliance. In January 2020 four Vienna bus drivers were dismissed for making the sign.
cases.cite: Austrian Symbols Act amendment in force 1 March 2019
cases.drop_reason: A ban on a movement's symbols is a ban, not infiltration.

cases.n: Austria's Operation Luxor raids later ruled unlawful
cases.d: On 9 November 2020 Austrian authorities searched about 60 addresses and questioned 70 people suspected of belonging to Muslim Brotherhood and Hamas networks, terrorist financing and money laundering. In August 2021 the Graz Higher Regional Court ruled that the house searches were unlawful.
cases.cite: Graz Higher Regional Court decisions, August 2021
cases.drop_reason: Police raids later ruled unlawful; the record shows no infiltration of any institution.

cases.n: UK proscribes Hizb ut-Tahrir (2024)
cases.d: Hizb ut-Tahrir is an international party founded in 1953 that calls for a single caliphate; it is banned in Germany, Turkey, Russia, Pakistan, Indonesia and most Arab states. After years of debate, the UK government announced in January 2024 that it would proscribe the group as a terrorist organisation, and the ban took effect on 19 January 2024 after Parliament approved it. Membership or support is now a criminal offence in the UK.
cases.cite: Terrorism Act 2000 (Proscribed Organisations) (Amendment) Order 2024, approved by Parliament January 2024
cases.drop_reason: Proscribing a group is a designation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Germany bans the Islamic Centre Hamburg as Tehran's outpost
cases.d: The Islamic Centre Hamburg, founded by Iranians in the 1950s, ran a large Shia mosque and was seen as aligned with Iran's government. In June 2022 Germany expelled its deputy director over ties to Hezbollah. In July 2024 the Federal Interior Ministry banned the centre as unconstitutional, closed the mosque and took the building under state administration; the centre's challenge was still pending at the Federal Administrative Court in 2025.
cases.cite: German Federal Ministry of the Interior ban order, July 2024
cases.drop_reason: Banning an Iran-aligned mosque centre; the record shows no one placed inside a German government body.

cases.n: Pope forces out Order of Malta's Grand Master
cases.rank: Prince and Grand Master of a sovereign order with UN observer status
cases.d: The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is a Catholic religious order that is recognised as a sovereign subject of international law and keeps its own diplomatic service. In December 2016 Grand Master Matthew Festing dismissed Grand Chancellor Albrecht von Boeselager over condom distribution in a charity project; Pope Francis set up an inquiry, Festing refused to cooperate, and in January 2017 the Pope asked him to resign. The Order reinstated Boeselager and the Pope named Archbishop Becciu as his special delegate. On 3 September 2022 Pope Francis promulgated a new constitution for the Order and made provisional appointments to its Sovereign Council; the Order's chapter confirmed most of them in January 2023.
cases.cite: Holy See and Order of Malta statements, January 2017; papal decree promulgating the Order's constitution, 3 September 2022
cases.drop_reason: The Pope openly exercising authority over a Catholic order is not hidden infiltration by an outside party.

cases.n: Scientology under German domestic-intelligence watch
cases.rank: Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV)
cases.d: Germany's government does not treat Scientology as a religion and says its aims run against the democratic order. The federal domestic intelligence service (BfV) and several state services have monitored it since 1997; in May 2008 Scientology dropped its legal fight against the surveillance after the Münster Higher Administrative Court refused to hear its appeal. A 2007–2008 attempt by interior ministers to ban it outright was abandoned for lack of legal grounds.
cases.cite: North Rhine-Westphalia Higher Administrative Court (Münster), 2008; BfV annual reports
cases.drop_reason: State surveillance of Scientology shows no one placed inside government.

cases.n: 'Loggia Ungheria' — secret-lodge claims against judges dismissed
cases.rank: judges, CSM members and senior officials named by a witness
cases.d: Lawyer Piero Amara told Milan prosecutors that a secret association, 'Loggia Ungheria', linked magistrates, officials and business people; he named more than 60 people. A Perugia judge closed the inquiry into the alleged lodge, and Milan prosecutors sent Amara to trial for slandering 65 people. The leak of his statements also led to the conviction of Piercamillo Davigo, a former member of the judges' governing council (CSM), for revealing official secrets; in December 2024 the Court of Cassation ordered a new appeal.
cases.cite: Perugia preliminary-investigations judge (archiving order); Brescia court and Court of Appeal judgments 2023–2024; Court of Cassation, 4 December 2024
cases.org_note: alleged lodge; investigators did not establish that it existed
cases.drop_reason: The secret-lodge claims were dismissed and the accuser sent to trial for slander; the record does not establish any infiltration.

cases.n: Macron makes first presidential visit to the Grande Loge de France
cases.d: The Grande Loge de France is one of France's main Masonic bodies. On 5 May 2025 Emmanuel Macron visited it, the first visit by a French president, and asked Freemasons to act as 'ambassadors of fraternity' for the 120th anniversary of the 1905 law separating church and state; he also welcomed their role in the end-of-life bill debate. The Élysée published the visit; Macron is not documented as a member.
cases.cite: Élysée Palace, official record of the visit, 5 May 2025
cases.drop_reason: A president's public visit to a Masonic lodge is not infiltration; he is not documented as a member.

cases.d: The Bilderberg Meeting is a private yearly conference of about 130 European and North American politicians, executives and academics, held under the Chatham House rule with no public record of what is said. The official list for the June 2025 meeting in Stockholm names Kyriakos Mitsotakis, who has been Greece's prime minister since 2019 and was in office at the time.

cases.n: French Senate inquiry into consultants; McKinsey tax-fraud probe
cases.d: McKinsey is a US management-consulting firm that sells advice to governments and companies. A French Senate commission of inquiry (chair Arnaud Bazin, rapporteur Eliane Assassi) reported in early 2022 that the state's use of consultants since 2017 was 'sprawling and opaque' and had real influence on policy, including during the Covid crisis; one example was a €496,800 McKinsey seminar for the Education Ministry. The Senate referred McKinsey's testimony on its French corporate tax to prosecutors in March 2022, and the National Financial Prosecutor (PNF) opened a money-laundering-of-tax-fraud investigation. On 4 September 2026 the PNF and Brussels prosecutors announced a €65 million seizure, about 96% of the tax loss they estimate; the investigation continues.
cases.cite: French Senate commission of inquiry on consulting firms, report 2022; Parquet national financier statement 4 Sept 2026 (via Public Sénat)
cases.drop_reason: The record describes consultants openly hired by the French state and a tax-fraud probe into McKinsey's own taxes, with no one placed inside or steering in secret.

cases.n: KPMG withdraws SARS 'rogue unit' report; nine executives resign
cases.rank: South African Revenue Service; finance minister
cases.d: KPMG is one of the 'Big Four' accounting firms. On 15 September 2017 KPMG South Africa withdrew all findings of its report on an alleged 'rogue unit' at the tax service SARS, a report that had fed criminal charges against former finance minister Pravin Gordhan, and apologised to him. KPMG International's review of the firm's audit work for Gupta family companies found risk checks had been skipped. CEO Trevor Hoole and eight other senior executives resigned, and KPMG offered to repay the R23 million SARS had paid for the report.
cases.cite: KPMG South Africa / KPMG International statement, 15 Sept 2017 (Business Day)
cases.drop_reason: KPMG withdrawing a flawed report and its audit lapses are failings by the firm's own people; the record does not show an outside party placing or paying anyone inside SARS through KPMG.

cases.n: Pfizergate — von der Leyen's texts with Pfizer's CEO
cases.d: In 2021 Commission President Ursula von der Leyen negotiated the EU's largest vaccine contract (up to 1.8 billion doses) partly by text message with Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla. The Commission refused to release the texts; the European Ombudsman found maladministration in July 2022. On 14 May 2025 the Grand Chamber of the EU General Court annulled the refusal in a case brought by The New York Times, holding that EU bodies must keep such documents or explain plausibly why they cannot; the Commission did not appeal. The European Public Prosecutor's Office confirmed an investigation into the vaccine purchases in October 2022.
cases.cite: European Ombudsman decision, 12 July 2022; EU General Court (Grand Chamber), New York Times v Commission, 14 May 2025
cases.drop_reason: A dispute over the Commission keeping text messages from an openly negotiated vaccine contract; no hidden control or payment is shown.

cases.n: John Dalli — EU health commissioner out after snus bribe request
cases.d: Swedish Match is a Swedish maker of snus, an oral tobacco banned for sale in most of the EU. The EU anti-fraud office OLAF reported in October 2012 that a Maltese associate of Health Commissioner John Dalli asked Swedish Match for €60 million in return for help with EU tobacco rules; it found no money changed hands but concluded Dalli knew of the approach. Commission President José Manuel Barroso required Dalli to leave on 16 October 2012. The EU General Court dismissed Dalli's challenge in May 2015.
cases.cite: OLAF report, Oct 2012; EU General Court, Case T-562/12 Dalli v Commission, 12 May 2015
cases.drop_reason: A Maltese associate solicited a bribe that Swedish Match did not pay; no outside party got anyone or any money inside the Commission.

cases.n: Barroso — ex-Commission president becomes Goldman Sachs chairman
cases.rank: former President of the European Commission
cases.d: Goldman Sachs is a US investment bank. In July 2016, about two months after his 18-month cooling-off period ended, José Manuel Barroso (Commission president 2004–14) became non-executive chairman of Goldman Sachs International. His successor Jean-Claude Juncker ordered an unprecedented ethics review; in October 2016 the ethics committee found 'not sufficient grounds' for a breach, accepting Barroso's assurance that he would not lobby for the bank.
cases.cite: European Commission ad hoc Ethical Committee opinion, Oct 2016
cases.drop_reason: A former official taking a private bank job after his cooling-off period, with an ethics finding of no breach; no one moved into a government post.

cases.n: African Union headquarters — data sent to Shanghai every night
cases.d: China built and paid for the roughly $200 million African Union headquarters in Addis Ababa, opened in 2012, and Huawei supplied most of its computer and network equipment. Le Monde reported on 26 January 2018 that from 2012 to January 2017 the building's data were copied each night to servers in Shanghai, and that bugs were found in desks and walls. The AU replaced its servers and declined Chinese offers to set them up. China called the report 'ridiculous', and Huawei said its equipment was not the source; no public evidence of a backdoor has been shown.
cases.cite: Le Monde, 26 Jan 2018 (summarised by New America)
cases.drop_reason: An unproven report of data copying; the record shows no one placed or paid inside the African Union and no evidence of a backdoor.

cases.n: Cambridge Analytica ran Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns
cases.d: Cambridge Analytica was a British political-data firm that closed in 2018. In an undercover Channel 4 recording broadcast in March 2018, managing director Mark Turnbull said the firm ran Uhuru Kenyatta's campaigns in 2013 and 2017, 'rebranded the party twice' and wrote its manifesto. The company then confirmed it was behind the TNA and Jubilee presidential campaigns.
cases.cite: Channel 4 News undercover investigation, 19 Mar 2018; company confirmation (The Star, Kenya)
