cases.drop_reason: Cambridge Analytica was hired by Kenyatta's own party to run its campaigns, a contracted service for the client rather than an outside party steering an institution.

cases.n: Kenya cancels Adani airport and power deals after US charges
cases.d: The Adani Group, an Indian conglomerate, had proposed to lease Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport and to build power lines. A day after Adani's directors were charged with bribery in New York in November 2024, President William Ruto cancelled both deals.
cases.cite: Statement by President William Ruto, Nov 2024
cases.drop_reason: Kenya cancelling Adani deals after US charges is a reaction to a case elsewhere; nothing here shows anyone getting inside Kenya's government.

cases.n: Gerhard Schröder — ex-chancellor on Russian state energy boards
cases.d: Rosneft and Gazprom are Russian state-controlled energy companies; Nord Stream built the gas pipelines under the Baltic. Gerhard Schröder, chancellor until 2005, became chairman of the Nord Stream shareholders' committee in 2006 and joined Rosneft's board in 2017, later chairing it; he gave up the chairmanship in 2022 and turned down a Gazprom board seat that year. In 2022 the Bundestag closed his ex-chancellor's office; Berlin courts rejected his challenges in 2023 and 2024. An SPD arbitration panel ruled in March 2023 that he could stay in the party.
cases.cite: Bundestag decision 2022; Berlin administrative courts 2023 and 2024
cases.drop_reason: Schröder took Russian company posts after leaving office; the record shows no one inside the German government acting for Russia.

cases.n: Karin Kneissl — ex-foreign minister on Rosneft's board
cases.d: Rosneft is Russia's state oil company. Karin Kneissl was Austria's foreign minister from December 2017 to June 2019, nominated by the FPÖ; Vladimir Putin attended her wedding in August 2018. In March 2021 the Russian government appointed her to Rosneft's board; she resigned in May 2022. She moved to Russia in 2023 and works at a research centre at St Petersburg State University.
cases.cite: Rosneft board appointment, March 2021 (Reuters and others)
cases.drop_reason: Kneissl joined Rosneft's board after leaving office; the record shows no decision while minister made for Russia.

cases.n: Kristalina Georgieva — Doing Business data changed for China
cases.rank: World Bank CEO; IMF Managing Director
cases.d: The World Bank's annual Doing Business report ranked countries' business rules and shaped investment and reform decisions. In September 2021 an inquiry by the law firm WilmerHale found that Kristalina Georgieva, as World Bank chief executive, had pressed staff to alter data in the 2018 report to raise China's (and Saudi Arabia's) ranking. She denied it; the IMF board, where she was Managing Director, said the evidence did not conclusively show wrongdoing and kept her. The IMF reappointed her for a second five-year term on 12 April 2024.
cases.cite: WilmerHale investigation for the World Bank Board, Sept 2021; IMF Executive Board statement, Oct 2021
cases.drop_reason: The inquiry found World Bank managers pressed their own staff to change data; the record shows no Chinese agent or payment inside the Bank.

cases.n: Interpol curbs Russia's direct use of its channels
cases.d: Interpol lets national police forces send each other wanted-person alerts. On 10 March 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine, Interpol's General Secretariat stopped Russia's bureau from sending alerts ('diffusions') directly to other countries; each must first be checked against Interpol's rules. The Secretary General also put Russia under enhanced supervision, endorsed by the Executive Committee, to prevent misuse against individuals.
cases.cite: INTERPOL General Secretariat statement, 10 Mar 2022
cases.drop_reason: Interpol limiting Russia's access is a safeguard; the record shows no misuse by anyone inside Interpol.

cases.n: French terror prosecutors open torture inquiry into Interpol president
cases.rank: UAE Interior Ministry inspector general; Interpol president
cases.d: Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, a senior UAE Interior Ministry officer, was Interpol's president from November 2021 to November 2025. Complaints were filed in Paris alleging torture of activist Ahmed Mansoor and of Britons Matthew Hedges and Ali Issa Ahmad in UAE custody. In March 2022 France's anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry into torture and acts of barbarism, and Hedges and Ahmad testified before Paris investigating judges in May 2022. Al-Raisi denies the allegations.
cases.cite: Parquet national antiterroriste (France), preliminary inquiry opened March 2022
cases.drop_reason: A torture inquiry into the Interpol president's conduct in the UAE; the record shows no Interpol decision steered for the UAE.

cases.n: Jimmy Morales ends CICIG while under its investigation
cases.d: CICIG, the UN-backed anti-impunity commission, was investigating irregular financing of President Jimmy Morales's campaign. In 2018 Morales said he would not renew its mandate and deployed armed forces near its offices; on 7 January 2019 he terminated the agreement. The UN rejected the move and the Constitutional Court ruled against it, but CICIG's mandate ended on 3 September 2019.
cases.cite: Government of Guatemala notice, 7 Jan 2019; Constitutional Court rulings 2019
cases.drop_reason: A president ending an investigative commission is a government acting against oversight, with no outside party getting inside.

cases.n: Erik Prince — UN panel finds he broke the Libya arms embargo
cases.d: Erik Prince founded the US private military company Blackwater. A UN Panel of Experts report in February 2021 found he violated the UN arms embargo on Libya in a 2019 operation to supply aircraft and personnel to forces of eastern commander Khalifa Haftar; the planned $80 million deal collapsed in June 2019. Prince denies wrongdoing.
cases.cite: UN Security Council Panel of Experts on Libya, report Feb 2021
cases.drop_reason: Supplying aircraft and personnel in breach of a UN arms embargo is sanctions-breaking, with no one placed inside an institution.

cases.n: Erik Prince — security deal with Ecuador's President Noboa
cases.d: Erik Prince founded Blackwater and now runs other private security ventures. In March 2025 he and President Daniel Noboa announced a deal for Prince to support Ecuador's security forces against gangs.
cases.cite: Joint announcement by President Noboa and Erik Prince, March 2025
cases.drop_reason: An openly announced security deal with Ecuador's government is a declared contract, not infiltration.

cases.n: Vectus Global — Prince's contractors in Haiti's anti-gang raids
cases.d: Vectus Global is a private security company run by Erik Prince, founder of Blackwater. Reuters reported in August 2025 that Prince planned to keep personnel in Haiti for ten years to fight gangs and help collect taxes. In January 2026 Haitian authorities confirmed Vectus took part in anti-gang raids.
cases.cite: Reuters, Aug 2025; Haitian authorities' confirmation, Jan 2026
cases.drop_reason: Contractors openly working for Haiti's authorities on anti-gang raids are a declared contract, not infiltration.

cases.n: Erik Prince sends men and drones to help Congo's army
cases.rank: Armed Forces of the DR Congo (FARDC)
cases.d: Erik Prince founded Blackwater. A UN report in 2023 described a proposed Prince mercenary deal for North Kivu, and in February 2026 Reuters reported that Prince sent men and drones to help Congo's army secure the eastern city of Uvira.
cases.cite: UN Group of Experts on the DR Congo, 2023; Reuters, Feb 2026
cases.drop_reason: Sending contractors and drones to help Congo's army is open mercenary contracting, not infiltration.

cases.n: Angola removes Universal Church's Brazilian leadership
cases.rank: government order dissolving the church's board
cases.d: The Brazilian-run Universal Church of the Kingdom of God built a large following in Angola. After Angolan pastors accused Brazilian leaders of racial discrimination and of pressing pastors into vasectomies, the Angolan government in June 2020 ordered the dissolution of the church's board and removed Bishop Honorilton Gonçalves. The church had already been suspended for 60 days in 2013 after a deadly crush at a Luanda stadium event.
cases.cite: Angolan government order, June 2020, via Wikipedia 'Universal Church of the Kingdom of God'
cases.drop_reason: Angola's government removing a church's leadership is the state acting against a religious body, not that body getting inside the state.

cases.n: William Ruto — plan for an 8,000-seat church at State House
cases.d: Ruto is an evangelical Christian who led a church choir of the Africa Inland Church and married in that church. In July 2025 he announced he would build a church in the State House grounds with his own money. The Daily Nation published designs for a building seating 8,000 people at an expected cost of about $9 million; Nairobi's Catholic archbishop and the Atheists in Kenya Society objected that it breached the secular state.
cases.cite: Daily Nation, July 2025, via Wikipedia 'William Ruto'
cases.drop_reason: A president building a church with his own money reflects his own faith; no outside party is shown placing people or steering decisions.

cases.n: Supreme Court voids president's 2019 pardon of BBS leader Gnanasara
cases.d: Gnanasara was sentenced in 2018 for contempt of court in the case of disappeared journalist Prageeth Eknaligoda, and President Maithripala Sirisena pardoned him in May 2019. He was jailed again in 2024 (four years) and January 2025 (nine months) over statements about Islam. On 10 September 2026 the Supreme Court ruled the 2019 pardon arbitrary and invalid, on petitions by the Centre for Policy Alternatives and Sandhya Eknaligoda, and in October 2026 the Court of Appeal ordered the rest of his sentence enforced.
cases.cite: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, 10 Sep 2026, via Daily Mirror; BBC, 10 Jan 2025
cases.drop_reason: A court voiding a presidential pardon for a monk's contempt conviction does not show Bodu Bala Sena placing people, money or control inside a government body.

cases.n: Ukraine bans church bodies tied to the Moscow Patriarchate
cases.d: The Russian Orthodox Church (Moscow Patriarchate) under Patriarch Kirill backs Russia's war on Ukraine. On 20 August 2024 Ukraine's parliament adopted a law 'On the Protection of the Constitutional Order in the Field of Activities of Religious Organizations' that bans the Russian church in Ukraine and gives affiliated Ukrainian bodies nine months to cut ties. The Security Service (SBU) has raided churches of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church since 2018 and courts have sentenced individual priests.
cases.cite: Law of Ukraine, 20 Aug 2024; via Wikipedia 'Ukrainian Orthodox Church (Moscow Patriarchate)'
cases.drop_reason: A national law banning a foreign-run church concerns a religious body, not a government, international body or company being taken over from outside.

cases.n: Estonia expels the Moscow Patriarchate's metropolitan
cases.rank: Police and Border Guard Board; Riigikogu
cases.d: The Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate has about 150,000 faithful. In January 2024 Estonia refused to renew the residence permit of its head, Metropolitan Eugene (Reshetnikov), calling his support for Russia's war 'a security risk'; he left on 6 February 2024. In May 2024 the Riigikogu declared the Moscow Patriarchate an institution that supports Russian military aggression, and in 2025 it tightened the churches law to cut foreign control.
cases.cite: ERR News, Jan 2024 and 2025
cases.drop_reason: Refusing a church leader's residence permit is a state measure against a religious body; no government body or company is shown being infiltrated.

cases.n: Latvia's parliament orders its Orthodox Church out of Moscow's control
cases.d: Until 2022 the Latvian Orthodox Church was a self-governing part of the Russian Orthodox Church. On 9 September 2022, on a bill tabled by President Egils Levits, the Saeima amended the law to make the church fully independent of any church authority outside Latvia, and required the President's chancery to be told of its bishops' appointments. No Orthodox church had recognised the new status as of mid-2026.
cases.cite: Law on the Latvian Orthodox Church, amended 9 Sep 2022; via Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: Parliament changing the legal status of a national church is open legislation about a religious body, not infiltration of a government body or company.

cases.n: UK sanctions Patriarch Kirill over support for the invasion
cases.d: Patriarch Kirill has led the Russian Orthodox Church since 2009; Swiss federal police files classified him as a KGB agent codenamed 'Mikhailov' from 1970. In 2022 the United Kingdom, Canada and Ukraine sanctioned him, the UK citing 'multiple public statements in support of the Russian invasion of Ukraine'. An EU listing proposed in May 2022 was dropped after Hungary objected.
cases.cite: UK sanctions notice, 2022; AFP; via Wikipedia 'Patriarch Kirill of Moscow'
cases.drop_reason: Sanctions on Patriarch Kirill are a designation, and the KGB link concerns a church, not a government body, international body or company.

cases.n: Belgium ends Saudi control of the Great Mosque of Brussels
cases.d: King Baudouin lent the building to Saudi Arabia in 1967 on a 99-year rent-free lease; from 1983 it was run with the Saudi-funded Muslim World League, with Gulf-trained imams. The parliamentary commission on the 2016 Brussels bombings recommended ending the concession, and on 16 March 2018 the Council of Ministers did so, citing foreign interference. In October 2017 the government had revoked the residence permit of the mosque's imam over his Salafi preaching.
cases.cite: Belgian parliamentary commission on the 22 March 2016 attacks; Council of Ministers, 16 Mar 2018; Washington Post, 19 Mar 2018
cases.drop_reason: Saudi Arabia ran the mosque under an open 99-year lease; a mosque is not a government body or company, and ending the lease is not infiltration.

cases.n: Belgian State Security finds foreign agents in new Brussels mosque body
cases.rank: Minister of Justice; State Security Service
cases.d: After Saudi Arabia lost the Great Mosque, a new Belgian management association was set up to run it. In December 2020 Justice Minister Vincent Van Quickenborne issued a negative opinion that halted its recognition, after the State Security Service found three of its members linked to Moroccan intelligence and one employed by Turkey's Diyanet.
cases.cite: Belgian Ministry of Justice, Dec 2020; via Wikipedia 'Great Mosque of Brussels'
cases.drop_reason: The foreign agents were found in an association seeking to run a mosque, a religious body rather than a government body, international body or company.

cases.n: Dutch parliamentary inquiry into Gulf and Turkish funding of mosques
cases.d: A parliamentary inquiry chaired by CDA MP Michel Rog reported on 25 June 2020 that donors from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar funded Dutch mosques to spread a hardline Salafi Islam it called anti-democratic, and influenced the choice of imams and teaching. It listed sums such as €2.5 million to The Hague's As-Sunnah mosque (2010–17). It found that Turkey's Diyanet, whose preachers are Turkish civil servants, exerts strong political influence over Turkish-Dutch mosques.
cases.cite: Parliamentary inquiry 'Ongewenste beïnvloeding uit onvrije landen', final report 25 Jun 2020, via DutchNews
cases.drop_reason: Foreign funding of mosques concerns religious bodies, not a government body, international body or company being steered from outside.

cases.n: Austria shuts seven mosques and reviews Turkish state imams
cases.d: Austria's 2015 Islam law bans foreign funding of religious bodies. On 8 June 2018 Chancellor Sebastian Kurz's government said it would close one Turkish mosque and dissolve the Arab Religious Community, which ran six mosques accused of Salafi preaching. It put under review the residence permits of about 40 imams employed by ATIB, the Austrian branch of Turkey's Diyanet, which it said had got around the funding ban. Turkey called the move 'anti-Islam' and 'racist'.
cases.cite: Al Jazeera, 8 Jun 2018
cases.drop_reason: Closing mosques and reviewing imams' permits is a state measure on religious bodies, not infiltration of a government body or company.

cases.n: Diyanet hands parliament imam reports on Gülenists in 38 countries
cases.rank: Grand National Assembly inquiry into the coup attempt
cases.d: The Diyanet is Turkey's state religious directorate; it employs imams as civil servants and runs over 2,000 mosques abroad. After the July 2016 coup attempt it instructed its imams abroad to gather information on followers of the Gülen movement and gave the Turkish parliament 50 intelligence reports from 38 countries. German federal prosecutors later investigated imams of its German branch, DITIB, on suspicion of informing on Gülen supporters.
cases.cite: Hürriyet Daily News, 2016; Wikipedia 'Presidency of Religious Affairs'
cases.drop_reason: Turkey's own state religious directorate gathering information on Gülen followers abroad is state surveillance, not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Germany investigates DITIB imams for spying for Ankara
cases.rank: Federal Prosecutor's Office; Federal Interior Ministry
cases.d: DITIB, founded in 1984 in Cologne as a branch of Turkey's Diyanet, is one of Germany's largest Muslim organisations; its imams are Turkish civil servants. In February 2017 German federal prosecutors opened an investigation into DITIB imams suspected of passing information on Gülen supporters to Turkey. Deutsche Welle later reported, under the headline 'Court says prosecutors can't prove Turkey spies via DITIB', that the case could not be proved. The Federal Interior Ministry cut DITIB's federal funding in 2018.
cases.cite: Politico Europe, 15 Feb 2017; DW, 5 Oct 2017 and 30 Aug 2018
cases.drop_reason: The spying case against DITIB imams could not be proved, and the target was a religious community rather than a government body or company.

cases.n: Germany keeps Scientology under domestic intelligence watch
cases.rank: Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV)
cases.d: Germany's domestic intelligence agency has monitored the Church of Scientology since 1997 as a group whose aims run against the constitutional order; several state agencies do the same. Scientology lost its challenge to federal surveillance in 2004, when the court relied on L. Ron Hubbard's writings that civil rights should be limited to Scientologists. The BfV estimates about 3,500 members in Germany, and monitoring continues.
cases.cite: BfV reports; Federal court ruling, Nov 2004; via Wikipedia 'Scientology in Germany'
cases.drop_reason: Domestic intelligence monitoring of Scientology is a designation; the record shows no one placed inside a government body or company.

cases.n: Moscow court bans the Church of Scientology of Moscow
cases.rank: Moscow City Court; Supreme Court of Russia
cases.d: In November 2015 the Moscow City Court banned the activities of the Church of Scientology of Moscow at the request of the Justice Ministry, partly because its name is a US trademark and so, the ministry argued, not a religion. Russia's Supreme Court upheld the ban in June 2016. The European Court of Human Rights had ruled against Russia's earlier refusals to register Scientology branches in 2007 and 2009.
cases.cite: Moscow City Court, Nov 2015; Supreme Court, Jun 2016; via Wikipedia 'Scientology in Russia'
cases.drop_reason: A court banning a religious group's branch is a designation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Belgian court acquits Scientology after 18-year case
cases.d: Belgian prosecutors spent ten years investigating the Church of Scientology's Belgian branch and European office and in 2007 sought charges including extortion, fraud and illegal medical practice. In March 2016 the Brussels court acquitted the church and the individual defendants of all charges and rejected demands to close the branch, ruling the case inadmissible because the defendants had been 'prosecuted primarily because they were Scientologists'. Prosecutors did not appeal.
cases.cite: Brussels court judgment, March 2016; via Wikipedia 'Scientology in Belgium'
cases.drop_reason: An acquittal on fraud and extortion charges involves no outside party getting inside a government body or company.

cases.n: Paris appeal court upholds Scientology fraud conviction
cases.d: France's government watchdog on cults (MIVILUDES) has classed Scientology as a dangerous cult since 2006. In October 2009 a Paris court convicted Scientology's Celebrity Centre and bookshop of organised fraud and fined them €600,000; it could not dissolve them because a 2009 legislative change had removed that penalty. In February 2012 the appeal court upheld the conviction, which Le Monde called a 'historic condemnation'.
cases.cite: Paris Criminal Court, 27 Oct 2009; Le Monde, 2 Feb 2012; via Wikipedia 'Scientology in France'
cases.drop_reason: A fraud conviction for Scientology's own staff and bookshop is ordinary crime with no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Three members of Congress open Scientology's Washington office
cases.rank: members of the US House of Representatives
cases.d: In September 2012 the Church of Scientology opened a National Affairs Office near the White House. Representatives Dan Burton (R-Indiana), Sheila Jackson Lee (D-Texas) and Danny K. Davis (D-Illinois) spoke at the opening, alongside a FEMA program manager.
cases.cite: Washingtonian, 14 Sep 2012
cases.drop_reason: Members of Congress openly speaking at an office opening is public support, not hidden placement of people or money inside Congress.

cases.n: Speaker Mike Johnson flies the NAR's 'Appeal to Heaven' flag
cases.rank: Speaker of the US House of Representatives
cases.d: Many NAR adherents use the Revolutionary-era 'Appeal to Heaven' flag to signal that Trump is chosen by God, according to scholar André Gagné. Press reports in 2024 showed the flag outside Speaker Mike Johnson's Capitol Hill office; it also flew at the vacation home of Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito. Johnson said in 2023 that the 'separation of church and state is a misnomer'.
cases.cite: Press reports, 2024; André Gagné (2024); via Wikipedia 'New Apostolic Reformation'
cases.drop_reason: The record shows a flag and statements, not that Speaker Johnson is a member of the New Apostolic Reformation.

cases.n: Doug Mastriano — Pennsylvania senator at NAR events
cases.rank: Pennsylvania state senator and 2022 governor nominee
cases.d: Mastriano has sat in the Pennsylvania Senate since 2019 and was the Republican nominee for governor in 2022. Salon and Media Matters reported that he attended NAR events and campaigned with Julie Green, an NAR 'prophet' who gave the opening prayer at one of his events. He worships at a Mennonite church.
cases.cite: Salon, Jul 2022; Media Matters, Aug 2022
cases.drop_reason: The record shows Mastriano attending NAR events and worshipping at a Mennonite church, not that he is a member of the movement.

cases.n: William Barr — Opus Dei centre board member to attorney general
cases.rank: Attorney General of the United States
cases.d: The Catholic Information Center in Washington is run by Opus Dei priests and is a meeting place for politically connected Catholics. Barr sat on its board from 2014 to 2017 and became Trump's attorney general in February 2019. Opus Dei has said Barr is not a member.
cases.cite: Wikipedia biography, citing Washington Post and America magazine
cases.drop_reason: The record shows only a board seat at an Opus Dei-run centre, and Opus Dei says Barr is not a member, so it does not show a member of the order holding office.

cases.n: José Antonio Kast — Schoenstatt Movement member as president
cases.d: The Schoenstatt Movement is a Catholic lay movement founded in Germany in 1914, present in over 110 countries, with 25 shrines in Chile. Kast is a practising Catholic and a member of the movement, as El Mercurio reported in a 2011 profile of his family. He took office as President of Chile in March 2026.
cases.cite: El Mercurio, 31 Jul 2011; via Wikipedia biography
cases.drop_reason: The record shows only a reported membership of a Catholic lay movement, not the movement steering the president's decisions.

cases.n: Eddie Villanueva — Jesus Is Lord Church founder as deputy speaker
cases.rank: Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives
cases.d: The Jesus Is Lord Church Worldwide is a Philippine evangelical church; Villanueva is its founder and spiritual director and also founded the Philippines for Jesus Movement. After presidential runs in 2004 and 2010, he entered the House in 2019 for the CIBAC party-list and was a Deputy Speaker from July 2019 to June 2022. His son Joel Villanueva is a senator.
cases.cite: House of Representatives records; Wikipedia biography
cases.drop_reason: A church founder openly elected to Congress on a party list is open political participation, not hidden placement or control.

cases.n: Fabricio Alvarado — Christian singer's party in Costa Rica's assembly
cases.rank: Legislative Assembly deputy and presidential runoff candidate
cases.d: Alvarado is an evangelical Christian singer and former journalist. As the only deputy of the National Restoration Party he reached the 2018 presidential runoff on opposition to an Inter-American Court ruling on same-sex marriage, losing to Carlos Alvarado. He founded the New Republic Party in 2019 and sat in the Legislative Assembly again from 2022 to 2026.
cases.cite: CRHoy; Costa Rican electoral tribunal results; via Wikipedia biography
cases.drop_reason: An evangelical singer openly running for office and founding a party is open political participation, not infiltration.

cases.n: Senator books Bellas Artes for La Luz del Mundo leader's homage
cases.rank: Senator; National Institute of Fine Arts (INBAL)
cases.d: La Luz del Mundo is a Guadalajara-based church with members in many countries. Senator Rogelio Zamora Guzmán (PVEM, allied with Morena) wrote to INBAL in January 2019 asking for the Palacio de Bellas Artes; on 15 May 2019 it hosted a homage for leader Naasón Joaquín García's 50th birthday. INBAL said it had been told it was an opera gala. García was arrested in Los Angeles in June 2019 and in June 2022 pleaded guilty to child sexual abuse, receiving 16 years and 8 months.
cases.cite: SDP Noticias; Los Angeles Times, 3 Jun 2022; New York Times, 9 Jun 2022
cases.drop_reason: A one-off venue booking under a misleading description does not show the church placing, paying or controlling anyone inside government.

cases.n: Cuba's ex-Grand Master admits he was a state-security officer
cases.rank: Department of State Security (Ministry of the Interior)
cases.d: José Manuel Collera Vento became Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Cuba in 2000 after government pressure. In 2011, after WikiLeaks cables exposed him, he admitted on the state TV series 'Las Razones de Cuba' that he had worked for state security as 'Agente Gerardo' and had been placed as Grand Master so the government could monitor Freemasons. The Pinar del Río provincial assembly gave him its highest award in April 2011.
cases.cite: Las Razones de Cuba (Cuban state TV), 2011; CNN; via Wikipedia 'Freemasonry in Cuba'
cases.drop_reason: The state security agent was placed inside a Masonic lodge, which is not a government body, international body or company within the map's scope.

cases.n: Cuban Justice Ministry steps into the Grand Lodge leadership crisis
cases.d: In January 2024 about $19,000 kept in the Grand Master's office safe for a Masonic retirement home went missing, and Grand Master Mario Urquía Carreño was expelled amid the dispute. Cuba's Ministry of Justice, which registers associations, then intervened and declined to recognise the lodge's newly elected leadership, 14ymedio reported. A former grand official who fled in 2023 said a state-security officer had told him agents had watched Cuban lodges for over 40 years.
cases.cite: 14ymedio, 2024; via Wikipedia 'Freemasonry in Cuba'
cases.drop_reason: A justice ministry refusing to recognise a lodge's leadership is state regulation of an association, not infiltration of a government body or company.

cases.n: Pope rewrites the Order of Malta's constitution and council
cases.rank: Holy See over the Sovereign Council of the Order of Malta
cases.d: The Sovereign Order of Malta is a Catholic religious order that is also a sovereign entity with diplomatic relations with 115 states and UN observer status. In January 2017 Pope Francis forced Grand Master Matthew Festing to resign after a dispute over Grand Chancellor Albrecht von Boeselager. On 3 September 2022 Francis promulgated a new constitution for the order and appointed its Sovereign Council himself; the order's chapter re-elected his appointees in January 2023.
cases.cite: Holy See decree, 3 Sep 2022; Wikipedia 'Sovereign Military Order of Malta'
cases.drop_reason: The Pope is the declared religious superior of the Order of Malta, so his rewriting of its constitution is open authority, not hidden infiltration.

cases.n: Bybit — North Korea steals US$1.5bn through a wallet supplier
cases.d: Bybit is a Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange. On 21 February 2025 attackers compromised the Safe{Wallet} software Bybit used to move funds and redirected about US$1.5 billion in Ether to their own wallets, the largest crypto theft recorded. On 26 February 2025 the FBI publicly attributed the theft to North Korea's 'TraderTraitor' hacking group, also known as Lazarus. The attack reached Bybit through a supplier rather than through Bybit's own staff.
cases.cite: FBI public service announcement PSA250226, 26 Feb 2025
cases.why: Official FBI attribution.
cases.drop_reason: This was a hack through a software supplier that stole funds; the record itself says no one got inside Bybit or steered its decisions.

cases.n: Salt Typhoon — Chinese state hackers inside telecom networks
cases.rank: core networks of AT&T, Verizon and other carriers
cases.d: Salt Typhoon is a hacking group widely attributed to China's Ministry of State Security. From about 2023 it sat inside the networks of at least nine US telecom companies, including Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile, Lumen and Spectrum, with access to call records and lawful-intercept systems; it was found in September 2024. In January 2025 the US Treasury sanctioned Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology for direct involvement, and in August 2025 agencies from 13 countries named three Chinese firms that supply the army and the MSS. The FBI said in August 2025 that at least 200 companies in 80 countries had been hacked.
cases.cite: US Treasury sanctions 17 Jan 2025; joint advisory of 13 countries Aug 2025; FBI statements
cases.why: US sanctions designation and a joint advisory by 13 governments.
cases.drop_reason: This is a network hacking campaign for espionage, not an outside party placing people, money or control inside the companies to steer their decisions.

cases.n: SolarWinds — Russian SVR code planted in a software update
cases.d: SolarWinds sells Orion, a network-management program used by companies and governments. Attackers got into SolarWinds' software-publishing system by September 2019 and, from March to June 2020, hid malicious code in Orion updates, which about 18,000 customers downloaded; Microsoft and FireEye were among the firms then breached. US agencies said in January 2021 that Russia was most likely responsible, and in 2021 the US government formally attributed the operation to Russia's foreign intelligence service, the SVR.
cases.cite: CISA/FBI/NSA/ODNI joint statement 5 Jan 2021; US government attribution to the SVR, April 2021
cases.why: Formal attribution by the US government.
cases.drop_reason: Planting malicious code in a software update is a hack, not an outside party getting its people, money or control inside SolarWinds to steer it.

cases.n: Juniper ScreenOS — 'unauthorised code' in firewall software
cases.d: Juniper Networks makes network equipment used by governments and companies. In December 2015 it announced that 'unauthorised code' had been inserted into ScreenOS, the software of its NetScreen firewalls: one change gave a hidden administrator password, the other altered a random-number generator (Dual_EC) so that VPN traffic could be decrypted. Researchers showed the Dual_EC mechanism was designed by the US National Security Agency, and that someone else, an unknown government, appears to have changed its key. Who planted the code has never been officially stated.
cases.cite: Juniper Networks security advisory, Dec 2015; academic analysis of the backdoor (Checkoway et al.)
cases.why: The code's presence is admitted by Juniper; who inserted it is a researchers' inference, not an official finding.
cases.drop_reason: Unauthorised code planted by an unknown party is a hack with no identified outside party inside Juniper steering its decisions.

cases.n: Supermicro 'Big Hack' — claimed Chinese spy chips in servers
cases.d: Bloomberg Businessweek reported on 4 October 2018, citing unnamed sources, that China's military had pressed Supermicro's Chinese subcontractors to add tiny spy chips to server boards used by about 30 companies, including Apple and Amazon, and by US agencies. Supermicro, Apple and Amazon denied it, and the US Department of Homeland Security and Britain's National Cyber Security Centre said they had no reason to doubt the companies. Supermicro later told US regulators it found no malicious chip. Bloomberg published further claims in February 2021; no public evidence of an implant has been produced.
cases.cite: Bloomberg Businessweek, 4 Oct 2018 and Feb 2021; company denials; DHS and UK NCSC statements
cases.why: Claimed by Bloomberg on anonymous sourcing; denied by all named firms and not backed by government findings.
cases.drop_reason: The spy-chip claim was denied by the companies and governments involved and no evidence of an implant has been produced.

cases.n: Kaspersky Lab — US bans sales over suspected FSB access
cases.rank: antivirus software installed on customers' computers
cases.d: Kaspersky is a Moscow-based maker of antivirus software that runs with deep access inside customers' computers. The US government has said the company has ties to Russia's FSB security service, which Kaspersky denies. In 2017 the US barred federal agencies from using its software; in June 2024 the Commerce Department banned sales in the US from July and software updates from 29 September 2024. Lithuania, the Netherlands and Australia have also restricted its use in government; the company moved some data processing to Switzerland and denies any spying.
cases.cite: US Department of Homeland Security directive 2017; US Commerce Department ban announced 20 Jun 2024
cases.why: US government designation on national-security grounds; no public proof of FSB use and the company denies it.
cases.drop_reason: US bans over suspected but unproven FSB ties are a designation; the record shows no proven placement or control inside Kaspersky.

cases.n: Bulgarian spy cell run from Moscow by ex-Wirecard COO
cases.rank: spy cell run by a former corporate executive
cases.d: Six Bulgarians living in Britain spied for Russia from 2020 to 2023 under the direction of Jan Marsalek, Wirecard's former chief operating officer, who the Crown Prosecution Service said is suspected of working for Russia's GRU and FSB. They watched the investigative journalist Christo Grozev and others, and staged a fake protest at the Kazakh embassy in London. They were convicted in 2025, and on 12 May 2025 the Old Bailey jailed them for a combined 50 years, from 10 years 8 months for ringleader Orlin Roussev down to 5 years for Ivan Stoyanov. The case shows a company executive turned into a handler for a foreign intelligence service.
cases.cite: Central Criminal Court (Old Bailey), London — sentences 12 May 2025
cases.why: Jury convictions; the prosecution named Marsalek as the director.
cases.drop_reason: Spying on journalists and staging a protest in Britain is espionage, not getting people inside a government body, international body or company.

cases.n: Huawei on trial for racketeering and stealing T-Mobile's 'Tappy'
cases.rank: company laboratories of T-Mobile, Cisco and three other US firms
cases.d: Huawei is China's largest telecom-equipment maker; under China's 2017 National Intelligence Law Chinese organisations must cooperate with state intelligence when asked. US prosecutors charge that over about 20 years Huawei stole trade secrets from five US companies, including source code from Cisco routers and the design of T-Mobile's phone-testing robot 'Tappy', and hid business in Iran. In 2017 a Seattle civil jury had already found Huawei liable for misappropriating T-Mobile's trade secrets. The criminal trial opened in federal court in Brooklyn in September 2026 and was expected to last about three months.
cases.cite: US District Court, E.D. New York — superseding indictment (racketeering), trial opened Sept 2026
cases.why: Charged and on trial; the earlier T-Mobile civil verdict is established.
cases.drop_reason: The charges are trade-secret theft and hiding business in Iran; the record does not show Huawei placing or recruiting people inside the victim companies.

cases.n: Three Germans tried for passing naval technology to China's MSS
cases.rank: a private firm used to approach companies and a university
cases.d: German federal prosecutors charge that Thomas R. worked for China's Ministry of State Security and used a company run by a married couple, Herwig F. and Ina F., to make contacts with German firms and research bodies. Prosecutors say they gathered information on ship engines, sonar, armoured-vehicle drives and drones, signed a research deal with a German university, and exported three special lasers to China in breach of EU dual-use rules. They were arrested in April 2024 and their trial opened in Düsseldorf on 13 May 2025.
cases.cite: Federal Prosecutor General of Germany — indictment; Düsseldorf Higher Regional Court trial from 13 May 2025
cases.why: Charged and on trial.
cases.drop_reason: Gathering technology through contacts and exporting lasers in breach of dual-use rules is technology acquisition, with no one placed inside an institution.

cases.n: Ex-ASML and NXP engineer jailed for passing chip know-how to Russia
cases.rank: former engineer of ASML and NXP
cases.d: ASML and NXP are Dutch chip-technology companies whose equipment and designs fall under export controls. In July 2025 the Rotterdam District Court sentenced a 43-year-old former engineer of both firms, reported by media to be the Russian national German Aksenov, to three years in prison for sending their files on chip-making equipment and processes to a contact in Russia, breaking EU sanctions, and for computer hacking. Media reported the recipient had links to Russia's FSB; prosecutors did not prove he sold the files.
cases.cite: Rotterdam District Court — verdict July 2025
cases.why: The leak is a court finding; the intelligence link is a media report.
cases.drop_reason: The conviction was for sanctions-breaking and hacking; an intelligence link was only reported and no recruitment by an outside party was proved.

cases.n: Hezbollah pagers — Mossad front firm licensed a Taiwanese brand
cases.rank: licensing and supply chain of a pager brand
cases.d: In September 2024 thousands of pagers and walk-talkies carried by Hezbollah members exploded across Lebanon, killing 42 people, including 12 civilians, and wounding several thousand. The pagers carried the brand of Taiwan's Gold Apollo, which said they were made under licence by BAC Consulting, a firm in Budapest; the New York Times reported that BAC was a front run by Israel's Mossad, with at least two other shell companies. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu acknowledged on 10 November 2024 that Israel carried out the pager operation.
cases.cite: Statement by PM Netanyahu, 10 Nov 2024; New York Times reporting; Lebanese government casualty figures
cases.why: Israel's prime minister acknowledged the operation; the front-company detail rests on NYT reporting.
cases.drop_reason: Mossad set up and ran its own front firm to sabotage devices; no existing government body or company was taken over from inside.

cases.n: NSO Group hacked WhatsApp's servers to plant spyware
cases.d: NSO Group is an Israeli company that sells the Pegasus spyware to government clients. In 2019 it used a flaw in WhatsApp's calling feature to install spyware on the phones of about 1,400 users in 20 countries, sending the attacks through servers NSO controlled. A US federal judge found NSO liable in December 2024 and a jury awarded Meta US$168 million in May 2025 (later cut to about US$4 million); in October 2025 the court barred NSO from targeting WhatsApp. NSO, now controlled by US investors, says it acts only for government clients.
cases.cite: US District Court, N.D. California — liability ruling Dec 2024, jury verdict May 2025, injunction Oct 2025
cases.why: Civil liability judgment and permanent injunction.
cases.drop_reason: Exploiting a flaw in WhatsApp to install spyware is hacking by a spyware vendor, not getting people or control inside WhatsApp.

cases.n: Leaked list of 1.95m party members working at Western firms in China
cases.rank: staff of foreign banks, drug makers and aircraft firms
cases.d: In December 2020 a database of about 1.95 million Chinese Communist Party members, mostly in Shanghai and organised in more than 79,000 branches, was leaked and passed to the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China. Reports said HSBC and Standard Chartered had about 600 members across 19 branches, Pfizer and AstraZeneca 123 in 2016, and that Airbus, Boeing and Rolls-Royce also employed members. The list showed membership, not spying, but members swear loyalty to the party and may be asked to help state intelligence.
cases.cite: Leaked CCP membership database via IPAC; Radio Free Asia, The Australian and Mail on Sunday reports, Dec 2020
cases.why: Membership is documented; any intelligence use is a suspicion only.
cases.drop_reason: The leaked list shows party membership of employees, and the record itself says it did not show spying or steering of company decisions.

cases.n: Kremlin seizes Danone's and Carlsberg's Russian units
cases.rank: management of Danone Russia and Baltika Breweries
cases.d: In April 2023 President Putin signed a decree allowing the state to take 'temporary management' of assets owned by companies from 'unfriendly' countries. On 16 July 2023 the federal property agency Rosimushchestvo took control of Danone's Russian business and Carlsberg's Baltika Breweries; Yakub Zakriev, Chechnya's agriculture minister and a nephew of Ramzan Kadyrov, became head of Danone Russia, and Taimuraz Bolloyev, a former Putin campaign representative, head of Baltika. Carlsberg said this was done without its knowledge; utilities of Fortum and Uniper had been seized the same way in April 2023.
cases.cite: Presidential Decree No. 302 (April 2023) and amending decree of 16 Jul 2023
cases.why: Seizure by published presidential decree.
cases.drop_reason: The Russian state openly seized the companies by published decree; this is expropriation, not hidden infiltration.

cases.n: Iran's Revolutionary Guards run a construction empire
cases.d: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is Iran's ideological military force. Its engineering arm, Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Headquarters, controls more than 812 registered companies, had received about 1,700 government contracts by 2012, and works in dams, tunnels, oil and gas fields and defence. In 2009 a Khatam-controlled group bought 51% of the naval shipbuilder SADRA. The US listed Khatam in 2007, the EU in 2008, and UN Security Council Resolution 1929 named it in 2010 as an IRGC entity.
cases.cite: US OFAC designation 25 Oct 2007; EU listing 24 Jun 2008; UN Security Council Resolution 1929 (2010)
cases.why: UN, US and EU designations.
cases.drop_reason: The Revolutionary Guards openly own their engineering arm and its companies; the record shows state ownership and designations, not hidden control.

cases.n: Turkey takes over 784 companies over Gülen links
cases.rank: ownership and management of seized companies
cases.d: After December 2013 graft probes and the July 2016 coup attempt, which the government blames on the Gülen religious movement, Turkey placed companies it said were Gülen-linked under the state trustee fund TMSF. The Treasury reported that 784 companies with TL 42.3 billion in assets were taken, including Bank Asya (transferred in May 2015, licence revoked 2016), Koza İpek Holding (now Türk Altın Holding) and Boydak Holding. More than 600 were later returned to owners, others were sold or liquidated; by October 2025 the TMSF controlled 1,056 businesses in all.
cases.cite: Turkish Treasury and Finance Ministry figures via Anadolu Agency; emergency decrees 2016
cases.why: Seizures by government decree; the Gülen link of each firm is the government's claim.
cases.drop_reason: The Turkish state openly took over companies by emergency decree; this is seizure, not hidden infiltration.

cases.n: Saudi 'Ritz-Carlton' purge forces business owners to hand over assets
cases.rank: owners and chairmen of major Saudi companies
cases.d: From 4 November 2017 a new anti-corruption committee under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman held princes and business leaders at the Ritz-Carlton in Riyadh, among them the chairmen of Saudi Binladin Group and of the broadcaster MBC. The government said settlements with 87 people recovered about US$107 billion in property, companies, cash and other assets; the committee closed in January 2019 after ordering 381 people detained. Some detainees later said they had been beaten and intimidated.
cases.cite: Saudi anti-corruption committee final statement, 30 Jan 2019
cases.why: Asset transfers announced by the Saudi government itself.
cases.drop_reason: The Saudi detentions and asset handovers were open state coercion, not an outside party getting inside an institution in a hidden way.

cases.n: Port of Darwin leased to firm whose owner has Party ties
cases.d: In 2015 the Northern Territory government leased Port Darwin for 99 years to Landbridge, a private company from Shandong owned by Ye Cheng, who has close ties to the Chinese Communist Party, for A$506 million. The port lies near a base used by US Marines. A 2021 review found no security grounds to cancel the lease, but before the May 2025 election both major parties pledged to return it to Australian ownership; in May 2026 Landbridge began investor-state arbitration to stop a forced sale.
cases.cite: Australian federal review 2021; government pledge 2025; ICSID claim May 2026
cases.why: Concern about state influence is raised by Australian officials and parties; no finding of misuse.
cases.drop_reason: The port was leased openly to Landbridge for 99 years; the record shows no hidden control or steering beyond the agreed lease.

cases.n: Philippine power grid 40% owned by State Grid of China
cases.rank: 40% stake and board seats in the national grid operator
cases.d: The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines runs the country's power transmission network under a concession won in 2007; State Grid Corporation of China owns 40% and names four directors, including the chairman. In December 2019 Senator Risa Hontiveros raised alarm that Chinese nationals held management roles and that 43 contracts went to Chinese firms, and the Senate opened hearings. In January 2025 the state Maharlika fund bought a 20% stake with two board seats.
cases.cite: Philippine Senate hearings, Dec 2019
cases.why: A senator's documented concern in Senate hearings; no finding of misuse.
cases.drop_reason: State Grid's 40% stake and board seats were openly agreed under the concession; the record shows concerns, not hidden control beyond that agreement.

cases.n: Waymo engineer took 9.7 GB of files to Uber
cases.rank: lead engineer of Google's self-driving car project
cases.d: Anthony Levandowski led work on Google's self-driving car unit (Waymo) and downloaded about 9.7 GB of its confidential files before leaving to found Otto, which Uber bought in 2016, putting him in charge of Uber's driverless programme. Uber settled Waymo's lawsuit in February 2018 by giving it equity worth about US$245 million. Levandowski pleaded guilty on 4 August 2020 to one count of trade-secret theft and was sentenced to 18 months in prison; President Trump pardoned him on 20 January 2021.
cases.cite: US District Court, N.D. California — guilty plea 2020; Waymo v. Uber settlement Feb 2018
cases.why: Guilty plea and civil settlement.
cases.drop_reason: Levandowski took files from his employer to his own start-up; no outside party placed him inside Waymo.

cases.n: Micron memory secrets — UMC pleads guilty, Fujian Jinhua acquitted
cases.d: US prosecutors charged in 2018 that engineers who moved from Micron's Taiwan unit to the Taiwanese chipmaker UMC took Micron's memory-chip designs for a joint project with Fujian Jinhua, a Chinese state-backed company. The US put Jinhua on its export blacklist in October 2018. UMC pleaded guilty in October 2020 to receiving a stolen trade secret and paid a US$60 million fine, but on 27 February 2024 a federal judge acquitted Jinhua, finding the evidence insufficient.
cases.cite: US District Court, N.D. California — UMC plea Oct 2020; Jinhua acquittal 27 Feb 2024
cases.why: UMC admitted guilt, but the Chinese company was acquitted at trial.
cases.drop_reason: Engineers who left Micron took designs to their new employer; no outside party placed or recruited people inside Micron, and Jinhua was acquitted.

cases.n: Ex-Samsung executive accused of cloning a chip plant in China
cases.rank: former senior Samsung and Hynix executive
cases.d: Choi Jin-seok worked at Samsung for 18 years and later at Hynix. Korean prosecutors charge that he and former Samsung staff took Samsung's chip-factory plans and more than 600 items of 20nm DRAM process data to CHJS, a company he set up in China with about US$340 million from the Chengdu government, to build a copy plant. He was detained in June 2023, released in November, and arrested again in September 2024; he denies the charges.
cases.cite: Seoul Central District Prosecutors — indictment 2023; Seoul Central District Court arrest warrant Sept 2024
cases.why: Charged and in custody; not yet convicted.
cases.drop_reason: A former employee is accused of taking data to his own new company; the record shows no outside party placing or recruiting people inside Samsung.

cases.n: 80 firms barred in Reggio Emilia for 'Ndrangheta ties in 2024
cases.rank: construction firms bidding for public works
cases.d: Italian prefects can issue an 'interdittiva antimafia' that bars a company from public contracts when it is found to be at risk of mafia control. Reggio Emilia's prefect, Maria Rita Cocciufa, reported that 80 companies received such bans in 2024, mostly family-run construction firms from Calabria owned by people from 'Ndrangheta families, as the province spent about €1.4 billion of EU recovery funds on 2,075 projects. The Edilgest consortium, with 160 members, was blacklisted on 1 March 2024.
cases.cite: Prefecture of Reggio Emilia — 2024 anti-mafia interdictions
cases.why: Administrative bans issued by the prefect.
cases.drop_reason: Bans on firms judged at risk of mafia ties are a designation, without a record of a specific clan placing people or control inside a named institution.

cases.n: Mizuho Bank lent to yakuza through Orient Corp.
cases.rank: joint loan business of Japan's second-largest bank
cases.d: The yakuza are Japan's organised-crime groups. In September 2013 Japan's Financial Services Agency found that Mizuho Bank had let about ¥200 million in loans, mostly car loans made through its consumer-finance partner Orient Corp., go to gang members over two years without acting, and ordered it to improve. Group CEO Yasuhiro Sato admitted that he and other executives had been told; he worked six months without pay and the bank's chairman stepped down from his bank post.
cases.cite: Financial Services Agency of Japan — business improvement order, Sept 2013
cases.why: Regulator's order and the bank's admission.
cases.drop_reason: The bank was ordered to improve for failing to stop loans to gang members; the record shows no crime group placing or paying staff inside Mizuho.

cases.n: Japan's yakuza exclusion rules for business
cases.d: Yakuza groups long worked through construction and property companies. Between 2009 and 2011 every Japanese prefecture passed an exclusion ordinance; Tokyo's and Osaka's made it an offence for businesses to deal with the gangs and let companies refuse bank accounts, leases and loans to members, treating ex-members as members for five years. The National Police Agency counted 9,400 members and 8,200 associates in 2025.
cases.cite: Prefectural organised-crime exclusion ordinances (Tokyo 2011); National Police Agency statistics 2025
cases.why: Laws and police statistics.
cases.drop_reason: Anti-gang ordinances for businesses are laws against organised crime, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: South Africa's 'construction mafia' demands 30% of building projects
cases.d: So-called 'business forums' in South Africa have since about 2015 forced their way onto construction sites, demanding '30%' of contract value in cash or subcontracts, citing a 2017 rule that applies only to state contracts. The practice began around Durban and spread to Gauteng and the Western and Eastern Cape. The Institute for Security Studies' ENACT programme estimated extortion's cost at about 0.7% of GDP, nearly R49 billion a year, and in November 2024 the police minister called the construction mafia public enemy number one.
cases.cite: ISS/ENACT analysis, Sept 2024; statement by the Minister of Police, Nov 2024
cases.why: Documented by the ISS and acknowledged by the police minister; few convictions.
cases.drop_reason: Extortion of construction sites from outside is a crime against firms, not a group placing people or control inside a government body or company.

cases.n: Lafarge paid Islamic State to keep its Syrian plant open
cases.rank: local management of Lafarge Cement Syria
cases.d: Lafarge, the French cement maker now part of Holcim, kept its Jalabiya plant in northern Syria running in 2013–14 by paying about US$5.92 million to the Islamic State and al-Nusra Front, which controlled the roads and raw materials. Lafarge pleaded guilty in the United States in October 2022 and agreed to pay US$777.8 million. On 13 April 2026 a Paris court convicted Lafarge and several former executives of financing terrorist groups.
cases.cite: US District Court, E.D. New York — plea Oct 2022; Paris Criminal Court verdict 13 Apr 2026
cases.why: Guilty plea in the US and criminal conviction in France.
cases.drop_reason: Lafarge paid armed groups to keep its plant running; the armed groups did not get inside Lafarge to steer it.

cases.n: Unification Church members ran 'spiritual sales' through companies
cases.rank: sales firms selling seals, vases and pagodas
cases.d: The Unification Church (Family Federation) has been tied for decades to firms selling seals, marble vases and miniature pagodas to people frightened about their ancestors. In 2009 the Tokyo District Court gave suspended sentences to church members who pressured passers-by to buy expensive seals; the church says it began a compliance drive that year. A lawyers' network counted about 34,500 complaints worth ¥123.7 billion from 1987 to 2021, and in March 2026 the Tokyo High Court upheld the order dissolving the church's Japanese branch.
cases.cite: Tokyo District Court 2009 judgment; National Network of Lawyers Against Spiritual Sales data; Tokyo High Court, Mar 2026
cases.why: Criminal convictions of members and civil rulings; the church denies the firms are its own.
cases.drop_reason: Fraudulent sales by church members through the church's own firms are crimes by the organisation's own people, with no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Boeing — case for deceiving FAA regulators dropped at DOJ request
cases.d: In January 2021 the Justice Department charged Boeing with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States, over its deception of the FAA about the 737 MAX's MCAS system. On 6 November 2025 Judge Reed O'Connor in Fort Worth dismissed the case at the Justice Department's request, under a non-prosecution deal in which Boeing pays a $243.6 million fine, $444.5 million more into a crash victims' fund and over $455 million on compliance and safety, with a compliance consultant in place of an independent monitor. The judge said the deal 'fails to secure the necessary accountability' but that he lacked power to block it; in 2023 he had called the crime 'the deadliest corporate crime in US history'.
cases.cite: US District Court, Northern District of Texas, dismissal order, 6 November 2025; Al Jazeera, 6 November 2025
cases.why: Federal charge, earlier deferred-prosecution admissions, and a court dismissal order under a non-prosecution agreement.
cases.drop_reason: Deceiving a regulator and the later dismissal of the charge involve no outside party getting inside the FAA; the inside angle is covered in the separate Boeing delegation entry.

cases.n: ExxonMobil lobbyist filmed describing work on senators
cases.d: In June 2021 Greenpeace's Unearthed project, posing as recruiters, filmed Keith McCoy, ExxonMobil's senior director for federal relations. He said the company spoke with Senator Joe Manchin's office weekly, called Manchin a 'kingmaker', described work to weaken climate parts of President Biden's infrastructure plan, said Exxon backed a carbon tax because it believed it would never happen, and spoke of using 'shadow groups'. Exxon chief executive Darren Woods said the comments did not represent the company and apologised; McCoy apologised.
cases.cite: Channel 4 News / Unearthed recording, 30 June 2021; NPR, 1 July 2021
cases.why: A recorded statement by the company's own lobbyist; the company disowned it.
cases.drop_reason: A lobbyist's boasts about access and lobbying are open influence-seeking; the record shows no Exxon people or money placed inside the Senate.

cases.n: Grenfell inquiry — cladding firms deceived the safety-testing system
cases.d: The Grenfell Tower fire in June 2017 killed 72 people. The public inquiry's final 1,700-page report of 4 September 2024 described 'systematic dishonesty' by the makers of the cladding and insulation. It found Arconic obtained UK safety certification for its plastic-core Reynobond panels on a false basis by supplying test results for a more fire-retardant version; Celotex rigged a full-scale fire test with hidden fire-retardant boards; Kingspan ran tests with concealed components and kept selling its insulation for tall buildings. The report also blamed government departments that ignored warnings. In February 2025 the UK government said it would open investigations to bar seven organisations criticised in the report from public contracts.
cases.cite: Grenfell Tower Inquiry, Phase 2 Report, 4 September 2024
cases.why: Findings of a statutory public inquiry.
cases.org_note: arconic used as lead; celotex and kingspan added as orgs.
cases.drop_reason: Manufacturers deceiving a safety-testing system is fraud from outside, not getting people, money or control inside a government body.

cases.n: Uber Files — Chancellor Osborne as 'a strong advocate' at TfL
cases.rank: Chancellor of the Exchequer; Transport for London
cases.d: The Uber Files, 124,000 internal documents from 2013 to 2017 leaked by former Uber lobbyist Mark MacGann to The Guardian and the ICIJ in July 2022, show Uber executives meeting heads of government and bypassing city regulators. Uber staff described George Osborne, then UK chancellor, as 'a strong advocate' who 'liked to believe that he's responsible' for Transport for London dropping plans to tighten rules on private-hire apps. The leak also showed a 'kill switch' that cut access to data when police raided Uber offices in six countries.
cases.cite: The Guardian / ICIJ, Uber Files, 10 July 2022
cases.why: Company documents published by The Guardian and ICIJ partners.
cases.drop_reason: The record shows open lobbying and a minister's support, but not hidden access or payments that changed Transport for London's decision.

cases.n: European Parliament revokes Amazon lobbyists' passes
cases.d: Amazon declined invitations to European Parliament hearings and warehouse visits in 2021 and 2023 and skipped a hearing on 23 January 2024 on workers' rights. On 27 February 2024 the Parliament's quaestors, at the Employment Committee's request, had the Secretary-General withdraw the 14 long-term access badges held by Amazon lobbyists, with no new ones issued until further notice. Lawmakers said they would not be lobbied by a company that refused scrutiny.
cases.cite: European Parliament Quaestors' decision, 27 February 2024; Euronews, 28 February 2024
cases.why: Formal access withdrawal decided by the Parliament's governing bodies.
cases.drop_reason: Amazon refusing to attend hearings and losing its lobbyists' badges is an open dispute over access, not anyone getting inside the Parliament to steer its decisions.

cases.n: Mediator — Servier convicted; drug regulator fined for failing to act
cases.d: Servier, a French drug company, sold benfluorex as 'Mediator' from 1976 to 2009; it is thought to have caused 500 to 2,000 deaths from heart valve damage. In March 2021 a Paris court convicted Servier of deception and manslaughter, gave former executive Jean-Philippe Seta a suspended four-year sentence, and fined the national medicines agency €303,000 for failing to act on warnings. In December 2023 the appeal court ordered Servier to repay more than €415 million to health insurers.
cases.cite: Paris Criminal Court, 29 March 2021; Paris Court of Appeal, 20 December 2023
cases.why: Criminal convictions of the company and of the state regulator.
cases.drop_reason: The record describes a drug company deceiving patients and a regulator failing to act on warnings, with no outside party shown placing people in, paying or controlling the regulator.

cases.n: Wirecard — financial regulator turned on the firm's critics
cases.d: Wirecard, a Munich payments company in Germany's DAX index, collapsed in June 2020 after admitting that €1.9 billion did not exist. In February 2019, while the Financial Times was reporting fraud, BaFin banned short-selling of Wirecard shares for two months and filed complaints against FT journalists and short-sellers. BaFin president Felix Hufeld later called the affair a 'complete disaster', and a Bundestag committee of inquiry examined the government's failures. Hufeld and his deputy left BaFin in January 2021.
cases.cite: Bundestag Wirecard Committee of Inquiry, 2020–2021; Reuters, 18 February 2019
cases.why: Regulator's own actions and admission, examined by a parliamentary inquiry; no finding that BaFin was paid.
cases.drop_reason: The record shows a regulator wrongly siding with a fraudulent company, but no outside party placing people in, paying or controlling BaFin.

cases.n: Rafale jets — French judge opens corruption investigation
cases.rank: Defence Ministry procurement of 36 Rafale fighters
cases.d: India agreed in 2016 to buy 36 Rafale fighter jets from France's Dassault Aviation. Critics said the choice of Anil Ambani's Reliance as an offset partner was imposed; former French president François Hollande told Mediapart that the Indian government proposed Reliance. India's Supreme Court found no irregularity in December 2018 and dismissed review petitions in November 2019. In June 2021, after Mediapart reports and a complaint by the NGO Sherpa, a French judge was appointed to investigate possible corruption and favouritism.
cases.cite: Supreme Court of India, 14 December 2018 and 14 November 2019; French judicial investigation opened June 2021
cases.why: An open French judicial investigation; the Indian Supreme Court found nothing.
cases.drop_reason: The record describes a dispute over the choice of an offset partner in a declared government-to-government jet deal, with no finding that anyone was paid or placed inside either government.

cases.n: Fossil fuel lobbyists outnumber most delegations at UN climate talks
cases.d: The Kick Big Polluters Out coalition, which includes Global Witness and Corporate Europe Observatory, counts fossil fuel lobbyists in the UN's official participant lists. It found at least 2,456 at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, more than every national delegation except Brazil's and the UAE's, and at least 1,773 at COP29 in Baku in 2024. In November 2025 The Guardian reported that more than 5,000 fossil fuel lobbyists had been given access to the summits over four years. The UNFCCC secretariat in Bonn runs the accreditation.
cases.cite: Kick Big Polluters Out analyses of UNFCCC participant lists, December 2023 and November 2024; The Guardian, 7 November 2025
cases.who: Oil, gas and coal companies and trade groups
cases.why: Counts drawn from the UN's own published participant lists.
cases.drop_reason: The lobbyists were openly accredited through the UN's published participant lists, and the record does not show them placed undeclared inside delegations or steering decisions.

cases.n: Philip Morris v. Uruguay — firm loses suit against health warnings
cases.d: Uruguay required graphic health warnings over 80% of cigarette packs and one variant per brand. In February 2010 Philip Morris International, based in Lausanne, sued Uruguay before the World Bank's investment tribunal (ICSID) under a Switzerland–Uruguay treaty, claiming its trademarks and investments were harmed. On 8 July 2016 the tribunal ruled for Uruguay and ordered Philip Morris to pay Uruguay's costs. The case is used as the leading example of the industry using investment treaties to deter health laws.
cases.cite: ICSID Case ARB/10/7, award of 8 July 2016
cases.why: Arbitral award on the record.
cases.org_note: status 'reported' because the company lost; the forum is an arbitral tribunal.
cases.drop_reason: An open lawsuit before an investment tribunal is a public legal challenge, not anyone getting inside Uruguay's government.

cases.n: Philip Morris Asia v. Australia — plain-pack claim thrown out
cases.d: Australia passed the world's first plain tobacco packaging law in 2011. Philip Morris, unable to sue under the US–Australia trade agreement, moved its Australian holding to its Hong Kong arm and in June 2011 claimed compensation under the Hong Kong–Australia investment treaty. In December 2015 the tribunal refused to hear the claim, finding the restructuring an abuse of rights because the dispute was already foreseeable.
cases.cite: Permanent Court of Arbitration, PCA Case 2012-12, award on jurisdiction, 17 December 2015
cases.why: Arbitral award on the record.
cases.drop_reason: An open treaty claim, even one built on a corporate restructuring, is a public legal challenge, not anyone getting inside Australia's government.

cases.n: FAO's partnership with the pesticide industry body CropLife
cases.d: CropLife International represents pesticide and seed makers including Bayer, BASF, Syngenta and Corteva. In October 2020 the UN Food and Agriculture Organization signed a letter of intent with CropLife under its private-sector engagement strategy. Pesticide Action Network and 430 civil society and Indigenous groups from 69 countries asked the FAO Council to end it, saying CropLife members had interfered in national pesticide policy and that the tie-up undermined the phase-out of highly hazardous pesticides.
cases.cite: FAO letter of intent with CropLife International, October 2020; PAN International open letter to the FAO Council
cases.why: Concern raised by named civil-society networks; no official finding of capture.
cases.drop_reason: The FAO's letter of intent with CropLife is an open, declared partnership, and the record does not show CropLife placing people inside the FAO or steering its decisions.

cases.n: Brumadinho — Vale and safety auditor TÜV SÜD charged
cases.rank: dam-safety certification relied on by mining regulators
cases.d: On 25 January 2019 a Vale tailings dam at Brumadinho, Minas Gerais, collapsed and killed 270 people. Engineers from the German certification firm TÜV SÜD, hired by Vale to inspect the dam, had signed its stability declaration; two of them and three Vale staff were arrested days later. In January 2020 prosecutors charged Vale, TÜV SÜD and 16 people, including former Vale president Fabio Schvartsman, with intentional homicide and environmental crimes. Brazil's dam-safety system relies on such company-paid declarations.
cases.cite: Minas Gerais State Public Prosecutor's Office, charges of January 2020
cases.why: Criminal charges filed; no final verdict.
cases.drop_reason: TÜV SÜD was openly hired by Vale to certify the dam, and the charges concern false safety declarations and homicide, not anyone placed inside or paid within a regulator.

cases.n: Nebrodi clans — EU farm subsidies, 50 final convictions
cases.rank: EU Common Agricultural Policy payments made through Italy's AGEA
cases.d: The Batanesi and Bontempo Scavo clans of Tortorici, in Sicily's Nebrodi mountains, put aside a feud to claim European Union farm subsidies on land they controlled or registered in other people's names. Prosecutors said a notary and staff at local agricultural assistance centres helped file the claims. The 2020 Operation Nebrodi led to a trial of 97 people; in 2022 the court in Patti convicted 90 defendants to more than 600 years in total, the appeal court upheld 65 convictions, and the Court of Cassation made 50 convictions final.
cases.cite: Messina anti-mafia prosecutors (Operation Nebrodi); Tribunal of Patti, 2022; Court of Cassation; ANSA and L'Indipendente
cases.who: Cosa Nostra clans of Tortorici (Batanesi, Bontempo Scavo)
cases.why: Final convictions by the Court of Cassation.
cases.drop_reason: The record describes subsidy fraud using land registered in other people's names, helped by a notary and claims-office staff, with no one inside a government or EU body shown working for the clans.

cases.n: State-Mafia negotiation trial — officers and politician acquitted
cases.d: Palermo prosecutors charged that in 1992–93, during Cosa Nostra's bombing campaign, Carabinieri officers opened talks with the mafia, offering relief from the strict 41-bis prison regime in exchange for an end to the attacks. In 2018 the Palermo assize court convicted the officers, Dell'Utri and mafia bosses. In 2021 the Palermo appeal court acquitted the officers and Dell'Utri while upholding the bosses' sentences, and in 2023 the Court of Cassation confirmed the acquittals.
cases.cite: Palermo Court of Assizes (2018); Palermo Court of Appeal (2021); Court of Cassation (2023)
cases.why: The state officials were finally acquitted; only the mafia bosses' convictions stand.
cases.drop_reason: The charge was that state officers negotiated with the mafia, not that the mafia placed or paid people inside the state, and the officers and politician were acquitted.

cases.n: Albania's decriminalisation law removes MPs with hidden records
cases.rank: members of parliament, mayors and civil servants
cases.d: After cross-party agreement in late 2014, Albania adopted a 'decriminalisation' law in 2015 that bars people with serious convictions, at home or abroad, from elected office and requires candidates to declare their records. By 2020 seven MPs had resigned or been dismissed, among them Mark Frroku and Arben Ndoka, who resigned, and Shkëlqim Selami, Gledjon Rehovica, Dashamir Tahiri and Aqif Rakipi, removed for hiding convictions. Three mayors lost office, including Elvis Roshi of Kavaja over an Italian drug-trafficking record, and about 600 state employees left their jobs.
cases.cite: Albanian decriminalisation law (2015); Central Election Commission decisions; Institute for Political Studies study reported by Exit News
cases.who: people with criminal records, including abroad
cases.why: Removals ordered by the Central Election Commission under the law.
cases.drop_reason: The record shows office-holders with past convictions being removed, but not that any crime group placed them in office or that they acted for one.

cases.n: Operation Troika — Spain acquits Duma deputy Reznik of mafia laundering
cases.d: Spanish police arrested alleged leaders of St Petersburg's Tambov and Malyshev groups, including Gennady Petrov, in 2008 under Operation Troika. Prosecutors said the group moved more than €50 million into Spanish property and named Duma deputy Vladislav Reznik among the defendants. In October 2018 Spain's National Court acquitted all 17 Russians tried, including Reznik, finding insufficient evidence that the investments came from organised crime.
cases.cite: Audiencia Nacional (Spain), verdict of October 2018
cases.why: Defendants including the Duma deputy were acquitted.
cases.drop_reason: The record is a money-laundering case in which all defendants were acquitted, and it does not show the group placing or paying anyone inside a government.

cases.n: Alaattin Çakıcı — MHP leader's ally freed by 2020 sentencing law
cases.d: Alaattin Çakıcı is a convicted crime boss and former Grey Wolves member who was used by Turkey's intelligence service (MİT) for covert operations abroad in the 1980s. MHP leader Devlet Bahçeli visited him in prison and in 2018 publicly demanded an amnesty that named Çakıcı; the government refused. He was released in 2020 under a sentence-reduction law passed by the AKP–MHP majority. After his release, rival boss Sedat Peker publicly accused him of ties to former ministers such as Mehmet Ağar.
cases.cite: Turkish court records; reporting by Hürriyet Daily News and Ahval
cases.why: Documented political contacts and a release under a new law; no forum has found that the law was written for him.
cases.drop_reason: A party leader openly campaigning for a crime boss's release, and a later public accusation by a rival boss, do not show Çakıcı placing, paying or controlling anyone inside the state.

cases.n: Keishu Tanaka — Justice Minister resigns over yakuza ties
cases.d: Keishu Tanaka became Minister of Justice in Yoshihiko Noda's cabinet on 1 October 2012. On 11 October the weekly Shūkan Shinchō reported that some 30 years earlier he had spoken at a party hosted by a boss of an Inagawa-kai-affiliated yakuza group and acted as matchmaker for one of its executives. Tanaka admitted the contacts, said he had not known of the yakuza link, and resigned on 23 October 2012.
cases.cite: Shūkan Shinchō, 11 October 2012; Tanaka's own statements and resignation
cases.why: The minister admitted the contacts and resigned.
cases.drop_reason: The record shows decades-old social contacts that the minister said he did not know were with yakuza, not a yakuza group acting through him in office.

cases.n: Yuen Long attack — white-clad men, slow police response
cases.rank: Hong Kong Police Force and a Legislative Council member
cases.d: On 21 July 2019 a crowd dressed in white attacked protesters and passengers at Yuen Long MTR station; at least 45 people were injured. Despite over 24,000 calls to 999, police arrived 39 minutes after the attack began. By April 2025, 13 members of the white-clad group had been convicted of rioting. Pro-Beijing legislator Junius Ho had urged villagers days earlier to 'wipe out' protesters who came to Yuen Long and was filmed greeting white-clad men that night; critics accused police of collusion, which the police deny, and the police watchdog IPCC's 2020 report called it a gang fight.
cases.cite: Hong Kong court convictions; IPCC thematic report (2020); reporting collected by Wikipedia
cases.who: Yuen Long village men including triad members
cases.why: Attackers were convicted; the claim of police and political collusion is made by critics and denied by police.
cases.drop_reason: The record contains allegations of police collusion that the police deny and the watchdog did not find, so no one inside a government body is shown acting for the attackers or triads.

cases.n: Taiwan moves to dissolve the Chinese Unification Promotion Party
cases.d: The Chinese Unification Promotion Party was founded in 2005 by Chang An-lo, the 'White Wolf', a former Bamboo Union triad leader. On 30 July 2026 Taiwan's Interior Ministry said it would ask the Constitutional Court to dissolve the party, citing work with China on espionage and election interference, attacks on Hong Kong activists, and use of the party as a cover for organised crime. Police counted 98 organised-crime cases linked to party members since 2010, with 141 suspects including 32 core cadres, and said 15 temples in seven cities and counties had been infiltrated.
cases.cite: Taiwan Ministry of the Interior, political parties review committee (January 2025) and announcement of 30 July 2026, reported by Focus Taiwan
cases.who: CUPP and Bamboo Union members, acting with China
cases.why: Official ministry findings and police case counts; the Constitutional Court has not ruled.
cases.drop_reason: The record concerns a party accused of crime and of working with China, but does not show anyone inside Taiwan's government bodies acting for it or for China.

cases.n: Pemuda Pancasila — paramilitary group woven into party politics
cases.d: Pemuda Pancasila is a paramilitary organisation founded in 1959 that took part in the 1965–66 killings and backed Suharto's New Order. It was formally part of Golkar from 1982 to 2001 and later ran its own Patriot Party. Its members are known for extortion, parking-fee collection and protection work; the 2012 documentary The Act of Killing showed leaders in Medan alongside officials and claimed three million members.
cases.cite: Academic histories of the New Order; 'The Act of Killing' (2012); reporting collected by Wikipedia
cases.why: Documented party affiliation and extortion reporting; no single forum finding.
cases.drop_reason: The record shows an open alliance with a ruling party and extortion by members, but not members placed in named government posts or steering decisions inside them.

cases.n: Lok Sabha 2024 — 251 of 543 MPs declare criminal cases
cases.d: Indian candidates must declare pending criminal cases in sworn affidavits. The Association for Democratic Reforms' analysis of the 2024 general election found that 251 of the 543 winning MPs (46%) declared criminal cases, and 170 (31%) declared serious cases such as murder, attempted murder, kidnapping or crimes against women. These are pending cases, not convictions.
cases.cite: Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) analysis of Election Commission affidavits, June 2024
cases.why: Self-declared sworn affidavits; cases are pending, not proven.
cases.drop_reason: Counting MPs with pending criminal cases shows nothing about any crime group placing or controlling them.

cases.n: Uzair Baloch — Lyari gang chief and the Sindh ruling party
cases.d: Uzair Baloch led the Peoples' Aman Committee, a Lyari gang aligned with the Pakistan Peoples Party, which governs Sindh; sources cited by Wikipedia say he was tied to the PPP until 2012. He was wanted in more than 50 cases of extortion and killings, was detained in Dubai in 2014 on an Interpol notice and taken into custody in Pakistan in 2016.
