A military court sentenced him in 2020 to 12 years for espionage, and the Sindh government released a joint investigation team report on him in July 2020; claims in that period that senior PPP leaders protected him are disputed by the party.
cases.cite: Pakistani military court (2020); Sindh government JIT report (July 2020)
cases.why: He is convicted, but the alleged protection by party leaders rests on disputed investigation records.
cases.drop_reason: The record shows a gang aligned with a party and an espionage conviction, but claims that office-holders protected him are disputed and not established.

cases.n: Kabul Bank — $900m fraud tied to the president's brother
cases.rank: Afghanistan's largest private bank, which paid public salaries
cases.d: Kabul Bank, founded in 2004, paid the salaries of the Afghan army and police. It nearly collapsed in 2010 after about $900 million was lost through insider loans to shareholders and their companies; shareholders included Mahmood Karzai, brother of President Hamid Karzai, and Haseen Fahim, brother of Vice-President Mohammad Fahim. Chairman Sherkhan Farnood and chief executive Khalilullah Frozi were arrested in 2011 and convicted by a special tribunal; the state took over the bank and re-launched it as New Kabul Bank.
cases.cite: Afghan special tribunal; Independent Joint Anti-Corruption Monitoring and Evaluation Committee report (2012)
cases.who: Kabul Bank insiders (Farnood, Frozi) and politically connected shareholders
cases.why: Convictions by a special tribunal; losses documented by an official committee.
cases.drop_reason: This was fraud through insider loans by the bank's own chairman, chief executive and shareholders, not an outside party getting inside the bank or the state.

cases.n: Canada sanctions Haitian senators for financing gangs
cases.d: Haiti's armed gangs, which joined in the Viv Ansanm alliance in 2023, control much of Port-au-Prince. In November 2022 Canada imposed sanctions on Haitian politicians including Senator Joseph Lambert and former senator Youri Latortue, citing 'the egregious conduct of political elites who provide illicit financial support to armed gangs', and added further politicians later that month. Those named deny funding gangs.
cases.cite: Global Affairs Canada, Special Economic Measures (Haiti) Regulations, November 2022
cases.why: Government sanctions designation (an executive finding, not a court verdict).
cases.drop_reason: The record shows politicians funding gangs from outside, not gangs placing people inside a government body.

cases.n: Los Dinámicos del Centro — licence-selling network in Junín government
cases.rank: Junín regional transport directorate and Perú Libre party
cases.d: Junín's anti-corruption prosecutors say a network inside the regional government's transport directorate sold driving licences from 2012. Prosecutor Bonnie Bautista argued in 2021 that the fees were diverted to finance the campaign of Perú Libre, the party led by former Junín governor Vladimir Cerrón that won the 2021 presidential election, citing statements by cooperating witnesses. Former regional transport director Eduardo Bendezú is among those accused; Cerrón was added to the investigation and has been a fugitive since October 2023 in a separate case.
cases.cite: Junín Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office; Junín Superior Court hearings, July 2021, reported by Gestión
cases.why: Formal criminal investigation with cooperating witnesses; no verdict.
cases.drop_reason: The record describes corruption by officials inside the regional government for their own party, with no outside party getting inside it.

cases.n: Tren de Aragua and Maduro — US agencies doubt state direction
cases.d: Tren de Aragua began in a Venezuelan prison and spread across South America and to the United States. A March 2025 US presidential proclamation under the Alien Enemies Act said it acts 'at the direction' of the Maduro government. A National Intelligence Council memo dated 7 April 2025, declassified in May, concluded that the government tolerates gangs but 'probably does not have a policy of cooperating with TDA'; FBI analysts held that some officials help members migrate and use them as proxies. Chilean prosecutors separately allege that the 2024 murder of exiled officer Ronald Ojeda in Santiago was ordered from Venezuela, naming Diosdado Cabello, who denies it.
cases.cite: US National Intelligence Council memo, 7 April 2025 (declassified); US presidential proclamation, March 2025; Chilean Public Prosecutor
cases.why: The US government's claim is contradicted by its own intelligence assessment; Chilean courts have not found a political motive so far.
cases.drop_reason: The record is about whether a government uses a gang, which US intelligence doubted, not the gang getting people inside the government.

cases.n: Jos Leijdekkers — Dutch fugitive cocaine boss at President Bio's church
cases.d: Jos Leijdekkers was sentenced in absentia in Rotterdam in June 2024 to 24 years for smuggling over 7 tonnes of cocaine. Reuters reported in January 2025, using facial-recognition matches, that he attended a New Year mass two rows behind President Julius Maada Bio in Bio's home town, and three sources said he is married to Bio's daughter Agnes; Dutch prosecutors said he had lived in Sierra Leone for at least six months. Sierra Leone said it was investigating, its immigration chief was later dismissed after footage showed him with Leijdekkers, and the government said the President did not know him.
cases.cite: Reuters investigation, 24 January 2025; Dutch Public Prosecution Service statements
cases.why: Reuters reporting with facial-recognition evidence and unnamed sources; Sierra Leone denies the President knew him.
cases.drop_reason: The record shows a fugitive living in Sierra Leone with reported family ties to the president, but no finding that anyone inside the government acted for his network.

cases.n: Tao Siju — police minister calls 'patriotic' triads respectable
cases.d: Tao Siju was China's Minister of Public Security from 1990 to 1998. In 1993 he said: 'The members of triads are not always gangsters. As long as they are patriots, concerned with maintaining the prosperity of Hong Kong, we should respect them.' Scholars and journalists cite the remark as evidence of Beijing's willingness to work with triads before the 1997 handover; no official body has found a formal arrangement.
cases.cite: Statement by Minister Tao Siju, 1993; San Francisco Chronicle, 28 May 1997
cases.why: A documented public statement by the minister; any working arrangement is inferred, not shown.
cases.drop_reason: A minister's public remark about triads shows no one placed, paid or in control inside a government body; any arrangement is inferred.

cases.n: Mungiki and Uhuru Kenyatta — ICC case withdrawn
cases.rank: Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister, later President
cases.d: Mungiki is a banned Kikuyu sect that ran extortion rackets in Nairobi's matatu transport and slums. Kenya's Waki Commission reported in 2008 that a meeting at State House coordinated revenge attacks during the 2007–08 post-election violence, which killed about 1,300 people, and named Uhuru Kenyatta among those who should face trial. The ICC charged Kenyatta in 2011 with organising Mungiki attacks; he denied any link, became President in 2013, and the ICC prosecutor withdrew the charges in December 2014, citing witness interference and lack of cooperation.
cases.cite: Commission of Inquiry into Post-Election Violence (Waki Commission), 2008; International Criminal Court, The Prosecutor v. Uhuru Kenyatta (charges withdrawn December 2014)
cases.why: An official commission named him, but the ICC case collapsed without a trial.
cases.drop_reason: The record alleges politicians organised a gang's attacks, not a gang getting inside government, and the charges were withdrawn.

cases.n: Nathan Rothschild — moving Britain's war money to Wellington and the allies
cases.rank: agent of the Commissariat for army pay and allied subsidies
cases.d: N M Rothschild & Sons was the London house of the Frankfurt Rothschild family of bankers. From 1811, in negotiation with Commissary-General John Charles Herries, Nathan Mayer Rothschild undertook to move money to pay Wellington's army in Portugal and Spain, and later to make Britain's subsidy payments to allies raising new armies after Napoleon's Russian campaign. The family's network of agents, couriers and shippers did the work; historian Niall Ferguson writes that the family made large profits from this government business over several years through exchange-rate and bond dealings. By 1825–26 the bank could supply the Bank of England with enough coin to help it through a liquidity crisis.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Nathan Mayer Rothschild' and 'Rothschild family' (citing N. Ferguson, The House of Rothschild, 1998)
cases.why: Government finance role recorded in Treasury dealings and standard histories (Ferguson); summarised by Wikipedia.
cases.drop_reason: Moving war funds for the British government was an open banking contract, not infiltration.

cases.n: Claim: Rothschild made a fortune from early news of Waterloo (myth)
cases.d: The story says Nathan Rothschild learned of Wellington's victory at Waterloo before the government, sold British bonds to fake a panic, then bought them cheaply and made a vast fortune. It first appears in an 1846 French pamphlet, 'Histoire édifiante et curieuse de Rothschild Ier, Roi des Juifs', by Georges Mathieu-Dairnvaell writing as 'Satan', and was repeated in later books and a 1934 Hollywood film. Historian Niall Ferguson finds the family lost more from the war's sudden end than it gained; Brian Cathcart (2015) traces the first news in London to Wellington's own dispatch, received by the War Secretary Lord Bathurst on the evening of 21 June 1815. The Jewish Chronicle (2017) notes the newspaper report the story relies on does not exist. Historians treat the tale as an antisemitic libel, not evidence of control over government.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Nathan Mayer Rothschild'; Brian Cathcart, 'The Rothschild Libel', The Independent, 3 May 2015; Robert Philpot, 'The Rothschilds, the banks and antisemitism: the truth and the myths', Jewish Chronicle, 11 Dec 2017
cases.why: Historians (Ferguson, Cathcart) find no basis; the story originates in an 1846 antisemitic pamphlet and still circulates.
cases.drop_reason: The record debunks a myth and shows no one getting inside a government.

cases.n: Rothschild and Montefiore raise the £15m loan to compensate slave owners
cases.rank: HM Treasury borrowing for the Slavery Abolition Act
cases.d: The Slavery Abolition Act 1833 freed enslaved people in most of the British Empire but paid £20 million in compensation to slave owners, not to the enslaved—about 40% of the Treasury's annual income. Nathan Rothschild and his partner Moses Montefiore arranged £15 million of this as a government loan. The Treasury says the debt was later rolled into a 4% consolidated loan of 1927 and was only fully cleared when the government redeemed its remaining undated gilts in 2015. University College London's Legacies of British Slavery database lists Rothschild himself as a claimant: as mortgage holder on an Antigua plantation with 158 enslaved people he received £2,571.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Nathan Mayer Rothschild', 'Slavery Abolition Act 1833'; UCL Legacies of British Slavery database; HM Treasury
cases.who: N M Rothschild & Sons (with Moses Montefiore)
cases.why: Loan and its redemption are on the Treasury record; the 'paid until 2015' point is a technicality of gilt refinancing, as the Treasury notes.
cases.drop_reason: Arranging a government loan is an open financial deal, not infiltration.

cases.n: Rothschild loan pays Brazil's price for Portugal's recognition
cases.d: Under the 1825 settlement Brazil agreed to pay Portugal £2 million to recognise its independence. N M Rothschild & Sons led the raising of this money for the new Empire of Brazil on the London market, including a £2,000,000 issue in 1825, and part of the price was that Brazil took over a £1,500,000 loan the Rothschilds had made to Portugal in 1823. The Rothschilds remained Brazil's main London bankers for decades.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Rothschild family' citing Caroline Shaw, 'Rothschilds and Brazil', Latin American Research Review 40 (2005)
cases.why: Documented in the Rothschild Archive and Shaw (2005).
cases.drop_reason: Raising a loan for Brazil on the London market is an open financial deal, not infiltration.

cases.n: Lionel de Rothschild lends Disraeli £4m to buy the Suez Canal shares
cases.rank: Prime Minister's purchase of a 44% state holding
cases.d: The Khedive of Egypt held 44% of the Suez Canal Company and in November 1875 offered his shares for 100 million francs. Rather than go to the Bank of England or wait for Parliament, Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli borrowed about £4 million from Lionel de Rothschild, a former Liberal MP for the City of London, who took a commission; the bank's money was at risk because Parliament could have refused to ratify the deal. The contract was signed in Cairo on 25 November. The holding made Britain the canal's largest shareholder, and the canal's security became a fixed aim of British policy, including the occupation of Egypt in 1882.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Benjamin Disraeli' (Suez section) and 'Lionel de Rothschild'
cases.who: N M Rothschild & Sons (Lionel de Rothschild)
cases.why: Recorded in parliamentary and Rothschild records; standard history.
cases.drop_reason: Lending the government money to buy Suez Canal shares is an open loan, not infiltration.

cases.n: Claim: the Rothschilds control governments, central banks and wars
cases.rank: governments and central banks worldwide (as alleged)
cases.d: A conspiracy theory dating from the 1840s holds that the Rothschild family secretly controls the world's money, central banks such as the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England, and the making of wars; it still circulates, for example in David Icke's talk of 'Rothschild Zionists'. The record shows a family bank that was the largest in 19th-century Europe and lent to many governments, but whose dominance was broken by joint-stock banks from the 1870s; Rothschild & Co today is a mid-sized advisory bank. Rothschild banks are not members of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and the 1825 Bank of England episode was a loan of coin that was repaid. Historians such as Jovan Byford describe the theory as antisemitic, with the Rothschilds standing in for Jews as a whole; Ferguson notes that by mid-century the family stood to lose from wars.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Rothschild family' (Conspiracy theories, citing Byford 2011, Ferguson 2008); Jewish Chronicle, 11 Dec 2017
cases.why: No evidence supports it; historians classify it as an antisemitic conspiracy theory.
cases.drop_reason: The record debunks a conspiracy theory and shows no one getting inside a government.

cases.n: Claim: Macron is 'the Rothschilds' president' (antisemitic trope)
cases.d: Macron's four years at Rothschild & Cie have been used to cast him as the bank's instrument. The Jewish Chronicle reported in December 2017 that Marine Le Pen had drawn 'none too subtle allusions' between 'the world of finance' and Macron, a former Rothschild banker, which an observer called conspiracy-mongering. What the record shows is a salaried partner who left the bank in 2012 (see the separate record); there is no evidence that the Rothschild family or bank directs French policy. The 'Rothschild puppet' framing is a form of the long-running antisemitic Rothschild conspiracy theory.
cases.cite: Robert Philpot, Jewish Chronicle, 11 Dec 2017; Wikipedia 'Rothschild family' (Conspiracy theories)
cases.why: Claim widely made; no evidence of bank control; historians class Rothschild-control claims as antisemitic.
cases.drop_reason: The record debunks an antisemitic trope and shows no one getting inside a government.

cases.n: Venezuela hires Rothschild & Co to map its defaulted debt
cases.d: Rothschild & Co's advisory arm is one of a few firms governments hire to restructure their debts, which puts the adviser inside a finance ministry's most sensitive negotiations. In April 2024 Bloomberg reported that Nicolás Maduro's government had hired Rothschild to give an overview of its foreign debt obligations, about $154 billion owed to creditors and largely in default, and to map who is owed what before any restructuring. In 2020 Rothschild had bid, unsuccessfully, to advise Argentina, which chose Lazard.
cases.cite: Bloomberg, 23 April 2024; Forbes Argentina (2020) on Argentina's adviser selection
cases.why: Bloomberg report citing people familiar; not officially announced.
cases.drop_reason: A government openly hiring a bank to advise on its debt is a declared contract, not infiltration.

cases.n: Morgan–Belmont syndicate rescues the US Treasury's gold
cases.d: During the Panic of 1893 the Treasury's gold reserve fell so low that the government risked being unable to redeem its notes in gold. In 1895 J. P. Morgan met President Grover Cleveland, told him the government could default that day, and used an old Civil War statute to have a syndicate of J. P. Morgan & Co. and the Rothschilds, through their New York agent August Belmont, sell about 3.5 million ounces of gold to the Treasury for a 30-year bond issue (about $65 million). The deal saved the Treasury, but William Jennings Bryan's wing of the Democratic Party attacked its terms and it helped end Cleveland's political career.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'J. P. Morgan' and 'Panic of 1893'
cases.who: J. P. Morgan & Co. with N M Rothschild & Sons
cases.why: Bond contract and congressional criticism are on the public record.
cases.drop_reason: Selling gold to the Treasury for bonds was an open deal, not infiltration.

cases.n: Panic of 1907 — Morgan runs the rescue from his library
cases.rank: US Treasury deposits; New York City finances
cases.d: With no central bank, the 1907 panic was handled by J. P. Morgan, who gathered bank and trust-company heads in his Madison Avenue library, decided which firms were sound, kept them until midnight to pledge $8.25 million for the Trust Company of America, and raised $23.6 million in minutes to keep the New York Stock Exchange open. Treasury Secretary George Cortelyou deposited about $25 million of federal money in New York banks, Morgan bought $30 million of New York City bonds to stop the city defaulting, and President Theodore Roosevelt approved U.S. Steel's takeover of Tennessee Coal, Iron & Railroad despite antitrust concerns. The crisis led to Senator Nelson Aldrich's National Monetary Commission and, in 1913, the Federal Reserve.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Panic of 1907' (citing Bruner & Carr 2007)
cases.why: Standard financial history; Treasury deposits and city bond purchase documented.
cases.drop_reason: A banker openly organising a rescue during a panic is not infiltration of a government or company.

cases.n: Claim: the Federal Reserve is owned by the Rothschilds and Jewish bankers
cases.d: A long-running claim says the Federal Reserve is a private bank secretly owned by the Rothschilds, Warburgs and other mostly Jewish banking houses who use it to control US money; the ADL traces versions through Eustace Mullins, Sheldon Emry, Aryan Nations, Liberty Lobby's Spotlight and a 1983 newsletter of the National Association of Retired Federal Employees. The record: the 1910 Jekyll Island meeting and Paul Warburg's role are real (see separate records), but the Fed is controlled by a Board of Governors appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate; member banks must hold stock in their regional Reserve Bank that cannot be sold, pays a capped dividend and gives no control; and the Fed remits its earnings to the Treasury. Rothschild banks are not members of the New York Fed. The ADL calls the claim a classic antisemitic myth.
cases.cite: ADL, 'Jewish Control of the Federal Reserve: A Classic Antisemitic Myth'; Wikipedia 'Federal Reserve'; Jewish Chronicle, 11 Dec 2017
cases.why: Contradicted by the Federal Reserve Act's structure; classed as an antisemitic myth by the ADL.
cases.drop_reason: The record debunks an antisemitic myth and shows no one secretly owning or controlling the Federal Reserve.

cases.n: J.P. Morgan & Co. becomes Britain's and France's war agent in the US
cases.rank: British government purchasing and finance in the US
cases.d: From the start of the First World War J.P. Morgan & Co.'s New York office was made the British government's main financial agent in the United States, after lobbying by ambassador Cecil Spring Rice; it took a similar role for France through its Paris affiliate Morgan, Harjes, and became France's main source of US loans. In October 1915 it led a joint $500 million Anglo-French loan from US investors, although Secretary of State William Jennings Bryan had argued that refusing loans to belligerents would shorten the war; Bryan resigned in 1915. By 1917 New York bankers held about $3 billion of Allied war loans.
cases.cite: Martin Horn, 'A Private Bank at War: J.P. Morgan & Co. and France, 1914–1918', Business History Review 74 (2000); Wikipedia 'American entry into World War I'
cases.why: Agency agreements and loans documented in business history and later Senate testimony.
cases.drop_reason: Acting as a government's declared financial agent is an open contract, not infiltration.

cases.n: Nye Committee — did bankers' Allied loans pull the US into the First World War?
cases.rank: US Senate Special Committee on the Munitions Industry
cases.d: The Senate's munitions committee, chaired by Gerald Nye (April 1934–February 1936), examined the wartime loans of J.P. Morgan & Co. and other banks and the profits of arms makers such as DuPont. It documented large arms profits, price-fixing and the industry's influence on policy, and argued that bankers had pressed Wilson to protect their loans; its funding was cut in early 1936 after Nye accused the late President Wilson of withholding information from Congress. Its work fed the Neutrality Acts, repealed in 1941. The view that a bankers' conspiracy caused US entry was popular with Progressives and revisionists such as Charles Tansill; other accounts give equal or greater weight to German submarine warfare, British influence and balance-of-power concerns, and the causal claim remains disputed.
cases.cite: Senate Special Committee on Investigation of the Munitions Industry, reports 1934–36; Wikipedia 'Nye Committee', 'American entry into World War I'
cases.who: J.P. Morgan & Co. and Wall Street lenders
cases.why: Loans and profits were documented by a Senate committee; that they caused US entry into the war is disputed by historians.
cases.drop_reason: A Senate inquiry into bankers' wartime loans and a disputed causal theory; no one shown inside a government steering it.

cases.n: Dwight Morrow — Morgan partner as US ambassador to Mexico
cases.rank: US ambassador; adviser to President Calles
cases.d: Dwight Morrow became a partner of J.P. Morgan & Co. in 1913 and was named US ambassador to Mexico by Calvin Coolidge (1927–30); the Mexican press expected 'a return to Dollar Diplomacy'. He held regular breakfast meetings with President Plutarco Elías Calles on oil, irrigation and the church conflict, gave the Mexican government economic and financial advice, and through the Calles–Morrow agreement reaffirmed the rights of US oil companies and helped delay nationalisation of the oilfields, which came in 1938. He also mediated the settlement of the Cristero War.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Dwight Morrow'
cases.why: Diplomatic record and standard histories.

arch.t: Vatican-Masonic Network — Roberto Calvi Murder; Banco Ambrosiano Collapse; P2 Lodge Member Directed Vatican Bank Investments (PROVEN)

cases.drop_reason: An open ambassadorial appointment of a banker, not hidden placement.

cases.n: Quigley: after 1925 the Round Table runs on Morgan, Lazard and Rockefeller-linked money
cases.rank: Round Table groups lobbying British and dominion governments
cases.d: Quigley writes that the Round Table's money came first from the Rhodes Trust, the Beit brothers, Abe Bailey and the Astors, and that 'since 1925 there have been substantial contributions from wealthy individuals and from foundations and firms associated with the international banking fraternity, especially the Carnegie United Kingdom Trust, and other organizations associated with J. P. Morgan, the Rockefeller and Whitney families, and the associates of Lazard Brothers and of Morgan, Grenfell, and Company.' He calls 'the chief backbone of this organization' the financial cooperation 'running from the Morgan Bank in New York to a group of international financiers in London led by Lazard Brothers', says Milner refused a Morgan partnership worth up to $100,000 a year in 1901, and counts 'the managing directorship of Lazard Brothers' among posts held by Milner's disciples. In The Anglo-American Establishment he names Lazard as the chief bank among the group's funders.
cases.cite: Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, p. 951; The Anglo-American Establishment, p. 4
cases.who: Lazard Brothers and J.P. Morgan & Co. (per Quigley)
cases.why: Rests on Quigley's reading of private papers; not independently documented.
cases.drop_reason: Banks funding a policy network is not anyone getting inside a government, international body or company.

cases.n: Quigley: central bankers' private 'world system of financial control', BIS at the apex
cases.rank: central banks and treasuries of the main powers (as described)
cases.d: Quigley writes that 'the powers of financial capitalism had another far-reaching aim, nothing less than to create a world system of financial control in private hands able to dominate the political system of each country and the economy of the world as a whole', run 'by the central banks of the world acting in concert, by secret agreements arrived at in frequent private meetings and conferences', with 'the Bank for International Settlements in Basle' at the apex. He names Montagu Norman (Bank of England), Benjamin Strong (New York Fed), Charles Rist (Bank of France) and Hjalmar Schacht (Reichsbank) as central bankers who sought to dominate their governments through Treasury loans and exchange markets. The documented part: the BIS, founded in 1930 and owned by central banks, held monthly private governors' meetings in the 1930s, with Norman and Schacht its most prominent figures. Quigley himself adds that the BIS's creation showed the 1914 system was 'in decline', and later wrote that bankers had 'great influence but not control of political life'.
cases.cite: Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 324–325; Wikipedia 'Bank for International Settlements', 'Carroll Quigley'
cases.who: Central bank governors via the BIS (per Quigley)
cases.why: One historian's interpretation; the private meetings are documented, control of governments is not shown.
cases.drop_reason: A historian's interpretation of central bankers' meetings; central banks meeting with each other is not an outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Quigley's 'network' recast as a world conspiracy — and his rebuttal
cases.rank: US government (as alleged by conspiracy writers)
cases.d: Carroll Quigley, a Georgetown University historian, described the Round Table network and international bankers in Tragedy and Hope (1966) and in The Anglo-American Establishment, written around 1949 and published in 1981 after his death. From 1970 W. Cleon Skousen's The Naked Capitalist, Gary Allen's John Birch Society bestseller None Dare Call It Conspiracy (1971) and later G. Edward Griffin's The Creature from Jekyll Island used him as proof of one all-powerful conspiracy. Quigley answered that Skousen's book was 'full of misrepresentations and factual errors', that 'I never called it a conspiracy and don't regard it as such', that Milner's papers held no evidence Milner financed the Bolsheviks, and that the bankers 'were much divided, often fought among themselves, had great influence but not control of political life and were sharply reduced in power about 1931–1940'.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Carroll Quigley' (citing Quigley's reviews and interviews); Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 949–950
cases.why: Quigley's own rebuttal; the single-conspiracy reading is not supported by his sources.
cases.drop_reason: The record is about a historian's work being misused and his rebuttal; no infiltration is described.

cases.n: BIS hands Czechoslovakia's gold to the Reichsbank
cases.rank: Czechoslovak National Bank reserves; UK Treasury bypassed
cases.d: In March 1939, after Germany occupied Prague, the Bank for International Settlements transferred 23 tons of gold it held for Czechoslovakia to the German Reichsbank. The Bank of England and Bank of France approved it; Bank of England governor Montagu Norman, a BIS director, did so without consulting the UK Treasury, saying 'I can't imagine any step more improper than to bring government into the current banking affairs of the BIS.' Historian David Blaazer (2005) showed from Bank of England memos that Norman knew the receiving account was the Reichsbank's. The transfer has been called the most controversial action the BIS ever took; at Bretton Woods in 1944 the Allies called for the BIS to be liquidated, a decision reversed in 1948.
cases.cite: D. Blaazer, Journal of Contemporary History 40:1 (2005); Wikipedia 'Bank for International Settlements', 'Montagu Norman'
cases.who: Bank for International Settlements / Bank of England governor
cases.why: Bank of England records and BIS history; acknowledged.
cases.drop_reason: A transfer decided by central bankers themselves has no outside party placed or paid inside an institution.

cases.n: Basel — central bank governors' closed meetings and the world's bank rules
cases.rank: central banks and bank regulators of 60-plus jurisdictions
cases.d: The BIS, owned by member central banks, hosts governors every two months (monthly in the 1930s). An inner group meets on Sunday evening as the Economic Consultative Committee followed by dinner, then a Global Economy Meeting and a Governors' Meeting on Monday; since Russia's suspension in 2022, 30 jurisdictions are members of the Global Economy Meeting and 22 attend as observers. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, set up by G10 governors after the 1974 Herstatt Bank collapse, writes the capital standards (Basel I–III) that national regulators and parliaments then adopt. The BIS is created and governed by states' central banks; critics such as Quigley saw this as private financial power, but its meetings and standards are public in outline.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Bank for International Settlements' (Basel Meetings; Basel Committee)
cases.why: Meeting format and standard-setting role described by the BIS.
cases.drop_reason: Central banks meeting and writing banking standards at their own body is declared and public in outline, not infiltration.

cases.n: M. M. Warburg cum-ex tax claim dropped after banker meets Hamburg mayor Scholz
cases.rank: Mayor of Hamburg; Hamburg finance authority
cases.d: M. M. Warburg & Co., the Hamburg family bank founded in 1798, took part in 'cum-ex' share trades that claimed refunds of tax never paid. Diaries of its co-owner Christian Olearius, seized by prosecutors, record three meetings with Hamburg mayor Olaf Scholz in 2016–17: on 26 October 2016 Olearius handed him a paper arguing against a €47 million tax claim, on 9 November Scholz phoned to suggest he send it to finance senator Peter Tschentscher, and on 17 November the tax office told Warburg the claim had been dropped. A second claim of €43 million was collected only after the federal finance ministry intervened. Scholz, later Chancellor (2021–25), told Hamburg's parliamentary inquiry he had 'no active memory' of the meetings and denies any influence; Olearius was indicted for serious tax evasion, but his trial was halted for health reasons in June 2024.
cases.cite: Hamburg Parliament committee of inquiry (testimony 19 Aug 2022); Irish Times, 19 Aug 2022; Bonn Regional Court
cases.why: Meetings documented by diaries and a parliamentary inquiry; influence on the tax decision is suspected but not proven, and Scholz denies it.
cases.drop_reason: A banker meeting a mayor to argue against a tax claim is lobbying; the record shows no money, people or control placed inside the city government.

cases.n: Jacob Schiff's Kuhn, Loeb raises $200m for Japan's war on Russia
cases.rank: Japanese government war borrowing (Bank of Japan)
cases.d: In April 1904 Jacob Schiff of Kuhn, Loeb & Co. met Takahashi Korekiyo, deputy governor of the Bank of Japan, in Paris and agreed to float Japanese war bonds on Wall Street. The loans, about $200 million in all, were the first major Japanese bond issues in the US and covered roughly half of Japan's costs in the Russo-Japanese War; Schiff was moved partly by the Tsarist state's persecution of Jews. Japan awarded him the Order of the Sacred Treasure (1905) and the Order of the Rising Sun (1907), presented in person by Emperor Meiji.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Jacob Schiff' (citing Kowner 2006)
cases.why: Bond issues and decorations on record.
cases.drop_reason: Floating war bonds for Japan was an open loan, not infiltration.

cases.n: Claim: Jacob Schiff financed the Bolshevik Revolution (antisemitic myth)
cases.d: From 1918 British and French officials, Russian émigré groups, American conservatives and antisemitic writers such as the journalist Henry Wickham Steed asserted that Schiff, Felix Warburg and other Jewish bankers had lent to the Bolsheviks in return for concessions; the claim still circulates online. Historian Priscilla Roberts, using Kuhn, Loeb records, finds that Schiff 'refused to give the Bolsheviks any financial aid': he had backed Kerensky's Provisional Government after it gave Jews equal rights, and in December 1917 demanded back a million roubles lent to it, which the Bolsheviks ignored. Schiff then funded anti-Bolshevik groups. The claim belongs to the antisemitic 'Jewish Bolshevism' conspiracy theory.
cases.cite: Priscilla Roberts, 'Jewish Bankers, Russia, and the Soviet Union, 1900–1940', American Jewish Archives Journal 49 (1997); Wikipedia 'Jacob Schiff'
cases.why: Archival research shows Schiff refused aid and opposed the Bolsheviks; the claim is an antisemitic myth.
cases.drop_reason: The record debunks an antisemitic myth; Schiff refused to fund the Bolsheviks.

cases.n: David Rockefeller's Chase campaign to admit the Shah — then the hostage crisis
cases.rank: President Carter's decision to admit the Shah
cases.d: David Rockefeller, chairman of Chase Manhattan Bank, which by 1979 had syndicated more than $1.7 billion in loans for Iranian public projects, ran a campaign with Henry Kissinger and John J. McCloy to persuade a reluctant President Jimmy Carter to admit the deposed Shah of Iran. Carter admitted the Shah in October 1979 for medical treatment in New York; on 4 November students seized the US embassy in Tehran and held 52 Americans for 444 days. In December 2019 The New York Times (David D. Kirkpatrick) used Rockefeller's private files to show the campaign's scale and that Carter was misled about the Shah needing treatment only available in New York; former hostages later sued JPMorgan Chase over the bank's role.
cases.cite: New York Times, 29 Dec 2019 (Kirkpatrick); Terence Smith, NYT Magazine, 17 May 1981; Texas Public Radio interview, 2 Jan 2020
cases.why: Rockefeller's own files, reported by the New York Times in 2019.
cases.drop_reason: A bank chairman's lobbying campaign from outside government is lobbying, not placing people or money inside it.

cases.n: Claim: the Rockefellers run a secret 'one world' cabal
cases.d: Since the 1970s writers such as Gary Allen, whose The Rockefeller File (1976) was promoted by Congressman Larry McDonald, have claimed the Rockefellers were following 'a plan to use their economic power to gain political control of first America, and then the rest of the world'. David Rockefeller's Memoirs (2002) answered: 'Some even believe we are part of a secret cabal working against the best interests of the United States ... conspiring with others around the world to build a more integrated global political and economic structure—one world, if you will. If that's the charge, I stand guilty, and I am proud of it.' The documented record is of open advocacy and access: he chaired the Council on Foreign Relations (1970–85), founded the Trilateral Commission (1973), whose members filled Carter's cabinet, and met heads of state as Chase chairman. No inquiry has found a hidden body directing governments; the quotation is often cut to read as a confession.
cases.cite: David Rockefeller, Memoirs (2002), p. 405; Wikipedia 'David Rockefeller'
cases.why: Open advocacy is documented; a secret controlling cabal is not.

arch.t: Trilateral Commission — 19/20 Carter Senior Appointments Were Members

cases.drop_reason: The record debunks a conspiracy theory and describes open advocacy, not hidden control.

cases.n: Rockefeller Foundation money reshapes the League of Nations
cases.d: The Rockefeller Foundation, endowed from the Standard Oil fortune, was the world's largest philanthropy by the 1920s and ran public-health campaigns with governments through its International Health Division from 1913. Although the United States never joined the League of Nations, the foundation funded League work, and historian Ludovic Tournès argues that by the 1930s US foundations had changed the League from a 'Parliament of Nations' into a think tank of specialist expertise. The foundation was also involved in the transition from the League to the United Nations (1939–46).
cases.cite: L. Tournès, International Politics 55:6 (2018) and J. of Modern European History 12:3 (2014); Wikipedia 'Rockefeller Foundation'
cases.why: Funding documented; the degree of influence is a historian's assessment.
cases.drop_reason: A foundation openly funding League of Nations work is declared funding; the record does not show hidden control.

cases.n: Rockefeller Foundation's Mexican Agriculture Program starts the Green Revolution
cases.d: In 1941, after the intervention of US Vice President Henry Wallace and Nelson Rockefeller, the Rockefeller Foundation began a maize research programme with the government of President Manuel Ávila Camacho; the foundation's own account gives a primary aim of stabilising the Mexican government and heading off communist influence. Its Mexican Agriculture Program (1943) was exported to other Latin American countries and in 1956 to India, again framed as an antidote to communism, and from 1959 drew in the Ford Foundation, USAID and the World Bank. This became the 'Green Revolution' of high-yield seed, fertiliser and irrigation, whose institutions still shape farming policy.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Rockefeller Foundation' (Agriculture); Anne-Emanuelle Birn, Marriage of Convenience (2006)
cases.why: Foundation records and histories.
cases.drop_reason: A foundation's farming programme run openly with a government is a declared partnership, not infiltration.

cases.n: Lazard inside the debt talks of Greece, Argentina and Lebanon
cases.rank: sovereign debt restructuring adviser to finance ministries
cases.d: Lazard's Sovereign Advisory group advises governments on debt. It advised the Greek government on the 2012 bond swap, called the biggest restructuring in history, and was rehired by the incoming Syriza government in 2015. In 2020 Argentina's Economy Ministry chose Lazard over Citi, Rothschild and Global Sovereign Advisory to advise its restructuring of foreign-law debt, while Lazard was also advising Lebanon. A government's restructuring adviser sees its full finances and shapes its offers to creditors.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Lazard' (citing Reuters, 5 Feb 2015); Forbes Argentina (2020)
cases.why: Mandates publicly announced by governments.
cases.drop_reason: Governments openly hiring a bank as debt adviser is a declared contract, not infiltration.

cases.n: Royal Mail sale — Lazard advised the price, its fund arm took shares
cases.rank: Department for Business (privatisation of Royal Mail)
cases.d: Lazard & Co was the government's financial adviser on the October 2013 sale of Royal Mail, for a £1.5 million fee, and advised against raising the 330p share price. The shares closed at 455p on the first day; the National Audit Office (1 April 2014) found new shareholders gained £750 million that day and judged the department's caution had cost taxpayers. Lazard's own fund arm, Lazard Asset Management, was one of 16 'priority investors' given larger allocations; it received six million shares and sold them within days for about £8 million profit. Lazard said its information barriers were 'rigorously maintained' and no rule breach was found; the Business Committee chair said advisers 'should be there to represent the interests of the government pure and simple'.
cases.cite: National Audit Office, The Privatisation of Royal Mail (HC 1182, 1 April 2014); Bureau of Investigative Journalism, 30 April 2014
cases.why: NAO report and parliamentary committee hearings.
cases.drop_reason: An adviser's fund arm buying shares is a conflict-of-interest question with no rule breach found, not an outside party inside government.

cases.n: Barings and Hope & Co. finance the Louisiana Purchase
cases.d: In 1803 Francis Baring and Co. became the US government's official banking agent in London and, with Hope & Co. of Amsterdam, financed the Louisiana Purchase. Alexander Baring helped the negotiators in Paris settle the price at 80 million francs ($15 million), down from 100 million that neither the Americans nor the bankers could provide. The banks bought $11.25 million of US bonds from Napoleon for $9.44 million and paid France in instalments, although Britain was at war with France and the money helped fund Napoleon's war. By 1818 Barings was called 'the sixth great European power' after England, France, Prussia, Austria and Russia.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Louisiana Purchase', 'Barings Bank'
cases.why: Bond contracts and Treasury records.
cases.drop_reason: Financing the Louisiana Purchase was an open banking deal, not infiltration.

cases.n: Wallenberg sphere — 35% of the Stockholm market through voting control
cases.rank: boards of Ericsson, ABB, Saab, SEB, Atlas Copco and others
cases.d: The Wallenberg family's foundations own about 23% of Investor AB, Sweden's most valuable listed company, but hold just over 50% of its votes. Through Investor and related holdings the family has major or controlling stakes in companies including Ericsson, ABB, Atlas Copco, SEB, SKF, Electrolux and the defence maker Saab. The family businesses employed 40% of Sweden's industrial workforce and made up 40% of the Stockholm market's value in the 1970s; one 2025 estimate puts its share at about 35%. The control is legal and disclosed, through dual-class voting shares.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Wallenberg family', 'Investor AB'
cases.why: Ownership and voting stakes are publicly disclosed.
cases.drop_reason: Legal, disclosed control of companies through voting shares is ordinary ownership, not infiltration.

cases.n: Goldman Sachs swaps hide €2.8bn of Greek debt
cases.d: In 2001, as Greece entered the euro, Goldman Sachs arranged cross-currency swaps for the Greek government that worked as a hidden loan of about €2.8 billion, not shown in debt figures reported under EU rules. Bloomberg reported in 2012 that Greece paid Goldman about €600 million in fees and that its obligation under the deal grew to €5.1 billion. The deals came to light in early 2010 as the debt crisis began; Goldman said they complied with EU reporting rules, while Christoforos Sardelis, head of Greece's debt agency at the time, said Greece did not understand what it was buying and that other EU states used similar deals until Eurostat stopped accepting them.
cases.cite: Der Spiegel, 8 Feb 2010; Reuters, 23 Feb 2010; Bloomberg (Dunbar & Martinuzzi), 5–6 March 2012; Wikipedia 'Greek government-debt crisis'
cases.why: Goldman acknowledged the trades; terms reported by Bloomberg and Der Spiegel.
cases.drop_reason: Selling swaps that helped a government hide debt is a product sold to a government, not someone getting inside it.

cases.n: Lucas Papademos — central banker during the Goldman swap, then unelected premier
cases.rank: Governor, Bank of Greece (1994–2002); Prime Minister (2011–12)
cases.d: Lucas Papademos was Governor of the Bank of Greece from 1994 to 2002, the years in which Greece entered the euro and the 2001 Goldman Sachs swaps were arranged, and then vice-president of the European Central Bank (2002–10). He never worked for Goldman, although he is often listed with Goldman alumni. In November 2011, after George Papandreou offered to resign, he was installed as prime minister of an unelected national unity government to secure the second EU–IMF bailout and the 2012 bond swap, serving until May 2012.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Lucas Papademos'
cases.why: Career on public record; listing as Goldman alumnus is incorrect.
cases.drop_reason: The record says he never worked for Goldman; an open appointment of a technocrat is not infiltration.

cases.n: BlackRock given a role in planning Ukraine's reconstruction
cases.rank: Office of the President (reconstruction investment framework)
cases.d: On 28 December 2022 it was announced that BlackRock and President Volodymyr Zelensky had agreed a role for the company in the reconstruction of Ukraine, after Zelensky met BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink; BlackRock's advisory arm was to help design a framework for public and private investment in rebuilding the country.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'BlackRock' (2020–present)
cases.why: Announced by the Ukrainian presidency and BlackRock.
cases.drop_reason: An openly announced advisory agreement with a government, not infiltration.

cases.n: Lebanon — 18 of 20 major banks tied to the political class
cases.rank: Parliament, cabinet and the central bank's debt financing
cases.d: Economist Jad Chaaban's study of 2014 ownership data (Economic Research Forum, 2016) found that 18 of Lebanon's 20 major commercial banks had major shareholders linked to political elites and that about 43% of the sector's assets could be attributed to political control, which affected the banks' lending and exposure to public debt. The banks lent heavily to the state and the central bank under Governor Riad Salameh (1993–2023), whose system collapsed in 2019 and froze depositors' savings. Salameh is under US, UK and Canadian sanctions, faced a French arrest warrant in 2023, and was detained in Lebanon in September 2024 and charged with embezzling $42 million of public funds.
cases.cite: J. Chaaban, 'I've Got the Power: Mapping Connections between Lebanon's Banking Sector and the Ruling Class', ERF Working Paper 1059 (2016); Wikipedia 'Riad Salameh'
cases.who: Lebanese commercial banks and their political shareholders
cases.why: Peer-reviewed ownership mapping; Salameh charges by Lebanese and French courts.
cases.drop_reason: The record maps disclosed political ownership of banks, not an outside party secretly getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Bank Rossiya — 'the personal bank for senior officials'
cases.d: Bank Rossiya was refounded in St Petersburg in 1991 by businessmen including Yury Kovalchuk, Vladimir Yakunin and Andrei Fursenko, members of the later Ozero dacha cooperative with Vladimir Putin. When the US Treasury sanctioned it on 20 March 2014 over the annexation of Crimea, it described it as 'the personal bank for senior officials of the Russian Federation', with shareholders from Putin's inner circle and Kovalchuk its largest shareholder; it was the first major Russian bank to expand into Crimea and is under US, EU and other sanctions.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release jl23331, 20 Mar 2014; Wikipedia 'Bank Rossiya'
cases.why: US Treasury designation.
cases.drop_reason: The record describes a bank owned by a leader's associates and its sanctions designation, not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Kolomoisky and PrivatBank — $5.6bn hole, US corruption designation, arrest
cases.rank: Dnipropetrovsk regional governor; Ukraine's largest bank
cases.d: Ihor Kolomoisky co-founded PrivatBank, Ukraine's largest bank, and was governor of Dnipropetrovsk region in 2014–15. In December 2016 the government nationalised the bank, needing a $5.6 billion bailout financed with IMF support; between mid-2015 and mid-2016 it had lent over $1 billion to firms of its managers, and Ukraine's courts upheld the nationalisation in 2022–24. In March 2021 the US State Department designated him for significant corruption as governor and cited 'ongoing efforts to undermine Ukraine's democratic processes and institutions'. He was arrested in September 2023 and charged by the SBU and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau with fraud, money laundering and embezzling about $250 million from PrivatBank.
cases.cite: US State Department designation (5 Mar 2021); NABU/SAPO charges (Sept 2023); Wikipedia 'Ihor Kolomoyskyi'
cases.why: Formal charges and a US designation; trial pending.
cases.drop_reason: An owner's own lending to his firms and embezzlement is the organisation's own crime, with no outside party inside it.

cases.n: NSA monitoring of Chancellor Merkel's mobile phone
cases.d: The US National Security Agency (NSA) is America's signals-intelligence service. In October 2013 Der Spiegel, working from documents leaked by Edward Snowden, reported that Chancellor Angela Merkel's mobile phone had been monitored, with the targeting going back to 2002 and ending in summer 2013. Merkel told reporters that 'spying among friends is not at all acceptable'. In March 2014 Der Spiegel reported she was one of 122 world leaders on an NSA surveillance list.
cases.cite: Der Spiegel reporting on the Snowden documents, Oct 2013 and Mar 2014; summarised in Wikipedia '2010s global surveillance disclosures'
cases.why: Snowden documents reported by Der Spiegel; Merkel protested publicly; no court ruled on it.
cases.drop_reason: Monitoring a leader's phone is espionage; no one was placed, paid or given control inside the German government.

cases.n: Operation Dunhammer — Danish intelligence helped NSA spy on neighbours
cases.rank: military intelligence service (FE) and its chief
cases.d: Denmark's Defence Intelligence Service (FE) let the NSA tap internet cables passing through Danish intercept stations such as Sandagergård. An internal FE review code-named Operation Dunhammer, finished in 2015, found the NSA used this access in 2012–2014 to wiretap German Chancellor Angela Merkel, foreign minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier and opposition leader Peer Steinbrück, and reportedly senior figures in Sweden, Norway and France. The defence minister was told in August 2020, and FE head Lars Findsen and three other officials were suspended. Danish broadcaster DR and partner media made the findings public on 30 May 2021.
cases.cite: Danish Defence Intelligence Service internal investigation 'Operation Dunhammer' (2015), reported by DR and partners 30 May 2021
cases.why: Finding of the Danish service's own internal investigation; led to suspension of its leadership.
cases.drop_reason: Tapping cables to eavesdrop on politicians is espionage; no one was placed, paid or given control inside a government.

cases.n: NSA bugs EU missions and hacks Commission networks
cases.rank: European Commission and EU diplomatic missions
cases.d: Der Spiegel reported in 2013, from the Snowden documents, that the NSA spied on the European Commission in Brussels and on EU diplomatic offices in Washington by placing bugs in offices and getting into computer networks. One method for bugging an encrypted fax machine at an EU mission was code-named Dropmire. The EU is the bloc's executive and its trade negotiator with the United States.
cases.cite: Der Spiegel, 2013 (Snowden documents); Wikipedia '2010s global surveillance disclosures'
cases.why: Leaked NSA documents reported by Der Spiegel; no official finding.
cases.drop_reason: Bugging and hacking EU offices is espionage; the record shows no one placed, paid or steering decisions inside the EU.

cases.n: NSA spies on UN headquarters and hacks its video system
cases.d: Der Spiegel reported in 2013, from the Snowden documents, that the NSA spied on United Nations headquarters in New York. The documents said the NSA got into the UN's internal video-conferencing system in summer 2012, in breach of the agreement under which the UN is hosted in the United States.
cases.cite: Der Spiegel, Aug 2013 (Snowden documents); Wikipedia '2010s global surveillance disclosures'
cases.why: Leaked NSA documents reported by Der Spiegel.
cases.org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is nsa_sigint
cases.drop_reason: Hacking the UN's video system is espionage; no one was placed, paid or steering decisions inside the UN.

cases.n: NSA monitors President Rousseff, her aides and Petrobras
cases.rank: president and top aides; state oil company
cases.d: Snowden documents reported in 2013 showed the NSA monitoring the communications of Brazil's president Dilma Rousseff and her top aides, and spying on the state-controlled oil company Petrobras. O Globo also reported mass collection of Brazilian emails and calls.
cases.cite: O Globo and TV Globo reporting on Snowden documents, 2013; Wikipedia '2010s global surveillance disclosures'
cases.why: Leaked NSA documents reported by Brazilian media.
cases.drop_reason: Monitoring a president's communications is espionage; no one was placed, paid or given control inside the government.

cases.n: GCHQ intercepts delegates at the 2009 London G20 summit
cases.rank: foreign delegations at an intergovernmental summit
cases.d: GCHQ is the UK's signals-intelligence agency. Documents leaked by Edward Snowden and published in 2013 showed that GCHQ intercepted the communications of foreign diplomats and officials attending the G20 summit the UK hosted in London in 2009.
cases.cite: The Guardian, June 2013 (Snowden documents); Wikipedia '2010s global surveillance disclosures'
cases.why: Leaked GCHQ documents published by the Guardian.
cases.drop_reason: Intercepting summit delegates' communications is espionage, not infiltration.

cases.n: Operation Socialist — GCHQ hacks Belgium's state telecom Belgacom
cases.d: Belgacom (now Proximus) is Belgium's main, majority state-owned telecom company, whose roaming hub carries mobile traffic for many foreign operators. Snowden documents showed GCHQ broke into its network from 2010 to 2013 using a 'Quantum Insert' attack and malware disguised as Microsoft software, aiming at the roaming (GRX) system. Belgacom noticed anomalies in 2012 and identified the malware in 2013. Snowden called it the first documented case of one EU member state mounting a cyber attack on another.
cases.cite: Snowden documents (Der Spiegel / The Intercept, 2013–14); Wikipedia 'Operation Socialist'
cases.why: Leaked GCHQ slides and the company's own discovery of the malware.
cases.drop_reason: Hacking a telecom network to intercept traffic is espionage; no one was placed, paid or steering decisions inside the company.

cases.n: CIA covert action in Venezuela, then US forces seize Maduro
cases.d: In October 2025 President Trump confirmed a New York Times report that he had authorised the CIA to carry out covert action inside Venezuela, while US forces were striking boats they said carried drugs. On 3 January 2026 US forces seized Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores in Caracas and flew them to New York to face a narco-terrorism indictment; Trump said the US would 'run the country' until a transition. Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez became interim president. Congress did not authorise the operation.
cases.cite: AP / OPB, 15–16 Oct 2025; PBS NewsHour, 3 Jan 2026
cases.why: Acknowledged by the US president; the seizure was announced by the US government.
cases.drop_reason: Covert action of unstated kind and an open military seizure are not someone getting inside a government.

cases.n: Danish intelligence: Americans ran an influence campaign in Greenland
cases.d: Greenland is a self-governing part of Denmark that President Trump has said the US should acquire. In August 2025 Danish media reported that at least three Americans, said by unnamed sources to have ties to the Trump administration, were trying to stir anti-Danish feeling in Greenland, using grievances such as the forced sterilisation of Greenlandic women. Denmark's police intelligence service confirmed an influence campaign was under way, and Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen summoned the top US diplomat in Copenhagen.
cases.cite: NPR, 28 Aug 2025; Danish police intelligence service statement
cases.who: Americans reportedly linked to the US administration
cases.why: The campaign was confirmed by Danish intelligence; the link to the US government rests on unnamed sources.
cases.drop_reason: An influence campaign aimed at the public is not anyone getting inside a government body.

cases.n: Australia bugs Timor-Leste's cabinet during oil-and-gas talks
cases.rank: cabinet room of a sovereign government
cases.d: In 2004 the Australian Secret Intelligence Service (ASIS) placed listening devices near Timor-Leste's cabinet room in Dili to gain an edge in talks over the Timor Sea oil and gas fields; the resulting CMATS treaty limited Timor-Leste's sea claims. After a former ASIS officer, 'Witness K', raised it, Timor-Leste took Australia to international bodies, and the International Court of Justice in 2014 ordered Australia not to interfere with Timor-Leste's legal communications. A new boundary treaty in 2018 split revenue 80–20 in Timor-Leste's favour. Australia prosecuted Witness K and his lawyer Bernard Collaery for disclosing the operation.
cases.cite: ICJ order of 3 March 2014; 2018 maritime boundary treaty; Australian prosecutions from 2018; Wikipedia 'Australia–East Timor spying scandal'
cases.why: Treaty set aside and renegotiated; Australia prosecuted the officers who disclosed it rather than deny it.
cases.drop_reason: Bugging a cabinet room to gain an edge in talks is espionage; no one was placed, paid or steering decisions inside the government.

cases.n: France names Monaco's police chief and senior judges
cases.rank: head of government, police command, judiciary
cases.d: Until a 2002 constitutional change, Monaco's head of government (Minister of State) had to be a French citizen picked from names put forward by Paris, and the prince still consults the French government before appointing one; Christophe Mirmand, a French senior civil servant, has held the office since July 2025. Key judicial posts are held by French magistrates proposed by the French government, Monaco's police are commanded by a French officer, and France is responsible for Monaco's defence.
cases.cite: Franco-Monegasque treaties and Monaco constitution; Wikipedia 'Monaco'
cases.why: Set out in treaty and constitutional arrangements.
cases.org_note: foreign_state = French state
cases.drop_reason: France's role in Monaco is set by open treaties and the constitution, not hidden placement.

cases.n: The French president is co-head of state of Andorra
cases.d: Under Andorra's 1993 constitution, the president of France is ex officio one of Andorra's two co-princes, with the Bishop of Urgell; Emmanuel Macron has held the role since 2017. Acting alone, the French co-prince appoints a member of the Constitutional Tribunal and of the Superior Council of Justice and must agree to treaty texts; jointly with Andorra's head of government he appoints the head of government, calls elections and signs laws into force. He is represented in Andorra by a personal representative.
cases.cite: Constitution of Andorra (1993); Wikipedia 'Co-princes of Andorra'
cases.why: Written into Andorra's constitution.
cases.org_note: foreign_state = French state
cases.drop_reason: The French president's role in Andorra is set openly by its constitution, not infiltration.

cases.n: Central African states still deposit half their reserves with the French Treasury
cases.d: The Bank of Central African States (BEAC) in Yaoundé issues the CFA franc for six countries: Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon. The French Treasury guarantees the currency's fixed peg to the euro, and in return member states must deposit half their foreign-exchange reserves with it. West Africa's CFA zone dropped this rule from 2021 after a 2019 reform, but it remains unchanged for Central Africa; a French Senate report in December 2024 called the reform incomplete.
cases.cite: CFA franc monetary cooperation agreements; French National Assembly vote May 2020; Wikipedia 'CFA franc'
cases.why: Treaty-based arrangement documented by both governments.
cases.drop_reason: The reserve-deposit rule is an open monetary agreement, not hidden control.

cases.n: Bosnia's High Representative can impose laws and sack officials
cases.d: The Office of the High Representative was set up under the 1995 Dayton peace deal and answers to the Peace Implementation Council of foreign governments. Since 1997 its 'Bonn powers' let it impose binding decisions and remove officials; by 2004 it had dismissed 139 officials, 58 of them in one day in June 2004. The current High Representative, Germany's Christian Schmidt, took office in 2021; Russia, China and some Bosnian politicians call his appointment illegitimate and have pressed at the UN to close the office.
cases.cite: Peace Implementation Council, Bonn conclusions (Dec 1997); Wikipedia 'Office of the High Representative'
cases.why: The powers are formally granted and openly used; their legality is disputed.
cases.drop_reason: The High Representative's powers were openly created under the Dayton peace deal, not infiltration.

cases.n: Israeli ministry funds covert campaign aimed at US lawmakers
cases.d: In June 2024 the New York Times reported that Israel's Ministry of Diaspora Affairs allocated about $2m to a covert online campaign run by STOIC, a Tel Aviv political marketing firm. Fake accounts on X, Facebook and Instagram pushed pro-Israel content at US lawmakers, especially Black Democrats such as Hakeem Jeffries, Raphael Warnock and Ritchie Torres. Meta banned STOIC in May 2024 and OpenAI also disrupted the network; the ministry denied involvement.
cases.cite: New York Times, 5 June 2024 (four current and former ministry sources); Meta and OpenAI threat reports, May 2024
cases.why: NYT confirmed the ministry link with four sources; platforms removed the network; ministry denies.
cases.drop_reason: A fake-account campaign aimed at lawmakers is an outside influence operation; no one was placed, paid or in control inside Congress.

cases.n: US officials: UAE arranged hack of Qatar's news agency that set off blockade
cases.rank: state news agency and emir's statements
cases.d: In late May 2017 Qatar's state news agency and government social media were hacked and carried false quotes attributed to Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani praising Hamas and calling Iran an 'Islamic power'. On 5 June Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Egypt and Bahrain cut ties with Qatar. In July 2017 the Washington Post, citing US intelligence officials, reported that senior UAE officials discussed the hacks on 23 May, the day before; the officials could not say whether the UAE did the hacking or paid for it. The UAE ambassador called the report false.
cases.cite: Washington Post, 16 July 2017 (US intelligence officials), via Al Jazeera
cases.why: US intelligence officials' account to the Washington Post; UAE denies.
cases.org_note: foreign_state = UAE
cases.drop_reason: A hack that planted false quotes is a cyber attack and disinformation, not anyone placed, paid or steering decisions inside Qatar's government.

cases.n: Project Raven — ex-NSA staff hacked for the UAE, including Qatar's emir
cases.rank: emir of Qatar and other foreign officials
cases.d: Project Raven was a UAE surveillance unit staffed partly by former US intelligence operatives, run from 2016 through the Emirati firm DarkMatter. Reuters reported in 2019 that it targeted other governments, militants and activists, including Qatar's Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Yemeni Nobel laureate Tawakkol Karman and the wife of jailed activist Ahmed Mansoor, using an iPhone exploit called Karma. In 2021 three former US operatives, Marc Baier, Ryan Adams and Daniel Gericke, signed deferred-prosecution agreements with the US Justice Department and paid $1.68m.
cases.cite: Reuters investigation, 2019; US Justice Department deferred-prosecution agreements, Sept 2021
cases.why: Reuters documents and interviews; US agreements confirm the hacking work for the UAE but not each target.
cases.drop_reason: A state hiring former US operatives to hack targets is a hacking operation, not anyone getting inside the governments targeted.

cases.n: Abu Dhabi Secrets — UAE paid Geneva firm Alp to target 1,000 Europeans
cases.rank: banks' risk databases, media and online reference sites
cases.d: From July 2023 the European Investigative Collaborations network, working from hacked files of Geneva intelligence firm Alp Services, reported that the UAE paid Alp at least €5.7m from 2017 to discredit people and groups in Europe it tied to Qatar or the Muslim Brotherhood. Alp compiled files on about 1,000 people and 400 organisations in 18 countries, planted articles, edited Wikipedia and fed names into banking-compliance databases. Businessman Hazim Nada says a false 'terrorism' listing ruined his company; he sued the UAE and Alp in the US in 2024. Swiss and French criminal cases were reported open in 2025; Alp says some files were falsified.
cases.cite: European Investigative Collaborations (Mediapart, Der Spiegel and others), July 2023; Wikipedia 'Abu Dhabi Secrets'
cases.why: Leaked company documents reported by a press consortium; criminal investigations opened in Switzerland and France.
cases.drop_reason: A state paying a private firm to run a smear campaign is a declared contract between them, with no one placed inside the targets.

cases.n: World Bank 'Doing Business' 2020 — data for Saudi Arabia, UAE, Azerbaijan altered
cases.d: The World Bank's Doing Business report ranked countries' business rules and was used by governments to attract investors. A WilmerHale investigation for the Bank's ethics committee, published in September 2021, found pressure on staff over data for Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Azerbaijan in the 2020 edition, in which Saudi Arabia rose 30 places to 62nd; it found no evidence that the President's Office or the board was involved in those changes. The Bank cancelled the report.
cases.cite: WilmerHale report to the World Bank Board ethics committee, Sept 2021; NBC News
cases.why: The inquiry found data irregularities that favoured these states but did not find they directed them.
cases.drop_reason: The record finds pressure on staff but does not show the three states placed, paid or directed anyone inside the World Bank.

cases.n: World Bank leaders lifted China's 'Doing Business' rank during capital talks
cases.rank: World Bank president's office and chief executive
cases.d: A WilmerHale investigation for the World Bank's ethics committee found in September 2021 that bank leaders put 'undue pressure' on staff to raise China's ranking in the 2018 Doing Business report, while the Bank sought China's backing for a major capital increase. After method changes China stood at 78th, seven places higher than the draft. It said the pressure likely came from President Jim Yong Kim's office and that chief executive Kristalina Georgieva, by then IMF managing director, and adviser Simeon Djankov pressed staff; Georgieva disputed the findings and the IMF board kept her. The Bank scrapped the report.
cases.cite: WilmerHale report to the World Bank Board ethics committee, Sept 2021; NBC News
cases.why: Finding of an investigation commissioned by the Bank; disputed by Georgieva; no finding that Beijing directed it.
cases.drop_reason: The record finds the World Bank's own leaders pressed staff; it does not show China placing, paying or directing anyone inside.

cases.n: UN human rights office gave China names of activists, whistleblower says
cases.rank: Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
cases.d: Emma Reilly, a staff member of the UN human rights office (OHCHR), alleged that the office confirmed to China, on request, the names of Chinese participants in UN human rights activities on several occasions from before 2012 to at least 2019, despite a ban on such sharing. She said emails showed it. OHCHR rejected her claims and said the disputed practice 'has not occurred since 2015'.
cases.cite: OHCHR statements; Emma Reilly's complaints; Wikipedia 'Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights'
cases.why: OHCHR's own wording implies the practice existed up to 2015; the later dates rest on the whistleblower.
cases.org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is China (prc_state)
cases.drop_reason: The record alleges a UN office shared names on request, but shows no one placed, paid or controlled by China inside it.

cases.n: Chinese swimmers' positive tests — claims WADA shielded China
cases.d: In early 2021, 23 Chinese swimmers tested positive for the banned drug trimetazidine; China's anti-doping agency blamed contaminated hotel kitchen food and WADA accepted that without a public case. The New York Times and ARD revealed it in April 2024; USADA's chief alleged a cover-up and a US criminal inquiry subpoenaed World Aquatics. WADA's appointed Swiss prosecutor Eric Cottier found in 2024 no favouritism or interference, while noting CHINADA had not followed some rules.
cases.cite: Independent prosecutor Eric Cottier, interim (July) and final (Sept 2024) reports; NYT/ARD April 2024; Wikipedia 'Doping in China'
cases.why: The cover-up claim was rejected by WADA's independent review; a US investigation was reported open in 2024.
cases.org_note: org = target body; claimed infiltrator is China
cases.drop_reason: The independent prosecutor found no favouritism or interference, and the record shows no outside party inside WADA.

cases.n: Fancy Bear — GRU hackers hit WADA after it exposed Russian doping
cases.d: In August 2016 hackers used an IOC-created account to enter WADA's ADAMS database and later published therapeutic-use files of about 250 athletes, including Simone Biles and the Williams sisters; WADA said some were forged. In October 2018 a US grand jury indicted seven officers of Russia's GRU military intelligence over a 2014–2018 hacking campaign; the Justice Department said one aim was to undermine WADA, which had published the McLaren report.
cases.cite: US grand jury indictment of seven GRU officers, Oct 2018
cases.why: US indictment; no trial because the accused are in Russia.
cases.org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is gru
cases.drop_reason: GRU hackers stole and leaked WADA database files; this is cyber-espionage, with no one placed or paid inside WADA to steer its decisions.

cases.n: Dutch catch four GRU officers trying to hack the chemical weapons watchdog
cases.rank: Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons network
cases.d: The OPCW was investigating the Novichok poisoning in Salisbury and the Douma chemical attack in Syria. On 13 April 2018 four men on Russian diplomatic passports parked a car next to its offices in The Hague with a Wi-Fi antenna, laptop and phones meant to steal network logins. Dutch military intelligence stopped them and expelled them; on 4 October 2018 the Dutch defence minister named them as GRU officers. One laptop had also been used in Malaysia against the MH17 crash inquiry.
cases.cite: Netherlands Ministry of Defence press conference, 4 Oct 2018
cases.why: Government finding and expulsion, with evidence shown publicly.
cases.org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is gru
cases.drop_reason: An attempted hack of the OPCW's network from a car park was stopped; no one inside the OPCW was recruited or controlled.

cases.n: Iran's cyberattack on Albania's government services leads to break in ties
cases.d: Albania hosts about 3,000 members of the Iranian opposition group MEK at a camp near Tirana. On 15 July 2022 a cyberattack shut down many Albanian government online services. On 7 September 2022 Prime Minister Edi Rama said an investigation found it was 'state aggression' organised and sponsored by Iran through four groups, and Albania cut diplomatic ties and gave Iranian embassy staff 24 hours to leave. The US backed the finding; Iran called it baseless.
cases.cite: Government of Albania, 7 Sept 2022; US National Security Council statement
cases.why: Official government finding backed by the US; diplomatic relations cut.
cases.org_note: foreign_state = Iran
cases.drop_reason: A cyberattack that shut down Albanian government services is sabotage, not an outside party getting people or control inside a government body.

cases.n: Azerbaijan accused of stirring New Caledonia's independence unrest
cases.d: Azerbaijan and France are at odds over France's support for Armenia. In July 2023 Baku hosted a conference of independence figures from French territories that created the 'Baku Initiative Group'. During deadly riots in New Caledonia in May 2024 over a voting-rights reform, French Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin said Azerbaijan, as well as China and Russia, was interfering in the territory, pointing to Azerbaijani flags at protests. Azerbaijan denied any link.
cases.cite: Statement of French Interior Minister, May 2024; Al Jazeera 17 May 2024
cases.why: Accusation by a French minister; no finding of payments to officials.
cases.org_note: foreign_state = Azerbaijan; existing caviar_lobby key may also fit
cases.drop_reason: A French minister's accusation of interference in New Caledonia names no office-holder or official working for Azerbaijan.

cases.n: Spain: Pegasus spyware found on Prime Minister Sánchez's phone
cases.d: On 2 May 2022 the Spanish government said Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's phone was infected twice in May 2021 and Defence Minister Margarita Robles's once in June 2021 with Pegasus, which NSO sells only to government agencies; the government said it had not authorised this. The High Court shelved the case in 2023, citing lack of cooperation from Israel, and reopened it in April 2024 after France shared data from its own Pegasus inquiry. No suspect state has been officially named.
cases.cite: Spanish government statement 2 May 2022; Audiencia Nacional, reopening 23 Apr 2024
cases.why: The infection is confirmed by the government; which state did it is not established.
cases.drop_reason: Spyware on the Spanish prime minister's phone is espionage by an unnamed state; no one inside the government was placed, paid or controlled.

cases.n: Pegasus Project: Macron's number on list linked to Morocco
cases.d: The Pegasus Project, a consortium of 17 media outlets, reported from 18 July 2021 on a leaked list of over 50,000 phone numbers believed to be of interest to NSO's government clients. It found President Emmanuel Macron's number on the list and linked his selection to Morocco. Morocco called this 'unfounded and false' and sued for defamation; France opened an investigation and Macron changed his phone.
cases.cite: Pegasus Project / Forbidden Stories, July 2021; Paris prosecutor investigation
cases.why: Suspicion stated by the Pegasus Project consortium; no infection of Macron's phone was confirmed; Morocco denies.
cases.drop_reason: Macron's number on a list of possible Pegasus spyware targets is espionage, not anyone getting inside the French government to steer it.

cases.n: IRGC hackers break into Trump campaign and leak its files
cases.d: In 2024 hackers took over Trump adviser Roger Stone's email and got into the Trump campaign; from 22 July an account called 'Robert' sent internal documents, including a 271-page vetting file on JD Vance, to Politico and other outlets and emailed stolen material to people tied to the Biden campaign. US intelligence agencies attributed the hack to Iran on 19 August 2024, and on 27 September 2024 the Justice Department charged three members of Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Iran denied it.
cases.cite: US intelligence community statement, 19 Aug 2024; US Justice Department indictment, 27 Sept 2024
cases.why: Official US attribution and indictment; not tried.
cases.org_note: foreign_state = Iran
cases.drop_reason: Iranian hackers stealing and leaking a campaign's files is a hack-and-leak operation, with no one inside a government body or company working for Iran.

cases.n: North Korean hackers steal $81m of Bangladesh's central bank reserves
cases.rank: central bank's account at the New York Fed
cases.d: On 4–5 February 2016 hackers inside Bangladesh Bank's network sent about three dozen fraudulent SWIFT payment orders for $951m from its account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; most were blocked, but $101m went out, $81m of it to the Philippines. Security firms tied it to the Lazarus Group, and US agencies to a unit under North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau; US prosecutors charged North Korean programmer Park Jin Hyok in 2018. About $66m was still unrecovered as of 2025.
cases.cite: US Justice Department complaint against Park Jin Hyok (2018); CISA alert on 'BeagleBoyz'
cases.why: US charges and agency attribution; the accused is beyond reach.
cases.drop_reason: North Korean hackers stealing $81m from Bangladesh's central bank is theft from outside, not placing people or control inside the bank.

cases.n: Ugandan special forces deployed to protect Kiir in Juba
cases.d: In March 2025, as President Salva Kiir's government detained ministers allied with First Vice President Riek Machar, Uganda sent special forces into Juba. Uganda's army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba said on 11 March that the army 'recognises only Salva Kiir' and that 'any move against him is a declaration of war against Uganda'. Uganda's parliament later endorsed the deployment; South Sudan at first denied Ugandan troops were present.
cases.cite: Uganda People's Defence Forces statement, 11 Mar 2025; Al Jazeera report
cases.why: Acknowledged by Uganda's army chief and parliament.
cases.drop_reason: Uganda sending special forces to protect South Sudan's president was an open, declared deployment, later endorsed by Uganda's parliament.

cases.n: Russia's Africa Corps in Togo under 2025 defence pact
cases.rank: armed forces and port of Lomé
cases.d: Africa Corps is the Russian defence ministry force that replaced Wagner in Africa. President Faure Gnassingbé and Vladimir Putin signed a defence agreement in November 2025 covering intelligence sharing, arms sales, joint exercises and Russian ships docking at Lomé. The Critical Threats project reports Africa Corps officers arrived in January 2026, about 300–350 soldiers were in Lomé and northern bases by mid-2026, and the sanctioned ship Mikhail Britnev unloaded vehicles at Lomé on 9 July 2026 for Africa Corps in Mali. Three opposition parties asked for a public debate on foreign troops.
cases.cite: Critical Threats (AEI) Africa File, 30 July 2026; Russian State Duma committee on the Togo agreement, July 2025
cases.why: The agreement is public; troop numbers come from open-source tracking, not official figures.
cases.drop_reason: Russian troops in Togo are there under an openly signed defence agreement.

cases.n: China's lending and base give Beijing leverage in Djibouti
