cases.d: China opened its first overseas military base in Djibouti in 2017, and a China Merchants subsidiary bought 23.5% of the Port of Djibouti in 2013. A US Congressional Research Service brief (June 2025) says Chinese institutions hold over half of Djibouti's 2.6 billion dollars of external debt, including a 1.2 billion dollar Exim Bank loan; Djibouti suspended repayments in 2022 and later agreed a moratorium. US officials have warned the debt 'could give Beijing undue leverage'. Djibouti says it will not hand port control to China.
cases.cite: US Congressional Research Service, 'China's Engagement in Djibouti' (IF11304), 6 June 2025
cases.why: Debt figures are documented; leverage over policy is a US concern, not a finding.
cases.drop_reason: Chinese loans and a military base in Djibouti are open, declared arrangements; warnings of leverage do not show hidden control inside Djibouti's government.

cases.n: Karapetyan arrested for 'calls to seize power' in Armenia
cases.d: Samvel Karapetyan is a Russian-Armenian billionaire whose Tashir Group ran Electric Networks of Armenia, the sole power distributor. He was detained on 18 June 2025 for public calls to seize power after backing the Armenian Church in its dispute with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, and later charged with money laundering. Parliament then passed amendments allowing the state to take over the grid company. His lawyers call the charges unfounded and critics see a political case before the 2026 election; no trial result has been reported.
cases.cite: Armenian Investigative Committee charges, June–July 2025; OC Media, 16 July 2025
cases.why: Charges filed by the government he opposes; no court ruling and the defence disputes them.
cases.drop_reason: A billionaire arrested for calling for a seizure of power describes a political prosecution, not an outside party inside a government body.

cases.n: 'Cyprus Papers' — Speaker filmed offering help with passport
cases.d: Cyprus sold citizenship to investors from 2007 to 2020. Al Jazeera published leaked files in August 2020 and on 12 October 2020 an undercover film in which House Speaker Demetris Syllouris and MP Christakis Giovanis appeared willing to help a fictional Chinese investor with a money-laundering conviction obtain a passport. Both resigned and the scheme was closed. A state inquiry led by former judge Myron Nicolatos found that more than half of the passports had been granted unlawfully; in 2022 four men were sent to trial and one was cleared in 2023.
cases.cite: Al Jazeera Investigative Unit, 'The Cyprus Papers', Aug–Oct 2020; Nicolatos inquiry report, 2021
cases.why: Resignations, closure of the scheme and an official inquiry finding unlawful grants.
cases.drop_reason: An undercover sting and unlawful passport grants by Cypriot officials do not show an outside party placing or paying people inside the state.

cases.n: Ivanishvili sanctioned for 'advancing the interests' of Russia
cases.rank: ruling party founder and honorary chairman
cases.d: Bidzina Ivanishvili made his fortune in Russia in the 1990s, founded the ruling Georgian Dream party and, as honorary chairman, nominates the prime minister. In December 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned him 'for undermining Georgian democracy and advancing the interests of the Russian Federation'; Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia also sanctioned him and the European Parliament describes him as having 'personal and business links to the Kremlin'. He denies acting for Russia.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designation, Dec 2024; European Parliament resolutions; Baltic states' sanctions
cases.why: US and Baltic sanctions designations; no evidence of direct Russian control has been published.
cases.drop_reason: The record shows US and Baltic sanctions saying Ivanishvili advances Russia's interests, but no mechanism by which Russia placed, paid or controlled anyone in Georgia's government.

cases.n: Zhao Wei crime group runs Laos's Golden Triangle zone
cases.d: Zhao Wei is a Chinese casino operator whose Kings Romans Group took a 99-year lease from the Lao government in 2007 to set up and run the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Bokeo province. In 2018 the US Treasury designated the 'Zhao Wei Transnational Criminal Organization' for drug trafficking and money laundering through the zone. UNODC has linked the zone to cyber-fraud compounds and flagged a 2020 river port built by a company tied to his organisation.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designation, Jan 2018; UNODC reports
cases.why: US Treasury designation; the lease from the Lao state is public.
cases.drop_reason: Kings Romans runs the Golden Triangle zone under an open 99-year lease from the Lao government; the record shows a US designation but no officials paid or placed.

cases.n: Chinese envoy lobbies Nepal's ruling party to stay united
cases.d: In May and July 2020, during a revolt inside the Nepal Communist Party against Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli, Chinese ambassador Hou Yanqi met Oli, President Bidya Bhandari and senior leaders Madhav Kumar Nepal and Jhala Nath Khanal, reportedly urging unity. Former ministers and diplomats criticised the meetings as interference, and in December 2020 China sent a delegation led by Guo Yezhou of the Communist Party's International Department. The Chinese embassy said it only wished to see the party united.
cases.cite: Kathmandu Post, 6 July 2020; The Himalayan Times on the Guo Yezhou delegation, Dec 2020
cases.why: Meetings were reported openly; whether they changed decisions is the critics' view, not a finding.
cases.drop_reason: A Chinese ambassador openly meeting Nepal's leaders to urge party unity is diplomatic lobbying, not infiltration.

cases.n: Iran's IRGC inside the Assad state (to Dec 2024)
cases.d: Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force advised and commanded alongside Bashar al-Assad's forces from 2012, with Hezbollah fighters in combat roles. About 2,000 Quds Force officers were reported in 2018 to command some 131 garrisons, and Iran was reported to hold 55 bases and 515 other military sites in 2023. Iran's officials acknowledged the 'advisory' mission. When Assad fell in December 2024 Iran evacuated its commanders, so the record is now about lasting effects.
cases.cite: Iranian official statements; reporting compiled on Wikipedia 'Iranian involvement in the Syrian civil war'
cases.why: Acknowledged by Iran; figures are press and monitor estimates.
cases.drop_reason: Iran's Quds Force advised and commanded alongside Assad's forces in an alliance both governments acknowledged, so the record shows an open military partnership rather than hidden placement.

cases.n: Australian spies bugged Timor-Leste cabinet during gas talks
cases.d: In 2004 the Australian Secret Intelligence Service planted listening devices in Timor-Leste's government building in Dili to learn its position in Timor Sea oil and gas talks, which led to the 2006 CMATS treaty. A former ASIS officer, 'Witness K', revealed it; Australia raided him and Timor's lawyer Bernard Collaery in 2013. Timor-Leste took Australia to the International Court of Justice and the Permanent Court of Arbitration, and a 2018 treaty replaced CMATS. Witness K pleaded guilty in 2021 to a secrecy offence; the case against Collaery was dropped in 2022.
cases.cite: ICJ provisional measures order, 3 Mar 2014; Permanent Court of Arbitration conciliation; ACT court proceedings 2018–2022
cases.why: Confirmed through court proceedings against the whistleblower and the treaty renegotiation.
cases.drop_reason: Australia bugging Timor-Leste's cabinet room was espionage to learn its negotiating position; no one inside Timor-Leste's government was placed or paid.

cases.n: Triad boss Wan Kuok-koi's push into Palau
cases.d: Wan Kuok-koi ('Broken Tooth') is the former head of Macau's 14K triad, sanctioned by the US in 2020 and said by Treasury to sit on a CCP United Front body. OCCRP reported in December 2022 that he visited Palau in 2018 as a 'guest of the government' and that a former postmaster general and a former Airai state governor were directors of his Palau Hongmen association, registered in early 2019 to plan a casino zone on Angaur. President Tommy Remengesau opposed the casino in April 2019 and the association applied to dissolve. OCCRP did not establish that the Chinese state directed the effort.
cases.cite: OCCRP, 'Pacific Gambit', 12 Dec 2022; US Treasury designation of Wan Kuok-koi, Dec 2020
cases.who: Wan Kuok-koi (14K triad / World Hongmen association)
cases.why: Company registrations and travel records documented by OCCRP; US sanctions on Wan.
cases.drop_reason: A triad boss's Palau association used former officials and its casino plan was rejected by the president; no one in office is shown working for him.

cases.n: UBS loan for Oil Search shares — PNG inquiry
cases.d: In 2014 the government of Peter O'Neill borrowed about 1.2 billion US dollars through UBS to buy shares in Oil Search, against cabinet advice and before parliament approved it; Treasurer Don Polye, who objected, lost his job. A Commission of Inquiry heard that the state lost about 432 million dollars while UBS earned about 83 million in fees and interest; its 2021 report found the loan unlawful and recommended a 10-year ban on UBS. O'Neill was later charged with giving false evidence to the inquiry.
cases.cite: Commission of Inquiry into the UBS Loan, report tabled 2021; RNZ and PINA reports
cases.why: Findings of a statutory Commission of Inquiry.
cases.drop_reason: The UBS loan was an unlawful decision by PNG's own government; the record does not show UBS placing or paying officials.

cases.n: Tonga's passport-sale fund lost under the king's 'court jester'
cases.d: Tonga sold passports to Hong Kong residents before 1997 and put the money into the Tonga Trust Fund. American adviser Jesse Bogdonoff, whom King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV named court jester in 1999, moved the fund into a viatical investment firm that went bankrupt in 2002, losing about 33 million dollars, around 40% of a year's state revenue. Tonga sued him and in 2004 he settled without admitting fraud.
cases.cite: Tongan government lawsuit and 2004 settlement
cases.why: Civil settlement paid to the state.
cases.drop_reason: An adviser openly appointed by Tonga's king losing a state fund in a failed investment is mismanagement, not hidden outside control.

cases.n: Banca Privada d'Andorra — US 'money-laundering concern' later cleared
cases.d: On 10 March 2015 the US Treasury's FinCEN named Banca Privada d'Andorra a 'primary money laundering concern', saying senior managers served criminal groups from Russia and China and Venezuelan money launderers. Andorra took over the bank and jailed its chief executive; its subsidiary Banco Madrid collapsed. FinCEN withdrew the finding in 2016, and Spanish courts between 2017 and 2019 dismissed money-laundering cases against the bank, raising questions about the information that triggered the alert.
cases.cite: FinCEN notice, 10 Mar 2015 (rescinded 2016); Spanish court rulings 2017–2019
cases.who: Russian and Chinese crime groups; Venezuelan launderers (alleged)
cases.why: The US finding was withdrawn and courts cleared the bank.
cases.drop_reason: The US withdrew its money-laundering finding against Banca Privada d'Andorra and Spanish courts dismissed the cases, so no crime group control is on record.

cases.n: Russia's hold over Belarus's state and army
cases.d: After the disputed 2020 election Vladimir Putin promised Alexander Lukashenko a 1.5 billion dollar loan. In February 2022 Russian forces launched part of the invasion of Ukraine from Belarus, and a referendum that month removed the ban on nuclear basing and allowed permanent Russian bases. Russia supplied nuclear-capable Iskander-M missiles in 2023 and Putin said warheads were delivered; he has said Russia keeps control of them. Both governments state these arrangements openly.
cases.cite: Joint statements of the Russian and Belarusian presidents; 2022 Belarus constitutional referendum
cases.why: Acknowledged by both governments.
cases.drop_reason: Russia's military and nuclear arrangements in Belarus are stated openly by both governments.

cases.n: Russian backing for Dodik's Republika Srpska
cases.d: Milorad Dodik led Bosnia's Serb entity, Republika Srpska, and pushed for secession. Its police signed a 2016 cooperation agreement with Russia's interior ministry on intelligence and counter-terrorism; Dodik met Putin at least five times from 2022 and received a Russian state order in 2023. The US sanctioned him in 2017 for obstructing the Dayton peace agreement and his family firms in 2023, but lifted the sanctions on 29 October 2025, a day after he met Russia's foreign minister. A Bosnian court banned him from politics for six years in 2025 for defying the international envoy.
cases.cite: Stanford International Policy Review, 30 Jan 2025; US Treasury designations 2017/2023 and delisting Oct 2025 (OCCRP)
cases.why: Formal police agreements and state honours are public; direction from Moscow is inferred by analysts.
cases.drop_reason: Russian support for Dodik through a signed police agreement, meetings and an award is open backing, with no hidden placement or payment shown.

cases.n: Belize immigration minister and a passport for Won Hong Kim
cases.d: In September 2013 Prime Minister Dean Barrow stripped Elvin Penner, minister of state for immigration, of his post after he was accused of selling and issuing a Belizean passport to South Korean national Kim Won Hong, who was then jailed in Taiwan. Penner was charged in March 2014, but the charges were dropped in July 2014 for lack of evidence.
cases.cite: Belize government statement, 19 Sep 2013; Belize Magistrate's Court, 2014
cases.why: The minister lost his post but charges were dropped.
cases.drop_reason: A single alleged passport sale by a minister to one buyer, with charges dropped, does not show an outside party steering a government body.

cases.n: Sanctioned Iranians bought St Kitts passports, US Treasury warns
cases.d: St Kitts and Nevis has sold citizenship since 1984. On 20 May 2014 the US Treasury's FinCEN said several Iranians under US sanctions had obtained Kittitian passports through the programme, which 'maintains lax controls', and that Iranians kept getting them after a 2013 suspension. FinCEN rescinded the advisory on 24 February 2026 after the passports expired and the programme was reformed.
cases.cite: FinCEN Advisory FIN-2014-A004, 20 May 2014 (rescinded 24 Feb 2026)
cases.why: A formal US Treasury advisory, now withdrawn.
cases.drop_reason: Sanctioned Iranians buying St Kitts passports through a scheme with weak checks is buying a product, not getting inside the government.

cases.n: Dino Bouterse — counter-terror chief convicted in US
cases.d: Dino Bouterse, son of then-president Dési Bouterse, headed Suriname's Counter-Terrorism Unit. He was arrested by the DEA in Panama on 29 August 2013 and convicted in New York of cocaine trafficking and of offering to let people he believed were Hezbollah operatives set up a base in Suriname; they were DEA informants. He was sentenced on 10 March 2015 to about 16 years.
cases.cite: US District Court (S.D.N.Y.) sentence, 10 Mar 2015
cases.who: Cocaine traffickers (and a staged Hezbollah offer)
cases.why: Guilty plea and US sentence.
cases.drop_reason: Dino Bouterse trafficked cocaine himself and made his base offer to DEA informants posing as Hezbollah, so no real outside party got inside Suriname's state.

cases.n: Desi Bouterse — head of state, later President
cases.d: Convicted in absentia by a Dutch court in 1999 of trafficking almost 500 kilograms of cocaine and sentenced to eleven years; with no extradition treaty the sentence was never executed and he was subsequently elected president twice. A separate 16-year Surinamese prosecution over the 1982 killing of fifteen political opponents produced a 20-year sentence upheld finally in December 2023. He did not surrender, vanished in January 2024, and died in hiding in December 2024 having served no time on either conviction.
cases.cite: Court of The Hague, cocaine conviction in absentia July 1999; Court of Justice of Suriname, December Murders verdict upheld 20 December 2023; death reported December 2024
cases.drop_reason: Desi Bouterse was convicted of trafficking cocaine himself; the record shows no outside group placing people or money inside Suriname's state.

cases.n: Vladimiro Montesinos — intelligence chief
cases.d: Head of the national intelligence service under Fujimori and, in practice, of the military, the courts and much of the press. He was convicted on a long series of counts including drug trafficking, and separately sentenced to twenty years for arranging an airdrop of ten thousand assault rifles to Colombian guerrillas. He was accused of sixty-three offences in all and pleaded guilty in 2024 to homicide and forced disappearance in the 1992 killing of six farmers. He videotaped himself paying bribes, which is how much of the record exists: the agency nominally responsible for counter-narcotics kept its own evidence.
cases.cite: Peruvian Supreme Court convictions from 2006; arms-trafficking verdict September 2006; guilty plea, January 2024
cases.drop_reason: The record lists Montesinos's own crimes (trafficking, an arms airdrop, paying bribes) but shows no outside party getting inside Peru's state through him.

cases.n: Cartel de los Soles indictment
cases.rank: head of state and general staff
cases.d: The US Department of Justice indicted Nicolas Maduro and more than a dozen serving and former officials, including senior military commanders, on narco-terrorism and cocaine importation charges in 2020. Treasury designated the group as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist in July 2025 and the State Department as a Foreign Terrorist Organization from 24 November 2025, saying the regime had corrupted parts of the military, intelligence apparatus, legislature and judiciary to serve it. That designation underpinned a maritime campaign in the Caribbean and Pacific and Maduro was taken into custody on 3 January 2026. Analysts and former officials dispute that it is a formally organised cartel or that he leads one, while agreeing there is government involvement in the trade; the charges have not been tried.
cases.cite: US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., indictment March 2020; OFAC SDGT designation July 2025; State Department FTO designation effective 24 November 2025; capture reported 3 January 2026
cases.drop_reason: A US terrorist designation and untried indictment of Venezuelan officials' own alleged trafficking does not show an outside group inside the state.

cases.n: Ousmane Conte — son of the head of state
cases.d: Arrested in February 2009 by the junta that took power after the death of his father, the head of state, and charged with trafficking. He confessed on state television to involvement in the cocaine trade; it was not clear whether the confession was coerced. Treasury designated him a kingpin in 2010 while he was held in a Conakry prison and standing trial. No verdict from a competent court followed, which is the pattern across the West African corridor: the admission exists, the judgment does not.
cases.cite: Guinean state television broadcast, February 2009; OFAC Kingpin Act designation, 2010
cases.drop_reason: A televised confession that may have been coerced and a US designation, with no verdict, do not show a trafficking group inside Guinea's state.

cases.n: Captagon production and the state
cases.d: The United States enacted the Captagon Act directing an interagency strategy against production assessed as linked to the Syrian government and associated networks; the UK and EU imposed sanctions on named figures. The assessments are governmental rather than judicial.
cases.cite: Captagon Act (US, 2022); UK and EU sanctions designations, 2023
cases.drop_reason: Assessments that Syria's government itself was linked to Captagon production describe a state's own trade, not an outside party inside it.

cases.n: Kamchybek Kolbayev — designated kingpin with state protection
cases.d: Designated under the US Kingpin Act, repeatedly released or lightly sentenced by domestic courts, and killed in a security operation in 2023. The record of releases is the documentary trace of protection.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, 2011; Kyrgyz court records
cases.drop_reason: The record infers protection from repeated court releases of a designated crime boss but shows no official placed or paid by his group.

cases.n: Provincial power and the opium economy
cases.d: Successive US government and UN assessments described provincial officials and police commanders taxing and protecting opium production. Very little of it reached a courtroom, which is itself the finding.
cases.cite: UNODC Afghanistan Opium Surveys; US SIGAR reporting
cases.drop_reason: General assessments that Afghan officials taxed opium name no outside party or official and give no case showing who was inside what.

cases.n: Border militias inside the state structure — Shan State
cases.d: Armed groups formally incorporated into the state as border guard forces operate in the areas producing the largest volumes of methamphetamine assessed anywhere. Myanmar scores 10 out of 10 on the synthetic drug indicator and 9 on state-embedded actors.
cases.cite: UNODC Synthetic Drugs in East and Southeast Asia; GI-TOC country profile
cases.drop_reason: Index scores and the open incorporation of militias as border guards do not show a drug network placing people or control inside Myanmar's state.

cases.n: Fabio Lobo — son of President Porfirio Lobo
cases.d: Arrested in Haiti in a DEA sting, he pleaded guilty in New York to conspiring to import cocaine and was sentenced to 24 years. He had arranged police escorts for shipments he believed belonged to the Cachiros.
cases.cite: US v. Fabio Porfirio Lobo, S.D.N.Y., plea 2016, sentence September 2017
cases.drop_reason: The record says Fabio Lobo arranged escorts for shipments he only believed belonged to the Cachiros, a DEA sting, so no real outside group got inside the Honduran police through him.

cases.n: Campo Flores and Flores de Freitas — the first lady's nephews
cases.d: Two nephews of Cilia Flores were arrested in Haiti after offering 800 kilograms of cocaine to DEA informants, convicted in Manhattan and sentenced to 18 years. Both were released to Venezuela in a prisoner exchange in 2022.
cases.cite: US v. Campo Flores and Flores de Freitas, S.D.N.Y., verdict November 2016; prisoner exchange October 2022
cases.undone: Both released to Venezuela in a prisoner exchange in October 2022, six years into 18-year sentences.
cases.drop_reason: The record shows two relatives offering cocaine to informants, not anyone placed or paid inside a government body.

cases.n: Air force sergeant on the presidential delegation flight
cases.d: A sergeant travelling with the presidential delegation to the G20 was caught in Seville with 39 kilograms of cocaine in his luggage aboard an air force aircraft. He was convicted by a Brazilian military court and sentenced to over ten years.
cases.cite: Superior Tribunal Militar, conviction 2019; Spanish Guardia Civil seizure, June 2019
cases.drop_reason: A serviceman smuggling cocaine in his luggage; the record names no outside group that placed or paid him to steer any decision.

cases.n: Baltimore Gun Trace Task Force
cases.d: An elite plainclothes squad was convicted of racketeering after robbing residents and dealers, reselling seized narcotics through a bail bondsman, and claiming overtime for hours not worked. Prosecutors and the courts have since reviewed hundreds of cases the unit built.
cases.cite: US v. Gondo et al. and US v. Hersl and Taylor, D. Md., pleas and verdicts 2017–2018
cases.who: Baltimore drug dealers and resale network
cases.drop_reason: Officers robbing people and reselling drugs themselves is crime by the unit's own members, not an outside party getting inside it.

cases.n: Jose Irizarry — DEA special agent
cases.d: An agent assigned to money-laundering operations in Colombia diverted laundered funds to himself and his associates, and was sentenced to 12 years. He had used the agency's own undercover accounts, which is why the losses took years to surface.
cases.cite: US v. Irizarry, M.D. Fla., plea 2020, sentence November 2021
cases.drop_reason: The record shows an agent stealing laundered funds for himself and associates, a fraud by an insider with no outside party steering the agency.

cases.n: Ronald Watts — Chicago police sergeant
cases.d: A sergeant and his tactical team ran a protection racket in a public housing development, taxing dealers and framing those who refused. He pleaded guilty to a federal theft charge; courts have since vacated more than 200 convictions built on his team's word.
cases.cite: US v. Watts, N.D. Ill., plea 2013; Cook County exoneration orders from 2017
cases.drop_reason: A police team extorting dealers and framing people is crime by the officers themselves, not dealers getting inside the police.

cases.n: Cameron Ortis — RCMP intelligence director
cases.d: The civilian head of the RCMP's National Intelligence Coordination Centre was convicted under the Security of Information Act of offering operational material to targets, among them the head of the encrypted-phone firm Phantom Secure. He was sentenced to 14 years.
cases.cite: R v. Ortis, Ontario Superior Court, verdict November 2023, sentence February 2024
cases.drop_reason: The record shows an official offering secrets to criminal targets on his own initiative, not an outside party placing or recruiting him.

cases.n: Moscow drug squad officers — the Golunov case
cases.d: Five officers of a Moscow district drug unit were convicted of planting narcotics on a journalist and sentenced to between five and twelve years. The case is the rare Russian instance where the fabrication of a drug charge by serving officers reached a verdict.
cases.cite: Moscow City Court, verdict 2022
cases.drop_reason: Officers planting drugs on a journalist is misconduct by the police themselves, with no outside party inside the force.

cases.n: The OCRTIS 'coups d'achat' file
cases.d: The former head of the national anti-drug office was placed under formal investigation over cannabis shipments run through an informer, in a case turning on how far a police service may let a trade operate to reach the people behind it. He denies wrongdoing.
cases.cite: French judicial investigation opened 2019, Paris; Cour de cassation rulings on related seizures
cases.drop_reason: The record describes a police tactic of letting an informer's trade run, not an outside party getting inside the anti-drug office.

cases.n: The Pong Su — a state-linked vessel
cases.d: A North Korean freighter delivered 125 kilograms of heroin to a beach in Victoria in 2003 and was boarded by Australian special forces. The captain and senior crew were acquitted of importation in 2006 — the jury was not persuaded they knew the cargo — and the ship was later sunk as a bombing target. The state link was never established in court.
cases.cite: R v. Song and others, Supreme Court of Victoria, acquittals March 2006
cases.drop_reason: A ship delivering heroin is smuggling; no one inside an institution was shown working for an outside party, and the state link was never established.

cases.n: Teddy Minahasa — police inspector general
cases.d: A two-star general days from taking command of the Jakarta police was convicted of ordering seized methamphetamine to be replaced with alum and sold on. Prosecutors sought death; the court imposed life imprisonment, later reduced on appeal.
cases.cite: West Jakarta District Court, verdict May 2023
cases.drop_reason: Ordering seized drugs to be swapped and sold is theft by a police officer himself, not an outside party inside the force.

cases.n: The 'ninja cops' and recycled seizures
cases.d: A Senate inquiry examined officers who reported partial seizures and resold the rest, a practice known locally as ninja cops. The chief of the national police resigned in October 2019 over his handling of a 2013 case in Pampanga; the administrative and criminal proceedings that followed produced no senior conviction.
cases.cite: Philippine Senate Committee on Public Order hearings, 2019; PNP internal affairs records
cases.drop_reason: Officers reselling seized drugs is crime by police themselves, not traffickers getting inside the force.

cases.n: Narcotics Control Bureau — the Mumbai zonal office
cases.d: The CBI registered a case in 2023 against the former zonal director of the Narcotics Control Bureau in Mumbai and three colleagues, alleging a demand for payment to keep a name out of a high-profile cruise-ship seizure file. He denies the allegation and the case has not been tried.
cases.cite: Central Bureau of Investigation FIR, May 2023; Bombay High Court proceedings
cases.drop_reason: An alleged payment demand by officials is extortion by insiders, with no outside party steering the bureau.

cases.n: Captagon on a private jet — the Beirut airport arrest
cases.d: A member of the Saudi royal family and four others were detained at Beirut airport in October 2015 while loading two tonnes of captagon onto a private jet. Lebanese prosecutors charged them; no verdict in the case has been made public.
cases.cite: Lebanese Internal Security Forces statement and public prosecution filing, October 2015
cases.drop_reason: Smuggling captagon by private jet, with no one inside a Lebanese institution shown working for the smugglers.

cases.n: Abba Kyari — deputy commissioner of police
cases.d: The head of the police Intelligence Response Team was charged by the drug agency with substituting seized cocaine and offering an officer 1,400 to stop it being tested. In March 2026 a judge acquitted him and two brothers on a separate 23-count asset-declaration charge, describing that prosecution as persecution. The cocaine trial continues before a different judge alongside four suspended officers of his unit; two traffickers originally charged with them pleaded guilty and were jailed. He has been in detention since 2022.
cases.cite: NDLEA charges, Federal High Court Abuja, from February 2022; acquittal on asset-declaration counts, March 2026; substantive drug trial continuing before Justice Nwite
cases.drop_reason: The charge is that police officers swapped and kept seized cocaine themselves, not that traffickers placed or paid them.

cases.n: Christiaan Prinsloo — police colonel, firearms to the Cape gangs
cases.d: A colonel sold roughly two thousand firearms from police stores to Cape Flats gangs, and was sentenced to 18 years. Ballistics have since linked the guns to more than a thousand shootings, many of them in the drug turf conflicts of the Flats.
cases.cite: Bellville Regional Court, plea and sentence 2016; SAPS ballistics evidence
cases.drop_reason: A police officer selling guns to gangs is an insider selling to criminals, not an outside party getting inside the police.

cases.n: Gustavo Petro — sitting President
cases.d: The United States designated the sitting Colombian president under its illicit-drug order in October 2025, citing a rise in coca cultivation under his administration and the handling of intelligence channels. Colombia rejected the finding, and the two governments' assessments of the same period diverge sharply. This is an executive designation rather than a charge, and belongs on the map as one.
cases.cite: OFAC designation under E.O. 14059, October 2025; Government of Colombia response
cases.drop_reason: The designation cites rising coca cultivation and policy choices; the record shows no trafficking group placing or paying anyone inside the government.

cases.n: The Assad family and the Fourth Division — the captagon designations
cases.d: Three cousins of the president were designated by the US, UK and EU across March and April 2023 over captagon production and smuggling, alongside the manager of the Fourth Division's revenues and militia leaders in the south. Treasury put one Latakia facility's output at 84 million pills in 2020. The EU stated the trade had become a regime-led business model; the findings are executive and no court has heard them.
cases.cite: OFAC designations under E.O. 13572 and 13582, March 2023; UK FCDO designations, March 2023; Council of the EU designations, April 2023
cases.drop_reason: The record describes a regime running the captagon trade itself, not an outside party getting inside the government.

cases.n: Taliban shadow ministry — the 2012 Kingpin designation
cases.d: A Taliban figure designated under the Kingpin Act in 2012 for his role in narcotics trafficking was, by late 2017, serving as the movement's shadow foreign minister and managing its relations with Iran. He also sits on the UN Security Council's 1988 sanctions list, which is the rare instance of the same person appearing on a drug list and a counter-terrorism list for the same conduct.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, November 2012; UN Security Council Resolution 1988 sanctions list
cases.drop_reason: A Taliban figure designated for trafficking and later holding a post in the movement's own shadow structure is not an outside party inside a government body.

cases.n: Los Cuellos Blancos del Puerto — the Callao judiciary
cases.rank: supreme court judge, court president and judicial council
cases.d: Wiretaps placed on a Callao trafficking organisation caught a different network on the same lines: a supreme court judge, the president of the Callao superior court and members of the judicial appointments council trading sentence reductions, promotions and favours. The judge fled to Spain, the court president was jailed, and the first conviction after a full trial came only in November 2025, seven years on. Several implicated judges were still sitting while under investigation.
cases.cite: IDL-Reporteros audio releases from July 2018; Corte Superior Nacional de Justicia Penal Especializada, first trial verdict November 2025
cases.drop_reason: The record shows judges and appointments officials trading favours among themselves; no outside party is shown steering them.

cases.n: General Dom Hak — military intelligence chief
cases.d: A two-star general was arrested with seven others after police found 35 kilograms of heroin and manufacturing equipment in a Phnom Penh house. The government burned the seizure publicly before prosecutors had begun, then released him within weeks for lack of evidence. It remains the highest-ranking Cambodian drug case to reach a court.
cases.cite: Phnom Penh Municipal Court, charge and release October 2003
cases.drop_reason: A general arrested with heroin and released for lack of evidence; the record shows no outside party placing or paying him.

cases.n: The vanished 975 kilograms
cases.d: The director of the judicial police said 975 of 980 kilograms seized in November 2021 had disappeared from official custody, and that police and security personnel were suspected of taking it. One officer was arrested. The country had not tried a drug case since 2005, which is the context for a seizure evaporating rather than becoming evidence.
cases.cite: Guinea-Bissau Policia Judiciaria statement, February 2022; US Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing record, 2009
cases.drop_reason: Police or security staff suspected of taking seized cocaine is theft by insiders, with no outside party shown placing them.

cases.n: Operation Eureka — 76 convictions
cases.d: A Reggio Calabria bunker court convicted 76 defendants and acquitted seven in October 2025, in a case built from a 2023 carabinieri operation that seized three tonnes of cocaine and arrested 108 people. Prosecutors described three trafficking associations run by the most powerful Ionian 'Ndrangheta families. It is the counterweight to the capture entries: the same state whose Calabrian councils are dissolved for infiltration also runs the courts that convict at this scale.
cases.cite: Tribunale di Reggio Calabria, Operation Eureka first-instance verdicts, October 2025; DDA Reggio Calabria and ROS carabinieri investigation, May 2023
cases.drop_reason: A trafficking prosecution of 'Ndrangheta families with no official or institution shown working for them; the record presents it as a counterweight to capture cases.

cases.n: Border Guard officers of the Vakhsh checkpoint
cases.rank: border guard officers and provincial police
cases.d: A military court in Khatlon sentenced five Border Guard Service officers to between three and 21 years, the longest for the former chief of the Vakhsh checkpoint on the Afghan frontier, in whose office investigators had found 20 kilograms of hashish. A senior Khatlon police official was arrested the same day with 12 kilograms of heroin. Roughly 90 tonnes of heroin cross Central Asia each year and most seizures are of small dealers; this is the rank at which the record stops.
cases.cite: Khatlon military court, sentences November 2012; State Committee for National Security statement, November 2012
cases.drop_reason: Officers caught holding drugs; the record does not show a trafficking group placing or paying them.

cases.n: The ambassador and the deputy interior minister
cases.d: Tajikistan's ambassador to Kazakhstan was arrested in Almaty in 2000 with 86 kilograms of heroin in his car. The following year the deputy interior minister was murdered, and prosecutors argued at trial that he was killed for refusing to pay for a 50-kilogram consignment. Estimates in 2014 put drug money at up to 30 percent of the country's economy.
cases.cite: Kazakh authorities, arrest in Almaty 2000; Tajik prosecution case in the 2001 killing; UNODC and academic estimates
cases.drop_reason: An ambassador caught smuggling heroin and a murder over a consignment show trafficking, not an outside party steering an institution.

cases.n: Operation Relentless — bribing the government that reported it
cases.d: South American and West African traffickers were recorded paying senior Liberian officials to guarantee safe passage and storage for multi-tonne cocaine shipments. The officials reported the approaches and worked with the DEA instead, producing extraditions to New York and convictions there. The DEA called the cooperation from the highest levels of the Liberian government unprecedented, which is the measure of how rare that response is on this map.
cases.cite: US v. Umeh, Salazar Castano, Kamara and others, S.D.N.Y., indictments and convictions from 2010
cases.who: Latin American and West African traffickers
cases.drop_reason: The officials reported the bribe offers and worked with the DEA, so no one inside the government served the traffickers.

cases.n: The Phantom Squad
cases.d: Guyana's most powerful trafficker ran an armed group that operated alongside the state during a period of killings in the mid-2000s, using construction and forestry businesses to launder cocaine proceeds moved from Colombia to the United States. He was convicted in New York and served 15 years. The squad's relationship to the government was examined publicly and never resolved in a Guyanese court.
cases.cite: US v. Khan, E.D.N.Y., conviction and 15-year sentence; Guyanese public inquiries into the killings of 2002-2006
cases.drop_reason: The record says the trafficker's armed group operated alongside the state but shows no one inside a government body working for it.

cases.n: The Fourth Criminal Court — Assad and the Fourth Division
cases.rank: head of state, division commander and security chiefs
cases.d: On 11 August 2026 the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus sentenced the deposed president to death in absentia for premeditated murder, torture and crimes against humanity, and his brother, who commanded the Fourth Armoured Division, to death in absentia; six other officials received the same sentence in absentia. Only one defendant was present, a cousin who ran political security in Deraa and had been sanctioned by the US Treasury in 2011; he stood in a cage in prison uniform to hear it and has the right to appeal. Both brothers are in Russia with political asylum and Moscow has refused extradition. Opposition activists accuse the Fourth Division of killings, torture, extortion and drug trafficking, and Western and regional governments treat it as the backbone of state captagon manufacture — but the convictions are for war crimes, not the trade. Human Rights Watch opposed the sentences and questioned whether a fair trial was guaranteed.
cases.cite: Fourth Criminal Court, Damascus, judgment 11 August 2026, reported by SANA and international agencies; US Treasury designation of the Deraa political security head, April 2011; Human Rights Watch statement, August 2026
cases.drop_reason: The convictions are for war crimes by the regime's own leaders; no outside party getting inside an institution is recorded.

cases.n: Nouh Zeaiter — the four-month sentence
cases.rank: trafficker sanctioned by the US and EU
cases.d: Sanctioned by the United States and the United Kingdom in 2023 over captagon manufacture and smuggling alongside relatives and associates of the Assad family, and already convicted in absentia by a Lebanese military court in 2021, which gave him life with hard labour, and sentenced to death in absentia in March 2024 for shooting at soldiers, one of whom was killed. The army took him in an ambush near Baalbek in November 2025 and called him one of the most dangerous wanted men in the country. In February 2026 the military court sentenced him to four months, finding him guilty in four minor matters — arms trafficking, shootings, unlicensed weapons and wearing military clothing — with weapons and radios confiscated. He denied trafficking and said he grew cannabis only between 2005 and 2008. The same court that had already sentenced him twice in absentia reached four months once he was in front of it.
cases.cite: US and UK sanctions designations, 2023; Lebanese military court convictions in absentia, 2021 and March 2024; Lebanese Armed Forces arrest, 20 November 2025; military court sentence, February 2026
cases.drop_reason: A trafficker's prosecution and light sentence, with no one inside an institution shown working for him.

cases.n: Louay al-Yasiri — a governor's son, pardoned
cases.rank: son of a former governor, intelligence service employee
cases.d: Sentenced to life in 2018 for drug offences, the son of a former provincial governor and himself an employee of the intelligence service. He was later pardoned and released. It is the clearest documented instance of a trafficker with direct government connections reaching an Iraqi court, and the sentence did not hold. Against it stands the volume the same judiciary produces: over 14,000 arrests in 2024, 144 death sentences for international traffickers and 434 life sentences for local offenders, and 973 convictions in the first quarter of 2025 alone.
cases.cite: Iraqi court sentence, 2018, and subsequent pardon; Supreme Judicial Council and Ministry of Interior figures for 2024 and Q1 2025; UNODC seizure data
cases.drop_reason: A well-connected person convicted of drug offences and pardoned; no outside party placing or paying anyone inside a government body is recorded.

cases.n: Revolutionary Court judges in the drug docket
cases.d: Defence lawyers describe the courts that try drug cases as security-dominated and fast-tracking low-level defendants while leaving trafficking networks and higher-level operators untouched. One attorney who handled more than seventy drug cases documented the conduct of two named Tehran revolutionary court judges, one of whom he alleges was involved in financial corruption, and submitted a report with case files; lawyers who pursue such cases report being turned on themselves. With no independent forum, the allegation cannot be tested. Iran scores 9.50 on state-embedded actors, the joint highest on this map, and hangs hundreds of people a year for drug offences.
cases.cite: Center for Human Rights in Iran, testimony of a defence attorney and analysis of drug sentencing, April 2025; Iranian judiciary announcements via Mizan Online
cases.drop_reason: The record describes harsh, fast drug trials and one unproven corruption allegation against a judge, but shows no trafficking network placing or paying anyone inside the courts.

cases.n: A mayor and 200 kilograms in his vehicle
cases.d: A local mayor was arrested with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle, an incident cited in investigative-journalism guidance for Africa as the model case of why a seizure is only the start: the work is unravelling the network behind the office rather than recording the arrest. No outcome is documented here. Niger sits on the Sahel corridor UNODC describes as a natural stopover between South America and Europe, and reporting on it carries physical risk to journalists.
cases.cite: Global Investigative Journalism Network, Guide to Investigating Organized Crime in Africa, chapter on drug trafficking; UNODC Sahel trafficking assessments
cases.drop_reason: The record shows a single arrest of a mayor with cocaine and no outcome; it does not identify a network or show the mayor's office being used on its behalf.

cases.n: Maher al-Assad — commander, Fourth Armoured Division
cases.d: The former president's brother, sanctioned by the United States, United Kingdom and European Union in 2023 over captagon production and export run through the division he commanded. The designations rest on intelligence findings and open-source investigation rather than a trial. After the government's collapse in December 2024 the production sites were opened to journalists and investigators, which corroborated the scale but not the individual attributions.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC and UK Foreign Office designations, March 2023; EU Council Implementing Regulation 2023/720; Centre for Operational Analysis and Research captagon reporting
cases.drop_reason: The Fourth Division was the Syrian state's own army unit running the captagon trade; the record shows no outside party getting inside it.

cases.n: President Joao Bernardo Vieira and the 2009 killings
cases.rank: head of state and armed forces chief
cases.d: The president and the army chief of staff were killed within hours of each other in March 2009, during the period when UNODC described the country as at risk of becoming Africa's first narco-state. No prosecution followed either killing. The link to the cocaine trade is the assessment of UNODC and of the UN Peacebuilding Support Office, not a court finding.
cases.cite: UNODC Transnational Organized Crime in West Africa; UN Security Council reporting on Guinea-Bissau, 2009-2012
cases.drop_reason: The record covers the unsolved 2009 killings of the president and army chief; it shows no traffickers placing or paying anyone inside the state.

cases.n: Rana Sanaullah — provincial law minister
cases.d: Arrested by the Anti-Narcotics Force in July 2019 on a charge of transporting fifteen kilograms of heroin. The case collapsed and he was acquitted in 2022; the ANF officer who filed it later disowned the recovery. The episode is on this map as a documented instance of narcotics charges being deployed against a political opponent, which is a distinct failure mode from capture and belongs in the same record.
cases.cite: Pakistan Anti-Narcotics Force case records; Lahore Special Court acquittal, 2022; Islamabad High Court proceedings
cases.drop_reason: The record is a collapsed drug charge against an opposition politician, which is misuse of the law by the state, not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: The 2017 official 'drug barons' list
cases.d: The president read out a list of alleged drug traffickers in public in 2017 and ordered arrests; a regional commissioner and several public figures were named. Few prosecutions were completed and most of those detained were released. The episode is recorded as an assertion by a head of state, not as a set of findings.
cases.cite: Tanzanian government statements, February 2017; Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime East Africa reporting
cases.drop_reason: The record is a president publicly reading out a list of alleged traffickers, an assertion with few prosecutions; it shows no network inside an institution.

cases.n: The judicial vetting
cases.d: An EU-monitored vetting of every judge and prosecutor in the country, running since 2017, has removed or forced out roughly half of those assessed, mostly on unexplained-wealth grounds. It is the largest deliberate purge of a judiciary attempted in Europe and the clearest admission by a state that its own courts had been captured. Individual outcomes are administrative rather than criminal.
cases.cite: Albanian Independent Qualification Commission and Special Appeal Chamber decisions; European Commission Albania progress reports
cases.drop_reason: The record describes a vetting programme removing judges on unexplained-wealth grounds; it names no outside party and shows no one placed or paid inside the courts by one.

cases.n: The dismantling of the anti-impunity capacity
cases.d: The UN-backed anti-impunity commission that produced most of the country's trafficking-linked prosecutions was expelled in 2019, and by 2023 more than thirty judges and prosecutors who had worked those cases had left the country under threat of arrest. The cases they built, several of them on this map, no longer have a domestic forum. This is capture achieved by removing the prosecutor rather than buying the judge.
cases.cite: UN International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) closure reporting, 2019; Inter-American Commission on Human Rights precautionary measures; US Department of State section 353 listings
cases.drop_reason: The record describes the expulsion of a UN anti-impunity commission and the exile of judges; it shows no named outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Operacion Necora — Galicia
cases.d: The operation that exposed the Galician rias as Europe's principal cocaine landing zone, run by tobacco-smuggling clans that had converted to cocaine for the Medellin and Cali organisations. Convictions followed for several clan leaders; a substantial number of defendants were acquitted, and the political and municipal protection alleged at the time was never proven in court. The landing infrastructure it described is still in use.
cases.cite: Audiencia Nacional judgment, Operacion Necora, 1994; Spanish Fiscalia Antidroga historical reporting
cases.drop_reason: The convictions were of the smuggling clans themselves; the political protection alleged was never proven, so no one inside an institution is shown.

cases.n: The Punjab synthetic drug racket
cases.rank: former deputy superintendent of police and political associates
cases.d: A former deputy superintendent of police was convicted over a synthetic drug network valued by Indian investigators in the hundreds of crores, in a case that reached into Punjab's political class through an associate of a serving minister. The wider political allegations were never proven; the police conviction was.
cases.cite: India Enforcement Directorate and Punjab Police case records; Special CBI Court, Mohali judgment
cases.drop_reason: The conviction is of a police officer who ran the racket himself; the link to a minister was never proven, so no outside party inside an institution is shown.

cases.n: Charges brought against a critic of the drug war
cases.d: A senator who had opened hearings into the killings was charged with drug offences in 2017 on the testimony of prison inmates and detained for almost seven years. Every charge was dismissed or ended in acquittal by 2023-2024 after witnesses recanted. This is the inverse of the pattern the rest of this layer records: not a state captured by the trade, but drug law used as an instrument against political opposition. Both are failures of the same institutions.
cases.cite: Philippine Regional Trial Court, Muntinlupa, dismissals and acquittals, 2021-2024; UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention Opinion 2018
cases.drop_reason: The record is false drug charges brought against a senator, which is state misuse of the law, not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: A legislator arrested in a narcotics operation
cases.d: A sitting deputy of the governing coalition was arrested in a police operation involving a cocaine sample, then released; parliamentary immunity was lifted and the case did not proceed to a verdict. Senegal's ports and airport sit on the West African route and the case is the only one to have reached the legislature.
cases.cite: Senegalese Division des Investigations Criminelles case records, 2019; Senegalese National Assembly immunity proceedings
cases.drop_reason: The record is the arrest and release of a deputy with a cocaine sample and no verdict; it shows no network using his office.

cases.n: The 30th Precinct — New York
cases.d: Thirty-three officers of one Harlem precinct were arrested for robbing dealers, reselling seized cocaine and perjury. Around 125 convictions were vacated. The Mollen Commission, reporting the same year, found that the department's internal affairs function had been structured to avoid finding what it eventually found.
cases.cite: Mollen Commission Report on Police Corruption, City of New York, July 1994; S.D.N.Y. prosecutions, 1994-1996
cases.drop_reason: The officers robbed dealers and resold drugs themselves; no outside party placed or paid them.

cases.n: Rampart CRASH — Los Angeles
cases.d: An anti-gang unit that planted evidence, shot unarmed people and dealt in seized narcotics. More than 100 convictions were overturned and the city entered a federal consent decree that ran for twelve years. Several officers were convicted; several convictions were later reversed on appeal, which is part of the record.
cases.cite: Los Angeles Board of Inquiry into the Rampart Area Corruption Incident, 2000; US v. City of Los Angeles consent decree, 2001
cases.drop_reason: The unit's officers committed the crimes themselves; no outside party placed or paid them.

cases.n: The Miami River Cops
cases.d: Officers of the Miami Police Department robbed cocaine loads from the river and resold them; three men drowned fleeing one raid. Nineteen officers were convicted after three federal trials. The department had expanded rapidly in the preceding years with reduced screening, which the subsequent review identified as the enabling condition.
cases.cite: US v. Garcia et al., S.D. Fla., 1986-1988; City of Miami internal review, 1988
cases.drop_reason: The officers stole and resold cocaine themselves; no outside party placed or paid them.

cases.n: The Philadelphia narcotics field unit
cases.d: Six officers were tried federally for robbing dealers and falsifying reports and were acquitted in 2015. The city nonetheless vacated around 1,000 convictions the unit had produced and paid several million dollars in civil settlements. An acquittal and a mass vacatur in the same case is the clearest illustration on this map of how differently the criminal and civil standards resolve.
cases.cite: US v. Liciardello et al., E.D. Pa., verdict May 2015; Philadelphia District Attorney's Office conviction review; city civil settlements
cases.drop_reason: The officers were accused of robbing dealers themselves and were acquitted; no outside party placed or paid them.

cases.n: The Camden narcotics squad
cases.d: Officers planted drugs and fabricated reports; around 200 cases were dismissed and the city later dissolved its police department entirely and rebuilt it under county control. It is one of very few instances anywhere on this map of an institution being abolished rather than reformed.
cases.cite: US v. Bayard et al., D.N.J., 2010; New Jersey Attorney General review; City of Camden police dissolution, 2013
cases.drop_reason: The officers planted drugs and fabricated cases themselves; no outside party placed or paid them.

cases.n: The BAC Nord case — Marseille
cases.d: Officers of the northern Marseille anti-crime brigade were charged with stealing seized cannabis, money and phones from the estates they policed. Convictions followed after a long procedural fight; several charges fell away. The estates in question are the same ones on this map's group layer.
cases.cite: Tribunal correctionnel de Marseille judgments, 2015-2021; Inspection generale de la police nationale reporting
cases.drop_reason: The officers stole seized cannabis and money themselves; no outside party placed or paid them.

cases.n: The Vught escape plot
cases.d: Prosecutors alleged a plan to free the principal defendant in the Marengo trial from the country's highest-security prison, involving contacts around the legal and custodial system. It followed the murders of the trial's crown witness's brother, his lawyer and a journalist. The Dutch state's response was to harden the prison regime, which is a measure of how far the threat was assessed to reach.
cases.cite: Dutch Openbaar Ministerie statements and Rechtbank Amsterdam proceedings, 2022-2024
cases.drop_reason: The record describes an alleged escape plan with vague 'contacts' and names no one inside the prison or legal system working for the organisation.

cases.n: The Noor 1 case
cases.d: Two tonnes of heroin arrived at Piraeus aboard a tanker and part of the load disappeared before it was secured. Convictions followed for the vessel's operators and associates; the Greek parliament held hearings on how the load moved through the port. It remains the largest single seizure in Greek history and the case that established Piraeus as an entry point rather than a transit stop.
cases.cite: Greek Court of Appeal judgments, 2016-2019; Hellenic Parliament committee proceedings
cases.drop_reason: The record describes a heroin load going missing at a port but shows no one inside an institution working for the importers.

cases.n: Police and political links in the Madush case
cases.d: The arrest in Dubai of a Sri Lankan trafficking figure produced photographs of him with police officers, entertainers and politicians at a party, triggering suspensions and an inquiry. He was killed in police custody in 2020 before any of it was tested. The inquiry did not conclude.
cases.cite: Sri Lanka Police Special Investigation Unit reporting, 2019-2020; Sri Lankan Human Rights Commission inquiry into the custodial death
cases.drop_reason: The record is photographs of a trafficker with officials and an inquiry that never concluded; it shows no one inside an institution working for him.

cases.n: The Teknaf yaba campaign and its aftermath
cases.d: The anti-drug campaign on the Myanmar border produced hundreds of killings in police custody or 'crossfire'. A former officer-in-charge of the Teknaf station and several colleagues were sentenced to death in 2022 for the killing of a retired army major who had filmed them. The convictions are for murder; the drug economy the campaign targeted was not disrupted.
cases.cite: Cox's Bazar District and Sessions Judge Court verdict, January 2022; UN OHCHR statements on Bangladesh drug operations
cases.drop_reason: The record is about killings by police in an anti-drug campaign and a murder conviction; it shows no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: The drug war killings
cases.d: Between 6,000 and more than 30,000 people were killed in anti-drug operations from 2016, depending on whether the count is the government's or that of human rights monitors. The International Criminal Court authorised an investigation into them as crimes against humanity in 2021, and the former president was surrendered to the Court in 2025. The trade itself continued through the campaign.
cases.cite: ICC Pre-Trial Chamber authorisation, September 2021, and arrest warrant proceedings, 2025; UN OHCHR report on the Philippines, 2020
cases.drop_reason: The record is about state killings in an anti-drug campaign; it shows no outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Jimmy Cherizier — former police officer, sanctioned gang leader
cases.d: A serving officer of the Haitian National Police until 2018, subsequently the leader of the largest federation of armed groups in Port-au-Prince and the first individual designated under the UN's Haiti sanctions regime in 2022. The trajectory from the force to the federation, rather than any single act, is what this entry records.
cases.cite: UN Security Council Resolution 2653 designation, October 2022; US and Canadian sanctions designations; UN Panel of Experts on Haiti reports
cases.drop_reason: The record traces a former police officer becoming a gang leader after leaving the force; it shows no one inside an institution working for the gang.

cases.n: HSBC
cases.d: Deferred prosecution and $1.9 billion after US authorities found its Mexican affiliate had moved Sinaloa and Norte del Valle proceeds through bulk cash deposits its monitoring did not catch. No individual executive was prosecuted; the DPA expired without charges.
cases.cite: US v. HSBC Bank USA NA, E.D.N.Y., DPA December 2012
cases.rank: Global bank — Mexican affiliate (banks & money transmission)
cases.who: Sinaloa and Norte del Valle cartels
cases.drop_reason: The record is a bank penalised for weak anti-money-laundering monitoring; it shows no crime group placing or paying staff inside it or controlling it.

cases.n: Wachovia
cases.d: Between 2004 and 2007 the bank took some $378 billion from thirteen Mexican currency exchange houses through correspondent accounts, money used among other things to buy aircraft for trafficking. In March 2010 it entered a deferred prosecution agreement in the Southern District of Florida: $110 million forfeited and a $50 million fine, at the time the largest penalty ever imposed for a Bank Secrecy Act violation. Charges were dismissed a year later on compliance with the agreement. No executive was prosecuted, and the sum is a fraction of one year's profit at the bank.
cases.cite: US v. Wachovia Bank N.A., S.D. Fla., deferred prosecution agreement approved 17 March 2010, Case No. 10-20165-CR-LENARD; consent agreements with the OCC and FinCEN; Wells Fargo Form 8-K, 17 March 2010
cases.rank: Global bank — correspondent banking (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: The record is a bank penalised for weak anti-money-laundering monitoring; it shows no crime group placing or paying staff inside it or controlling it.

cases.n: Rabobank National Association
cases.d: The California subsidiary of the Dutch bank pleaded guilty in February 2018 to a felony conspiracy charge and paid $368.7 million, the largest financial penalty in the Southern District of California. The offence is not the laundering itself: the bank admitted conspiring with former executives to obstruct an examination by its regulator, concealing the deficiencies in its anti-money-laundering programme after learning that large numbers of customer transactions indicated trafficking and organised crime. A former vice-president had taken a deferred prosecution agreement two months earlier and was cooperating.
cases.cite: US v. Rabobank National Association, S.D. Cal., guilty plea 7 February 2018 before Magistrate Judge Jill Burkhardt; Department of Justice statement; deferred prosecution agreement with a former vice-president, 14 December 2017
cases.drop_reason: The record is a bank penalised for weak anti-money-laundering monitoring; it shows no crime group placing or paying staff inside it or controlling it.

cases.n: Banamex USA (Citigroup)
cases.d: Forfeited $97 million under a non-prosecution agreement over failures in monitoring remittances to Mexico, where a small compliance staff generated fewer than ten suspicious activity reports against millions of transactions flagged by its own systems.
cases.cite: US DOJ non-prosecution agreement, May 2017
cases.drop_reason: The record is a bank penalised for weak anti-money-laundering monitoring; it shows no crime group placing or paying staff inside it or controlling it.

cases.n: Danske Bank — Estonia branch
cases.d: Pleaded guilty to bank fraud conspiracy and forfeited $2 billion over roughly €200 billion in non-resident flows through a single branch. Laundering infrastructure rather than drug-specific: the same channel serves any proceeds needing distance from their origin.
cases.cite: US v. Danske Bank A/S, S.D.N.Y., plea December 2022
cases.rank: Correspondent banking — non-resident portfolio (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: The record is a bank penalised for weak anti-money-laundering monitoring; it shows no crime group placing or paying staff inside it or controlling it.

cases.n: Western Union
cases.d: The company entered a deferred prosecution agreement on 19 January 2017 admitting willful failure to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering programme and aiding and abetting wire fraud between 2004 and 2012, and forfeited $586 million — the largest forfeiture ever imposed on a money services business — to be used to reimburse defrauded consumers. The specific failure is the one worth recording: it filed suspicious activity reports about its customers but not about its own agents, whom it knew were complicit. Prosecutors said employees fought to keep high-volume agents because of their turnover. Twenty-six agents in the United States and Canada had already been convicted since 2001. New York fined the company a further $60 million in 2018 and France penalised it in 2019.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission deferred prosecution agreement and consent order, 19 January 2017, with the US Attorneys for the Middle and Eastern Districts of Pennsylvania, the Central District of California and the Southern District of Florida; FinCEN civil money penalty; New York Department of Financial Services penalty, 2018
cases.rank: Money transmission — agent network (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: The record is the company failing to police its own agent network; it shows no outside group placing people inside Western Union or steering its decisions.

cases.n: Westpac
cases.d: Paid an A$1.3 billion civil penalty, the largest in Australian history, over roughly 23 million reporting breaches. Cited here as scale evidence on monitoring failure rather than as a drug case.
cases.cite: AUSTRAC v. Westpac Banking Corporation, Federal Court of Australia, 2020
cases.drop_reason: The record is a bank penalised for weak anti-money-laundering monitoring; it shows no crime group placing or paying staff inside it or controlling it.

cases.n: ING Groep
cases.d: Settled with Dutch prosecutors for €775 million after clients used its accounts for laundering over years while customer due diligence was under-resourced. No individuals were charged, a decision later challenged in the Dutch courts.
cases.cite: Openbaar Ministerie settlement, September 2018
cases.rank: Universal bank — client onboarding (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: The record is a bank penalised for weak anti-money-laundering monitoring; it shows no crime group placing or paying staff inside it or controlling it.

cases.n: ABLV Bank
cases.d: Named by FinCEN as a primary money-laundering concern; the designation triggered a deposit run and the bank's self-liquidation within weeks. A demonstration that designation can end an institution without a trial.
cases.cite: FinCEN Section 311 notice of proposed rulemaking, February 2018
cases.rank: Correspondent bank — shell-company clients (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: The record is a US designation that closed a bank; designation alone shows no outside party inside the institution.

cases.n: Binance
cases.d: Pleaded guilty to Bank Secrecy Act and sanctions violations and agreed to $4.3 billion in penalties; its founder pleaded guilty personally. Filings describe transactions with darknet markets and ransomware actors passing through with no effective monitoring.
cases.cite: US v. Binance Holdings Ltd, W.D. Wash., plea November 2023
cases.drop_reason: The record is a crypto exchange's own compliance failures; it shows no outside party placed or paid inside it.

cases.n: BTC-e / Alexander Vinnik
cases.d: An exchange indicted as a laundering vehicle for roughly $4 billion, including narcotics proceeds; its operator was arrested in Greece, convicted in France, and later pleaded guilty in the United States.
cases.cite: US v. BTC-e and Vinnik, N.D. Cal., indictment 2017; US plea 2024
cases.drop_reason: The exchange was run as a laundering service by its own operator; no outside party got inside an institution.

cases.n: Hydra Market
cases.d: Seized by German police with its servers and about €23 million in bitcoin, and sanctioned by the US Treasury the same day. It was the largest darknet drug marketplace, with laundering services sold alongside the product.
cases.cite: BKA seizure and OFAC designation, April 2022
cases.drop_reason: The record is a darknet market run by its own operators and seized by police; no outside party got inside an institution.

cases.n: Tornado Cash
cases.d: Sanctioned by OFAC as a laundering tool; a developer was convicted in the Netherlands in 2024. The US designation was later vacated in part on appeal, leaving the question of whether software can be sanctioned unresolved.
cases.cite: OFAC designation August 2022; Van der Linde ruling, Rechtbank Oost-Brabant, 2024; Van Loon v. Treasury, 5th Cir., 2024
cases.drop_reason: The record is a software tool being sanctioned; no outside party got inside an institution.

cases.n: Amarvel Biotech and other PRC precursor suppliers
cases.d: US indictments charged China-based chemical companies and their executives with trafficking fentanyl precursors, alleging they marketed the chemicals to Mexican buyers and advised on concealing shipments. The companies are outside US jurisdiction in practice.
cases.cite: US v. Amarvel Biotech et al., S.D.N.Y., indictments June 2023
cases.drop_reason: The record is foreign chemical companies selling precursors to cartels, an outside sale, not someone getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Precursor diversion — acetic anhydride
cases.d: The reagent required to convert morphine into heroin is a mainstream industrial chemical. The INCB tracks legitimate trade and repeatedly reports diversion at the distribution layer rather than at manufacture, which is where controls are weakest.
cases.cite: INCB Precursors Report, annual
cases.drop_reason: The record describes diversion of a legal chemical in trade, with no outside party inside any institution.

cases.n: McKesson, Cardinal Health, AmerisourceBergen
cases.d: The three largest US drug distributors agreed to pay about $21 billion over 18 years to settle claims that they shipped opioid volumes their own monitoring systems flagged. Diversion out of a licensed supply chain, not capture by an outside group.
cases.cite: National Prescription Opiate Litigation, N.D. Ohio, settlement July 2021
cases.drop_reason: The record says itself that this was diversion from a licensed supply chain, not capture by an outside group.

cases.n: Purdue Pharma
cases.d: Pleaded guilty to three felonies including conspiracy to defraud the United States and violating the anti-kickback statute, with $8.3 billion in penalties. The Sackler settlement structure was rejected by the Supreme Court in 2024 and renegotiated.
cases.cite: US v. Purdue Pharma LP, D.N.J., plea November 2020; Harrington v. Purdue Pharma, 2024
cases.drop_reason: The crimes were the company's own; no outside party got inside Purdue Pharma.

cases.n: Rochester Drug Co-Operative
cases.d: The first US distributor charged criminally over opioid diversion; its former chief executive was later convicted. Establishing personal criminal liability at this layer took two decades of the epidemic.
cases.cite: US v. Rochester Drug Co-Operative, S.D.N.Y., deferred prosecution 2019; US v. Doud, conviction 2022
cases.drop_reason: The crimes were the company's own; no outside party got inside the distributor.

cases.n: Suncity Group
cases.d: Its chairman was convicted in Macau of running a criminal syndicate and illegal gambling and sentenced to 18 years. Junket credit systems moved value across borders in a form that generated no bank record.
cases.cite: Court of First Instance, Macau SAR, January 2023
cases.drop_reason: The record is a junket operator's chairman convicted of running his own syndicate; no outside party got inside an institution.

cases.n: Crown Resorts
cases.d: A NSW commission found the company unsuitable to hold a licence after evidence that junket partners with organised-crime links used its accounts to move funds; AUSTRAC later obtained a A$450 million penalty.
cases.cite: Bergin Inquiry report, February 2021; AUSTRAC v. Crown, Federal Court, 2023
cases.drop_reason: The record is a casino found unsuitable for letting junket partners use its accounts; it does not show a crime group placing staff inside or controlling Crown.

cases.n: Wynn Las Vegas
cases.d: Forfeited $130 million to resolve allegations it let unlicensed money transmitting move funds for foreign patrons. The mechanism was informal value transfer routed around the banking system entirely.
cases.cite: US DOJ non-prosecution agreement, September 2024
cases.drop_reason: The record is a casino penalised for letting patrons move money informally, a compliance failure with no one placed inside it.

cases.n: Mossack Fonseca
cases.d: The firm at the centre of the Panama Papers; its founders and 26 others were acquitted of money laundering by a Panamanian court in 2024, the judge citing insufficient and improperly gathered evidence. The acquittal is the record and belongs on the map as much as a conviction would.
cases.cite: Duodécimo Juzgado Penal, Panama, verdict June 2024
cases.rank: Offshore formation agent (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: The record is a law firm's founders acquitted of laundering; no outside party got inside an institution.

cases.n: UK company formation — Scottish Limited Partnerships
cases.d: Structures registered in the UK for a few pounds, with no verified beneficial owner until recent reform, appeared repeatedly in laundering schemes traced by journalists and regulators. Not a firm but a jurisdictional product, and the reason gatekeeper prosecutions are so rare.
cases.cite: UK Government SLP consultation and reform; Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023
cases.rank: Corporate registry as a service (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: The record is about a type of UK company structure misused by launderers; no outside party got inside an institution.

cases.n: Phantom Secure
cases.d: Its chief executive pleaded guilty to running a criminal enterprise, the first US prosecution of a company for knowingly supplying encrypted devices to trafficking organisations. Devices were sold with the camera and microphone removed.
cases.cite: US v. Ramos, S.D. Cal., plea October 2018
cases.rank: Encrypted handset provider — chief executive (encrypted communications)
cases.drop_reason: The company sold encrypted phones to criminals, a sale, not someone getting inside the company to steer it.

cases.n: Sky Global / Sky ECC
cases.d: Its chief executive was indicted in the United States for racketeering; Belgian and Dutch police had already penetrated the network, producing about a billion messages that underpinned hundreds of European prosecutions. Five years on the charges remain untried: the company’s distributor spent four years in a French jail before release on bail in 2025 and awaits a trial listed for late 2026, and both men maintain their innocence. The evidence the takedown produced has convicted hundreds of others in the meantime.
cases.cite: US v. Eap, S.D. Cal., indictment March 2021; Belgian federal police operation, March 2021; French proceedings against the distributor, bail June 2025, trial listed late 2026
cases.drop_reason: Sky ECC sold encrypted phones that criminals used and police then hacked; selling a product to criminals is not someone getting inside the company.

cases.n: EncroChat
cases.d: French and Dutch authorities compromised the network's servers in 2020. The resulting material produced thousands of arrests across Europe and remains the single largest evidentiary source in modern European organised-crime prosecutions; its admissibility has been litigated in several countries.
cases.cite: Operation Emma/Lemont, Eurojust, 2020; national admissibility rulings 2021–2024
cases.drop_reason: The record is police hacking an encrypted phone network used by criminals, which is not infiltration.

cases.n: NTR Metals / Elemetal
cases.d: Three traders were convicted or pleaded guilty over a scheme importing roughly $3.6 billion in illegally mined South American gold, laundering drug proceeds through metal purchases. Gold converts cash into an exportable commodity with a legitimate invoice.
cases.cite: US v. Barrage, Granda and Rodriguez, S.D. Fla., pleas 2017–2018
cases.rank: Gold refiner — trading desk (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: The record is the company's own traders laundering through gold purchases; no outside party placed or paid people inside it.

cases.n: Chiquita Brands International
cases.d: Pleaded guilty in US federal court to making payments to the AUC, a designated terrorist organisation and one of Colombia's largest cocaine traffickers, and paid a $25 million fine. A Florida jury found the company liable in a civil case brought by victims' families in 2024.
cases.cite: US v. Chiquita Brands International, D.D.C., plea March 2007; civil verdict S.D. Fla., June 2024
cases.drop_reason: The record is a company paying a paramilitary group; the group did not get people or control inside Chiquita or a state body.

cases.n: Dubai gold trade — Kaloti and the refining chain
cases.d: A DEA-led task force spent three years assembling a case against one of the world’s largest gold traders and refiners, concluding it bought metal from sellers suspected of laundering for drug traffickers, often paying cash and wiring funds for suspect clients. Treasury abandoned the case. An auditor’s 2012 inspection had already found more than $5.2 billion in cash-for-gold deals, about 45 percent of the firm’s business that year, and 2.4 tonnes taken in more than a thousand transactions from customers who provided no paperwork; the partner who reported it was forced out and sued his firm. Dubai’s regulator removed the refinery from its approved list in 2015. The company denies the allegations and continues to trade.
cases.cite: Ernst & Young inspection report, 2012, and whistleblower disclosure, 2014; DMCC delisting, 2015; ICIJ FinCEN Files reporting on the abandoned Treasury case, 2020-2024
cases.rank: Gold refining and bullion trading — cash purchase (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: The record is a gold trader buying from suspect sellers and failing checks; it shows no outside party placed inside or controlling the firm.

cases.n: Lebanese Canadian Bank
cases.d: Named by FinCEN as a primary money-laundering concern for moving proceeds of a cocaine network that shipped through West Africa and settled its accounts by buying used cars in the United States for resale in Africa. The bank's assets were sold and its successor forfeited $102 million; no banker was prosecuted.
cases.cite: FinCEN Section 311 finding, February 2011; US v. Lebanese Canadian Bank SAL, S.D.N.Y., settlement August 2013
cases.rank: Retail and correspondent bank — used-car trade finance (banks & money transmission)
