cases.drop_reason: Countries added to a FATF monitoring list, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: Correspondent banking as the enforcement mechanism
cases.d: When FATF names a jurisdiction, correspondent banks worldwide restrict or price in the risk regardless of whether their own regulator requires it, which is how a listing bites without any prosecution. The UAE's grey listing in 2022 and removal in 2024 moved the cost of moving money through Dubai in both directions without a single case being tried.
cases.cite: FATF listing and delisting decisions, 2022 and 2024; correspondent banking practice
cases.rank: Bank-to-bank relationships as a control point (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: A description of how correspondent banks react to FATF listings, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: The Akwesasne cross-border route
cases.d: Three dual Canadian-American citizens were arrested in July 2026 over an international trafficking operation running through Akwesasne, a territory whose land crosses the US-Canada border and two Canadian provinces. The investigation required US, Canadian and tribal law enforcement to act jointly, which is the difficulty the route exploits: jurisdiction changes several times inside a few kilometres.
cases.cite: US v. Lazore, Arquette and Ransom, N.D.N.Y., arrests 30 July 2026
cases.rank: Territory straddling an international boundary (shipping, freight & ports)
cases.drop_reason: A cross-border smuggling route and arrests; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: Balloons over the Jordanian border
cases.d: With Syrian production disrupted after December 2024, smugglers moved captagon south first on quadcopter drones and, when those proved expensive and low-yield, on large heavy-lift helium balloons carrying GPS guidance and timed remote-release mechanisms that drop the payload once across the border. Launching from the empty Hamad desert removed the need for inhabited areas or local help. Jordan intercepted 21 attempts from Sweida between January and July 2025 and 128 more between July 2025 and April 2026, and has struck inside Syria five times since Assad fell, most recently with F-16s against six locations on 3 May 2026. At least 46 million pills have been intercepted since mid-2025, most of them off balloons. When the state that ran a trade stops running it, the method improves rather than the volume falling.
cases.cite: Charles Lister, Middle East Institute, data published in New Lines Magazine, May 2026; Jordanian Armed Forces 'Operation Jordanian Deterrence' statements, 3 May 2026; SANA and Arab News reporting, 14 May 2026
cases.rank: GPS-guided helium balloons with timed release (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: Smuggling captagon by balloon across a border; no one inside an institution.

cases.n: Sweida after the fall
cases.d: Once a transit route for narcotics moving to Jordan and the Gulf, Sweida became the country's principal drug-trafficking centre after December 2024, with laboratories and smuggling routes held by local armed factions rather than the state. Syria's interior ministry said domestic production was virtually eradicated by late 2025 after raids on former regime facilities, and UNODC recorded fifteen industrial-scale laboratories and thirteen smaller storage sites dismantled within a year; a significant share of what now moves through Sweida arrives from Lebanon instead. Under Assad the model was centralised and industrial, tied to regime and militia structures. What replaced it is smaller, dispersed and harder to reach by conventional border enforcement — 177 million tablets were intercepted across the Arab region between December 2024 and December 2025.
cases.cite: Middle East Eye, June 2026; UNODC research paper, December 2025; Syrian Ministry of Interior statements, late 2025; Karam Shaar Advisory analysis reported by Arab News, May 2026
cases.rank: Production relocating from state facilities to a province (chemicals & precursors)
cases.drop_reason: Drug production by local armed factions after Assad's fall; no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: J and C Import and Central Logistica de Servicios
cases.d: Two Guatemala-based import and export companies designated on 23 April 2026 within a single 23-target action against a synthetic opioid procurement network tied to the Sinaloa Cartel. One received 116 kilograms of N-Boc-4-Piperidone over two months, sourced from Indian suppliers designated in the same action; the other shipped both precursors and finished fentanyl. The action names every stage at once — Indian chemical suppliers, a Guatemalan broker and his freight companies, and Mexican precursor brokers arrested a month earlier — so the supply chain is described as a chain rather than as separate national problems.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release sb0468 and OFAC designations under E.O. 14059, 23 April 2026
cases.rank: Guatemala City import-export firms on the precursor route (chemicals & precursors)
cases.drop_reason: Freight companies openly supplying chemicals to a cartel's supply chain; sales, not infiltration.

cases.n: Abou Merhi Group — the Joumaa maritime network
cases.d: Four Lebanese nationals, two Germans and eleven companies were designated in October 2015 for supporting the Joumaa organisation, which Treasury describes as a laundering ring benefiting Hezbollah. At the centre is a Lebanese holding company with subsidiaries across Africa, the Middle East and Europe, and five named vessels; the individuals were listed for their management roles rather than for handling drugs, two of them the owner's children. The vessels carried used cars for the network, which is the mechanism — value moves in the price and paperwork of goods on ships the network itself owns. Lebanese media reported in March 2016 that the family and companies had been cleared; Treasury said that was false and that all remained designated. The trafficker the action was built around, indicted in Virginia in 2011 over 85 tonnes of cocaine and more than $250 million laundered, remains a fugitive.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release jl0196, OFAC Kingpin Act designations, October 2015, coordinated with DEA and Customs and Border Protection; Joumaa organisation designated 26 January 2011; indictment E.D. Va., November 2011; Treasury statement rebutting reports of clearance, March 2016
cases.rank: Shipping holding company and five named vessels (shipping, freight & ports)
cases.drop_reason: A shipping group designated for supporting a laundering network; the record shows no outside party placed inside or controlling an institution.

cases.n: The 2026 designation rate
cases.d: By mid-July 2026 the administration had charged at least 291 individuals for cartel-related activity and added more than 380 Latin American individuals and entities to the sanctions list. Five criminal groups were designated foreign terrorist organisations in under seven weeks: two Brazilian groups on 5 June, an Ecuadorian gang on 1 July, and two Mexican groups on 16 July. April alone brought 172 additions and 30 vessels identified as blocked property. The pace matters for reading this layer. A designation in 2015 marked an organisation as exceptional; a designation in 2026 places it among hundreds listed the same year, and the compliance consequence has broadened faster than any adjudication behind it.
cases.cite: Miller & Chevalier, Where FTO-Designated Cartels Operate: 2026 Update, July 2026; Hughes Hubbard sanctions summary, April 2026; State Department FTO designations of 5 June, 1 July and 16 July 2026
cases.rank: The pace of listing, as context for the layer (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: Statistics on the pace of US designations, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: Chone Killers and the Ecuadorian FTO tranche
cases.d: Designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization and Specially Designated Global Terrorist on 1 July 2026 over attacks on civilians, police and government officials including assassinations. It is the third Ecuadorian organisation designated in ten months, after Los Choneros and Los Lobos in September 2025, and it was listed separately from the parent group it split from in 2020. Ecuador now carries more designated organisations than most producing states, in a country that appeared in almost no enforcement record a decade ago.
cases.cite: US Department of State, Terrorist Designation of Chone Killers, 1 July 2026; earlier designations of Los Choneros and Los Lobos, 4 September 2025
cases.rank: Coastal gang designated as a terrorist organisation (shipping, freight & ports)
cases.drop_reason: A gang designated as a terrorist organisation; designation alone is not infiltration.

cases.n: The Canaries-Azores corridor
cases.d: A two-week operation led by the Spanish Guardia Civil and coordinated through Europol, 13-26 April 2026, worked the eastern Atlantic between the Canaries and the Azores: 11 tonnes of cocaine and 8.5 of hashish seized, eight vessels intercepted, 54 arrests. The method is staged. Mother vessels — container ships, bulk carriers, small non-commercial craft — collect in Latin America and run hundreds to thousands of nautical miles into international waters; cargo moves mid-ocean onto fast long-range boats; a final transfer puts it into small craft landing at remote Portuguese and Spanish coastline. Europol calls these fragmented maritime routes, and the fragmentation is the purpose: no single vessel or party carries the whole exposure. It is the direct answer to the port enforcement recorded elsewhere on this layer — if terminals are watched, the cargo never enters one.
cases.cite: Europol newsroom release, Atlantic operation 13-26 April 2026, led by the Spanish Guardia Civil with Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, UK and US DEA participation
cases.rank: Mother vessels, mid-ocean transfers and landing craft (shipping, freight & ports)
cases.drop_reason: A maritime smuggling operation and seizures; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: Eight tonnes in a banana shipment
cases.d: 8,064 kilograms of cocaine were found on 13 July 2023 in twelve pallets of bananas shipped from Ecuador via Panama, the largest seizure in Dutch history and almost double the previous record of 4.5 tonnes. Sniffer dogs found it and a container scan confirmed it; the discovery was withheld for a month for the investigation, and no arrests had been made when it was announced. The customs chief noted that recent seizures had been much smaller, as though smugglers were spreading their risk — the fragmentation the Atlantic operation would document three years later. Dutch seizures fell from 45.5 tonnes in 2023 to about 26 in 2024, while Vlissingen rose slightly.
cases.cite: Rotterdam Public Prosecution Service statement, 10 August 2023, seizure of 13 July 2023; Dutch customs and police annual seizure figures, January 2025
cases.rank: Container terminal and a fruit consignment (shipping, freight & ports)
cases.drop_reason: A record cocaine seizure with no arrests and no insider named.

cases.n: Dutch brokers inside Colombian supply chains
cases.d: One of three actions Europol announced together in December 2025: a Dutch-led network embedded in Colombian supply chains, a Brazilian maritime operation and a Greek at-sea transfer group — organisers, transport and receivers taken as one chain rather than three cases. The Dutch suspect, based in Ibiza and travelling frequently, is alleged to have organised shipments with his two sons using direct access to high-level Colombian traffickers. The case first surfaced in Sky ECC material and was developed years later, which is the pattern the Sky Global entry records: the archive keeps producing prosecutions long after the takedown.
cases.cite: Europol newsroom, three coordinated cocaine supply-chain actions, December 2025; case originating in Sky ECC material
cases.rank: A broker with direct access to Colombian suppliers (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: A trafficking network with contacts among Colombian traffickers; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: The Rzeszow logistical hub
cases.d: Twenty suspects were arrested in Czechia, Slovakia and Ukraine on 18 June 2026 over a network that bought methamphetamine in Western Europe, moved it through Czechia to a logistical hub at Rzeszow in Poland, then on to Slovakia for distribution and to Uzhhorod in western Ukraine. Investigators put the traffic at about 50 kilograms of methamphetamine and two of cocaine, close to 950,000 euros in proceeds from the methamphetamine alone. The group ran separate units for procurement, transport, distribution and financial flows, and changed concealment methods continuously, carrying loads in passenger cars and buses. The direction is the finding: almost every route on this map runs toward Western Europe, and this one runs out of it.
cases.cite: Europol and Eurojust press releases, 7-8 July 2026, on the joint investigation team of Czech, Slovak and Ukrainian authorities; action day 18 June 2026
cases.rank: Poland as a staging point on a west-to-east corridor (encrypted communications)
cases.drop_reason: A methamphetamine distribution network; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: Constructora FR de Venezuela
cases.d: A real estate construction company with offices in Caracas and Puerto La Cruz, designated on 13 September 2012 with its founder, director and majority shareholder. Treasury described him moving significant quantities of cocaine each year by aircraft from Venezuela to Africa and by sea from Ecuador to Mexico, and laundering the proceeds through the Venezuelan economy. He had been indicted in the Southern District of Florida in December 2011, and was arrested in Panama City and handed to US authorities the day after the designation. It is the earliest Venezuelan company on this layer and it predates by thirteen years the designation of the network the state itself is now said to run.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation and notice, 13 September 2012; indictment S.D. Fla., 13 December 2011; arrest in Panama City and transfer to US custody, 14 September 2012
cases.rank: Real estate construction company, Caracas and Puerto La Cruz (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: A trafficker laundering money through his own construction company; no outside party.

cases.n: The Tren de Aragua support network
cases.d: Designated a foreign terrorist organisation in February 2025, its leaders sanctioned in June and July, and a network of individuals and entities designated in December for providing material support. The sequence is the standard shape of a designation campaign: the organisation first, then the people, then the businesses that carry the money.
cases.cite: US Department of State FTO designation, 20 February 2025; OFAC designations, June, July and December 2025
cases.rank: Individuals and entities providing material support (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: A sequence of US designations against a gang; designation alone is not infiltration.

cases.n: Six states, one refusal, one contrary vote
cases.d: After the United States listed the Venezuelan military network, Ecuador and Paraguay declared it a terrorist organisation in August 2025 and Argentina, Peru and the Dominican Republic followed. Colombia's president said the cartel does not appear in any of the country's drug investigations and called it an invention; on 17 September 2025 the opposition-majority Senate voted, after an intense debate, to declare it a terrorist organisation anyway and urged the president to honour Colombia's treaty commitments. Academics have also questioned the label, noting that a cartel by definition sets prices and regulates trade. The same body of evidence produced designations in six countries, a refusal in one government and a contrary vote in that government's own legislature.
cases.cite: National designations by Ecuador, Paraguay, Argentina, Peru and the Dominican Republic, 2025; Colombian Senate plenary proposition, 17 September 2025, and presidential statements, September 2025; US State Department FTO designation announced 16 November 2025, effective 24 November
cases.rank: National designations following the US listing (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: Countries' differing decisions on designating a group, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: Strikes on vessels at sea
cases.d: On 2 September 2025 the US military struck a vessel said to be carrying drugs from Venezuela, killing eleven people reported to be Tren de Aragua members; strikes continued through September, October and December, and in early October the United States declared itself in an armed conflict with drug cartels. A Senate bill requiring congressional approval for further strikes was defeated on 8 October, and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights called for an investigation on 31 October. Every other maritime record on this layer ends in a seizure, a crew list and a court file. These end with none of the three.
cases.cite: Congressional Research Service, Venezuela: Political Crisis and U.S. Policy (IF10230), updated 2025-2026; UN High Commissioner for Human Rights statement, 31 October 2025; US Senate vote, 8 October 2025
cases.rank: Military strikes replacing interdiction (shipping, freight & ports)
cases.drop_reason: US military strikes on boats at sea, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: Oil licences alongside the designations
cases.d: Treasury revoked and then granted a restricted licence to a US oil major in 2025, reportedly halving what it could export, then in July permitted its joint ventures to resume operations while barring cash payments to the Venezuelan government. The Cartel de los Soles was designated a global terrorist in July 2025 and a foreign terrorist organisation in November. Three days after Maduro's capture on 3 January 2026, an announced energy deal had the United States market and sell Venezuelan oil into US-controlled accounts, with roughly $3 billion in sanctioned oil to be handed over; OFAC has issued new licences to other companies and is reported to be weighing an expanded one. The layer records companies barred from the American financial system; here the same authority admits others to a market it has named as narco-terrorist.
cases.cite: Congressional Research Service, Venezuela: Overview of U.S. Sanctions Policy (IF10715) and Venezuela: Political Crisis and U.S. Policy (IF10230), 2025-2026
cases.rank: Export licences issued into a designated market (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: US oil licensing policy toward Venezuela, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: Grupo MBS and the Maputo Shopping Centre
cases.d: Three businesses were designated on 1 June 2010, the same day President Obama identified their owner as a Mozambican drug kingpin: a family-owned conglomerate, a retail store and a shopping mall in the capital. He was among the country's most prominent businessmen, with reported links to the ruling party. The designation reached him through commerce rather than a court: within a month three banks had closed their branches inside his shopping centre, which is the correspondent-banking effect operating at street level. He was never prosecuted, and in 2014 was abducted at gunpoint from the shopping centre's own yard. Mozambique's protected heroin corridor, recorded separately on this map, ran through the same years.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release TG-729 and OFAC Kingpin Act designations, 1 June 2010; Presidential identification, 1 June 2010; State Department International Narcotics Control Strategy Report, 2010; Mail & Guardian, July 2010; reporting on the 2014 abduction
cases.rank: Family conglomerate, a retail store and a shopping mall (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: A businessman designated as a drug kingpin over his own companies; the record shows no one placed inside an institution.

cases.n: Botanica 2000 — a pharmacy making pills
cases.d: A chemist running clandestine laboratories in Guadalajara obtained precursors for the Chapitos faction and used his own pharmacy to produce fentanyl-laced pills for shipment to the United States. OFAC's own listing files the company under retail sale of pharmaceutical and medical goods, cosmetics and toilet articles — the designation and the trade classification describe the same premises. He was arrested at Madrid airport in November 2025, detained immediately after passport control off a flight from Mexico City, and designated on 23 April 2026 in the same 23-target action as the Indian suppliers and the Guatemalan freight companies. A licensed outlet is both a legitimate purchaser of chemicals and a plausible place for pills to exist.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release sb0468 and OFAC designations under E.O. 14059 and E.O. 13224 as amended, 23 April 2026; arrest in Madrid, November 2025
cases.rank: Licensed retail pharmacy used as a pill press (chemicals & precursors)
cases.drop_reason: A chemist using his own pharmacy to make pills; no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Fictitious trading and the HK$8.9 billion file
cases.d: Hong Kong Customs identified a laundering operation running about HK$8.9 billion through fictitious trading activity, announced in December 2025, alongside a separate syndicate handling HK$2.6 billion broken up in September. The instrument is the Organized and Serious Crimes Ordinance, which criminalises dealing with property a person had reasonable grounds to believe was crime proceeds — a lower threshold than proving knowledge, and the reason company accounts rather than individuals carry the charge here.
cases.cite: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department announcements, 16 September and 23 December 2025; Organized and Serious Crimes Ordinance, Cap. 455
cases.rank: Trading companies invoicing goods that never moved (lawyers, brokers & formation agents), Hong Kong
cases.drop_reason: A laundering operation through fake trading, with no insider or captured institution.

cases.n: Personal bank accounts after a narcotics seizure
cases.d: Two Customs files traced HK$53 million and HK$61 million of suspicious transactions through the personal accounts of people already arrested in drug cases, the money moving through ordinary retail banking rather than any corporate structure. Customs pairs each announcement with a warning that lending an account to move money from unknown sources is itself the offence, which is what the layer records: the smallest available laundering unit is a person with a bank card.
cases.cite: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department announcements, 20 November 2024 and 23 May 2025
cases.rank: Individual accounts used as laundering channels (banks & money transmission), Hong Kong
cases.drop_reason: Laundering through personal bank accounts; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: The Chinese money laundering organisation model
cases.d: Six defendants pleaded guilty to laundering more than $92 million, largely proceeds of drugs imported through Mexico. The structure explains why these networks displaced older methods: Chinese nationals wanting to move money out of China buy cartel dollars already in the United States, so the cash never crosses a border and no wire is sent. The final three pleas were entered in July 2025.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice and IRS Criminal Investigation, guilty pleas concluding July 2025
cases.rank: Brokerage matching cash holders to currency buyers (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: A money-laundering method using cash swaps; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: The Anbar underground and the Syrian border
cases.d: Captagon seizures rose about 3,380 percent between 2019 and 2023, with more than four tonnes taken in 2023 alone and 17,500 kilograms found buried in Anbar in 2024; a single day in May 2024 produced 2.5 million pills. Most of it crosses a 600-kilometre border with Syria. Iraq has built the apparatus around it — a national narcotics authority since 2017, a 2023-2025 strategy, mandatory drug testing for government employees — and the country has moved from transit route to production site while that was happening. The state's own institutions are the test case: testing was extended to teachers and officials, which is an admission about where the trade had reached.
cases.cite: UNODC seizure data 2019-2023; Iraqi Ministry of Interior announcements, May 2024 and 2025; New Lines Institute analyses, 2026
cases.rank: Border crossings and storage on a 600km frontier (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: Captagon seizures and Iraq's drug policy; the record names no one placed inside an institution.

cases.n: The Maraya and Alwefaq Ltd
cases.d: Treasury designated a Libyan operator, two associates, a Malta-based company and the vessel itself for smuggling fuel out of Libya and moving drugs through it to Malta, running between the port of Zuwarah and Hurd's Bank just outside Maltese territorial waters, a known transfer point for illicit maritime cargo. The finding worth recording is the paperwork: he kept all official documentation clear of his name while organising the operation. The company is the registered owner and he is not on it.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release sm1083 and OFAC designations under E.O. 13726, 2020
cases.rank: A vessel and a Malta-registered company (shipping, freight & ports)
cases.drop_reason: Fuel and drug smuggling by sea through a shell company; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: Subsidised fuel and the two governments
cases.d: Fuel is bought by Libyan authorities at international prices, sold domestically at a heavy subsidy — official price around 0.15 dinars a litre against two or three on the black market — and resold abroad. Crisis Group's assessment is that the racket helps hold the peace between rival elites in Tripoli and Benghazi, both of which tap the unofficial income. Security Council measures allow interdiction if the designated Libyan government contact signals a cargo is suspect; no such signal has arrived in years, which the analysis attributes to the complicity of government agencies and their political bosses. The instrument exists and the state that must trigger it is the beneficiary.
cases.cite: International Crisis Group, Watch List 2026 Spring Edition, March 2026; UN Security Council Resolutions 2146 (2014) and 2362 (2017)
cases.rank: State fuel subsidy resold abroad (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: Fuel subsidy smuggling benefiting Libya's own officials; no outside party getting inside.

cases.n: Maltese and Libyan oil brokers
cases.d: Six individuals, 24 entities and seven vessels were designated in 2018 for smuggling Libyan oil to Europe, the designees Maltese, Libyan and Egyptian. It belongs beside the drug records rather than apart from them: the same routes, ports and vessels carry both, and Treasury's Libya designations reach fuel and narcotics through one executive order.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release sm0298 and OFAC designations under E.O. 13726, 2018
cases.rank: Brokers, companies and vessels moving Libyan oil (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: Oil smuggling designations; smuggling with no one inside an institution.

cases.n: Execution as the enforcement instrument
cases.d: Saudi Arabia executed 330 people in 2024, up from 172 the year before and 196 in 2022, a large share for drug offences; Amnesty recorded 37 executions for drug crimes in a single month, 34 of them foreign nationals from Egypt, Ethiopia, Jordan, Nigeria, Pakistan, Somalia and Syria. The kingdom is the destination market for the captagon this map tracks from Syria and Lebanon through Jordan and Iraq. The record at the receiving end consists almost entirely of executed couriers, most of them foreign; no Saudi official appears in any adjudicated case on this layer. Severity and capture reach different people.
cases.cite: Amnesty International execution figures, 2025; Reprieve compilation verified by Reuters; Saudi Ministry of Interior and Saudi Press Agency announcements, 2024-2026
cases.rank: Capital punishment applied to couriers (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: Saudi execution statistics, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: Captagon plants in Khartoum and Blue Nile
cases.d: Manufacturing facilities have been identified at Khartoum, Blue Nile and Jabal Awliya, with both foreign and domestic actors involved, and Kassala has become a trafficking hub with product entering through the eastern borders and the Red Sea ports. The Rapid Support Forces and Darfur rebel movements are implicated in the trade. Captagon's appeal here is the same as everywhere on this map: it mimics legal medicine closely enough to be disguised as one. Sudan scores 8.50 on state-embedded actors and produces no adjudicated case at all.
cases.cite: GI-TOC Organized Crime Index country profile for Sudan, 2025; ENACT Africa reporting
cases.rank: Manufacturing sites and a Red Sea entry corridor (chemicals & precursors)
cases.drop_reason: Captagon production in Sudan; the record names no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: The tramadol chain from India through Kinshasa
cases.d: Shipments originate with Indian manufacturers and travel through the Democratic Republic of Congo before reaching the Central African Republic, where high-dose tablets are distributed under a local name meaning the cocaine of the poor. Miners at the gold operations take it to work long hours and fighters take it in combat. University research has linked rising consumption to a near-20 percent increase in deaths from fighting over mining areas, around 500 in a year. It is the same legal-pharmaceutical origin as the Indian export records on this layer, arriving at the opposite end of the chain.
cases.cite: Wall Street Journal reporting, 12 July 2026; Uppsala University research on tramadol consumption and mining violence; GI-TOC Central Africa Observatory, June 2026
cases.rank: Pharmaceutical shipments repurposed as a stimulant (pharmaceutical supply)
cases.drop_reason: A tramadol trafficking chain; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: Gold, timber and a fuel monopoly
cases.d: Illicit gold exports are estimated at $180 million a year, moved abroad on military cargo aircraft registered in the country and laundered through UAE-linked exporters, with a government-backed fuel monopoly generating a further $17.5 to $30 million in unjustified profits annually. The drug revenue is the smaller line and the one that buys weapons. GI-TOC's assessment is that high-ranking political and military figures, co-opted criminal actors and transnational groups have aligned to consolidate control over the country's criminal markets.
cases.cite: GI-TOC Central Africa Observatory report, June 2026; Wall Street Journal reporting, July 2026
cases.rank: Extractive revenue alongside the drug trade (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: Illicit gold, timber and fuel profits; the record describes no specific outside party placed inside an institution.

cases.n: Standard Chartered
cases.d: Penalised repeatedly by US and UK authorities over sanctions and anti-money-laundering failures, with settlements in 2012 and again in 2019 totalling well over a billion dollars, and a deferred prosecution agreement extended three times because the monitor kept finding the controls inadequate. The failures were in the correspondent channel that trade-based laundering depends on.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice deferred prosecution agreements, 2012 and 2019; UK Financial Conduct Authority final notice, April 2019
cases.rank: Correspondent and trade bank (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: A bank penalised for weak sanctions and money-laundering controls; no outside party inside it.

cases.n: Commonwealth Bank of Australia
cases.d: Paid A$700 million, then the largest civil penalty in Australian corporate history, after admitting more than 53,000 breaches of anti-money-laundering law. A software update disabled the automatic reporting on its intelligent deposit machines and the failure went unnoticed for three years, during which syndicates fed cash through them in structured amounts.
cases.cite: AUSTRAC v Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Federal Court of Australia, settlement June 2018
cases.rank: Retail bank — deposit machines (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: A bank fined for failed automatic reporting on deposit machines; no outside party inside it.

cases.n: Raiffeisen Bank International
cases.d: Subject to European Central Bank supervisory pressure and US scrutiny over its Russian and eastern European exposure and its correspondent relationships. No penalty has been imposed for drug-proceeds laundering specifically. It is on this map because Vienna is the regional correspondent hub for the Balkan corridor and the supervisory record is open rather than closed.
cases.cite: European Central Bank supervisory requirements, 2023-2024; US Treasury correspondence reported by the bank in filings
cases.rank: Regional and correspondent bank (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: Supervisory pressure on a bank with no penalty and no insider named.

cases.n: Nordea and SEB — the Baltic branches
cases.d: Both were found by journalists and by Baltic regulators to have processed very large non-resident flows through Estonian and Latvian branches during the same period as Danske. Swedish and Estonian regulators fined and censured the successor entities. The flows were mixed-origin; the share attributable to narcotics has never been separated out and this map does not claim it.
cases.cite: Swedish Finansinspektionen and Estonian Finantsinspektsioon decisions, 2019-2020; European Banking Authority review
cases.rank: Nordic banks — Baltic branch networks (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: Banks censured for weak controls on non-resident flows; no outside party inside them.

cases.n: Pilatus Bank
cases.d: Its licence was withdrawn after its owner was arrested in the United States; he was convicted in 2021 of running a scheme to evade Iran sanctions through the bank. Malta's failure to act on earlier warnings was one of the findings that put the country on the FATF grey list in 2021.
cases.cite: US v. Sadr Hashemi Nejad, S.D.N.Y., conviction 2020 (later vacated on prosecutorial grounds); European Central Bank licence withdrawal, November 2018; FATF plenary decisions
cases.drop_reason: A bank owner's own sanctions evasion; no outside party getting inside.

cases.n: Versobank
cases.d: Licence withdrawn by the European Central Bank on the Estonian regulator's proposal for long-running and serious anti-money-laundering failures across a largely non-resident client base. It is the second Baltic bank closed by supervisors within months, the other being ABLV, and together they mark the point at which the Baltic non-resident channel was shut by regulators rather than by courts.
cases.cite: European Central Bank licence withdrawal decision, March 2018; Estonian Finantsinspektsioon findings
cases.drop_reason: A bank closed for weak money-laundering controls; no outside party inside it.

cases.n: Exchange houses in the OFAC designations
cases.d: Successive OFAC actions have designated Gulf-based exchange houses moving funds for sanctioned and trafficking networks, alongside the Afghan hawala designations already on this map. The UAE was itself grey-listed by FATF from 2022 to 2024. Dubai's role as the settlement point for several networks mapped elsewhere here rests on this infrastructure.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, 2021-2024; FATF plenary listings, March 2022 and February 2024
cases.rank: Money exchange and hawala houses (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: Exchange houses designated for moving funds; service provision, not infiltration.

cases.n: The black market peso exchange
cases.d: Not a company: the oldest and still the largest mechanism for repatriating US drug proceeds, in which the dollars are sold to importers who need them and the peso equivalent is paid to the trafficker at home. Nothing crosses a border as money. It has survived every generation of anti-money-laundering rules because the transactions on each leg are ordinary trade.
cases.cite: US Treasury FinCEN advisories on trade-based money laundering; UNODC and GAFILAT typology reporting
cases.rank: Trade-based value transfer mechanism (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: A description of a laundering method, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: Correspondent de-risking in the Caribbean
cases.d: Global banks have withdrawn correspondent relationships from small Caribbean jurisdictions faster than from anywhere else, on compliance-cost grounds. The consequence is that legitimate remittance and trade flows move to less transparent channels, while the trafficking flows the withdrawal was meant to address were never dependent on those relationships in the first place.
cases.cite: IMF and World Bank correspondent banking withdrawal reporting; Caribbean Financial Action Task Force statements; Financial Stability Board reviews
cases.drop_reason: Global banks withdrawing services from the Caribbean, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: Suex OU
cases.d: The first cryptocurrency exchange ever designated by OFAC. Treasury found that more than forty per cent of its known transaction history involved illicit actors, including darknet market and ransomware proceeds. Nominally Czech-registered, operationally Russian.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designation, September 2021
cases.drop_reason: A crypto exchange designated for serving illicit users; selling a service, not infiltration.

cases.n: Chatex
cases.d: Designated two months after Suex as a successor operation sharing infrastructure with it, along with three supporting companies in Latvia and Estonia. The pattern of a designated exchange reappearing under a new name within weeks is the central enforcement problem in this sector.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designation, November 2021
cases.rank: Crypto exchange and messaging bot (crypto & digital rails)
cases.drop_reason: A successor crypto exchange designated; selling a service, not infiltration.

cases.n: Blender.io and Sinbad.io
cases.d: Blender was the first mixer designated by OFAC, in May 2022; it shut down and reappeared as Sinbad, which was designated in turn in November 2023 and taken down by Dutch and Finnish police. Mixers are the point at which darknet drug proceeds and state-sponsored theft proceeds use the same rails.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, May 2022 and November 2023; Dutch FIOD and Finnish NBI takedown, November 2023
cases.drop_reason: Crypto mixers designated and taken down; selling a service, not infiltration.

cases.n: Genesis Market
cases.d: Taken down in April 2023 by an operation across seventeen countries and simultaneously designated by OFAC. It sold the account access used to move and cash out proceeds rather than the drugs themselves, which is why it belongs in this layer: the laundering supply chain has its own market.
cases.cite: Operation Cookie Monster, Europol coordination, April 2023; US Treasury OFAC designation, April 2023
cases.drop_reason: A criminal marketplace taken down by police; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: Bohemia, Cannabia and Monopoly
cases.d: Three of the largest remaining darknet drug markets, closed between 2023 and 2024 by Dutch, German and US operations. Monopoly's takedown fed Operation SpecTor, which produced 288 arrests across nine countries — the largest darknet drug enforcement action recorded.
cases.cite: Dutch Politie and Openbaar Ministerie announcements, 2023-2024; Europol Operation SpecTor, May 2023; German BKA operations
cases.drop_reason: Darknet drug markets closed by police; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: Huione Guarantee
cases.d: A messaging-based marketplace where laundering, stolen data and fraud services were bought with a parent company acting as escrow, processing tens of billions of dollars before it announced its own closure in May 2025 following the FinCEN action against its parent. It sat at the junction of the compound fraud economy and the regional drug proceeds channel.
cases.cite: FinCEN section 311 final rule on Huione Group, May 2025; Elliptic and Chainalysis transaction analysis
cases.drop_reason: A criminal marketplace closed after regulatory action; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: Dollar stablecoin settlement in Southeast Asia
cases.d: UNODC's 2024 regional assessment identified a dollar stablecoin on a low-fee chain as the preferred settlement instrument for Southeast Asian laundering networks and compound operators, moving value between the fraud economy, the underground banking system and the drug proceeds channel. Issuers have frozen substantial balances at law enforcement request and no enforcement action has been taken against any of them. The finding is about what the instrument is used for, not about who issues it.
cases.cite: UNODC Casinos, Money Laundering, Underground Banking and Transnational Organized Crime in East and Southeast Asia, January 2024
cases.rank: Dollar-denominated stablecoin on a low-fee chain (crypto & digital rails)
cases.drop_reason: A stablecoin used by launderers; use of a product, not infiltration.

cases.n: Cryptex and PM2BTC
cases.d: Designated by OFAC and named in US indictments in September 2024 as part of a Russian-based cash-out infrastructure; servers were seized in coordination with Dutch authorities. The same operation named an individual as a laundering broker for multiple criminal categories rather than for one trade.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC and FinCEN actions, September 2024; US Department of Justice indictments; Dutch police server seizures
cases.rank: Exchange and payment processor (crypto & digital rails)
cases.drop_reason: Crypto cash-out services designated; selling a service, not infiltration.

cases.n: Samourai Wallet
cases.d: Its founders were charged in April 2024 with conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business and to launder proceeds, over a coin-mixing feature. The case is the sharpest test in this layer of where a software tool ends and a money services business begins, and it is unresolved.
cases.cite: US v. Rodriguez and Hill, S.D.N.Y., indictment April 2024
cases.rank: Non-custodial wallet and mixing service (crypto & digital rails)
cases.drop_reason: Charges over a coin-mixing software feature; selling a tool, not infiltration.

cases.n: The container lines
cases.d: The world's largest carriers appear repeatedly as the vessel owner in multi-tonne seizures and are almost never charged, because the load is inserted and extracted by shore-side crews without the line's knowledge. Several have joined port-security partnerships and fund scanning. The entry records where the volume physically travels, not an allegation against the carriers.
cases.cite: Europol and World Customs Organization port security reporting; national seizure records; industry security programme documentation
cases.drop_reason: Shipping lines whose containers are used without their knowledge, explicitly not an allegation of infiltration.

cases.n: The Colon Free Zone
cases.d: The largest free zone in the Americas and the second largest in the world, through which goods pass without entering Panamanian customs territory. Both the trade-based laundering literature and multiple OFAC designations, including one already on this map, run through it. Panama has tightened beneficial-ownership rules; the volume has not fallen.
cases.cite: FATF and GAFILAT free trade zone typologies; US Treasury OFAC designations; Panamanian Superintendency reporting
cases.drop_reason: A free trade zone used for trade-based laundering; no one placed inside an institution.

cases.n: The rip-on rip-off mechanism
cases.d: The dominant method in the Atlantic cocaine flow: the load is inserted into a legitimate container at origin without the exporter's knowledge and removed at destination before customs clearance. It requires no complicity from the shipper and no falsified paperwork — only physical access at both ends. It is why port employment screening, not manifest analysis, is where the enforcement effort concentrates.
cases.cite: Europol EU SOCTA 2025; Belgian and Dutch customs technical reporting
cases.rank: Container insertion and extraction (shipping, freight & ports)
cases.drop_reason: A smuggling method that the record says needs no complicity from the companies involved.

cases.n: Semi-submersible construction
cases.d: Purpose-built low-profile and fully submersible vessels are constructed in mangrove yards on the Pacific coast, each carrying several tonnes. Colombian and Ecuadorian forces seize them regularly; the builders are occasionally charged. The design has improved steadily across two decades, including transatlantic-capable hulls recovered in Europe.
cases.cite: Colombian Armada Nacional and Ecuadorian Fuerzas Armadas seizure records; Spanish Guardia Civil recovery of a transatlantic vessel, 2019 and 2023
cases.drop_reason: Construction of smuggling submarines; no institution infiltrated.

cases.n: Wuhan Yuancheng Gongchuang Technology
cases.d: One of the earliest Chinese firms indicted in the United States over fentanyl and precursor exports, charged alongside individuals in a 2018 case that described a marketing operation with English-language sales staff and multiple domain names. The company continued to appear in later enforcement reporting under related names.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice indictment, 2018; US DEA and Congressional-Executive Commission on China reporting
cases.drop_reason: A Chinese company openly selling fentanyl and precursors; sales, not infiltration.

cases.n: Acetic anhydride diversion
cases.d: The essential reagent for converting morphine to heroin has no substitute and large legitimate uses. INCB tracks the licit trade and repeatedly reports diversions in transit through Turkiye, Central Asia and the Gulf toward Afghan laboratories. It is the single chokepoint in the opiate chain where a control regime already exists and still fails.
cases.cite: INCB Precursors report, annual; UNODC Afghan Opiate Trade Project
cases.drop_reason: Diversion of a chemical in transit; no one inside an institution named.

cases.n: Laboratory equipment suppliers
cases.d: Dutch and Belgian prosecutors have charged suppliers of industrial reactors, tabletting machines and glassware with knowingly equipping synthetic drug production sites in the border region. The equipment is unrestricted and has ordinary industrial buyers, so the charge turns on knowledge rather than on the goods.
cases.cite: Dutch Openbaar Ministerie and Belgian federal prosecution filings, 2020-2024; EMCDDA/EUDA production reporting
cases.rank: Reactor vessels, tabletting and glassware (chemicals & precursors)
cases.drop_reason: Equipment suppliers selling to drug labs; sales, not infiltration.

cases.n: Johnson & Johnson
cases.d: Agreed to pay $5 billion over twenty-five years as part of the $26 billion national opioid settlement, and separately $230 million to New York. Its Tasmanian poppy operations supplied a large share of the narcotic raw material used by other manufacturers, which is the part of its role least visible in the settlement documents.
cases.cite: National Opioid Settlement agreement, 2021; New York Attorney General settlement, June 2021
cases.rank: Manufacturer and active ingredient supplier (pharmaceutical supply)
cases.drop_reason: A drug maker's opioid settlement; its own conduct, no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: McKinsey & Company
cases.d: Paid $573 million to states in 2021 over advice to Purdue on how to 'turbocharge' oxycodone sales, then a further $650 million to the US Department of Justice in December 2024 under a deferred prosecution agreement, with a former partner pleading guilty to obstruction for deleting records. A consultancy is on this map because the strategy documents were the product.
cases.cite: State attorneys general settlement, February 2021; US Department of Justice deferred prosecution agreement, December 2024
cases.drop_reason: A consultancy hired openly by Purdue to boost sales; an open contract, not infiltration.

cases.n: Publicis Health
cases.d: Paid $350 million to settle claims that it designed and ran the marketing campaigns behind opioid prescribing growth, including targeting materials for individual prescribers. The first advertising group to settle in this litigation.
cases.cite: Multistate attorneys general settlement, February 2024
cases.drop_reason: An advertising group hired to market opioids; an open contract, not infiltration.

cases.n: Kroger, Albertsons and the grocery pharmacies
cases.d: Settled state and local opioid claims for roughly $1.4 billion and $224 million respectively, following the larger settlements by the three national chains already on this map. Dispensing data showed sustained volumes in counties where the prescription rate exceeded the population.
cases.cite: Multistate settlement agreements, 2023; ARCOS dispensing data cited in In re National Prescription Opiate Litigation
cases.drop_reason: Pharmacy chains settling opioid dispensing claims; their own conduct, not infiltration.

cases.n: Entain
cases.d: Paid £585 million under a deferred prosecution agreement with HMRC over bribery in its former Turkish business, the largest such settlement in UK history, alongside a separate £17 million regulatory penalty for social responsibility and anti-money-laundering failures. Online gaming accounts are a standing route for layering small amounts at scale.
cases.cite: UK Crown Court deferred prosecution agreement, 2023; UK Gambling Commission regulatory settlement, August 2022
cases.rank: Online betting and gaming group (casinos & junkets)
cases.drop_reason: A gambling company's settlement; the record does not say who was bribed or how anyone got inside an institution.

cases.n: SkyCity Entertainment Group
cases.d: Agreed a NZ$4.16 million penalty with New Zealand's financial intelligence unit and separately faced Australian proceedings over its Adelaide casino, in both cases for failing to monitor high-value play. New Zealand pays the highest methamphetamine prices in the world and the casino floor is where that cash surfaces.
cases.cite: New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs civil proceedings settlement, 2024; AUSTRAC v SkyCity Adelaide, Federal Court of Australia
cases.drop_reason: A casino operator fined for weak monitoring; no crime group shown inside it.

cases.n: Trident Trust and Asiaciti Trust
cases.d: Two of the largest offshore providers in the Pandora Papers, administering structures for clients including sanctioned and criminally implicated figures. Asiaciti was fined by Singapore's regulator for anti-money-laundering failures. Neither has been charged over drug proceeds; both supply the layer of the chain where ownership stops being traceable.
cases.cite: ICIJ Pandora Papers, October 2021; Monetary Authority of Singapore composition penalty, 2021
cases.rank: Offshore trust and corporate services (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: Offshore service providers fined for weak checks; no outside party inside an institution.

cases.n: Citizenship and residence by investment
cases.d: Programmes selling citizenship or residence for investment have been used by figures under sanction or investigation to acquire travel documents and banking access. The European Commission opened infringement proceedings against Malta and the European Court of Justice ruled against the scheme; five Caribbean states came under joint US and EU pressure to tighten theirs. The mechanism is legal and the due diligence is the whole of the control.
cases.cite: European Commission infringement proceedings and CJEU judgment, 2025; US-EU-UK joint statements on Caribbean CBI programmes, 2023-2024
cases.rank: Passport and residence programmes (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: Citizenship-for-investment schemes; a legal programme, not a case of infiltration.

cases.n: The Dubai free zones
cases.d: Free zone companies can be formed with beneficial ownership visible only to the zone authority. Investigative reporting has repeatedly traced structures used by sanctioned and trafficking-linked figures to these registries, and the UAE's FATF grey listing between 2022 and 2024 turned on beneficial-ownership access. The registries were reformed rather than opened.
cases.cite: FATF plenary decisions, March 2022 and February 2024; Dubai Unlocked and related investigative reporting, 2024
cases.rank: Free zone company formation (lawyers, brokers & formation agents)
cases.drop_reason: Opaque company registries in free zones; no specific infiltration case.

cases.n: Michoacan agriculture
cases.d: Extortion of avocado and lime growers, packing houses and hauliers is documented by Mexican federal authorities and by US inspection suspensions after threats to inspectors. The organisations mapped in Tierra Caliente take a fee per hectare and per shipment. Growers and packers are victims of the arrangement, not parties to it, which is why the entry names the sector rather than a company.
cases.cite: US Department of Agriculture APHIS inspection suspensions, 2022 and 2024; Mexican Fiscalia General de la Republica reporting; Michoacan state agricultural association statements
cases.rank: Avocado and lime supply chains (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: Cartel extortion of farmers and packers, who the record says are victims rather than captured; no one inside an institution.

cases.n: Amazon gold and timber
cases.d: Illegal gold from the Brazilian, Peruvian and Venezuelan Amazon enters refining chains that also process legitimate metal, and the proceeds settle alongside cocaine proceeds moving on the same rivers. OFAC has designated related networks and Brazilian operations have seized aircraft and dredges at scale. Gold is the preferred store of value on this corridor because it does not decay and carries no serial number.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designations; Brazilian IBAMA and Policia Federal operations, 2021-2024; UNODC and Igarape Institute Amazon reporting
cases.drop_reason: Illegal gold and timber trade; no institution infiltrated.

orgs.d: France's English-recognised 'regular' Grand Lodge, founded in Paris in 1913 by a lodge that broke from the Grand Orient and an independent lodge in Bordeaux. In December 2009 Grand Master François Stifani faced a revolt over €17 million spent; in January 2011 a court put the Grand Lodge under an appointed administrator. The United Grand Lodge of England suspended relations on 14 September 2011 and withdrew recognition on 12 September 2012, then restored it in June 2014 after Jean-Pierre Servel replaced Stifani. Membership of francophone African heads of state is widely reported but is not documented in the source used here.
orgs.cite: UGLE withdrawal of recognition 2012 and restoration 2014; Wikipedia 'Grande Loge Nationale Française'
orgs.reach_src: The source used gives no list of GLNF lodges abroad; only France is documented.
orgs.drop_reason: Description covers an internal financial dispute and recognition by other lodges; it says itself that membership of African heads of state is not documented.

orgs.d: Italy's main Masonic body, founded in 1805 under the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy. Mussolini suppressed Freemasonry in 1925; it was restarted after the Second World War. It originally chartered the P2 lodge and revoked the charter in 1974. The United Grand Lodge of England withdrew recognition in 1993, citing corruption and Mafia accusations, and restored it in March 2023. In September 2015 it reported 22,675 members in 842 lodges.
orgs.cite: UGLE derecognition 1993 and re-recognition 2023; Wikipedia 'Grand Orient of Italy'
orgs.reach_src: Home jurisdiction; no foreign lodges documented in the source used.
orgs.drop_reason: Description shows only its history and loss of English recognition over accusations; no documented case of it getting inside an institution (P2 has its own entry).

orgs.hq: Palazzo Malta, Via dei Condotti, Rome
orgs.d: A Catholic lay order descended from the Knights Hospitaller (papal recognition 1113), seated in Rome since 1834, with about 13,500 knights, dames and chaplains. It is a sovereign subject of international law, a UN General Assembly observer since 1994, and has formal diplomatic relations with 114–115 states. In 2016–17 Grand Master Matthew Festing removed Grand Chancellor Albrecht von Boeselager over condom distribution in a Myanmar aid project; in January 2017 Pope Francis ordered Boeselager reinstated, required Festing to resign and named Archbishop Giovanni Becciu his special delegate.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Sovereign Military Order of Malta'; 'Foreign relations of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta'
orgs.reach_src: States with full diplomatic relations, per Wikipedia 'Foreign relations of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta' (115 incl. Holy See). National associations exist in other countries (e.g. US, UK, France) but are not listed in the source.
orgs.drop_reason: Description covers its diplomatic status, which is open, and an internal leadership dispute; no infiltration of another institution.

orgs.hq: Mexico City (founded); general direction in Rome
orgs.d: A Catholic congregation founded by Marcial Maciel in Mexico City on 3 January 1941, part of the Regnum Christi Federation. It runs a network of private schools and universities for Mexico's elite, including the Anáhuac University Network, and its priests serve as chaplains to business leaders in Latin America. The Vatican removed Maciel from ministry in 2006 and in 2010 said his actions were real crimes.
orgs.cite: Holy See communiqués 2006 and 2010; Wikipedia 'Legion of Christ'
orgs.reach_src: Education centres and 2009 apostolic visitation regions named in Wikipedia 'Legion of Christ'.
orgs.drop_reason: Description shows schools, chaplaincies and its founder's crimes; no case of it placing or paying people inside a government or company.

orgs.d: A Catholic traditionalist movement founded in Brazil in 1960 by Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira; national TFPs followed in about 30 countries. Its campaign against land reform is described as contributing to Brazil's 1964 coup. Chile's Frei government banned the Chilean TFP, which welcomed the 1973 coup; South Africa's P. W. Botha wrote to commend it in 1987; Venezuela's Lusinchi government moved to ban it after an investigation found it operating outside the constitution. Successors include the Heralds of the Gospel (2001) and the Instituto Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira; Poland's Ordo Iuris was founded by a TFP-linked association.
orgs.reach_src: National TFP associations and founding years listed in Wikipedia 'Tradition, Family, Property'.
orgs.drop_reason: Description shows open campaigning and support for coups by a lay movement; no placement of people or control inside institutions.

orgs.d: A church founded by Apollo Quiboloy in Davao City on 1 September 1985. A US federal grand jury indicted Quiboloy in 2021 for child sex trafficking and misuse of donations, and the US Treasury sanctioned him in 2022. In March 2024 its broadcaster SMNI said former President Rodrigo Duterte had been made administrator of its properties. Police raided the Davao compound from 24 August 2024 and arrested Quiboloy in September 2024.
orgs.cite: US v. Quiboloy (C.D. Cal. 2021); US Treasury sanctions 2022; Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Jesus Christ (church)'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia (FBI raids in California, Texas, Hawaii).
orgs.drop_reason: Description covers its leader's indictment and a former president managing its property; no case of the church getting inside an institution.

orgs.d: A self-help company founded near Albany in 1998 by Keith Raniere and Nancy Salzman, with centres in the US, Canada and Mexico; prosecutors called it a front for crime. Its secret women's group DOS branded members and held 'collateral'. Raniere was convicted in June 2019 and sentenced on 27 October 2020 to 120 years; the Second Circuit upheld it in 2022. Emiliano Salinas, son of former Mexican president Carlos Salinas, and Ana Cristina Fox, daughter of Vicente Fox, have been accused of involvement; NXIVM kept dossiers on officials and pushed officials to investigate critics.
orgs.drop_reason: Description shows crimes within a self-help company; the claim that it pushed officials to act is too vague to stand as infiltration without invention.

orgs.hq: Cairo (operations centre); founded at a Kenyan resort
orgs.d: An intelligence alliance chartered on 1 September 1976 by the spy chiefs of France, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran, named after the Kenyan resort where it first met; it ran an operations centre in Cairo. Saudi Arabia paid, France supplied technology, and Egypt and Morocco supplied troops and arms. In 1977 French aircraft flew Moroccan and Egyptian troops into Zaire's Shaba province; it armed Somalia in the Ogaden war and gave about $5 million to UNITA in Angola. Saudi intelligence chief Prince Turki al-Faisal described it in a 2002 speech at Georgetown.
orgs.cite: Turki al-Faisal, Georgetown speech 2002; Wikipedia 'Safari Club'
orgs.reach_src: Member intelligence services, per Wikipedia 'Safari Club'.
orgs.drop_reason: An alliance of governments' spy chiefs acting abroad together is covert state cooperation, not one party getting inside another's institutions.

orgs.d: A cross-border repression system set up at a meeting called by Chile's DINA in Santiago on 25–28 November 1975; Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia signed, Brazil joined in 1976 and Peru and Ecuador later. Members shared intelligence and kidnapped, tortured and killed exiles across borders; John Dinges documented 654 victims from 1976 to 1980. Operations reached Washington (the 1976 Letelier–Moffitt car bomb) and Europe. In 2016 a Buenos Aires court convicted 15 former officers, the first court ruling to recognise Condor.
orgs.cite: Buenos Aires federal court 'Plan Cóndor' verdict 2016; US National Security Archive, 2025 briefing book
orgs.reach_src: Member states per the National Security Archive and Wikipedia 'Operation Condor'.
orgs.drop_reason: Cross-border kidnapping and killing by cooperating governments is state repression, not infiltration of an institution.

orgs.d: A fake press agency set up in Lisbon in September 1966 under Salazar's regime, run by ex-OAS captain Yves Guérin-Sérac, with Italian neo-fascist Stefano Delle Chiaie among its founders. It allegedly worked against independence movements in Angola, Mozambique and East Timor. Italian judge Guido Salvini found its instructors trained Avanguardia Nazionale members in explosives and linked it to groups behind the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing. After the 1974 Carnation Revolution its staff fled; a document titled 'Our Political Activity' set out the aim to 'create the conditions favouring the installation of chaos'.
orgs.cite: Investigations of Judge Guido Salvini (Milan); Wikipedia 'Aginter Press'
orgs.drop_reason: Description shows a front press agency training militants; the record shows no one placed inside a government, international body or company.

orgs.d: A merchant bank founded in Sydney in 1973 by lawyer Frank Nugan and former US Green Beret Michael Hand, which opened overseas branches and hired retired senior US military and intelligence officers, with former CIA director William Colby as a lawyer. Nugan was found dead near Lithgow in January 1980; Hand destroyed records and fled Australia in June 1980. The 1985 Stewart Royal Commission found banking-law violations and money laundering but no credible evidence of drug smuggling, arms dealing or CIA involvement; the 1980–83 Joint Task Force on Drug Trafficking disputed that.
orgs.cite: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking (Stewart), 1985; Joint Task Force on Drug Trafficking 1980–83
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Nugan Hand Bank' (branch list not given).
orgs.drop_reason: The Royal Commission found banking violations and laundering by the bank's own people but no credible evidence of intelligence involvement; hiring retired officers is not infiltration.

orgs.d: Founded in Rome in 1968 by Aurelio Peccei and Alexander King; based in Hamburg and, since 1 July 2008, in Winterthur. Its 1972 report 'The Limits to Growth' sold about 30 million copies. Its membership is drawn often from current and former heads of state; honorary members include Mikhail Gorbachev, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, King Juan Carlos I, Horst Köhler, Princess Beatrix and Manmohan Singh. It has national associations in 35 countries and territories.
orgs.reach_src: Founding city and successive HQs; the 35 national associations are not listed in the source.
orgs.drop_reason: Description shows a forum with eminent members and an influential report; no placement of people or control inside institutions.

orgs.d: A state foundation created by decree of Vladimir Putin on 21 June 2007 to promote Russian language and culture abroad, working with the Russian Orthodox Church. The EU sanctioned it in July 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine. Observers describe it as a tool of Russian soft power and propaganda.
orgs.cite: Presidential decree 21 Jun 2007; EU sanctions July 2022; Wikipedia 'Russkiy Mir Foundation'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Russkiy Mir Foundation' (only the São Paulo centre is named).
orgs.drop_reason: A state cultural foundation that was sanctioned is open soft power; no placement of people or control inside institutions is shown.

orgs.d: Private non-profit created by Congress in November 1983 and funded almost wholly by annual congressional appropriations. It gives grants directly and through four core institutes (the party institutes NDI and IRI, the Chamber of Commerce's CIPE and the AFL-CIO's Solidarity Center). Its founder Allen Weinstein said in 1991 that much of its work 'was done covertly 25 years ago by the CIA'. Russia banned it as 'undesirable' in 2015 and China sanctioned it in 2019.
orgs.reach_src: Lindsey O'Rourke (Reagan-era NED programmes); LeoGrande (Nicaragua); The Intercept (Venezuela grants); Irving Brown/UNI grants (France, 1980s)
orgs.drop_reason: NED is funded openly by Congress and gives declared grants; open funding is not infiltration.

orgs.d: Boston engineering firm founded in 1893, known for hydroelectric and water-resource work abroad, such as Turkey's Sarıyar Dam in the 1950s and a plan for the Jordan River valley. It also sold economic forecasts and feasibility studies. Parsons Corporation bought it in 1985. Its former chief economist John Perkins describes it as a vehicle for loading countries with debt; that account is his own.
orgs.drop_reason: Description shows an engineering firm's open contracts; the claim it served as a debt vehicle is one author's account only.

orgs.n: US-Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation
orgs.d: Bilateral commission set up in 1974 after the oil embargo, co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary and the Saudi Finance Minister. The GAO found in 1979 that US technical help under it was paid almost entirely from a Saudi trust account held in the US Treasury, so it ran outside the normal congressional appropriations. It placed US experts in Saudi ministries and agencies on infrastructure and planning projects.
orgs.drop_reason: US experts worked in Saudi ministries under an openly agreed bilateral commission paid by Saudi Arabia; an accounting irregularity in Washington is not infiltration.

orgs.d: Anglo-American dining society founded in London on 16 July 1902 by Sir Harry Brittain; the US society first met at the Waldorf Astoria, New York, on 13 January 1903. It welcomes each new US ambassador to Britain, and US ambassadors in London and secretaries of state are customarily admitted ex officio; the two societies share membership. Churchill spoke to it as Prime Minister on 18 March 1941.
orgs.reach_src: Ex officio membership of US ambassadors and secretaries of state
orgs.drop_reason: A dining society that welcomes ambassadors is open social activity, not infiltration.

orgs.d: Paramilitary formation of Russia's defence ministry that took over and rebranded most of Wagner's African operations from late 2023. It provides troops, regime protection and training to governments that have expelled French or US forces. Estimated deployments: Mali about 1,000–2,000, CAR 1,500–2,000, Libya 800–1,800, Burkina Faso about 300, Niger 100–300, Equatorial Guinea about 200.
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia, citing CTC Sentinel, ISPI, BBC, Al Jazeera
orgs.drop_reason: A defence ministry formation supplying troops to governments under open agreements is military contracting, like the Erik Prince case, not infiltration.

orgs.d: Party cadre school in Kibaha, Tanzania, built with a $40 million grant from the Chinese Communist Party's Central Party School and taught partly by CCP instructors. It is run jointly by the CCP and six southern African ruling or former liberation parties. The ANC says it had trained over 1,405 participants by January 2024.
orgs.cite: Africa Center for Strategic Studies (2022); ANC statement (23 Jan 2024)
orgs.drop_reason: An openly run party school training ruling-party cadres is declared party-to-party cooperation, not infiltration.

orgs.d: London public relations firm that ran a paid campaign for the Gupta-owned Oakbay Investments in 2016–17 using fake social-media accounts and 'white monopoly capital' messaging. Expelled by the PRCA on 4 September 2017; went into administration on 12 September 2017.
orgs.drop_reason: A PR firm openly hired by a client to run a smear campaign is a contract, not infiltration.

orgs.d: Israeli maker of Pegasus phone-hacking spyware, sold only to governments under Israeli export licences. Investigations tied state clients including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Morocco, Rwanda and Togo to surveillance of journalists, dissidents and foreign officials. Added to the US Entity List in November 2021.
orgs.cite: US Commerce Department (2021); Citizen Lab; Pegasus Project
orgs.drop_reason: Selling spyware to governments under export licences is an open sale; the brief lists this kind of case as not infiltration.

orgs.d: Israeli private hacking and disinformation outfit led by Tal Hanan, exposed in February 2023 by the Forbidden Stories 'Story Killers' consortium. Hanan claimed to have worked on 33 presidential elections, many in Africa, and worked with Cambridge Analytica in Nigeria in 2015.
orgs.drop_reason: Description rests on the outfit's own claims of election work; hacking and disinformation for hire, with no one shown placed inside an institution.

orgs.d: Israeli political consulting firm banned from Facebook in May 2019 for coordinated fake accounts aimed mainly at African elections, after spending about $1.1 million on ads.
orgs.reach_src: Facebook takedown report as reported by CNN and DFRLab
orgs.drop_reason: Running fake Facebook accounts around elections is disinformation, not placing or paying people inside an institution.

orgs.d: British political data and influence firms. Cambridge Analytica worked on Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 Kenyan campaigns and, with Team Jorge, on Nigeria's 2015 election; executives claimed work on over 200 elections. Both firms closed in 2018 after the Facebook data scandal.
orgs.drop_reason: Campaign data and messaging work for hire is an open contract with candidates, not infiltration.

orgs.d: A Catholic lay movement founded in October 1914 by priest Josef Kentenich at Schoenstatt near Vallendar, Germany. It is active in more than 100 countries and every Latin American country, with nearly 80 shrines in Chile, Argentina and Brazil. Chile's President José Antonio Kast was raised in it; his brother Miguel Kast was Pinochet's planning minister and Central Bank president.
orgs.drop_reason: The record shows only that Chile's president was raised in the movement and that his brother served Pinochet, not that Schoenstatt works to place members in office or steer policy.

orgs.d: A transnational criminal organisation operating mainly out of India and led by Lawrence Bishnoi. Canadian officials said in October 2024 that targets identified through Indian diplomats were attacked by the gang. Canada listed it as a terrorist entity on 29 September 2025.
orgs.drop_reason: The record shows Indian diplomats identifying targets for a gang to attack in Canada, which is a state using criminals abroad, not anyone placed inside Canada's institutions.

orgs.d: Cambodian financial group whose units include Huione Pay (payments), Huione Guarantee (an escrow marketplace on Telegram) and a crypto exchange. Hun To, cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet, is a major shareholder and director of Huione Pay. Cambodia's central bank revoked Huione Pay's banking licence in March 2025, and in May 2025 the US Treasury's FinCEN found the group a primary money laundering concern that moved over US$4 billion in illicit funds from 2021 to 2025.
orgs.drop_reason: The record shows a relative of Cambodia's prime minister as a shareholder and a US money-laundering finding against the group, but no one placed inside a government body or company to steer it.

orgs.hq: Nairobi (first branch); national bodies in each country
orgs.d: Overseas counterpart of India's RSS, started as a branch in Nairobi on 14 January 1947 by RSS volunteers; it says it is active in 156 countries with about 3,289 branches. The UK branch dates from 1966; the Charity Commission for England and Wales investigated it after a 2015 ITV programme and in 2016 found trustee mismanagement but no evidence of formal links to the RSS. The RSS said in 2014 the two work closely together but are separate. No case of HSS reaching into a government was found.
orgs.cite: Charity Commission for England and Wales, inquiry report, 2 September 2016
orgs.drop_reason: The record itself states that no case of the HSS reaching into a government was found; it describes only the organisation's existence and a charity inquiry.

orgs.d: Pro-democracy party founded in 1982 by Vietnamese exiles, with members in the diaspora and inside Vietnam. Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security designated it a terrorist organisation on 4 October 2016; rights groups and the US government dispute the label. Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of membership.
orgs.cite: Vietnam Ministry of Public Security, 4 October 2016
orgs.drop_reason: Viet Tan is an exile opposition party that Vietnam designated as terrorist; being designated is not reaching inside an institution.

orgs.d: Unofficial offices abroad linked to the public security bureaus of Chinese cities such as Fuzhou, Qingtian, Nantong and Wenzhou. Safeguard Defenders reported in September and December 2022 that they were used to pressure people wanted by China, including dissidents, to return; China says they renew documents and fight fraud. Ireland and the Netherlands ordered stations closed in 2022, the UK said in 2023 they had closed, and US prosecutors charged two men in 2023 over a station in Manhattan (one pleaded guilty in 2024, one was convicted in 2026).
orgs.cite: Safeguard Defenders reports 'Patrol and Persuade' and '110 Overseas', 2022; government statements of Ireland, Netherlands, UK, US
orgs.reach_src: Safeguard Defenders 2022 list as reproduced on Wikipedia, plus governments that announced investigations (Spain, Portugal, Canada)
orgs.drop_reason: The record shows unofficial Chinese offices pressuring people abroad, but not anyone inside the host countries' institutions working for them.

orgs.n: United Russia party – foreign party cooperation agreements
orgs.d: United Russia is Vladimir Putin's ruling party. It signs formal cooperation agreements with foreign parties covering delegation exchanges, contacts between legislators and economic cooperation: Austria's FPÖ signed one on 19 December 2016 (expired end 2021) and Italy's Lega on 6 March 2017 (renewing automatically every five years). Bulgaria's Russophiles party signed a memorandum with it for the 2021 elections.
orgs.cite: Agreement texts published by Il Foglio (Lega) and reported by Vindobona (FPÖ)
orgs.drop_reason: The record describes formal, published cooperation agreements between parties, which are open and declared, not hidden placement of people or money.

orgs.n: First Czech Russian Bank (Pervyi Chekhoslovatsko-Rossiiskii Bank)
orgs.d: A Moscow bank that lent €9 million to France's Front National in 2014, confirmed by Marine Le Pen in November 2014. Party officials told Mediapart it was the first part of a €40 million facility.
orgs.cite: Marine Le Pen statement, November 2014; Mediapart
orgs.drop_reason: The record shows a loan that the Front National openly confirmed, which is declared financing of an opposition party, not hidden placement inside an institution.

orgs.d: A Russian state think tank. Bulgarian prosecutors charged pro-Russia activist and former MP Nikolay Malinov in 2019 with collecting state secrets for it from 2013 to 2019; a Sofia court acquitted him in May 2026.
orgs.cite: Bulgarian Specialised Prosecution Office, 2019; Sofia court, May 2026
orgs.drop_reason: The only case recorded ended with the accused, a former MP, acquitted in May 2026, so the record does not establish anyone inside an institution working for the think tank.

orgs.n: DITIB – Turkish-Islamic Union for Religious Affairs
orgs.d: Founded in 1984 as the German branch of Turkey's state religious authority, the Diyanet; it runs about 900 mosques in Germany. Its imams are trained in Ankara and paid as Turkish civil servants. German federal prosecutors investigated imams in 2017 for spying on Gülen supporters (case dropped in December 2017), and Germany's interior ministry cut its funding in 2018.
orgs.cite: German Federal Prosecutor's Office 2017; Federal Ministry of the Interior 2018
orgs.drop_reason: The record shows open Turkish state control of a German mosque association and an inquiry into imams spying on individuals that was dropped, not anyone placed inside a government, international body or company.

orgs.d: A Shia religious centre founded by Iranian residents of Hamburg in the 1950s and seen as aligned with Iran's government. Germany expelled its deputy director in 2022 over Hezbollah ties and banned the centre in July 2024 as unconstitutional, taking over its mosque building.
orgs.cite: German Federal Ministry of the Interior ban order, July 2024
orgs.drop_reason: The record shows a religious centre aligned with Iran and banned in Germany, with no one placed inside German institutions.

orgs.d: US pharmaceutical company. Its CEO Albert Bourla negotiated the EU's largest Covid-19 vaccine contract partly by text with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen; the EU General Court ruled in May 2025 that the Commission wrongly refused access to the texts.
orgs.drop_reason: The record shows a vaccine contract negotiated partly by text and a court ruling on access to the texts, not anyone placed inside the EU's institutions.

orgs.d: British political-data and campaign firm, part of SCL Group, that closed in 2018 after it was found to have harvested Facebook users' data. Its executives were recorded saying it ran Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns in Kenya.
orgs.drop_reason: Running election campaigns for a candidate under contract is open, declared work, and the data harvesting was a breach of users' privacy, not placing people inside an institution.
